paragraphs.text: BY COMMAND OF CONSTANTINE, THE CHRIST-LOVING AND PORPHYROGENITUS EMPEROR, SON OF LEO, THE MOST WISE EMPEROR AND AUTOCRATOR. It begins where Theophanes left off [?] with the emperor Michael, son of Theophilus, the kouropalates, that is, from the reign of Leo the Armenian. The same emperor Constantine diligently collected the individual events and set them out in a clear overview, so that [?] of the reign might become clear to those who come after. And this is surely among your good deeds, most philosophical emperor, together with many other great ones: to bring back to new life and rebirth what had slipped away with time and passed into nothingness, and to take care for the good of history, so that it is not neglected as it was by those who held imperial rule before you. Those who strove after what good men do not strive after may be left out of our account. Some have been eager to differ from the many in nothing, except that they have been nurslings not of learning but of boorishness [?]. For what should an emperor practise that does not [?] bring the benefit that comes from what is done with learning? He must care for men and above all for rational knowledge, from which the strength of the empire comes, so that men, robbed of reason, may not be carried headlong without noticing it, and so that the very thing by which we surpass all creatures may not be in danger of being handed over to speechlessness.

But how much you have toiled, most gentle emperor, over learning and the care of men, so that the rest [?], the wise will see, since you too are wise; or rather, you will see it clearly, since they too are wise. You yourself write the history, taking only our hand to serve you, of what was done in the lives of those before you, even if it contains plenty that is mean and not splendid, since even from such things the earnest can hunt out what is useful. Indeed, having valued zeal for learning above all business and idleness, since learning above all breeds emulation and virtue in subjects who love learning and history, you gathered material partly from writings and partly from oral tradition, and you nobly resolved to set it before everyone as a kind of common school. You judged that the best beginning for this history was the point where the blessed Theophanes ended, [and so to put into words the deeds of all the emperors up to the present time and your own reign. And since the deeds of your celebrated grandfather Basil, glorious among emperors, have been recounted by you, and published by your most learned knowledge with all clarity and elegance of language, according to the plain and sincere truth of what happened, it would be superfluous to narrate any of them here.] Since by kinship and close relation it has fallen to you to be his grandson, you amply honor him from your own achievements, and in turn receive from him some

Theophanes, then, ended with the reign of Michael the kouropalates and the defeat that befell him at the hands of the Bulgarians when he was betrayed by his own men. He mentioned only the proclamation of Leo, and made nothing clear to his readers about where Leo came from or how he was brought up. We, however, as if joining the other members to the head, present the history whole-bodied and not half-finished, and carry it on to the following and later period for those who do not live too carelessly, providing them with gain and not loss, if indeed it is good, and a sure road to safety, to come to know the lives of both the good and the wicked.

ON THE REIGN OF LEO. 1. The homeland of the said Leo was Armenia. By descent he was partly from the Assyrians and partly from the Armenians themselves. His parents, out of unholy intent, had handed their own parents over to bloody slaughter and were condemned to exile; and there, struggling through a life of poverty as fugitives, they begot the beast in question. When Leo was just entering youth, he exchanged his homeland for a village called Pidra, which belonged to the theme of the Anatolikon. There he reached manhood and, being counted among the most warlike and bloodthirsty, won fame for his bravery. At that time the reins of empire were held by Nikephoros, who became a trophy in Bulgaria. He had sent out Bardanes, surnamed the Turk, as sole general administering the oversight and care of the five themes of the East, because of his daring in war and the other virtues that flourished in him. Bardanes, who loved to master his enemies and was always dreaming of the throne, enrolled among his bodyguards and attendants this Leo of whom we speak, who had a striking look and a noble stature and seemed besides to be witty in conversation. Before him, or shortly after, he enrolled Michael the Stammerer and Thomas from Lake Gazouros, all of them humble and obscure men who were only then coming to the notice of those entrusted with military commands. 2. These men, then, hung upon Bardanes and anchored their worldly hopes in him. And he, being a lover of the throne, shared his intent and desire for it with a certain monk who lived in the region of Philomelion, and begged him to send up supplicating prayers to God to guide his crown and award him the empire. But at once he heard: “You must not dare such things, Bardanes, for through them the loss of your property, the cutting out of your eyes, and misfortune besides will befall you, and it will go badly for you. But if you can be persuaded by me, I advise you to leap away from these things at once, and not to admit into your mind even the beginning of such affairs.” The man was filled [?] with dejection and

gloom on hearing these words, and in the end he left the room full of despondency and grief. But when the monk saw the men mentioned above, Leo, Michael and Thomas, bringing the horse for him to mount, he called the general back; and Bardanes, expecting to hear something new and strange, came back quicker than words. But the monk again begged him not to desert to the dangers he hoped for, and not to exchange his present prosperity for misfortune still to come. And about these very men he bore witness with prophetic tongue, declaring: “The first and second of these will become masters of the empire you long for, but you will not; and the third, who will share only in acclamation and proclamation, will not prosper at all, but will break off his life miserably.” Struck in his soul by these words, Bardanes let his face change through many colors, and went off home again, at once hurling blasphemies and insults at the man and at the same time reporting his predictions to the three and pouring much laughter on what had been said. 3. So, bidding farewell to the monk's words, on the nineteenth of July of the eleventh indiction he gathered a great force against the reigning Nikephoros, brought the four themes under his command over to his views (all except the Armeniakon, which did not yield to him), and began the revolt. At that time his subjects hated Nikephoros, being oppressed by the weight of the public taxes, and this became in a way both a pretext for the revolt and a support for it; but there was also another cause. For when Bardanes had fought bravely against the Hagarenes and had distributed the abundant plunder with just foresight, setting out the prizes in proportion to those who had struggled in the war and not by favor, he seemed to them worthy to share in the empire as well. So he was proclaimed emperor by public acclaim, and was deemed worthy by the people of many other privileges and honors, to the point that they raised and built a church in his name, and he took the road leading to Nicomedia. But the reigning Nikephoros fielded a sufficient and equal force, and by the multitude of those arrayed against him made him despair of the future and persuaded him to be the first to ask for pardon. For first Leo and then Michael slipped away to the emperor and carried off rewards: the one the command of the foederati, together with the imperial house of Zeno and the Dagisthaeus; the other the office of count of the tent and the house of Karianos. This made Bardanes think poorly of his own prospects. So, asking the emperor for pardon for himself and the army, he withdrew as far as Malagina. There he received assurances of immunity and the little gold cross worn by Nikephoros, which had been sent to him [?]

as security and pledge, and then he fled by night to the monastery of Herakleios with only Thomas sharing his danger, eager to have the hair of his head cut off. The superior of the monastery would not allow this; so he cut off his locks himself with the sword he wore, put on poor clothing, and set out for the island of Prote, where he had a well-built estate and where the emperor allowed him to remain in confinement. Having crossed over there and received the customary prayers and the divine habit of monks, he was renamed Sabbas, and gave proof of many ascetic struggles. Not much time passed before some men from Lycaonia set upon him and deprived him of his eyes, with the knowledge and awareness of the reigning emperor, and took refuge in the great and divine church of God. And so the prediction of the monk who lived at Philomelion was fulfilled. But Bardanes prayed for them as for benefactors and kept to a harsher rule of life, abstaining entirely from wine, fish and oil, and always going bareheaded and barefoot, even when the winter was very severe. He also wore only a single tunic, a leather one in summer and a hair one in winter. He did not live on wheat, but made himself bread baked in the ashes from barley flour. And so he passed his life, lasting until Leo became master of the empire. He also had his wife Domnika tonsured in his own house, together with their daughter and his sons, renaming her Athanasia, and of course he distributed all his wealth to the poor. Such, then, is the story of Bardanes. 4. Leo held on to his glory and exulted in it, now that from being lowly and obscure he had become conspicuous in the command of the foederati. But he did not refrain from ingratitude either, having shown himself such toward his benefactor. Still, he persevered, and adding battle to battle against the Ishmaelites he fought bravely, since in this field he brought great strength both by nature and by practice. Once, however, he was entrusted by Nikephoros, who held the scepter, with distributing the soldiers' pay. He cared nothing for the imperial orders and carried none of them out, but wasted his time in ease and negligence in the small town of Euchaita and put off giving the army what was due to it. He took no care for security, neither of the public funds, nor of his own person, nor of the men under his command. So when the Hagarenes made a raid and plundered Roman territory, it was he, and no one else, who supplied them with their booty without their having to struggle for it: not in his own person, for he secured his safety by swift flight, but by abandoning the soldiers' funds and all but placing them in the enemy's hands. For this he paid a penalty, though not the one he deserved, to Nikephoros, who had trusted him: he was subjected to blows on his back

and chest, and paid for the loss with perpetual exile. But Nikephoros campaigned against the Scythians and fell, wounded in the camp during the war, on the twenty-sixth of July of the fourth indiction. His son Staurakios was mortally wounded in the war, so that he survived only two months and eight days, having previously reigned with his father for eight years and seven months. After Staurakios departed this life on the second of October, Michael the kouropalates, who was Nikephoros' son-in-law, was descended from the family of Rangabe and lived at the place called Mangana, received the rule of the empire in the month of October of the fifth indiction. Then Leo was released from exile, according to the custom of clemency that prevailed among the Roman emperors. He was brought back from exile and enrolled among the staff-bearers of this same Michael who attended at the palace; not long after he was honored with the dignity of patrikios and appointed general of the Anatolikon. At that time he also renewed his old friendship with Michael, who had been brought up with him and whom his desertion from Bardanes had rewarded with the post of count of the tent. Making him the confidant of his secrets, he had in him the most trustworthy of his household and the most capable in affairs outside it. 5. But the villain was destined to be caught again on a charge of ingratitude, raised as he had been with cruelty and nurtured in savagery, and to cover his former deeds with his later ones. Krum, the ruler of the Bulgarians, had just feigned agreements and friendship and was seeking a peace treaty, on condition only that what used to be given each year should be given to him, as tribute, I suppose, as had been agreed in earlier times. He added that refugees, both Bulgarians and Romans as well, should be handed back to their own nation. The matter of the refugees seemed improper to the members of the senate, even though the reigning Michael wholly shared the ruler's opinion, in his desire not to miss the chance of peace. But the council prevailed, with the magistros Theoktistos confirming and supporting its view, and they broke off once more into acts of war, leaving the words empty. And this rightly seemed good. For how could anyone be thought humane and compassionate if he handed over to the cruelty of the Scythians, who differ in no way from wild beasts, a man who through some mischance had gone astray and renounced the land that bore him, than which nothing is sweeter, as they say, and his wife and children too, and had fled to the Roman state as to an inviolable altar? For many of them cannot bear the fearful and savage things the Scythians do, and for this reason frequently desert to our gentleness and mildness; and so their leaders, afraid that little by little they might find themselves emptied out into our land, have often raised this matter, even with us. [?]

But, as the proverb says, they plucked an empty string, since they came up against firm men. 6. So after a short interval they took up arms against each other. Michael asked his lieutenant Leo to come back quickly and cross over from the East with his forces; and in the man he meant to use as a helper, he found an implacable enemy. Krum had sent boastful words and threats against the Romans, threatening slaughter of people, devastation of land, cutting down of trees and burning of houses, and in short declaring that he would rush upon us like a torrent and bring everyone under his power. But the emperor had just taken the field and curbed those extravagant threats, and all but forced him to stay within his own borders rather than leap out and plunder ours. Michael often challenged him to pitched battle, but Krum did not presume; recognizing his own weakness, he did not dare raise his hand against the emperor. So Michael thought it enough to have shut up his rashness and arrogance within his own territory, and not to join battle, since the future was uncertain. “For since,” he said, “we cannot call them out to fight a pitched battle, but are forcing them to avoid battle and stay on their own ground, what would we gain by using force?” For this reason he wished to return quietly and gradually to his own capital. But Leo thought it unseemly, and unworthy of an emperor of the Romans, to turn his back on the enemy—that is what he called that most excellent counsel—because his own thoughts were not upright or sound but rotten and treacherous, and he was scheming to bring the whole Roman dominion under himself. “We must go against them, O emperor,” he said, “and today you will see me plainly crowned with victory over the enemy and shown to be victorious, relying on your confidence and prayer and fighting for them.” Michael, swayed and shaken by these words, ordered the battle to be joined. But as soon as the engagement began, Leo turned his back and embraced flight, still always seeking the throne. For a time this was unclear both to Michael himself and to the enemy. Nothing had yet happened, as usually does in war, no feat of valor on either side; the battle was still at its very beginning, and it was hardly known that they had even clashed. So it seemed to the Bulgarians themselves and to everyone that the thing was a stratagem, and that the Romans meant to draw them apart and then turn back and defeat them. But when both sides realized that the flight was no stratagem but real, then the enemy fell upon them and wrought great slaughter of the fugitives with youthful vigor, while Michael with a few men tried to save himself rather than

make a stand. That is how some have handed down to us in writing that this battle went. But there are others who instead give Leo the credit for saving the forces and fighting stoutly, saying that it was the imperial tagmata who deliberately played the coward and betrayed their own line, and not Leo's part of the army. In any case, the Bulgarians won beyond all hope, while the Romans, caught in a heavy and frightful defeat, sent the emperor off in fear for his life. He was escorted to the imperial palace, leaving Leo outside as a kind of bulwark to keep watch, so that the enemy would not carry off more plunder. But Leo, seizing a suitable opportunity, stirred up the mass of soldiers and drove them to hurl insults at the emperor. He said it was not right, as in the fable, for a deer to lead lions—one who had embraced flight. “And now,” he said, “he has fled to his wife's bosom, leaving us, his own people, as prey for the enemy.” His speech had not yet come to an end among those who shared in his words when it could be seen turning into action, spread by the glib talk and support of flatterers. And finally came his proclamation on the spot, and the smallest fraction of the day saw the same man both private citizen and emperor. 7. Now, just as he was being acclaimed by the army, fears and alarms crept over him. Either he was really putting on an act, so as to have an excuse later, or he was genuinely reckoning the adverse consequences that follow such deeds, since those eager to seize what belongs to others tend to find their daring softening in the face of danger; and above all he wondered how he might gain possession of the imperial palace, camping in the open and quartered somewhere far away. But he was certainly destined to take up residence in the palace himself, and for this reason a most wicked spirit roused Michael the Stammerer to threaten to strike him a mortal blow if he did not gladly accept the proclamation, saying that he himself would take care of all the apparent difficulties, including this very matter of reaching the palace. Which indeed also

8. Now there was a certain man, John Hexaboulios, who had charge and care of the walls. When he learned that this Leo had been left behind on guard at the time of the emperor's entry (he was clever, it seems, at guessing a man's nature from afar), he said that Leo's command of the armies was not in good hands. So he advised the emperor to devise some plan and remove the man skillfully. Yet the beast hidden until then in the fleece had at some point to be uncovered, and God's elect had to be tested like gold in a crucible. This is often permitted to happen in some cyclical course of time, for reasons, I think, [?]

[?]…demonic [permission?], as in the case of Job: for the knowledge and discernment of the pious, but for the estrangement and rejection of the wicked.

9. The words had not yet come to an end when a rumour, running ahead, announced the proclamation of the usurper. When it arrived, the city was almost driven out of its mind by such news and could barely hold itself together, dreading civil war, which has often sunk whole cities with all their people. The emperor was struck to the soul, but he was not shaken in his judgement. He condemned only the man's ingratitude, and quietly murmured that it is good to follow the divine will. Then he calmed the alarm and turmoil in the city and urged everyone to go out and meet Leo, so that he might keep his city undefiled and clean of civil bloodshed. Some urged him to stand firm against the danger and to settle the matter by battle, and promised to stay loyal to a gentle and faithful emperor. His wife Prokopia herself supported this, as did a certain Manuel, one of the Amalekites, who was protostrator at the time. But he said that the empire had no need to be drenched in the blood of brothers. So he gave some of the imperial insignia to one of his trusted attendants and made him go to Leo. At this his wife, distraught and as if seized by frenzy, is said to have cried out in horror at the thought that Barka (as she called Leo's wife) should place the crown on her head. But he rebuked her with stern words, entrusted himself wholly to God, and awaited what was to come.

Soon it was announced that the usurper was entering through the Golden Gate. The whole senate met him at the holy church of the Forerunner, which Stoudios had built from its foundations, and received him with outstretched hands, escorting him and hailing him as chosen by God. As he approached the palace, he was about to stop before the holy image of God the Word, who became man for our sake, at the place called the Chalke, to offer his prayers. He was wearing an unbelted cloak embroidered in purple, after a military custom (those who are refined in such matters call it an "eagle" or a "sea"), and at once he took it off. Michael, who bore a mark on his tongue and was then in charge of Leo's horses, took it in his hands and immediately put it on. To many this seemed an omen that he would obtain the empire after Leo. When they reached the Skyla, as a certain place at the palace entrances is called, Michael, hurrying along somewhat recklessly and running close on Leo's heels, trod with the tips of his feet on the hem of the cloak where it fell to the foot. Leo himself noticed, and suspected some reckless move on his part. But that came about later.

10. Then, when Leo appeared, Michael, together with

his children and his wife, had his hair shorn and fled to the sanctuary of God called the Pharos. It is so named because it kindles a light for all and guides them by night to safe harbours, in imitation of the lighthouse that stands at Alexandria and bears the same name. There he sought Leo's goodwill. Leo did not think it right to drag a man away from God and deprive him of his life. Instead he banished him to the island of Plate and allowed him to live there in quiet, supplying him with a sum of gold each year. They say that there he took the monastic habit, was renamed Athanasios, and lived on for thirty-two years. With him was his son Eustratios, who was tonsured and castrated at the age of twenty on Leo's orders. Niketas was also with him. As a boy he had held command of the Hikanatoi, because he wished to be on friendly terms with the soldiers and with those who live in the field, and to gain experience in many matters. Now he too had his hair shorn, was called Ignatios, and stayed with his father, devoted to the solitary life. Leo separated Michael's wife from him, tore her away, and moved her to another place, the monastery called Prokopia's, although Michael begged him earnestly not to do so.

Michael departed this life on 11 January in the year 6302 [?]. He laid aside his dust on that same island and was buried on the right side of the church. Eustratios lived for five [and ten] years after his father's death and then he too fell asleep, on 15 January in the year 6327 [?], and was laid on the left side of the church. Ignatios, formerly called Niketas, obtained the presidency of Constantinople. Many years later his holy body was laid in the monastery called Satyros, which he had recently built from its foundations. This monastery is also called "of the Rising One", and here is how it got these names. It is called Satyros because a short distance from it lies a place named Old Satyros, where there was a temple built by the pagans to Satyros himself. Because the monastery is close by, it is called by the same name. The emperor Theophilos, who built the palaces of Bryas, took the material from that temple and used it to build them. It is called "of the Rising One" for the following reason. Once the emperor Nikephoros was hunting in the area where the monastery now stands, which was wooded, hard to get through, and well suited for hunting game. A very large deer appeared and was chased and caught on the very spot where the monastery's altar now stands. There an old table was found, resting on a column and bearing this inscription: "This is the altar of the Archistrategos Michael the Rising One, which the apostle Andrew set up [?]." But these things did not happen then; they happened a long time afterwards.

11. But we must bring the account back and look for the cause that persuaded both men, as though by agreement: Michael, not to resist at all on behalf of his throne (for, as the proverb says, even an ant has bile), and Leo, to step boldly in and take [?] possession of it. I would say that this alone is the truest education and training for political affairs: the clearest cause, and the explanation laid bare [?] of why it was this and not that. Without it, stripped and bare, I do not know what benefit any historical book could offer its readers.

Michael had a maidservant attached to his household who, at certain periods, became frenzied and possessed, and would [?] and utter prophecies. And at the shore of [?]… [?] she would come there [?] and say: "Come down from there, come down, most noble [?] Michael; strip off [?] and [?] to the best [?]," as though throwing it down to him. Now this happened often and did not go unnoticed. It did not let those who wished [?] spend their lives in good cheer, but [?] it reached the imperial [ears?], causing a stir and a certain unexpected [?]. Michael (for everyone likes to air what troubles him to those he loves) shared [?] the words with a certain Theodotos, who was thought to be a trusted man of the Melissenos family and whose surname was Kassiteras. Theodotos advised him to adopt a plan, a truly auspicious and unfailing one [?]. It was this: at the moment when the girl fell into her frenzy, he should find out precisely, by every means, what the house of the future emperor was, what name he bore, and what he looked like. Michael decided to do this. The girl, possessed by a spirit of divination, held nothing back and said: "At [?], when you are at such-and-such a place, two men will come in. The one riding a mule is named Leo, the other has another name. It is this one who will be blessed with the empire."

That God-hated man then denied all this on oath to the emperor and reported none of what had happened. He called the words nonsense with nothing sound in them. But to him it was no nonsense [?]. He went off at once and found the man, as he had heard, in the shrine of St Paul, whose task it is to care for orphans. He sat down with him, bound him with pledges, reassured him, told him to take heart and rejoice, and said: "I have been secretly taught the future by a divine voice, and it loudly proclaims you emperor." These whispered words were like a second layer of colour in a painting, laid over the first shadings (I mean those first revealed by the monk at Philomelion). They made Leo see the empire no longer as an image and a reflection, but bare and clear, as though already accomplished. This set smouldering again Leo's flame of hope, which had burnt down and, as it were, withered away, while it plunged Michael into a deep abyss of despondency. It raised up the tower of the one man's soul and shook down that of the other. [?]

It was not only that woman who did this, but also Kassiteras, who was trusted and was in fact a deceiver. But we must return to the history.

When Leo had taken the sovereign power and had been publicly proclaimed in the month of July of the sixth indiction, he enrolled Michael, the one who lisped, in the rank of patrician, having earlier sponsored his son at holy baptism. He appointed Thomas, his especially close contemporary and childhood playmate, turmarch of the federates. He also enrolled Manuel, Michael's protostrator, among the patricians and honoured him with the command of the Armeniakoi. Then he said to him: "You should not have armed yourself for war against me by becoming adviser to the emperor and to Prokopia." Manuel answered with great frankness: "Nor should you have raised your hand against your benefactor, who was also your child's godfather." At these words Leo fell silent, out of respect for the man's virtue.

13. He heard that the ruler of the Bulgars, puffed up by his earlier victory, was again ravaging the neighbouring land. He was stripping and plundering the fields, carrying off many people and many cattle, burning houses here and there, and was altogether intolerable. At first Leo thought he should remind him of the peace through an embassy. When this failed to persuade him, Leo had the ruined parts of the walls rebuilt under his own direction and marched out quickly to the rescue. Arriving at the city of Mesembria, he used the following stratagem. For a number of days he sat in a certain place, having entrenched himself and his army. They were supplied regularly from our own territory and lacked nothing they needed, nor even luxuries. Then he heard that the Bulgars encamped nearby and armed against him were short of necessities. So he left the place where he had been lying in wait by night, with a good number of soldiers trained in strength and endurance, revealing his plan to one man only. He went to lie in ambush on a certain hill, after giving the signal for battle and the hour. When day dawned and the general [?] of the emperor [?], everyone concluded that he, the emperor that is, had fled, since they knew nothing of what had happened. The enemy took heart and could no longer stay where they were at all [?]. They rose up and thought they had the army in their hands. When night came, Leo came down from the ambush upon them while they expected no harm. He fell upon men who had put down their arms and were relaxed in sleep and in their confidence at the emperor's flight. As the Romans poured in from all sides at the signal, he caused such destruction and slaughter that the whole camp was taken and, as the saying goes, not even the fire-bearer escaped. What is more, he made people of every age the spoil of raiding and plunder, dashed their children against the rocks and the ground, and his own

[land] he quickly regained. From that time on the hill has been called Leo's, and the Bulgars who pass that way always shake their heads, point at it with their fingers, and [do not?] forget the evils of that time.

14. This success made him bolder and more reckless, and drove him back into his inborn cruelty. To him there was no difference between a small offence and a greater one. Against everyone caught for anything there was a single sentence: to have some vital limb cut off and to be hung up on high. These things bred in everyone a hatred and a fierce enmity toward him. He practised his native savagery undiluted, not tempered or inclined toward mildness, and mercilessly degraded the nature he shared with others. As his wages he got hatred, not friendship.

15. While he was doing these things, he remembered the monk at Philomelion and thought he would repay him for the prophecy. He sent him thank-offerings, supposedly asking for victories for his reign. But the monk had already departed from among men, and a wicked and envious demon had taken over the old man's cell under a show of piety. I would not call him a man, the one who confounded and troubled everything and, like the ancient serpent, poured poison into the ears of wretched Leo, whose whole mind was unstable. He was called Sabbatios. He heaped reproaches on the imperial messenger and spoke insults against the emperor openly, not in secret. He even begged the messenger to report everything without holding anything back: "You will not reign long while you cling to idols" (oh, that accursed tongue!) "and dare [?] … those honoured by the leopardess and Thuis [?] and Taraxios." With an unbridled tongue he spoke this way about the holy images, calling the empress Irene and Tarasios, who is among the saints, by these names.

Leo was truly an idol of demons, a slave of ignorance, more voiceless than a shadow. He should have disregarded these words. Failing that, he should at least have exposed them and laid them before the man who held the reins of the Church, and convened a synod to examine great matters in a great way. Instead [?] he turned to men who had no sound thoughts and cared nothing for his interests (alas for friendship joined with deceit!), but who looked after and arranged their own. He confided in his beloved Kassiteras and brought the messages to light for him. Kassiteras did not cure evil with evil or madness with madness; he stirred them up. He introduced to the emperor another man who held the same opinion about the holy images and lived at the portico of Maurianos. He chattered endlessly about lofty things, affirmed that this man was more than an angel, and said:

"Make use of this man, then, O emperor, concerning the matters at hand [?]. If you do whatever he tells you, you will not fall short of what is needed."

16. Once the plan had been settled, he decided to hurry ahead to the monk. He drenched him with nonsense and added: "Tomorrow night I will bring the emperor himself here to you, dressed as a private citizen, to take counsel about the faith and other matters of real importance. Promise him that he will steer the [empire?] for seventy-two years, count him as the thirteenth of the apostles, and tell him he will see his children's children on the imperial throne, provided he agrees in some way with the doctrine of Leo the Isaurian. If he will not promise this but refuses, swear to him that ruin and destruction, cliffs and pits are threatened against him by God." Having coached the monk in these things out of mischief and malice, he brought the emperor at the appointed time. When they had come in with Theodotos and were beginning their secret talk, the monk said: "You ought not, O emperor, to lay aside the purple, disguise yourself as a private citizen, and go nibbling at the opinions of the crowd in this way." Leo was astounded and struck by these words, and supposed that they came from divine foreknowledge. From then on he truly followed the monk as a shadow follows a statue, and hung entirely on his words, dangling by the ears like an earthenware jar. But these things have also been told in verse by those who came before us.

17. At once he proclaimed the removal of the holy icons. He demanded that the patriarch (this was Nikephoros) give his consent in his own handwriting, unless he wished to be sentenced to exile. Nikephoros had already gathered from other signs the tyrant's hostility toward the divine. He judged it better to be led away than to agree with such a man, and he was led off to the confession for which he had been condemned. Theodotos Kassiteras received the throne of the hierarchy as his prize at the time of holy Easter. It is worth not passing over the evidence for this hostility. Nikephoros, as head of the priesthood, had asked Leo to affirm his assent to the divine faith in a sacred [written statement?]. Leo said he would not do it now, but would put it off until his proclamation as emperor had been fully completed. The postponement showed that he had been gripped by the madness of the heresy from birth.

18. There is another sign, clearer than the one just mentioned. When he had just been proclaimed and needed the diadem, the high priest had to place it on his abominable head. As Nikephoros came near and touched the head, he felt not soft hair, as it seemed to be, but thorns and caltrops, which was what was truly there. It was as though he were being pricked with points and his hand pierced with pain. But these things

happened earlier. At the time we are speaking of, the patriarch had received the vote deposing him and was going into exile. It is said that as he was being carried on a merchant ship, at a certain place along the coast he saw far off the blessed Theophanes greeting him with incense and lamps, as though sending an escort ahead to honour that noble confession. He welcomed him, as was fitting, and commended him to God in prayer. Then, raising his hands on high, he embraced him, as it were, giving him a last greeting from afar. One of his companions asked him, "To whom are you giving this greeting, with such prayer and longing?" He answered with a prophetic tongue: "To the confessor Theophanes, superior of the monastery of Agros." And this came to pass not long afterwards, for he never saw Theophanes again, and Theophanes won the crown of confession. So much for the patriarch.

19. Leo, for his part, made this handling of the Church's affairs the beginning of his reign, as though it were an auspicious start [?]. Sick with ambition like few others, he took the public affairs in hand. Like the wasps, he carried his sting with him everywhere. He trained the soldiery himself, rebuilt from their foundations under his own direction cities in many parts of Thrace and Macedonia, and went about everywhere, so that he was fearsome and terrifying even to the enemy. For this reason they say that the holy Nikephoros once remarked, after Leo's murder, that the city had lost a man who, though a scourge, still took good care of the public interest.

He also took great pains over offices and commands, not only civil ones but military ones as well. He himself was above money, and preferred the most incorruptible men of all, honouring everyone by merit rather than by wealth. He wanted to be called a lover of justice, but he did not become one. Still, he laid claim to it, and settled many cases himself, sitting in the Lausiakos. Once a man brought a complaint before him about the abduction of a wife: one of the prominent men had carried off his wife, and he said, "I have not even been given a hearing, though I have often pestered the eparch." The eparch was summoned at once and confirmed that it was so. Leo removed him from office, called him to account, and poured great bitterness on him, and he ordered the adulterer to be handed over to the law.

20. By such things he courted the citizenry and, as one might say, bargained for their goodwill toward himself. But in matters of faith he raged violently, so much so that he did not even think it right to name God. For when he concluded on oath the thirty-year treaty with the nations called the Bulgars, and made peace agreements,

…since he was to confirm and secure these terms by oaths, he did not use our oaths, which call on God, or the heavenly powers, or the Mother of Christ our God according to the flesh as overseers and witnesses of what is said and done. Instead, like some barbarian soul cut off from piety, he used dogs, and the things that the lawless nations sacrifice, as witnesses of the proceedings. He cut them apart and did not shrink from taking the oath on his own lips to confirm it, using the things by which they [?] swear. Meanwhile, it seems, he entrusted the faith of the Christians to men who were one day to be brought over to it by us. In this way he was plainly not ashamed of his impiety. By casting the pearls of the faith before swine, as the Lord puts it, and forcing the barbarians to take them on their lips, the man deserved loathing for his impiety. And by being initiated into their rites without a blush, though he himself governed the empire and realm of the Romans, and that in a public theatre full of both unbelievers and believers, he deserved nothing but the eternal worm and fire. He tortured bitterly and terribly all those he found keeping the orthodox doctrine. At the same time he gathered and assembled bands and companies of those who thought as he did, placed them at his side and flooded them with favours. Among these was enrolled John the Grammarian, a man trained in nothing good. Leo ordered these men to draw up a document that sprang from a new and foul faith, and so he pursued his course against the holy icons. The head of the sacred body and clergy of the imperial palace also fanned him up, as it were, and puffed him up and raised him high, for Leo was light-headed and moved toward nothing with a reasoning mind. This man had long lain in wait for him, as if in ambush, eager to catch his Proteus. On one occasion that divine text was proclaimed to the assembled congregation: "To whom have you likened the Lord, and with what likeness have you compared him? Has not a craftsman made an image, or has not a goldsmith melted gold and gilded it, or fashioned a likeness?" When this rang out and was proclaimed in the church of the Pharos, the man quietly slipped forward, put himself in view and said: "Understand, O emperor, what the sacred oracle says. Do not regret what you have begun. Get rid of every image that seems divine, and hold to the right worship of those who do not venerate them." By these words, as I have said, Leo was kindled further without any reasoning, and his wretched soul was set entirely ablaze. He turned his whole frenzy against the pious, and against the impious he stirred up the divine and just wrath. By decree he summoned all the bishops from the outlying regions, despoiled them, and kept them far from the sight of the patriarch,

denouncing them, as though he would make them obedient to his own will. In fact, because they would not be persuaded by him, he persuaded many to take up the noble witness of martyrdom. 21. But God, as is his way, is not abrupt but long-suffering: he whetted his sword but did not yet let it fall. Now plagues and droughts and scorching suns came upon them, now earthquakes and upheavals. At other times flames seemed to be hurled through the air, and elsewhere civil strife, the most extreme of terrors, was brandished over them. But that soul could not be restrained, and rushed like a swine down a cliff. So at last a sword that strikes a fatal blow came forth from God, so that nail might be driven out by nail and evil cured by evil. This was Michael. He had held the command of the federates at that time, and had been caught on a charge of treason, which he managed to shake off only with great labour and toil. But Leo, who kept him always between his teeth, was soon to make him a sacrificial victim, as it were, for what he had done. For Michael in any case cultivated a forward and reckless tongue, and never stopped parading his beastly character, since he had grown up together with Leo and was proud of the prowess of his hand. Leo (for one who rules over all cannot bear to be bested by a single fool, unless he is truly made master not only of men but of his own temper) set a band of eavesdroppers on him, so that Michael's words might be carried across to him as if by a ferry. For he suspected what was coming. The prophecy at Philomelion had by no means faded from his soul, and it had declared that Michael would be proclaimed emperor after Leo. One of these spies was Exaboulios, a man able to read a person's character and nature. As time went on, Michael did not let up on his loose talk and mockery. Like a river in flood that churns up all its mud at the wrong moment, he threatened Leo with utter ruin and whatever else his wicked temper was nursing. These things were reported to the emperor, Michael was seized on the spot, and finally, as his accusers confirmed the charge, he was found guilty of plotting a usurpation. It was the day before the coming and incarnation among us of the Word, Christ our God. The emperor himself examined him in the offices of the secretaries, and he was caught out on every side. There was no escaping what he had dared, so he was condemned to death, and to no ordinary death. So that he might have the emperor himself as both spectator and executioner, whether Leo was overcome by the passion of his anger or simply delighted in cruelty, Michael was to be flung into the furnace of the imperial bath as fodder for the fire. This was decided, and Leo himself hurried ahead to watch the spectacle. But his wife (this was Theodosia, the daughter of Arsaber) leapt up and ran just as she was, as if driven mad by some Bacchic frenzy. She held him back and checked his impulse, calling him accursed and a fighter against God, since he did not even keep that day in reverence, although he was about to partake of the divine body. Terrified

then by these dreadful prospects, and afraid that it would displease God, he granted Michael for the moment a reprieve that was to turn back on himself. He entrusted him to the custody of the papias, though he saw fit to keep the key of the iron fetters in his own keeping. And he said to his wife: "Before long, wife, you and the offspring of my loins will see what comes of this, even if today you have freed me from the sin of that deed." With these words he foretold and proclaimed the future. 22. For a fear had settled in his soul because of an oracle, which said that on the day of the birth of Christ our God according to the flesh he would be stripped of all the prosperity and rule that had grown so great. The oracle was a Sibylline one, kept in a book in the imperial library. The book contained not only oracles in plain words but also figures and portraits of the future emperors in colour. There was a beast drawn there, a lion, with the letter Chi marked on it from its spine down to its belly. Behind it a man ran up and dealt the beast a fatal blow with a spear through the Chi. The picture was shown to many people for interpretation, but only the man then holding the office of quaestor explained the oracle: an emperor called Leo, like the lion, would be handed over to a violent death on the day of Christ's birth. [P. 23] 23. His mother's vision also came back to him and filled him with fear. When she had told it to him he had made nothing of it, but now it pressed upon his soul and gnawed at it sharply. She constantly visited the holy church at Blachernae, and there a maiden appeared to her, surrounded by many figures in white, and the whole church was full of blood. The maiden told one of those standing by to fill a pot with blood and give it to Leo's mother to drink. She pleaded her long widowhood, in which she had tasted neither meat nor anything with blood in it, so that she had no need of the pot. "How so?" the maiden replied angrily. "Does your son not keep on filling me with much blood, and by this provoking my Son and God?" From then on she often begged her son to abandon the heresy of the icon-burners, telling the vision with all its tragic force. 24. Another vision by night frightened him no less. He heard Tarasius himself, the celebrated patriarch, who had long since departed this life, urging a certain Michael by name to leap upon him, deal him a fatal blow and hurl him down a cliff above an abyss. On top of this came the words of the monk at Philomelion, and also the too hasty change of robe. Putting all this together,

he shook with fear and his soul was in turmoil, and sleep would not come to him that night [?]. So, in the dead of night, taking a counsel more clever than kingly, he broke open the small doors leading to the papias's quarters (for he was strong in the hands) and made his way to him. When he entered the room he saw a sight that astonished him beyond measure. He saw the condemned man lying comfortably on the papias's couch, and found the papias himself sleeping on the floor. He put his hands on Michael and on his head, wanting to learn whether he was sleeping a carefree and sweet sleep, or the anxious and tormented sleep that commonly comes to those in misfortune. He found him at ease and free of every care (indeed he did not even wake at his touch). These unexpected sights fed his anger all the more, [P. 24] and he went away shaking his head menacingly, not only at Michael but at the papias as well. This did not escape the notice of the papias's people. One of the attendants guarding Michael recognised the emperor by his purple shoes and reported everything plainly. They were deeply shaken, and seized by an overwhelming fear they contrived a plan to save themselves. 25. Day was just dawning when Michael put forward a pretext through Theoktistos, whom he later honoured with the dignity of keeper of the imperial inkstand: he claimed to be burdened with certain stains on his soul and wished to confess them to one of the men dear to God. This was allowed and granted by the emperor. Michael then told Theoktistos to threaten that he would disclose to the emperor all those who had shared in the plan with him, unless they did something bold to save him from this death and prison. When the conspirators heard this, they stitched together the following plan. It was the custom then for the sacred clergy to spend the night not inside the palace, as they do now (the practice began from that time), but in their own houses. At the start of the third watch they would gather at the Ivory Gate to render the morning hymn of praise to the Lord God. The conspirators, carrying daggers under their arms, mingled with the clergy, escaped notice thanks to the darkness and the priestly vestments, and boldly went in with them. They hid in a dark place and waited for the signal. As the hymn was drawing to its close, the emperor was somewhere near the singers, often leading off the chant he loved so well, "From love of the Ruler of all they scorned…" (for he had a naturally fine voice and was the sweetest singer of the men of his time). Then they rushed in all together. At their first attack they missed their mark and went for the head of the clergy by mistake, whether because of some resemblance and similarity of build or because of the similar covering on his head. For the season was frosty and wintry, and both men were wrapped in cloaks and had their heads covered with very pointed felt caps. But the head of the clergy escaped the danger, for at once

he bared his head and won his safety with his bald pate. Leo, however, dragged himself into the sanctuary and was not saved, though he did his best to defend himself. He seized the chain of the censer, or, according to some, a holy cross, and tried to stand up to his attackers. But they rushed at him in numbers, not one at a time, and wounded him, even as he defended himself and turned aside the thrusts of their swords with the wood of the cross. But he grew exhausted, struck from all sides [P. 25] like a beast. Then in despair he begged and openly implored, by an oath on the grace that dwells in the church, a certain huge, giant-like man who was about to deal the blow. This man came of the family of the Krambonitai. But he answered, "This is a time not for oaths but for slaughter," and swearing in his turn by the divine grace, he struck straight down on Leo's arm so powerfully that he not only tore it terribly away from the collarbone, but the arm of the cross was also cut off and flew a long way. Someone else cut off his head as well, leaving the body like a stump. 26. Such was the end of Leo's life, in the month of December (it was the tenth hour of the night). He had reigned seven years and five months, and practised cruelty and impiety as much as any of his predecessors; and by these he disgraced the care he had shown for public affairs and the strength and courage of his hands. It is said, too, that at that very hour a voice burst forth from heaven announcing his downfall to many. Some sailors heard it, wrote down the time and the night, and on later inquiry found that it was

ON THE REIGN OF MICHAEL OF AMORION. 1. After Michael's party had killed Leo, as we have related in the previous book, they dragged his corpse pitilessly and without mercy through the [?] and brought it out to the Hippodrome. They no longer had any fear, since the imperial palace was full of plotters and conspirators. Along with him they also brought out his wife and their four children: Symbatios, who was renamed Constantine at his coronation, Basil, Gregory and Theodosius. They put them in a small boat and took them to the island of Prote. There the boys were castrated, and it befell Theodosius to lose his life and to share his own father's grave.

2. Michael was brought up from the papias's custody with his feet still bound in iron, because the key, which Leo had kept for safety, could not be found for the time being. He sat on the imperial throne, [P. 27] was proclaimed emperor, and received the obeisance of all who were then in the palace. By midday the news had spread everywhere. His fetters had been broken, with difficulty, by a hammer. Without washing his hands, without taking the fear of God into his mind, without doing anything else that was proper, he went off to the great and holy church, eager to receive the crown from the patriarch's hand and to be acclaimed by the whole people. His only fence and rampart were those who had shared in the murder and conspired with him. Here one might well wonder at the wrong-headedness of both men. Of the one, that he had none of his many flatterers and friends to help him at that moment, since all of them had crept into holes like reptiles. Of the other, his fearlessness [?] and bloodthirstiness toward everyone. Like a prize-winner returning from victory, and not like an executioner, he paraded through the street (this came about by the Providence that governs all things), when he ought to have covered his face and lamented. He should have lamented not for having shed blood that deserved to be shed in justice (and even that is not praiseworthy), but for having shed it in an unfitting place, a place divine and pure, the only place where the Lord's blood is poured out every day as the ransom for our sins. 3. But let our history turn now to the land that reared him, take him into its midst and tell his story. He was born in the city of Upper Phrygia called Amorion, where a great number of Jews and of certain Athinganoi have always lived. From their mixing and constant contact a heresy has grown up there, with a new way of life and new doctrines, and he himself belonged to it, having inherited it from his fathers. This heresy allows its initiates to receive the divine washing of baptism, since it is held to bring salvation and is acknowledged as such among them. But it keeps and observes everything else according to the Law of Moses, except circumcision. Whoever has been initiated into it keeps in his own house a Hebrew man or woman as teacher and leader, so to speak, one who abstains entirely from divine baptism. To this person he entrusts not only his spiritual affairs but also the management of his household, and he puts himself under that person's hand. [P. 28] He belonged to this sect from childhood, and his soul was taken over by it in advance. Yet even so he did not keep that early belief pure. Becoming a kind of meeting-place of unbelief, he at once corrupted the sect itself by not holding close to it, adulterated the faith of the Christians, and debased that of the Jews. For a while he held to it and grew up to manhood, with boorishness and ignorance growing up together with him like tendrils on a vine,

or rather, held fast by them and schooled by them, he took up lessons to match. Often, even when he had gained control of the imperial power, he could be seen taking more pride and delight in these than in his own diadem. Rational learning he despised entirely and deliberately cast out of his soul, because it overturned the views he put forward and was able to persuade him and teach him otherwise, so that he would not follow his own heresy and religion. And yet he could have revered his own beliefs without dishonouring ours, since he could not compete with so great a chorus of men [?] for wisdom, who prevailed both by their antiquity and by their numbers. 4. In any case, he valued his own accomplishments. These were: to predict of a newborn litter of piglets which would be well fed and would not lack size of body, and which would suffer the opposite; to know how to stand close to kicking horses, but cleverly to keep as far away as possible from kicking donkeys; to be an excellent judge of mules, both of those fit and suited for carrying loads and of those that carry their riders smoothly without growing panicky at some sudden fright. More than that, with a mere glance of the eye he could tell which horses were by nature vigorous and swiftest for racing, and which kept their endurance for war; he could judge how well sheep and cattle would breed, and which of them had been given by nature an abundance of milk; and, greatest of all, even when the mothers and their newborn young made no sound, he knew how to tell which young belonged to which mother. These were the lessons and the boasts of his early years, and, one might say, of his last years too. 5. When he had reached his prime, he was living a pauper's life and enduring it [?], and he was eager to shake it off by any means. Once he presented himself to his general, [P. 29] showing himself off and drawing the commander's attention by the stammer of his tongue. One of the Athinganoi, who was known to the general and on intimate terms with him, declared that this Michael and another man would soon be famous and would before long attain the empire itself. The general's soul was set aflame by this. Harvesting the future in advance, as it were, he decided not to let the opportunity slip by delay, for it would be neither easy nor simple to find it again. So a table was laid at once, and, leaving out all the others, he invited these men to a feast. When the drinking was at its height, the general brought in his daughters, gave them away and pledged them to the men as brides. The strangeness and unexpectedness of it at first left them astonished and speechless, but afterwards they accepted and agreed, acknowledging the hand of God in it, perhaps, rather than that of man.

6. There are, then, many things that fall under the art of divination: the flights of birds, swarms of dreams, and the inspection of the entrails of all kinds of bodies. I will not argue this at length, so that I am not one man quarrelling with many. But neither I nor, I think, anyone else of sound mind would say that it is pure and free from the service of certain demons, who are eager to drive man far from God [?]. For we have heard that people who pursue no sincere or pure life, but a careless and servile one, have gained exact knowledge of it. Why have I raised this question here? So that no one should think that those who busy themselves with such things reveal anything of this kind by divine inspiration, and so make God the cause of their unjust purpose, or, what comes to the same thing, of their rule. Nor should anyone suppose that those who give themselves over to such men have any sense, since many of them fail every day and become the cause of their own ruin. Rather [?], let him blame the serpent, the author of evil. He walks about the world, seizes suitable instruments, and sows the seeds of empire not in this man or that man alone but in many. He persuades and stirs them to make the attempt, persuading them to overturn peoples and stir up civil wars, like a blind man who often throws stones at people: by throwing at many, he may perhaps now and then hit his target, though barely and without seeing it. We have said this as a digression, so that no one should attribute such deeds, or the more wicked kinds of rule, to the Divine. We rely on that testimony of Scripture: "They set up kings for themselves, but not through me" [?]. 7. Michael had taken the voice of the Athinganos soothsayer to heart as a divine prediction. Much later, as I said before, he fulfilled the prophecy given at Philomelion by rather boldly carrying out the murder of Leo. From then on he made this his constant concern, and he also boldly made his entry into the holy church sooner than he should have. He showed himself wicked toward his first benefactor, the Bardanes already mentioned, and more wicked toward the second, Leo, all the more because he had become godfather to Leo's son at holy baptism. Still, he set aside a portion of Leo's confiscated property and arranged for it to be provided for the use of Leo's children, together with their mother, Leo's wife. He also gave them some of his own servants, though not all of them. He ordered with full authority that the mother and wife should live in safety in the monastery called that of the Despotai, and the male children on the island of Prote, as was said. There Constantine, renamed Basil, was somehow struck speechless after his genitals were cut off. He prayed to God that his voice might be set free and that his tongue might once more become clear, and he also prayed to the one who shone in theology,

Gregory, whose image happened to be set up somewhere there. The saint yielded and heard his prayer at the feast of Lights. For at dawn he saw that divine figure speaking to him and saying, "Take the candle and read." He believed what was said, went in, and read in a bright, clear voice the words "[?] my Jesus." From then on he never stopped loathing the folly he had inherited from his father and its ingratitude toward the holy icons. He changed his mind and never stopped embracing the images of the saints. But this happened late in time, much later on. 8. When Michael had now taken up sole rule and was managing its affairs as he pleased, the blessed Nikephoros sent him a letter. He urged that the faith be restored and that the icons once again receive veneration. But Michael replied: "I have not come forward to make innovations in any doctrine of the faith, nor to attack in any way what has already been handed down and confessed. So let each do what seems good and desirable to him, and remain a stranger to toil and untouched by grief." However, he did not keep to this resolve to the end, for he had never been a true Christian from the beginning. Instead, the more firmly he gained control of the empire, the more, with his ill-starred nature and [?], he fanned the flames of war against the Christians and his own countrymen. At one time he spat on the monks, surrounding them with every kind of horror and devising punishment after punishment. At another he consigned the rest of the faithful to prisons and drove them into exile. So it was that he expelled from the city Methodios, who shortly afterward took over the patriarchal throne, and Euthymios, then bishop of Sardis, because they did not yield to his will or deny the honour due to the icons. He handed the holy Methodios over to prison on the island of the Apostle Andrew, near which Akritas lies. He put the blessed Euthymios to death through his own son Theophilos, and Euthymios was beaten mercilessly with ox-sinew whips. As much as he oppressed Christ's inheritance and fed on it like some wild beast, so much did he make the Jews free and exempt from taxes, loving and cherishing them above all other people. Painters take beautiful creatures as their models. This man, however, took the life of Kopronymos as a kind of stamp and prototype and strove to imitate it to the utmost. So he drove on to the very citadel of impiety. At one time he decreed fasting on the Sabbath, and at another he sharpened his tongue against the holy prophets and disbelieved the coming resurrection and the good things that follow it. He insisted that there was no devil at all, since Moses had not handed one down. He embraced fornication and decreed that in all matters one should swear by God alone, and

with an unbridled tongue he counted Judas among the saved. He mocked the feast of saving Easter as celebrated wrongly and at the wrong time. He spat on Greek learning, and despised our own sacred learning so much that he would not let the young be educated anywhere. He did this so that no one would ever be able to stand up to his ignorance and refute it, or, carried along by sharp eyes and a quick tongue thanks to education, force him to take second place. For he was so slow at joining letters together and reading syllables that someone could more easily have read through a whole book than he, with his slow mind, could get through the letters of his own name. But we must leave these matters aside, since the holy men of that time have already held them up to ridicule. Whole books are full of works that expose his doings. Let us move on to the next part of the history, the results of his impious deeds.

9. At this time a civil war broke out in the East and filled the world with every kind of evil, leaving few men out of many. Fathers armed their right hands against their sons, brothers against those born of the same womb, and at last friends against those who loved them most. The leader of all this was Thomas, about whom two accounts are told. We are only human, and because so much time has passed, we have learned these parts of the history by hearing and not by sight. So, in order to preserve the truth on every side, we must record both versions that have been handed down, not just one. Such uncertainty and variation does no harm to our subject. In fact, it is safer for those who are always arguing that things were not this way but that way. It would be best if the truth were naked and we humans could know everything without a veil. But since the long passage of time, laid over us like a covering, weakens our knowledge, we must trust rumour and report and bring events to light as far as we can, rather than hand them over entirely to the river of forgetfulness. 10. The first account, which I myself follow because I have confirmation from certain written sources, says that this Thomas was born of obscure and poor parents, and moreover of Slavic stock, from those who had often been settled in the East. Living in poverty and hoping to trade up his fortune, he ran away from his homeland and came to this great city. He attached himself to one of the senators to serve and wait on him, but his lust drove him to shame and defile his master's bed and marriage. When he was caught and was unable [?] the blows for

this, he fled to the sons of Hagar. He gave them sufficient proof of his loyalty, both by fitting deeds over many years (he was spending his twenty-fifth year there) and by denying Christ our God. He became the commander of a war band and took up arms against the Christians, promising to bring the empire of the Romans under their power with a mighty hand. To make sure no one among the Romans would stand in his way, and that all would instead side with him and run risks on his behalf, he declared and spread it about that he was Constantine, the son of Irene. Her folly and the cruelty of her character had long before deprived Constantine of his rule along with his eyes, and by that time he had departed this life. The scale of the undertaking and the hopes that sustained him called for a partner in affairs, for he did not think he could otherwise make his position by land and sea secure. So he also adopted a son, a man of no relation to him, whose deformed body revealed the madness of his soul. He gave him enough troops and renamed him Constantius, and ordered him to ravage and overrun the land of the Romans from one direction while he himself did so from another. At that time the reins of empire were held by Leo the Armenian, at a later time [?]. Leo gathered a force against him, but not a considerable one. He made it fail, for it turned to flight at the first face-to-face encounter, and he made Thomas bolder and more confident in his own prospects. This is how the first and more widespread account says this uprising and revolt began. 11. The other account does not differ on the name. It says that this Thomas was the one who had long ago been an associate of Bardanes and had been honoured by Leo when Leo was in power. He was then in command of the foederati and stationed in the Anatolikon theme. When he heard that Michael had just killed Leo, he raised a hostile hand. He did so to avenge Leo, to satisfy his own anger (for he had been at odds with Michael since they were young), and because he feared the monk of Philomelion's prophecy about Michael. It was no small or weak hand but a heavy, manly and vigorous one, for he had with him men of every age able to wield a spear. For Michael happened to be hated by everyone for other reasons as well. He had taken part in the evil heresy of the Athinganoi, as was said. He had a stammering tongue and was decried for cowardice and softness. Much more than that, he had a soul no less lame than his tongue, so he was loathed and considered a burden by most people. Thomas, on the other hand, though lame in one leg and a barbarian by race, was venerable for his grey hair. He was also better loved, because from boyhood he had been used to the affability and good humour that soldiers love, and in bodily strength and courage

he seemed second to none. He won over the collectors of the public taxes and worked hard, through generous gifts, to bring the many under his command. So from small he became great, and from a tiny band he became mighty. Some he led by persuasion and friendship, namely those who had a love of revolution and wealth. Others he led by force and against their will, namely those who had already experienced the evils of civil strife. So the civil wars broke out, and like the cataracts of the Nile bursting open, they drenched the earth not with water but with blood. So slaves turned against masters, soldiers against officers and captains against generals, all arming their murderous hands, and the whole of Asia groaned as it sank. Some of the cities, swayed by fear, were taken by Thomas with all their men. Others resisted again and again and kept faith with the ruling emperor, but they were subdued later with much slaughter and enslavement. In the end all Asia went over to him, except for Katakylas, general of the Opsikion, and Olbianos, general of the Armeniakon. These two alone, among so many generals, were seen to keep faith with Michael. He rewarded them for not betraying him by remitting one miliaresion of the so-called hearth tax that was paid into the imperial treasury. All the others, these themes included, had paid two miliaresia from of old, but now one was remitted because of their loyalty. 12. When the Hagarenes learned of this, it seemed welcome to them and a real delight. Seizing the opportunity, they overran every land and island without fear, since no one stood in their way. Thomas heard of this. He feared that his own men would stir up some movement or revolt if he took no care for their homes and the rest of the East and let their children and wives be plundered and carried off. So he judged it best for the time being to check the enemy's onslaught by appearing in person, to overawe them with the size of his forces, and to cunningly draw them into peace. And so it happened. When he invaded their land in turn and seemed irresistible to the Saracens, he entered into negotiations with the barbarians, made peace treaties and called them into an alliance. He agreed and promised, as was said before, to betray the borders of the Romans and to bring their empire under the Saracens' power. So he did not fail in his plan. He even received a crown and was proclaimed emperor by Jacob, who at that time laid claim to the throne of Antioch. He gathered a large army, or rather received one, to strengthen his position. For he drew not only on these Hagarenes who are our neighbours and

[?] Book II. Michael [?] share our borders, but also on those who live further inland: Egyptians, Indians, Persians, Assyrians, Armenians, Chaldians, Iberians, Zechs, Kabeiroi, and all who followed the doctrines and oracles of Mani. Fortified by these, as it were, and fenced in on every side, he thought it best, in keeping with his habits, to change his name and adopt a son, as [?]

13. So he invaded, ravaging the whole East and every age group that did not come over to him through persuasion. When the emperor heard this, he judged the report to be greater than the reality. He sent against him an army that was neither adequate nor considerable. Thomas engaged it and gulped some of the men down as a thirsty man gulps a drink. He turned the rest to flight and made his own position stronger. He fitted out biremes, along with round-hulled ships that followed him carrying grain, and horse transports. He then also gained control of the thematic fleet and ordered the whole navy to gather at Lesbos. Meanwhile he himself, now believing he had no rival, plundered all of Asia. He commanded eighty thousand men and drove them with a single word, and he set out on the road to Abydos in order to cross over. He had overrun everything and reduced to ash and dust not only the humbler places but even the stronger ones. But one well-situated place was left that had suffered nothing from their ravages, and he entrusted his adopted son with overrunning it with the troops under his command. The son was puffed up by some demonic sorcery and had filled his soul with divination. On the day before, he shouted out in the hearing of his men the exact day on which, he declared and affirmed, he would enter the imperial city. Then, riding out boldly, the wretch danced his way into disaster. For he was advancing with his men scattered, thinking the place was empty of enemies, and he fell into an ambush laid by Olbianos. His head was cut off on the spot and sent to Emperor Michael. Michael sent it on to the man's father, who had in no way slackened in his advance or in his dreadful and cruel deeds. Thomas had just received it, but he shrank from nothing. From a place by the sea called Horkosion he watched for the time when the moon was dark at its conjunction, and then crossed over into Thrace at many points. Michael had been concerned about this even before Thomas crossed. So he went around the whole of Thrace, urging the people to stand firm against the rebel and appealing to them to take his side to the point of shedding their blood, renouncing neither their loyalty to the emperor nor their own courage and valour. But it seems that the sight of a man is something most people cannot resist. Once Michael had withdrawn to the capital and Thomas appeared before them in person, they all changed sides with ease, so that

[?] they did not even need to be persuaded, and at once joined his campaign as he led them toward the capital. 14. The emperor learned of these things very quickly. So he gathered an army from those who still remained from Asia and assembled forces through Katakylas and Olbianos, [?] skilfully the danger that now threatened the empire. Nor did he neglect the navy, but with great skill he prepared forces to oppose Thomas by land and sea. He was in such difficulty and straits that he even stretched an iron chain from the Acropolis to the opposite shore at [?], keeping the inner passage blocked. Now on Skyros, one of the Cyclades, there was an exile who had often served as a general and had recently become embittered against Michael. His name was Gregory, called Pterotos. He was Leo's nephew, and when Leo was murdered he became an exile. He did not keep silent: with a heart boiling with love for Leo, he came in to do obeisance to Michael, heaped many reproaches on him, and made the murder the charge behind his words. Michael said to him at the time, "I know the sea of your despondency and the depth of your grief," and let him bear what had happened. But when the third day had passed, he exiled him to that place in the Cyclades. Thomas took him as an ally and made him general of a land army of about ten thousand men. He also fitted out the fleet that had come over to him [and set another general over it], and sent both ahead as a kind of vanguard, judging it useful to attack by land and sea at the same time. This was done, and the naval and land forces appeared together in the gulf by Blachernai, for the iron chain that had been set up proved neither a hindrance nor a help. But their arrival was considered of little or no importance, and so they accomplished nothing worth mentioning. Thomas, however, had certain engineers build rams, tortoises and siege engines with which he thought he could shake the walls. He also adopted a certain Anastasios, who had recently given up the monastic life and returned to this vagabond worldly life, a man black in complexion and black in soul, and he proclaimed him his partner in the revolt. Then, flowing on with a great army and force, he advanced against the capital. He thought the citizens would open the gates to him as soon as he came into view, out of hatred for Michael. But he was disappointed in this hope. Instead he was drenched with their insults and abuse. Then he pitched his general's tent and his camp at the house of Paulinus, where the precinct of the venerable Anargyroi is built like a palace, and all the region as far as the Euxine and Hieron and the

He went on beyond these small towns with a detachment of his army to win them over, so that he would have no enemy at his back. When these matters seemed to him to be in hand, he allowed himself a few days for preparation. Then, from some lookout, he saw Michael, who had fixed the war standard on the roof of the church of the Mother of God and from there was asking for and receiving strength against his enemies. He also saw Michael's son Theophilus going around the whole circuit of the city walls with the clergy, carrying the life-giving wood of the cross and the robe of the all-pure Mother of Christ our God. At this he fell into deep despair about his prospects, and like the chameleon his mind changed this way and that, since he might be forced to fight not only visible powers but invisible ones as well. Not knowing what to do, but emboldened above all by the sheer size of his host, he decided to let a battle be the judge of these deliberations. So the next day at first light he sounded the call to battle and led his men out. To his son he entrusted the pressing of the war and the attack on the landward circuit of the wall. He himself, with the bulk of the forces and the siege engines with which he meant to test the city wall, made his assault at the towers of Blachernae. He brought up ladders to match the height, tortoises from one side and rams from the other, and used arrows and stone-throwers everywhere, hoping that by appearing in every form from every side he would terrify the citizens and take the city. Nor did he neglect the sea walls: he surrounded the city on all sides with his fleet and ordered them to use fire and arrows without stint, and also certain four-legged siege towers. To put it plainly, all this mighty force of men accompanying him accomplished nothing to his advantage. For a contrary wind sprang up at once, dragged the fleet apart and scattered the ships in every direction, since this was an extraordinary winter storm. On land, those in the city fought back bravely. For a time they made his ladders useless with the heavier missiles hurled from the towers. In some places the other engines did not reach the wall, which weighed heavily in the outcome and bore witness to his inexperience in war.
