Those that did reach and make contact were very feeble, incapable of a vigorous fight or of shaking walls, and could not even make the men standing on the towers give ground. So it became clear that things were not going as the earlier rumor [?] had noised and trumpeted everywhere, but worse, as if they were being steered and carried through by a very feeble mind. The besieged city at once took heart, and used such long-range [?]

missiles that it forced the attackers to camp far off, abandon their many engines, and look to their own safety. Since the siege had not gone as he expected but had proved tougher than he had reckoned, and since the season was also making the time harsher, because winter had set in and Thrace is more wintry than other regions, he turned to wintering and withdrew his army. 15. When spring was already shining gently and compelling the soldiery to leave their holes and burrows, he decided to attack Constantinople again from both sides, by land and by sea. But he found Michael not as before: he had just gathered a military force, and by sea another naval one. So he went again in arms to the same quarter as before, the gulf of Blachernae. When day dawned, the signal for battle was given, and he was about to shake the wall of Blachernae, Michael spoke with some of them from the top of the walls. He proclaimed an amnesty for their crimes and promised to give them many good things if only they would change sides and refuse to be stained with the blood of their kinsmen and brothers. But, as the saying goes, he poured these words into a leaky jar. He only made them bolder because they were being entreated, and so, as it were, loosened the cohesion that fear had given them, while he himself grew steadier and firmer. Then suddenly, when they did not expect it, he streamed out against them through many posterns, engaged some of them in battle, inflicted considerable slaughter, and won a brilliant victory. By sea his victory was even greater than on land. The imperial triremes put out and were about to come to grips. The rebel fleet had just begun the battle and was hurling stones when, I know not what came over it, it was struck by terrors and confusion, backed water and put in to shore. Some of the men took courage and changed sides, deserting to the emperor. Others ran off to their own army's camp on land, utterly refusing to stay at sea and fight. Thus the fleet was broken up without effort and came to nothing, having achieved nothing worthy either of the number of ships or of the men who had embarked on them. 16. Then Gregory, the man mentioned earlier, saw that this rebel was contemptible and would become more so as time went on, since he was given to drinking and largely lacking in prudence, through which, more than by any other means, victories are usually won. So he took a portion of the regiment under him and, after first communicating with the emperor through a monk of the Stoudios monastery sent by the emperor, planned a breach and fell upon the rebel's rear. In this way he meant both to frighten him and fill him with confusion and, at the same time, for his own offenses against the emperor, and also

for his wife and children, to obtain reconciliation and pardon (for they were being held in custody because he had joined Thomas). But the emperor did not learn of this in time, for he was so cut off from the outside that he could not know whether anyone at all had taken his side, not only among those nearby but even among those farther away. Thomas, dreading that Gregory might suddenly grow powerful, and wishing to [?] fear among his own men, did not move his camp from the city. He was guarding against exactly this, and took care not to be pursued from behind. Instead he took a few men, as many as he knew were a match for a fight with Gregory, went out against him, overcame him, caught him in flight and killed him. Then he quickly returned to the forces besieging the city and sent letters everywhere announcing his success, claiming that he had won, which was not the case. He also ordered the fleet that was lying idle [?] in Hellas to put to sea quickly, so that he could attack the seaward parts again with a stronger force. These ships, numbering three hundred and fifty warships together with biremes and grain transports, sailed with a fair wind and anchored in the harbor of Byrides in Thrace. But the imperial fire-bearing fleet attacked them there while they suspected nothing. It captured many of the ships with their crews and burned others with a very strong hand. Only a very few escaped the disaster, and they made every effort to reach the gulf of Blachernae and join the land army, which they did. So affairs at sea were steered and directed in this way. On land there were constant skirmishes here and there and killings, as now Michael, now his son Theophilus went out against them with Olbianos and Katakylas, at times dealing and receiving fatal blows. Yet there were no brilliant, vigorous contests in pitched battle between evenly matched forces, since Michael was much weaker and unable to face Thomas's well-equipped army and cavalry. 17. While matters stood thus, Mortagon, the ruler of the Bulgarians (for the report had spread through the world that the emperor of the Romans was under siege), secretly sent men to the emperor. Of his own accord he offered to send an allied force and promised to give him all the help he needed. But Michael, whether he truly felt shame and pity for the multitude of his own people, or wanted to spare his money (for out of stinginess he kept his hands closed far more than other emperors), judged the intention worthy of acceptance [?] but declined his help, and let him know that even if something should happen at the rebel's hands, he did not want his assistance. But Mortagon, who

in any case delighted in wars and loved to reap the spoils they brought, and who also sought to confirm and strengthen the thirty-year treaty made with him by the previous emperor, Leo, made ready his army against the usurper. He openly entered Roman territory and encamped at the place called Kedouktos. This news spread and could not escape the rebel. He was shaken, as was natural, and stunned in mind, but when he came to himself again he armed his army against the Bulgarian. If he divided his forces in two, it was clear that he would be very weak and easily overthrown. The queen of cities, under siege, required not a small army but a very large and considerable one, since Michael was already gathering no mean forces, was able to stand on his heels, and had often been able to inflict destruction on them. The power of the Bulgarians also required no small detachment and army, but a great and far from ordinary battle line. So, lest by dividing himself in two, like some violent torrent, he should seem weaker to his enemies than he was and become easy to subdue, he withdrew entirely from the city. Judging himself a match for the Bulgarian, he drew up his line at the place mentioned and joined battle. 18. When they came to blows, the usurper was decisively defeated. He inflicted no slaughter but suffered it at the hands of the enemy. Since there was no other way to save themselves, they found safety in flight, and scattered in some rough country they considered how they might regroup. But the Bulgarian leader at once took the captives he had won, and having seized a great deal of plunder he returned to his own land, elated and exulting in his victory over Thomas. When the remaining fleet, the one besieging the city, heard this, it went over to the emperor and joined him. Yet the rebel reached such a pitch of boldness, empowered, it seems, by the demons who fought on his side, that although he was crushed and battered on every side and reduced from many to few, and had never won a clear victory, either in a pitched battle or with the engines brought daily by many hands against the city walls, he gathered his men again on a plain called Diabasis. It lay a good many stades from the city and was well suited for a camp because of its vegetation and abundant flowing water. Using it as a base for raids, he ravaged and burned all the beauty that lay before the city, but he no longer showed himself to those in the city as he had before. Michael understood this. He assembled a considerable army and, with Olbianos and Katakylas and their fresh, intact regiments, marched against him. He found him neither dreading nor afraid, but coming to meet him with

haste, and he joined battle with him, wishing to decide the whole matter. There Thomas, meaning to outwit the emperor, was outwitted by his own plan and missed his whole aim. As soon as the battle began, he ordered his men to turn their backs on the emperor. He did not understand the mood of his forces: these were men who had long been deprived of their wives and children because of him, and who were defiling their hands with the blood of their brothers. They had expected their time in the field to be short and not drawn out so long, and at first they had obeyed him in everything. But by now the time had stretched on (the third year was being completed), and judging from what was happening every day they seemed to be attempting the impossible, slaves to the desire and madness of one man. So they seized on the order as a windfall and carried it out not as he wished but as they thought best. He had allowed them to give way only far enough to break up the emperor's line and then to turn back firmly and slaughter. But they knew that the emperor's army was running behind them in good order and with tactical skill, and was not as easy to break as he had thought, and so they fled in disorder and scattered, each in a different direction. The rest went over to the emperor and submitted to him, a few now and others later. Thomas himself escaped with a few men to Adrianople and halted his flight there. His bastard and adopted son Anastasios, in his flight, seized the fortress of Bizye. This happened, I think, not by chance but by a kind of providence, so that each of them, by drawing the emperor's siege upon himself, might give the other respite and an opportunity to forage. 19. But the emperor, following hard on their heels, decided first to besiege Thomas and pay him back for what he had done to him. So he laid siege to him. He did not try to take him with engines or any other means, partly to avoid civil war and partly because he wanted the inhabitants of Scythia to remain ignorant of such devices. Instead he relied on famine and the lack of necessities, of which the city was evidently short and in want, having no stores laid up. This was his decision, and the operation began. The besieged man first drove out every kind of animal not fit for eating [?], and then people of every age from the city. He conducted most of his affairs not with persuasive words, as one might say, but with a tyrannical and self-willed mind, and this stirred up and renewed the hatred against him. Then, as the famine reached its height, there was no hope of safety anywhere, and the belly compelled them and relentlessly demanded its taxes. Some secretly through posterns, others let down from the walls, went off: some gave themselves up to the emperor, while others

fled to the son at the fortress of Bizye. They had eaten not only what was needed but also what was loathsome and wretched, and their food had come down to rotten leather and shoe soles. Then some of those in the city opened talks with the emperor, asked for and received an amnesty for their offenses, surrounded Thomas, seized him with their own hands and brought him to his enemy. The emperor first did what had long been the emperors' practice and had become a custom: he set him beneath his feet. Then he had him mutilated, cut off his hands and feet, and paraded him on a donkey before everyone, while he cried out only this lament: "Have mercy on me, O true emperor!" When the emperor asked whether any of the friends who were with him, or others, shared his views, he might well have denounced many, had not a man named John, of the Hexaboulion, said: "It is not right, O emperor, indeed it is absurd, to believe enemies against friends." With these words he averted the heavier punishments from the wretched citizens and from his own friends. So the rebel ended his life in the middle of October, his soul torn from him by gradual torments, like some animal dying hard. At the beginning he had seemed magnificent and daring and able to carry through what he set out to do, but as he went on he proved far inferior to himself and to the expectations of outsiders. Whether this happened because he himself changed for the worse, or because of a change in those fighting against him, is not worth much discussion. As long as the war was an internal one, which he had first kindled with a self-willed and daring mind, and his hold on power was uncertain, his deeds were no less vigorous than his words, and things went as he intended. But once he had subjected almost all of Asia and crossed over to Europe with no mean confidence, finding no one in his way, then, as a man who started not from learning and education but from vulgar company and the ways of a vagabond, he became inflamed and puffed up and lost his wits, carried away and swept further on toward love affairs and unchaste marriages by his daily drunkenness and revelry. As for the conclusion of these events, we leave others free to think otherwise, if they do not wish to follow our account. But enough about these matters. The people of Bizye also quickly changed their minds, fearing the danger that lay before them. As soon as they learned of Thomas's misfortunes, they did the same as had been done in the same circumstances and brought Anastasios bound hand and foot. He too was forced to suffer the same fate and departed this life like his father. 20. Yet even after things had turned out in this way, the coastal cities of Thrace, Panion and Heraclea, did not stop siding with the usurper. So great

was the hatred that had grown in everyone against Michael, perhaps for other reasons too, but much more because he would not put an end to the [?] that had been kindled against the holy icons. But when he approached these cities, an earthquake struck and the wall of Panion was thrown down, so that Michael entered it without effort. Heraclea still held out, but when it was mastered from the seaward side it too was taken without bloodshed. It stopped siding with the usurper and gave pledges of loyalty to the emperor. Such was the end of Thomas's affairs, from the beginning described above. So the emperor returned in triumph from the mainland cities. He devised no other punishment for the rebels than to make them pass through the hippodrome, at a spectacle held for this purpose, with their hands tied behind their backs, and to exile those most to blame. Next there were Choireas and Gazarenos the Koloniate, men who kept faith with Thomas. Choireas held Kabala and Gazarenos held Saniana, and from there they made many raids, living like brigands and tyrants. Michael at once sent them a chrysobull promising them great honors, the rank of magistros, and an amnesty for their crimes, and informing them of Thomas's death. But the envoy did not persuade them, for they were arrogant men of untamed spirit. He did, however, quietly win over some of their subordinates and bring them into allegiance to the emperor. He persuaded them that when their masters went out on their usual raids, they should shut the gates of the walls against them and leave them outside without a word. And this is what happened. When the two found the gates shut, they hurried off on the road to Syria, stricken with fear. But they were caught alive, hanged on the gallows, and departed this life. It is worth not passing over how Gazarenos was betrayed and shut out of his walls. The envoy befriended a rustic man who took care of his voice and took melodious delight in loose, rustic songs, and composed a song for him addressed to Gazarenos's steward. It went word for word like this: "Listen, master steward, to what Gyberin says: If you give me Saniana, I'll make you a metropolitan and give you Neocaesarea." This song, sung over and over, made the steward take notice. So, when he understood its meaning and how matters had changed, he shut the gates against Gazarenos one day when he had gone out, and left him outside. So much for these little towns perched high in the clouds, and so their [?] again by Michael [?]
21. But the torrent of evils was not to stop there. Rather, of the two continents, Asia and Europe, I mean, in [?] of the Lord, as of a kind of head [?]

87 THEOPHANES [?]
[?] and tail. Even though they did not understand, they were chastised by murders, fires, earthquakes, plunderings, raids of civil war, unexpected overthrows of cities, signs from heaven and signs from the air; and finally the terrors fell on the wretched islands as well, as on a kind of middle part, so that the blow might strike the whole body. But there was no chastening those who had refused to venerate the form of the God-man. So it was that just when Thomas's revolt had begun, and news of it was heard everywhere, the Hagarenes who live in the western gulf of Iberia, bordering on the Ocean (the long flow of time has renamed them Spaniards), had grown in numbers and in the prosperity of their people. They saw that the western side of their land was poor and only moderately prosperous. It fell far short in the quality and abundance of its soil, and lagged even behind the eastern and southern parts of Iberia (for not all of Iberia is suited and fertile for every kind of produce; the western side, as has been said, is parched and poorer than the rest). It could therefore neither feed nor support men of large bodily build who thrive on an abundance of good things rather than on want. So these men went to Apochaps, their emir [?], and asked that a colony and a migration to a new land be granted them, since they were cramped by their numbers and hard pressed by a shortage of necessities. He fitted out some long ships and put on board no small force of these very men. For the moment he turned to piracy, keeping his real intention hidden, against the islands lying to the east that belonged to us. In this way he both fulfilled their desire, glutting them with other people's goods, and at the same time spied out whether any of the islands was fertile and rich enough for them to settle in. [P. 47] As he approached many of the islands he found no one to oppose him with a ship, small or large, for all of them had been stripped of their defenders, who had just gone to help against Constantinople and were sailing with Thomas. From every island where he put in he reaped and carried off great spoils. He came to the Cretans as well. He raided them, plundered them and enslaved as many as he could, and from every side he learned the excellence of the land and how fertile it was for every delight and for an abundance of good things. "This," he said, "is none other than the land flowing with milk and honey." Then, laden with good things of every kind [?], he went home and with every hand and all his strength fitted out a fleet. When the winter was over and spring was beginning to shine, he manned forty ships with fighting men, waited for a favourable wind, and set out on a straight course for Crete, counting the other islands as nothing. Soon he drew near, and he put in and anchored at the promontory called Charax. When nothing untoward befell them either at the landing or at the disembarking,

but as they went out for booty and pillage [?] the plan and the enterprise went forward easily, he sent the able-bodied men out on the usual foraging raids to carry off the enemy as slaves. He himself kept the rest with him, and just when the wind was at its height and the others were already ten or fifteen stades away, he set fire to the ships and burned them all, sparing not a single one. At first the whole army was dumbfounded at the strangeness of the deed (for they came back at once). In terror they asked the reason and began to talk of mutiny. But then they heard what he had long been brooding over: "You yourselves are the cause of this, since you were seeking a colony and good land. In my judgement no land is better than this one, and so I took this course, both to procure good things for you and to free myself of the trouble you were giving me." When they spoke of their wives and showed concern for their children, he said: "Here are your wives, the women you are taking captive, and before long there will be children from them." Silenced by such words and judging that what he said deserved to be accepted, they first dug a deep ditch and set a palisade in it (whence the place to this day keeps a name of the same meaning, being called Chandax). There they spent the night, posting the proper guards and storing up their spoils.
22. Not much time passed before rumour had told the emperor everything. He appointed the protospatharios Photeinos to administer all the affairs of Crete. Photeinos [P. 48] was the great-grandfather of Zoe, the God-crowned Augusta of blessed memory, and was then general of the Anatolikon theme. When he arrived there and had seen some things and heard of others, he informed Michael more clearly of what was going on, and asked him to send a force that would drive the enemy out of the island. So the emperor sent Damian, count of the imperial stable and protospatharios, with a large force and much equipment, to help the general Photeinos. They joined forces and opened the war against the Hagarenes, but the outcome came to nothing useful. For Damian, as has been said, fell wounded at the very start of the battle and was slain, and this made the rest not conquer and stand firm but flee in defeat. In this rout Photeinos too barely escaped in a single small boat to Dia, and brought the news of what had happened to the emperor himself. But since he was always held in honour by the emperor, he [received] in turn the command of Sicily [instead] of Crete [?]

23. While the Spaniards were still living in some turmoil and anxiety, a monk who came down from the mountains of the island told them that there was another place better suited for them to found a town and
[Apparatus: 82 [?]. 83 ὑμεῖς ("you")] αἴτιοι ὑμεῖς ("you are the cause"). 84 εἰς ("to")] ὥστε ("so that"). 85 [?]]

to secure their continued existence and dominion for the future. At once he took them and showed them Chandax, where their city is built to this day; and Apochaps then became its ruler. Setting out from it as from a kind of citadel, they overran this whole island, and no fewer of the neighbouring islands, so that they even settled in them and enslaved the inhabitants and natives themselves. Light-armed troops and foot soldiers together, they captured twenty-nine cities of Crete. From then on only one remained untaken and unharmed: it was subject to them in name, but kept its own customs and its Christianity untouched. At that time too Cyril, the bishop of Gortyn, was slaughtered like a spotless sacrificial victim, because he would not go along with them in denying Christ. His blood still remains, crying out unchanged to God like that of Abel or of Zechariah. The faithful can draw myrrh from there, soaking it up with sponges, but the stain of the blood cannot be altered. Moreover, coffins and tombs have been raised there for the many others who were martyred for Christ at that time, and for the ten renowned martyrs. [P. 49] In such a way, then, and at that time, the Cretans were snatched from the midst of the Christians.
24. Late and with difficulty, Michael shook off the enemies who had surrounded him and clamoured about him. He ought then to have turned to God and propitiated him, making him gracious through his deeds. Instead he acted and conducted himself contrary to what the civil laws require, as one saved not by God but by himself. When his wife died, he wished to have the reputation among the people of mourning her unforgettably. So by secret and private messages he got the senate to resolve to persuade him to be joined to a wife again. They were not only to urge this on him but to force him, and to rise in revolt if it did not happen: "For it is not possible," they were to say, "for an emperor to live without a wife, and for our wives to be deprived of a mistress and empress." At length he let himself be persuaded by these feigned words, which time would not let stay hidden. First he demanded from everyone signed pledges concerning things that neither existed nor would exist: that after his death they would never cease to protect and fight for his future wife and the children born of her, but would have her as their mistress and them as their emperors after him, as was fitting. Thus he thought he would rule not only his own age but the age after him as well, when he ought to have made everything hang on God, not on their hand, on God through whom kings reign and tyrants rule the earth. Nevertheless, he who was lord of all the earth bowed to the senate's command, and he who had chosen a chaste life reluctantly agreed to marry. So he was led to marry

93 BOOK II. – MICHAEL
not this woman or that, but a woman who had long since renounced the world and its things and been betrothed to Christ, and who from childhood had devoted herself to ascetic exercises in the monastery on the island of Prinkipos, attending to God. Her name was Euphrosyne, and she prided herself on being the daughter of Constantine, who by a just judgement had suffered blinding at his mother's hands. These things he carried through, and by them he not only failed to make God gracious but even provoked him to anger.
25. He sent another army against those who had seized Crete and were ravaging it. Its general was a man named Krateros, who at that time governed the theme of the Kibyrrhaiots. Taking seventy biremes from those under his command and from all the themes, he landed, roaring and full [P. 50] of pride. The enemy, for their part, saw fit not to shrink back but to go into battle and display their strength and courage (for these are by nature more capable than the other Hagarenes). Both sides joined battle boldly, entering the contest just as the sun was spreading its rays over the earth, and neither gave way until midday; fighting bravely, they displayed their experience and strength. But when the Cretans, worn out, turned to flight as the sun was already declining, the Romans killed many of them and took even more captive as they threw down their arms, pursuing close on their heels. And perhaps by pressing on they would have taken the city that same day, had not night, already coming on, turned matters around [?] and brought forth, for men seeking rest, not safety but slaughter. For the Romans, thinking themselves already victorious and hoping to capture them all next day in short order, since they were few, gave themselves up to drinking and luxury as if they were in their own land and not a foreign one. They took no thought for any watch or any other safeguard prescribed by the law of war, but only for sleep and for the carelessness and slackness that easily overturn and destroy everything. So about midnight the Cretans, who in their desperate straits were keeping awake, learned through their own scouts that the men in the Roman camp were overcome by sleep and wine. At once they came out and put them all to the sword, so that not even a messenger, as the saying goes, made it back and escaped from there, except only the general, who boarded a merchant ship and sought safety. But the leader of the Hagarenes searched for him everywhere and could not find him; and when he heard that he had fled, he ordered officers to hunt for him in cargo ships. They caught him on Kos, hanged him on a gibbet, and put him to death. Such were the events of that battle and contest, which brought great disaster on the Romans: not only the disaster of that defeat, but also the many-headed hydra which from then on held sway and

has persisted, always being cut off there and elsewhere, but always sprouting again somewhere else.
26. After this a man of military experience, and not lacking in prudence and shrewdness either, surnamed Ooryphas, by imperial order gathered an army then called the Tessarakontarioi [P. 51], because forty gold pieces were distributed to each of them. He overran the other islands, where very few of the enemy were to be found, laying ambushes for some and fighting others openly, and he wiped them out and gave them over to destruction. Crete, however, it seems, he left to us. But its affairs will certainly be God's concern, and they will be ours too, who spend our souls on its behalf night and day.
27. At the same time a certain Euphemios, who was serving as tourmarch in Sicily, fell in love with a virgin who lived in a convent and had long since taken the monastic habit, and he made great efforts to fulfil his passion by somehow taking the virgin as his wife. Since he had an example not far off that did not hinder or deter him, namely this very Michael (for, as has been said, he too had dared something of the kind), he snatched the virgin from the convent and took her to himself against her will. Her brothers went to Michael and told him the story. He ordered the general, if he found the truth to be so, to cut off the nose of the presumptuous Euphemios according to the strictness of the law. When Euphemios learned of this, and of the law being enforced against him and of the emperor's threat, he took as fellow conspirators both the men under his command and some of his fellow tourmarchs. He drove away the general who had come for this purpose and fled to the emir of Africa, promising to bring all Sicily under him and to pay much tribute, if only he would proclaim him emperor and furnish him some help. So the emir proclaimed him emperor of the Romans and gave him a large force, and he became master of Sicily, receiving it from Euphemios himself, though not from him alone: others too joined in to bring about the ruin of such regions. This is shown most clearly and more fully by the letter written at that time to Theognostos, the author of the work on orthography, which has come into our hands; whoever wishes may consult it and learn the details. Not long afterwards, however, Euphemios received as the prize for his rebellion and his lawlessness the loss of his head. For he went, in imperial dress, to Syracuse, and having moved away from his own escort and bodyguards about a bowshot, he came up to the city and spoke to its people in the manner of a tyrant [P. 52] and an emperor. As he was approaching, [?]

two brothers recognized him. They had become [?] and, being of one mind, approached him peaceably, paying him the honour due to an emperor. Euphemios gladly welcomed their acclamation and listened to the rest of what they had to say, and he called them to him to return their greeting kindly. As he bent his head and pressed his mouth to theirs, he was seized firmly by the hair by one of the brothers, and the other cut off his head. Such was the end of Euphemios's life.
28. From then on the Hagarenes became masters not only of Sicily but also of Calabria and Lombardy, overrunning, plundering and encamping in the whole country until the reign of the emperor Basil of blessed memory. But the history of his reign will make these things known. Michael died after holding power for nine years and eight months of his reign, seized by the disease of dysuria, which began in his kidneys. He had not put an end to his enmity toward God, for he would not venerate the form of him who took on flesh for our sake; rather, he even deposed those who venerated it, Methodios and Euthymios, of whom we have spoken. He had also increased the implacable war with the Hagarenes, since God, because of his wickedness, had sent upon him the troubles of Thomas and of the Cretans, and indeed of the Africans mentioned above. All Dalmatia, too, then broke away from the empire of the Romans, and all its people became self-governing and independent until the reign of Basil of glorious memory [?]; for then they were again made subject to the Romans. The oracle about him was also fulfilled, which runs as follows:
"A beginning of evils shall befall the land
when a dragon rules over Babylon,
utterly halting of tongue and greatly fond of gold."
His body was laid in the church of the Holy Apostles, in the heroon of Justinian, in a green Thessalian sarcophagus.

ON THE REIGN OF THEOPHILOS, SON OF MICHAEL
[P. 53] 1. The deeds of Michael the Stammerer, who reigned nine years and eight months, have been set out in the book before this one. His son Theophilos, already of man's age, succeeded to his father's rule and empire in the month of October of the eighth indiction. In word he wished to be called a kind of ardent lover of justice and

a strict guardian of the civil laws, but in truth he put on this show to keep himself out of reach of plotters, so that no one would make any rash attempt against him. So, suspecting the danger that hung over him, he resolved to deliver to destruction and slaughter all those who had given the empire to his father through their conspiracy and had risen against Leo. He therefore issued a decree that everyone who enjoyed any imperial honours, and moreover everyone who had any share in imperial dignity whatsoever, should assemble at the Magnaura. When this had been done, and no one dared disregard the order, [P. 54] he hid for the moment the savagery of his soul as in darkness, and in a quiet and gentle voice spoke briefly, roughly as follows: "My father, whose child and heir I am [?], wished and longed to reward with many honours and many other benefits and privileges those who stood by him and bravely [?] [won him] the empire. But since he departed from among men sooner than he had planned, and passed out of time before the time for his purpose came, he has left me, so that he might not seem ungrateful to many, not only as successor to the empire but also as debtor to these men for such a benefit. So let each of them come forward from the crowd and make himself known to us." Taken in by these words and their minds beguiled, each of them revealed himself and was plain for all to see. At once he commanded the eparch to apply the civil law. "Come now, you," he said, "repay these men as their lives deserve, not only because they did not fear God and stained [?] their right hands with human blood, but because the wretches killed the Lord's anointed, the emperor." With these words he dissolved that first and truly remarkable assembly. Even if someone should choose to praise it as lawful, I do not know whether it would be found close to a most gentle and mild soul. Thus, then, he removed such men from among the living. He added to this a praiseworthy and good deed as well: he drove out his stepmother Euphrosyne and made her go back to the monastery in which she had earlier been tonsured. The history has recorded her as Michael's second wife, and those signed pledges and many oaths that we spoke of there, which were neither made nor given in holiness, availed nothing. Why [?]? Because he did not take a wife trusting in the Lord (for then he would have taken a lawful wife and not one already vowed to Christ), but trusting in his own audacity and in those [?] mighty oaths, which had sent everyone far away from God.
2. Such were his first acts. After that he laid claim to justice and was fearsome to all the wicked and admirable to the good: admirable to the good because he hated wickedness and was just, fearsome to the wicked because he was stern and severe. Yet he could not keep himself clean of every evil. And so he held to devotion [?] toward God and his all-pure mother, as he used to say, [?]
[Apparatus: 91 [?]. 93 προστάγματος ("order")] πράγματος ("matter"). [?] ἔχοιτο] ἕλοιτο ("should choose").]

…faith, but he also clung to the foul heresy of the Iconoclasts handed down from his father. With it he harassed the pious and all-holy people and subjected them to every kind of affliction, never allowing them any rest for the whole of his reign. For this reason his deeds of valour in war did not shine as they should have; he was always defeated and never came home as an emperor ought.

3. Even so, he held fast to justice, and also to his faith in and devotion to the Mother of God. Every week he rode out along the broad avenue and main thoroughfare through the middle of the city to the holy church at Blachernae, escorted by his guards. He went out to make himself available to everyone, but above all to those who had been wronged. They could then pour out their grievances, and no evildoers who feared punishment could stop them. His second purpose was to pass through the marketplace and look at the goods for sale. So he would ask the market price of every item being sold. He did not do this in passing, but with great energy and persistence. Nor did he ask about one kind of thing only, but about everything that can feed a person, whether food or drink, and everything used for warmth and clothing; in short, about everything set out in the market for those who wished to buy. For this reason one would hardly ever have seen him go out in procession except to show his great zeal and care for public affairs, now in the law courts and now, as has been said, on the [?] days of the week.

4. Things that offer a feast for the eyes outside the city usually draw emperors to them. So he extended the seaward walls of the palace beyond their ancient foundations. Toward the sun-terraces, where there had once been a cistern in which an emperor's son happened to drown, he laid out gardens. In this way he supplied what was lacking, and he took pleasure and refreshment in them, as was natural. Once, as the story goes, while he was spending time there or perhaps dining, a huge merchant ship sailing before a fair wind under full sail overshadowed the harbour with its size and filled the emperor with amazement. He at once asked whose freighter it was and what provisions it carried. When he heard that it belonged to the Augusta, there was no keeping it from him. At the time, it is said, he held his peace and let things wait until the day he usually went to Blachernae. When that day came, and the emperor had learned from someone where the ship was moored, he set out on the road leading to the ship; it lay in the Bosporus. When he arrived, he stood by the ship's stern with his retinue following and asked the senate, not once only but twice and

three times, whether any of them needed provisions: grain or wine or anything else used up in a household. After being asked many times they barely answered once: "We lack nothing, so long as we enjoy your lordship and reign." They added that they knew nothing about what they were being asked. Then he said, "So you do not know that God made me emperor, but the Augusta, my consort, has made me a ship-owner? Who ever saw an emperor of the Romans, or his wife, turned merchant?" (I say this, he added, with bitterness of soul.) When they had no reply to this, he ordered on the spot that the people alone be put off [?] and that the ship be set on fire, anchors, sails, cargo and all. Afterwards he spoke harshly against the empress and heaped every kind of insult on her. He even threatened to put her to death if she were ever again caught doing such a thing.

5. Now Theodora (for this was the Augusta's name) could claim Paphlagonia as her homeland, and the village of Ebissa. Her father was Marinus, no obscure man or private citizen, but a drungarios, or according to some a turmarch. Her mother was Theoktiste, also called Phlorina. Both had been brought up in piety. They did not deny the veneration of the holy icons, as everyone did at that time, but embraced it and held it close to their hearts with extraordinary devotion. Theodora had long since been crowned with the imperial diadem, and her mother Theoktiste had been honoured with the rank of zoste patrikia. At her own house, where the monastery of Gastria now stands (she had bought it from the patrician Niketas), this Theoktiste used to summon Theodora's daughters. There were five of them: Thekla, Anna, Anastasia, Pulcheria and Maria. She would win them over with presents and the other things that naturally appeal to the female sex. Then she would take them aside and beg and implore them not to be soft or remain mere women, as they were. They should act like men, she said, and think thoughts worthy and fitting of the breast that had nursed them: they should reject their father's heresy and kiss and embrace the images of the holy icons. At the same time she would put the icons into their hands (she kept them in a little chest) and press them to the girls' faces and lips. So she sanctified them and stirred up their love for the icons. She did this constantly, rekindling her granddaughters' love for the icons, and it did not escape Theophilus. He asked them what their grandmother had given them and what kindness she had shown them. The other girls, being right-minded, deftly slipped his questions, as a wrestler slips out of holds. But Pulcheria, being a baby in years and in mind, told of the kindnesses and of the heaps of fruit. She also counted the veneration of the holy icons among them, thinking and speaking in her childish way: she said she had many "dollies" in the chest, and she put them

on her head and face and kissed them. When these words were reported to the emperor, they drove him to fury. But he was kept from doing anything harsher or more bitter to his mother-in-law by her venerable age and her piety. No less did her outspokenness restrain him. She openly mocked and rebuked him for the daily persecutions of the confessors and for the heresy already mentioned, and she was almost the only one who made plain the hatred everyone felt for him. He only cut back his daughters' visits to her and stopped them from being frequent.

6. Something similar also happened to the empress Theodora. The emperor had a half-witted little fellow, in no way different from Homer's Thersites. His name was Denderis. He uttered gibberish and made people laugh, and he lived in the palace for the sake of amusement. Once he burst into the empress's bedchamber and caught her holding holy icons and earnestly pressing them to her eyes. When the fool saw them, he asked what they were and came closer. She answered in the same rustic way: "My pretty dollies, and I love them very much." The emperor was then dining at table. When the fellow went straight to him, he asked where he had been. Denderis said he had been with "Mama", meaning Theodora, and had seen her take pretty dollies out from under the pillow. The emperor understood. Filled with anger, he rose from the table and went to her, poured insult after insult on her and with unbridled tongue called her an idol-worshipper. He repeated what the fool had said. She calmed his anger for the moment and answered readily: "It is not that, O emperor, not what you have supposed. I was gazing into my mirror with my maidservants, and Denderis saw the figures reflected there, came, and foolishly reported it to my lord the emperor." So for the moment she quenched his anger. As for Denderis, a few days later she [?] him so that he would never speak of the pretty dollies to anyone again. Once, at a drinking party, Theophilus was boasting and gloating over the empress. He asked Denderis about her: was "Mama" again kissing the pretty dollies? Denderis put his right hand to his lips and his left on his backside and replied, "Hush, hush about the dollies, emperor!" So much for that.

7. There was a man who distinguished himself in war. He had a vigorous arm and a clever horse. It happened that the general under whom this soldier served fell in love with the horse, which had saved the man and often rescued him from death. Many times the general asked for it, trying every means and favour (for he promised to give the man a great deal), but his request was refused. The general was [?], and when even so he could not get [?], he struck the man from [?] of his command and spoke

against him at length to Theophilus. So the soldier was left on his own, with the horse as his delight. A good while passed, which [?] summoned the man to war out of rivalry and also wore him down terribly, as tends to happen to the unfortunate. Then, at the time of the man's misfortune, Theophilus began looking for a good horse. So he wrote to all those holding office and rank and ordered them to search out such and such a horse and send it to him. The general seized on this pretext, took the horse from the man against his will, and sent it to the emperor as his own. That was the cause of the horse being lost. Later, in some crisis, the emperor ordered everyone to go out to war, even those who had been discharged for whatever reason. This man went out too, and for lack of a good horse he lost his life, leaving a wife and poor children. What then did the wife do? She heard that the emperor was ready to listen and loved justice. She was burning with love for her husband, and she had no means of providing her children with the necessities of life. So she came to the imperial city. On the day Theophilus usually went to Blachernae, she saw him riding her husband's horse. She fell on her knees, wailing, and begged the emperor while holding the horse's bridle. She told him how the horse was hers, and how no one else but the horse's taker was the cause of her husband's death. The emperor was astonished and amazed at the woman's boldness [?], and he knew nothing of what she was saying. For the moment he ordered that she be kept until he returned to the palace. Hurrying back, he said that the woman should be called, and she appeared at once and explained and related everything clearly. The emperor then ordered the general to come and conducted a vigorous inquiry about the horse. The general insisted that the horse had been sent from his own house and nowhere else, and not taken by force. So the emperor set the woman before him, face to face, to refute his story and accuse him. When the general looked at the woman's face, he could not bring himself to brazen it out with a lie. At once he became a pitiable suppliant and clasped the emperor's feet in tears. What then did the emperor do? He made the woman and her children co-heirs of the general's property, with shares equal to his own children's, and he removed him from his command. His just judgment and his hatred of robbers became plain to all.

8. No less did he show his diligence in devoting himself to building. He rebuilt the lower walls from their foundations, scraping off their old age, as it were, and raising them high and handsomely, and so made them wholly impassable to enemies. To this day they display his name inscribed on them. Not only that, but
[?] were preserved. ⁷ ⁸ ἐκπλαγεὶς B. ⁸ καὶ δὴ] τότε δὴ. ³ τὸν] αὐτὸν. ³ ἐξάρας.

and prostitutes, [?] out of the brothels. He cleansed that whole district and built there a hostel bearing his name. It was the loveliest of buildings and the largest, airy and with fine views, a place where destructive diseases are washed away and saving remedies are gained. That was how he dealt with prostitutes. Yet they say that he was once captivated by the beauty of one of Theodora's maidservants and lay with her, at a time when he was living carelessly. When he realized he had fallen from what was right, Theodora too had found out; she was downcast, neglected her appearance, and went about in gloom. From then on he told her, swearing an oath and lifting his hands to God in awe, that he had truly slipped then and only then, and he begged his wife's forgiveness. In addition, with a lavish hand he raised and built a house and palace for his daughters near the place called ta Karianou. Some remains and mounds of it have preserved their memory down to our own day.

9. Following an old custom, he wished to make the affairs of his reign known to the Hagarenes, either to share his joy with them or rather to appear formidable to them. For this mission he chose John, then synkellos and formerly, as we said earlier, his teacher. He loved this man, who was full of civic refinement, who also stood by him in his heresy, and who was moreover powerful in debate against opponents. He honoured him above everyone around him. For this reason he sent him to the ruler of Syria. He gave him many things for which the empire of the Romans is admired and at which foreign peoples stand in awe, and in addition gold amounting to more than four kentenaria. The other things he sent to the amermoumnes as gifts. The gold was for John to spend on lavish displays of generosity, both for show and to increase his prestige. For if the envoy can scatter gold like sand as he pleases, how much more must the sender be admired for his heaps of wealth! So he also gave him two vessels made of gold and precious stones, which common, impure speech calls chernibóxesta, exalting and adorning his envoy in every way. When John arrived and reached Baghdad, he appeared [?] from his inner intelligence and his prophetic [?] speech, and great from the wealth and dignity that bloomed about him outwardly. He gave no small gifts to those sent to him and to those who visited him, but great ones, fit only for the emperor of the Romans. For this he was admired, and his name became [?]. But first, as soon as he reached the borders of the barbarians, he astonished

everyone. Those who came to meet him to pay their respects and merely asked how the emperor was, he left marvelling at the abundance of his gifts and his gold. Then he approached the Ishmaelite ruler, stood before him face to face and delivered the emperor's message. When he had delivered it, he withdrew to his lodging. Wishing to exalt the cause of the Romans more and more, he would give everyone who came to him, for any reason great or small, a silver vessel filled with gold, out of munificence. Once, while dining with the barbarians, he told his servants to lose one of the two hand-basins mentioned above on purpose; he had brought them for his own use. Over its loss there arose no small uproar. All the barbarians had been struck to the soul by its beauty, its dignity and its magnificence, and they made a great search and inquiry, leaving no stone unturned, as the saying goes, to bring the stolen basin to light. Then he ordered the other one to be thrown out as well, saying, "Let this one go too!" He astonished the Saracens and put an end to their search. The amermoumnes, vying with him in generosity and unwilling to be seen to come second to him, courted him with other gifts. John was not won over by these, but threw them down before him like dust. The ruler also offered him a hundred prisoners, just brought out of prison and dressed in fine clothes, their captive rags taken off. John praised this generous gift highly and welcomed it, but he would by no means accept the prisoners. He said they should stay with the Saracens for the time being, at ease and free, until he could arrange an exchange; then he would hand over other Saracen prisoners to them and receive ours. This astonished the Saracen ruler. He regarded John no longer as a foreigner but as one of his own household. He kept inviting him, showing him his treasures, the beauty of his buildings and his splendour. He was seen to honour him in this way until he sent him back to Constantinople with great magnificence. As soon as John came before Theophilus and told him about Syria, he persuaded him to build the palace of Bryas in imitation of the Saracen palaces. It differed from them in no respect whatever, in design or in decoration. The work was supervised and carried out according to John's description by a man named Patrikes, who held the dignity of patrician. He did only this beyond the Saracen model: in the bedchamber he built a church dedicated to our most holy Lady the Theotokos, and in the forecourt of the palace the triconch church, which was exceedingly beautiful and larger than many others. Its central part was dedicated

to the Archangel, commander of the heavenly host, and the parts on either side to holy women martyrs.

10. In matters like these Theophilus seemed and was considered magnificent and admirable. But toward us, the faithful, who venerate the holy and divine icons, what was he like? Like some savage and harsh barbarian, eager to outdo all who had been cruel in this respect before him. His predecessors were Leo and Michael, his father. Michael decreed that the word "holy" should not be inscribed on any painted icon, wherever icons happened still to be painted, on the ground that it is fitting to inscribe it on no one but God. His mind did not hit the mark. For God has shared with human beings even the title "God", which is loftier, calling them gods not by nature, I mean, whether or not it was he himself who spoke through the prophet. How then would he deprive them of "holy", which is far lower? At any rate, Theophilus said: "One of them decreed this, and the other, Leo, that icons should not even be venerated. But I decree that they should not even be painted or given form at all [?], since a creature bound to the earth ought not to be dazzled by such things, but should look to the truth alone." From then on the divine images were taken down in every church. Wild beasts and birds were put up and painted in their place, exposing his bestial and slavish mind. From then on the sacred treasures were outraged by profane hands and paraded through the marketplace. Some were thrown on the ground and given to the fire, and precious objects that bore the divine images engraved on them were treated as common. From then on the city prisons were full of those who honoured the icons: painters, monks, bishops, shepherds and their flocks. The mountains and caves were full of those put to death like criminals by hunger and thirst, and of no fewer who died under harsh siege. He had just ordered that the cities be kept closed to monks and decreed that they be driven off everywhere as something accursed, so that they did not dare to show themselves even in the countryside. So he openly turned their monasteries and hermitages into graveyards and lodgings for laymen. Some of the monks, refusing to betray virtue and the holy habit, wasted away from hunger and hardship and died. Others could not even face so great a struggle, so they gave up their habits but managed somehow to secure their own salvation. Still others lived more carelessly and embraced a relaxed and dissolute life, neglecting the divine hymns, odes and chants. For the tyrant did not want even these assemblies to be held, which often alone are able to preserve [?]…

…a kind of bridle for those who slide, without restraint, into the passions. 11. Yet boldness of speech and freedom had not vanished from among men altogether. Some of the more fervent, some one at a time and others in groups, such as those who came from the monastery of the Abrahamites, reasoned with him. From what our Fathers, the divine Dionysius, Hierotheus and Irenaeus, had said, they showed that the life and institution of monks had not been devised yesterday or the day before, but was ancient, primordial and dear to mankind. They also showed that the depiction of the divine images went back to the apostles and belonged to their age, since the divine Luke painted the likeness of the Mother of God, and Christ himself, our Master and God, impressed his own likeness on a cloth and left it to us, not made by hands. These most divine men provoked the tyrant's madness and savagery by speaking so boldly. After many other tortures they were driven out of the city and fled to the house of prayer of the Forerunner on the Black Sea, the one called "of Phoberos". There, utterly worn down by the unbearable strokes of the whips, they were found worthy of the lot above. Their holy bodies lay carelessly thrown on the ground for a long time and were not even granted burial, yet they were kept whole and uncorrupted until they became known to the faithful. Then they were buried and honoured as befits those who bore witness for Christ. [P. 61] 12. A certain monk also rivalled these men. He had just risen to the first rank of the priesthood, and in his zeal he resolved to rebuke the tyrant and, if possible, persuade him about the holy icons. He stood before him face to face and went through many arguments, among them the saying of the apostle Paul which declares: "If anyone preaches to you a gospel other than what you received, let him be accursed." The emperor had him beaten many times. Then, since he saw that the monk spoke more wisely and argued more forcefully than he could, he sent him to John, who had been his own tutor and teacher, and ordered John to overthrow him with dialectical proofs. But the noble contender left John too more speechless than a fish, using no sophistic or dialectical proofs, only the words of the apostles and the Gospels. For the time being he got away from there. Later he went to the mountain called Kalon, where he found Ignatius, a God-bearing man, and was granted ordination. He taught Ignatius about events and emperors still to come, lived on until the Christ-loving Leo and his children, and then departed to the Lord.

13. The tyrant resolved that all who painted the divine figures should be removed from among men. If they chose to live, they had to spit on the images, throw them on the ground like profane things and trample them, and so save themselves. He resolved to force the monk Lazarus as well, who was renowned at that time in the art of painting. But he found him stronger than flattery and stronger than his own will, and he was rebuked by him not once or twice but many times. So he tortured him so savagely that at first his flesh flowed away with his blood, and many thought he was no longer alive at all. Then he heard that Lazarus, shut up in prison again and barely recovered, was busy with his art, setting up the likenesses of the saints on panels. He ordered red-hot iron plates to be laid on his palms. The fire ate away his flesh and [?], until at last he gave out and lay half-dead. But grace had to preserve him to be a spark [?] later on. So when the emperor learned that the holy man was breathing his last, he yielded to the pleas of the Augusta and of some others close to him and released him from prison. Lazarus hid himself in the church of the Forerunner called "of Phoberos". [P. 65] There, though his wounds still pained him, he painted an icon of the Forerunner that has survived to our own day and works many cures. That was then. After the tyrant's death, when Orthodoxy shone forth again, he set up with his own hands the image of the God-man Jesus Christ at the Chalke. When the illustrious Theodora asked him to forgive her husband and to pray for forgiveness for him, he said: "God is not so unjust, O empress, as to forget our love and our labours for him and to prefer that man's hatred and boundless madness." But this happened later. 14. Once the emperor summoned the confessor Theophanes and his brother Theodore to the triclinium of the Lausiakos to debate publicly about the faith, since he knew they surpassed most men in learning. "Come now," he said, "you accursed men! Persuaded by which sayings of Scripture, and emboldened by [?], do you worship idols", as he called the holy icons with his godless and foolish tongue, "and assure the many simple folk that it is right to do so?" In a loud voice he added other blasphemous and harsh words against the image of Christ God. The blessed men said: "May the mouth be stopped that speaks lawless words against God!" His insolence was [?], for an unjust emperor cannot bear to be rebuked to his face, and for the time being he played the flatterer [?]…

…and asked for testimonies from the prophets that led to this very point, that the icons should be venerated. The blessed Theophanes cited a passage from the prophecy of Isaiah. Theophilus objected that it did not read that way, and at the same time he unrolled his own book and showed [?] the words. The saint cried out that not only this book but every book that had come into his hands had been falsified by him. He told the emperor to have the book brought that lay in the patriarchal library in the Thomaites, at such and such a place, to confirm what he said. Someone was sent and brought it quicker than words. The emperor deliberately failed to find the passage and, out of shame, unrolled the book at other places. But when the blessed Theophanes showed him, pointing with his finger…

[?] these were seen [?] in the venerable place,
Wicked vessels of superstitious error.
[?] there, having done many shameful and terrible things
Impiously, out of unbelief,
They were driven out from there as apostates.
They fled to the city of the empire,
But did not abandon their lawless follies.
So, branded on the face [?] as criminals,
They are condemned and driven out again.

This was quickly done. The two men put on the crown of confession and martyrdom, while the emperor, haughty and the most wretched of all wretches, was shown to everyone to be a blasphemer and a persecutor, and more heretical than any heretic before him. Besides these, he also shut up in prison Michael, the synkellos of the church of the Holy City, together with many other ascetics, contriving [?] by prolonged ill-treatment. 15. Such were his outrages against the faithful and the saints. In this way he insulted him who for our sake appeared as man while being true God. He also mistreated his holy servants, not for a short or limited time but for his whole life, and subjected them to incurable misfortunes. 16. He composed hymns and set stichera to music, and he urged that they be sung. Among them were the one in the fourth mode, "Bless ye", and, from the one in the eighth mode, "Hear, O daughter" [?]…

…which he rearranged and gave a rhythm to, and he ordered them to be sung in the Church of God in everyone's hearing. There is even a story that this same Theophilus was so smitten with love of the melody, as fathers are with their offspring, that he did not refuse to conduct with his hands in the Great Church at a splendid festival. [P. 67] For this he gave its clergy a hundred pounds [?]. They also say that the sticheron for Palm Sunday, "Go forth, you nations, go forth, you peoples", was the offspring of his soul. 17. By nature he had rather little hair on his head [?]. So he decreed that everywhere hair should be cropped close to the skin and that no Roman should be allowed to wear it below the neck. Anyone caught doing so was to be beaten with many [blows] and brought [?] to virtue [?], for people of old [?] also took pride in that kind of hair. He therefore issued a law that no one at all should dare to let it grow below the nape of the neck.

18. He also had to provide for his own affairs and those of his family and arrange them as he saw fit. At that time he happened to be the father of five daughters but had no male offspring. So he decided that the youngest of them all, Maria, who was truly loved more than the others, should be married. The husband came from the family of the Krenitai, from the land of the Armenians. His name was Alexios and his surname Mousele. He was handsome in appearance and [?] rather tall, and he lived in the area of the acropolis, at the houses called "of the Krenitissa". Because of his affection for his daughter, the emperor first honoured him with the rank of patrician and anthypatos, then proclaimed him magistros, and finally Caesar. Then, since some pressing need had arisen, he gave him a sizeable army and sent him off to Lombardy. Alexios went and handled his business well and as the emperor wished. As a result the emperor's affection for him grew, but men's envy of him grew along with it. Some reviled him and spread slanders against him, saying that he coveted the imperial power and that the "theta" was fated at some time to prevail [?]. When the Caesar Alexios heard the slanders stitched together against him, he wished to guard himself against envy, and he begged the emperor earnestly to take pity on him and allow him to change over to the monastic life. At that time the emperor did not allow it, pleading that his daughter would be left a widow, and the Caesar stayed on in great quiet, occupied with public affairs. Then Theophilus fathered Michael, and his daughter, the Caesar's wife, departed this life. He honoured her so highly that he placed her remains in a silver-plated coffin, and by iambic verses carved on it he granted the privilege of asylum to people convicted on any charges whatever…

…who took refuge there. Alexios, however, secretly changed his way of life [P. 68] and put on the monastic habit. Since the emperor could not persuade him to cast it off again, he reluctantly allowed it, though he heaped many reproaches on him for choosing not to be with him but to live in some out-of-the-way place and corner. He then gave him as a gift the imperial monastery at Chrysopolis, together with the monastery of Byrseus and the one at Elaia. Alexios lived in the one at Chrysopolis. Once, when he needed a walk, he came to the place of Anthemios, which at that time belonged to the imperial mangana estates. Saying that each monastery bears the undying name of those who build it, he chose to buy it by imperial order and make it his own. This was done through the empress Theodora, his mother-in-law. He rebuilt it well and brought it under monastic rule. When he departed this life he was laid to rest there, and his tomb, with his portrait inscribed above it, bears witness to what has been said. His brother Theodosios, who had been enrolled in the rank of patricians, is also laid near him, and left many tokens of his excellent life in the monastery.

19. The Hagarenes were pressing hard, and Ibrahim was campaigning against the Romans with many myriads. Theophilus too, out of love of glory and nobility of spirit, went out to war, with no cowardly or soft thought in his mind. If he felt any fear at all, the experience and courage in war of the men with him turned it aside and drove it far away. These men were called Theophobos and Manuel. Manuel was formidable in courage and known to all the enemy. He was Armenian by birth, had commanded the army of the Anatolikoi under Leo, and under Michael before him had been chief count of the stable; they call this post protostrator. The account will also show where Theophobos came from: how, being descended from the Persians, he became known to the emperor and married his sister. A man of the Persian royal line once came to Constantinople on an embassy. He fathered Theophobos, not from a lawful union but from a secret and clandestine one, and went home. Now among the Persians there is an inviolable law [P. 69] that no one may hold power over them unless he belongs to the royal line. Those of the royal stock, however, had died out through continual wars and through migrating here and there as the Hagarenes drove them. Yet much was said about him among those who remained in Persia: that someone in Byzantium was called Theophobos, for this was the name given him by the father who had begotten him at that time. So the leading men of the Persians decided to send some men secretly to search for the one they sought. They reached our country and at last, with difficulty, found him living with his mother and residing at the Oxeia. Then, since not only from…

…certain resemblances but from the very marks of his soul and body the one they sought was then revealed and recognized, and a neighbour moreover testified to the woman's union with the Persian (for nothing is hidden that will not become known to many), the envoys made themselves known to the emperor and explained the whole story. They promised peace, treaties and the submission of the entire nation if he would not refuse to hand Theophobos over [?] to them. The emperor was delighted at the promises. Finding that the truth was as they said, he had Theophobos lodge and live in the palace and saw to his studies and education. 20. There is also another account of Theophobos, and it is good to give both. It seems to differ a little at the beginning, but in other respects it keeps close to what has been written and matches it. This account says that he did not come of illegitimate seed from an ambassador. Instead, through one of the reversals that happen in war, his father, who was either a king or closely related to the king, fled from Persia and came to the Queen of Cities, where he lived a poor and hard life. There he served a woman who kept a tavern, and eventually, out of love for her and in lawful marriage, he fathered Theophobos. Then the father passed from among men. The Persians learned of Theophobos through astronomy and divination (for they say these sciences still flourish among the Persians) when they inquired whether anyone descended from the royal stock existed anywhere. Once they learned of him, they hurried to Constantinople to search for the one they sought. In this way he was found and became known to the emperor. [P. 70] His appearance and his being alive became known to everyone in Persia through the returning envoys. So it seemed [?] desirable to them to plan a revolt from the Hagarenes and go over to Roman rule, since they had found their leader by birth. 21. It also happened that Babek, the leader of the Persians, had already been in revolt from the amermoumnes for five years and had lifted his heel against him with seven thousand men. [?] Moved by longing for Theophobos and by fear of the Hagarene from whom he had revolted, he came over to Roman territory at the city of Sinope and made himself and the whole nation subject to the emperor. For this reason Theophilus enrolled Theophobos in the rank of patricians and gave him his own sister in marriage. He decreed that each of the Persians should be joined with the Romans and bound to them by intermarriage, and he raised many of them to imperial dignities. He also entered them in the military rolls, established a regiment called the Persian regiment, and ordered them to be counted among the Romans who went out to war…

…against the Hagarenes. 22. Encouraged by these men, and knowing besides that they were brave, Theophilus went out to war against the Hagarenes, since Ibrahim, as has been said, had marched against us. The leader of the Saracens and Theophilus came near each other, and a council was needed. Manuel said it was not right for the emperor of the Romans to fight against an amermoumnes [?], but that someone should take part of the troops and go out to face the enemy, and do so by day. Theophobos wanted the emperor to be in the battle line, but to attack them by night with the Persian infantry and then, when the moment came, to surround them with the cavalry. He did not persuade the emperor, because many said that Theophobos was claiming the Romans' glory for himself and wanted to fight at night for that reason. So it was decided to join battle openly by day. Ibrahim, whether out of plain boastfulness or because fear of the emperor closed in on him, took part of the army and withdrew. But he sent Abouchazar with eighty thousand men to fight the emperor. Both sides fought very bravely for a long time, [P. 71] but in the end the enemy forced the scholae and their domestic to give way and turn to flight. The emperor, with the imperial phalanx and two thousand Persians, Theophobos also among them, took refuge on a hill, fearing for his life. Until evening there was heavy fighting around him. One side hoped to capture him, and the other fought back and held out rather than abandon him. So as soon as night fell, those with the emperor clapped their hands and shouted as if they were rejoicing, and made the air ring with lyres, strings and the blare of trumpets, wishing to rouse no small apprehension in the enemy. And so it turned out: the enemy withdrew six miles, dreading an attack and an encirclement. Having gained a little respite, the emperor's men fled far off by night and secured their safety. They got through safely to the army that had betrayed him and turned its back to the enemy. The emperor heaped much blame on the army that had betrayed him, but he gave Theophobos and his men special favours and honours. As a result the Persians burned with a fiery love for Theophobos. Heartened by an inexpressible joy, they begged to undertake the war against the Hagarenes with him and declared that they would rout them with invincible force. For this reason the emperor wanted Theophobos to be their commander. 23. In the following year he went out again with [?]…

[?] …force, Theophilus also went to the Charsianon, where the Ishmaelites were full of arrogance and boasting after their earlier victory. He engaged them, overcame many of them, took plunder amounting to as many as twenty-five thousand head, and returned to the capital with a brilliant victory. Now it happened that one of the Hagarenes, a man famous for his skill in arms, had been taken prisoner. The domestic of the scholai testified in written commendations to his great prowess in war. He declared that the man was a skilled horseman and of powerful bodily strength, and that he rode against his opponents wielding two spears with great art and skill. So when the domestic's triumph was being celebrated in the Hippodrome, this man walked at the head of it, confirming the reports about him by the size of his body and the loftiness of his spirit. When the emperor saw him, he was perhaps carried away by the praises, and he ordered the man to mount a horse, take two spears and display his skill and prowess to the whole city. This was done, and it delighted the eyes of the less experienced. But Theodore, called Krateros, who shortly afterwards became leader of the band of the holy forty-two martyrs, was standing near the emperor, and he sneered at the Hagarene, saying that he was showing nothing brave or astonishing. The emperor was annoyed at him and said, "And do you yourself have the strength to do anything like this, you effeminate and unmanly [?] fellow?" At once he replied, "I cannot handle two spears, Emperor, since I never learned how, and in war there is no need for such idle display. But with one spear I have firm confidence in God that I will unseat this man and throw him from his horse." The emperor could not bear such boldness, and he swore, calling the oath down upon his own head, that he would put the saint to death unless he really turned his words into deeds. So Theodore mounted a horse, took a spear in his hands, and quicker than it takes to tell, in only a few passes he unseated the Saracen and left him no reason at all to think much of himself. The emperor [?] was ashamed to see the Saracen thrown down by a eunuch, and no man of valor at that. But he was crafty, and he respected the man's virtue, so he spoke to him kindly and presented him with robes and garments out of respect for his way of life. 24. As spring was again beginning and arming warriors against one another, Theophilus gathered a large force and went out against the Saracens. He had released the holy Methodius from prison and was taking him along. He did this not only now and for the first time but always, keeping him somewhere near him. Perhaps it was so that, through the wisdom that dwelt in Methodius, Theophilus could have obscure matters unknown to most people explained and made clear to him, for Theophilus was very inquisitive about hidden things. Or perhaps he was guarding against some uprising [?]

that he might suffer at Methodius's instigation because of his war against the holy and venerable icons. For he seemed to honor the man in no small degree and to revere the excellence and godliness of his life, and for this reason he thought it a dignified thing to take him along rather than leave him behind. When the armies clashed and the Ishmaelites were getting the upper hand, the emperor was surrounded by the enemy and found himself in danger for his life [?]. Then Manuel the stratelates thought it a terrible thing, and worse than terrible, that the emperor should be taken captive. He encouraged those around him, saying, "Men, take shame from the bees, which out of love fly after their king," and he charged [?] like a lion fighting for its cubs, searching for the emperor. He found him exhausted and despairing of safety out of cowardice, though he pretended that he did not want to escape and leave the army behind. "Come, Emperor," Manuel said, "follow me." [?] he broke through the line and slaughtered many. But when Manuel came out and found that the emperor, who was very afraid and terrified, was not following him, he again broke into the line with many men, wanting to rescue him. When he missed him again, a third time, with a still more resolute spirit, he cut through the line that hemmed the emperor in and came near enough to tie the emperor's horse to his own with straps and drag him out once more. The man was wounded in his soul by the fear that the emperor of the Romans would become a captive and a footstool for his enemies. So he turned back more quickly and more skillfully and threatened the emperor with death if he did not follow him. At last, and only barely, he brought him safely out of danger, while a few men behind them fought off the attack, and he restored him to his own people. For this the emperor rewarded him lavishly with honors, showed him favor with fitting gifts, and often called him his benefactor and savior. 25. But envy prevailed against him. The man who had shown such valor against so many tens of thousands and had saved the emperor from his enemies was brought down by a few men of his own side. He was unreasonably accused, out of slander, of treason and conspiracy, and he saw that the envy against him was great. Then he learned through a trusted man, once Manuel's slave but at that time serving Theophilus as cupbearer and attendant by the emperor's favor, that the emperor intended to blind him and take away his eyes. So he dared to defect and went over to the Hagarenes. He was held in high regard among them and honored with great honors. He pressed hard against their neighboring enemies, called the Kormatoi, and won no ordinary victories, since he surpassed many in experience and intelligence. What is beyond words is that he achieved these things with the Roman captives who were held in prisons, giving the Hagarenes a pledge on their behalf that they would not flee [?] … thinking this terrible and beyond terrible [?] …

He is also said to have seized Khorasan and subjected it to the amermoumnes. He did this not only because he surpassed them in bravery but also because he appeared to them in a novel and unfamiliar way: the change of dress and the unexpected change of language drove the enemy to fear. Moreover, he freed the Hagarenes from many savage beasts that were ravaging and harming them. Having become the cause of great benefits to them, he was loved exceptionally by the ruler himself and by his council. 26. When the emperor heard of these things, they made him regret what he had done and caused him much grief, and he decided to leave no stone unturned to recall the man and make him come back.
