Some say that he made a peace agreement with him through the monk Jannes, at the time of the exchange of prisoners, and brought him back to his own country, when he also sent him a chrysobull and oaths guaranteeing his immunity, both through Jannes and through many others before him. Others say it was indeed through Jannes himself, but not through an open meeting and interview. It was rather a secret one, unknown to most. By Theophilus's decision Jannes was removed from among us, disguised, and made to look like the ragged Iberians and monks who travel in humble dress [?] to Jerusalem. He was slipped into the house in Baghdad where Manuel was living and established there, pretending to beg and informing Manuel of the emperor's change of heart. As proof of what he said, he gave him the emperor's encolpion and the chrysobull, which announced his goodwill and a complete amnesty for past wrongs. Manuel took these into his hands, and with his spirit rekindled, as it were, he began to plan his return home. Over time, and through the deeds against the enemy that we have related, the Hagarenes' trust in him did not diminish but grew from day to day. So he informed the amermoumnes that he wished to campaign against the Romans and take revenge on his enemies, the men who had denounced him to the emperor and who had their homes in Cappadocia. He asked the amermoumnes to send his son with him as a further guarantee of the undertaking. The Ishmaelite granted his requests and sent him out against those he wished to attack. When they came near the Roman borders, he revealed his intentions and his return to the Romans to the strategos of Cappadocia. At the same time he instructed him to set an ambush at a certain place, "so that when I arrive there, having persuaded the son to send the Saracen raiding parties off to some other place, I may join the ambush and make my own way back to the Roman lands." And so it happened. As soon as he drew near that place, he embraced the son of the Ishmaelite warmly and said, "Go in good health.

Go, my child, to your father. And know that I am going to no other than my true emperor and lord." Having escaped from there to the capital, he went to the holy church at Blachernai, knowing [?] that Theophilus had no ordinary trust in him. As a result he was honored with the rank of magistros, was from then on called the emperor's co-father, and was promoted to domestic of the scholai. There are some who say that Manuel did flee to the sons of Hagar and did return through Theophilus's efforts, as has been described, but that he did not flee under Theophilus on a charge of treason. Rather, they say he fled under Michael the Stammerer, Theophilus's father, either because of the hatred he bore him or because he feared Michael's old anger. Jannes was ordained bishop of Constantinople on the twenty-first of April, a Sunday, receiving the priesthood as a prize for his impiety and unbelief and for refusing to venerate the holy icons. 27. Theophilus was inquisitive and very eager to know the men who would reign in the future. From certain people he learned of a woman taken from the Hagarenes in these wars who was possessed by a spirit of divination. Theophilus brought her to himself and asked who would be the men whose reign would last a long time. She declared and prophesied that his successors would be his son and his wife, and that afterwards the Martinakioi would hold the empire for a long time. At once he had this Martinakes tonsured as a monk, even though he was in some way related to him, and turned his house into a dwelling for God and monks. That was not all, for the woman also foretold many other future events. She indicated that Jannes would be removed far from the patriarchal throne, and she plainly announced the restoration of the venerable icons. Theophilus was pained in his soul by these predictions and could not shake them off. He kept repeating them constantly to his wife, and he also urged the logothete Theoktistos and bound them both with a multitude of oaths that Jannes should not be sent into exile and that the icons should not receive veneration. So thoroughly did he search out and track down what concerned the empire that, through Jannes, by means of lecanomancy, he clearly saw Basil, who would later take over that rule. Moreover, the woman disclosed to Constantine of the Triphyllios family what would happen to him, when he begged her earnestly and questioned her: that he and his sons would be made to take the clerical habit under Basil, which indeed came to pass. She also foretold that George, who was in charge of the military rolls, would be killed by a sling in the Hippodrome and that his property would be taken into the imperial treasury. These things he saw, as Plato says, [?] … 28. In the following year the Hagarenes and Theophilus went out to war against each other, but they did nothing at all, [?] each other

[?] and returned to their own lands. At the same time the khagan of Khazaria and the bek [?] sent envoys to the emperor Theophilus asking that a fortress called Sarkel be built for them. The name means "White House," and it lies on the river Don, which divides the Pechenegs on one side from the Khazars themselves on the other. Three hundred Khazar soldiers are stationed there, relieved every year. Theophilus was persuaded by their request and entreaty, and he sent the spatharokandidatos Petronas, of the family known as Kamateros, with imperial chelandia and the katepano of Paphlagonia, ordering him to carry out their request. As soon as Petronas reached Cherson, he moored the warships there and left them on shore, put his men on round-hulled merchant ships, and carried them across as far as the Don, where he was to build the city for them. Since there were no suitable stones, he burned lime in kilns from the small pebbles of the river and clay from the ground beneath, and made bricks. With difficulty, but brilliantly thanks to the large workforce, he completed the task assigned to him and returned to the capital. He also gave the emperor his opinion and advice about Cherson, as a man who had gained experience of both the people and the places there: "You will never rule that country and those places completely unless you appoint your own strategos, rather than entrusting yourself to their rulers and leading men." For until then no strategos of ours had ever been sent out to look after their affairs. Instead, the so-called proteuon, together with the fathers of the city, administered everything. On this advice the emperor Theophilus judged that the aforementioned Petronas, and no one else, was experienced with the place. He honored him with the rank of protospatharios and sent him out as strategos, decreeing that the proteuon and the others should obey him without hesitation. From that time down to our own day it has been the rule to appoint strategoi from here to Cherson. This, then, is how Sarkel came to be built and how strategoi began to be sent from here to the Chersonites. 29. Theophilus again went out against the Hagarenes, more vigorously this time, [?] unwilling to fall short of his father's daring. He advanced deeper into Syria, at once ravaging and laying waste the land, plundering it and taking captives. He took two other cities and subdued the country as far as [?], and he besieged and took Sozopetra itself, the homeland of the amermoumnes. On its behalf the amermoumnes tried to persuade Theophilus by letter to withdraw from his homeland, but he found no willing listener. Having settled these matters, Theophilus returned to the capital, after urging Theophobos to set the affairs of the Persians in order and come back to him quickly. But the Persians detained him at Sinope and proclaimed him emperor against his will.

But he, moved by respect and fear toward the emperor, refused, and told them they would suffer terribly for their audacity. They made light of the emperor's threats all the more, held to their purpose, and kept him among them, encouraging him. But Theophobos secretly told the emperor what had happened and assured him on oath that it was not he but they who were responsible for this audacious act. The emperor gladly accepted his intentions, summoned him to the palace and restored his former good fortune. He granted pardon and an amnesty for their wrongs to all the others and made them leave Sinope, or according to others Amastris. Since they had multiplied and grown to as many as thirty thousand, the emperor did not think it advisable for them to remain free and unrestrained. After careful thought he sent two thousand to each theme, to be under the command of those appointed as strategoi, and he also set tourmarchai over them. That is why, down to our own day, the tourmai of the themes in which they were dispersed have borne the name "Persian." This audacious act seemed to Theophilus rather bold and reckless. It led him to have them scattered and distributed, and not long afterwards it cost Theophobos his life. There was also a second cause, which the narrative will reveal in due course. 30. The amermoumnes was so wounded in his soul by the capture and sack of his homeland that he decreed and proclaimed everywhere that men of every age from Babylonia, Phoenicia, Coele Syria, Palestine and lower Libya should assemble and write "Amorion" on their shields, boldly hinting at his coming invasion against it. He gathered his forces at Tarsus, and from small beginnings his army became huge, while his soul burned with fury at the disgrace of his homeland. Theophilus came out to meet him at Dorylaion, which lies about three days' journey from Amorion. Many advised him to move the population of Amorion elsewhere and so escape for the time being the irresistible onslaught of the Saracens, for their army had grown great and kept bringing up endless numbers. But this seemed absurd and unmanly to Theophilus. He thought it good, and the path of courage, rather to fortify the city further and preserve it through the counsels of a noble strategos. This was the patrician Aetios, strategos of the Anatolikon. And since a large force was also needed, Theophilus sent this as well, so that Aetios could resist on every side and defeat the enemy. In addition he gave him as leaders and commanders the men who shortly afterwards would become martyrs: Theodore Krateros, Theophilus and Babutzikos. They became leaders not only of that army but also of the band of the forty-two martyrs. 31. When the leader of the Saracens arrived at Tarsus with his proud spirit and his army, it did not seem good to him, as he consulted the omens and [?] deliberated,

to advance on Amorion at once. Instead he would first test the strength of the Romans through his son, who would take part of the army and march against the emperor. "For if he is victorious," he said, "victory will surely follow for his father too. If not, it is better to keep quiet, since victory is not on my side." So his son took Amer, who was then governing Melitene, and some ten thousand Turks, together with the whole army of the Armenians and the archon of archons, and attacked at Dazimon. Theophilus also marched against him with no mean army, made up of Persians and of troops from the West and from the East. When he reached the place called Anzen, he wanted to see the enemy's assembled forces before engaging. So Manuel, the domestic of the scholai, took him up a hill higher than the surrounding country. Judging by estimate, the number of Saracens seemed somewhat smaller. Manuel, however, did not agree; to him the swarm of spears looked equal. "But, Emperor," he said, "if you want an accurate estimate, look at the forest of spears on both sides." Since it now seemed that the enemy's army was somewhat stronger than their own, they needed to devise a bold plan. This plan, proposed by Manuel and Theophobos, was to attack the enemy by night. But others [?] argued that daytime was better, and the emperor was persuaded by them. When day dawned, a fierce battle took place. The imperial tagmata fought ardently, and the Ishmaelites turned to flight and gave up the fight. But the Turks kept up a steady barrage of arrows and drove back the Romans who were pursuing, and they persuaded the Saracens to stand and not flee. So the Saracens regrouped and, shooting bravely with their bows from a distance, turned the tide of the battle. The Roman army could not get near them, nor even see them from a distance, because they were being shot at so hard. They turned their backs and abandoned the emperor. The commanders of the imperial tagmata, however, along with the Persians, did not dare to do this, or even think of it. They stood around the emperor and tried to save him, while the enemy encircled them on every side and shot at them. They would all have perished had not night fallen and a brief shower of rain come on. The rain slackened the bowstrings with which the enemy were defending themselves and holding the advantage, gave the Romans relief from the arrows, and barely afforded them a chance of escape. 32. When the night was already far advanced and Manuel was busy with the watches, he overheard the body of Persians speaking with the Saracens in their language, negotiating with them somehow [?], and agreeing again

[?] to betray the Roman army and go over to the head from whom they had revolted. He made this known to the emperor in secret, and urged him to save himself with picked men and not wait to be captured. When the emperor asked, "And how will this great host be saved if they stay by me [?]", he said, "Let you alone, Emperor, be saved by God; these men will quickly settle their own affairs." So late in the night, toward dawn, the emperor took flight and escaped safely to Chiliokomon. The generals who had deserted their posts came to meet him and said that they did not deserve to live, having abandoned their emperor in war. At the same time they bared their swords and laid them at his feet, their cheeks wet with tears. But Theophilus, wounded in soul even more than they were by this unexpected turn, said, "If I have been saved by God, you too will be saved if you fight against

33. This stratagem of the enemy, then, and the night-time parley, so to speak, with the Persians, which is as much as to say a truce, became for Theophobos's enemies, who were voting for his death, a second cause and a timely pretext for slander. For the caliph, who had heard of no small victory, it also led to the raid against Amorion. So the two armies were joined at the emperor's native city, the caliph's own and the army of his son that had fought so fiercely before; they threw a palisade around it and began the siege. Meanwhile Theophilus, having withdrawn to Dorylaeum, made an attempt to persuade the caliph with gifts to leave the place and return home. But he was not persuaded, for he nursed in his heart the capture and sack of the emperor's native city. Rather he scorned him, calling him a slave and a coward, sneering at him and mocking him, since he had not been persuaded by him before, but now [?], when he stood on a razor's edge. He also kept the envoys who had been sent somewhere there, as observers and witnesses of what was being done. 34. And indeed, given time, the city would have escaped destruction. The one side brought every form of siege to bear, the other overthrew them, and many men were killed on both sides, both defenders and besiegers, while the Hagarenes remained for the time being unsuccessful and their great arrogance was brought low by the multitude of their men who had been killed. In fact about seventy thousand were found to have fallen when they were counted after the capture. But there was no escaping the sword of God threatened from on high against those by whom the Divine was being insulted as the heresy grew. For this reason a man of the lower ranks (the wretch was called Boiditzes), when they were already about to withdraw and return home in shame, sent letters by arrows, saying, "Why, you men, after enduring so much hardship, are you about to [?], worn out, unsuccessful and [?]? Come then to those towers [?]

where a little ox of stone stands above and a lion of marble outside; and finding me there, for I am on your side and am arranging things for you, and since they are weaker there anyway, there at the battlements you will become masters of what is inside and will reckon me worthy of much." They came as he had said and entered with the assault, striking and wounding those they caught. There was no one who did not die. All were slain and fell, setting rivers of blood flowing. So Amorion was taken and betrayed, more lawlessly than lawless, into lawless hands. Only those survived who were sent on to Baghdad, the magnates and more powerful men serving in the themes, among whom the forty-two martyrs were numbered. All the others became a trophy of the sword of war. For not even so did Theophilus persuade the enemy, though he sent a second embassy, to let him buy back and redeem from the enemy the captive people for two hundred kentenaria, or if not, then at least those who were close to him by kinship and had been sent there to fight as his allies. But, greatly exulting and greatly puffed up, the caliph sent back both the first envoys and these second ones, mocking them and drenching them with insults, and saying, "Do you want to ransom them for only so many kentenaria, when as many as a thousand have been spent [?] for the sake of display and as gifts to you?" Theophilus was stricken to the heart at this, and as though seething with some fire or driven by it, he asked for [?] water brought from snow. When this seemed lukewarm to the burning of his heart, it happened that from that drink he was seized by the disease of dysentery and, against his will, passed out of life through this disease. Such were the events at Amorion.

35. When the Hagarene had returned to his own country, he shut up the commanders we have mentioned in a dark prison, securing them in the stocks, and ordered that they live on a little water and bread. They were kept in such darkness that not even at high noon did they see a glimmer of light; they recognized one another only by their voices, they had the company only of the guards, deprived of all other people, and they lived as if in the deepest desert. They endured these hardships for seven [?] whole years. Then on the fifth of March the man who had betrayed Amorion and denied Christ, Boiditzes [?], came to the prison and called Constantine, a prudent man brought up in wisdom (this Constantine served the patrician as his secretary). "I do not want any of those inside to be with you and hear [?] my secrets," he said. When Constantine assured him that no one was there, he said, "Come, my child [?], dearest of [my] kin [?],

my sweet soul (for you know how my longing for you has been part of me from the start), agree, together with the patrician, to pray with the chief counsellor and to apostatize tomorrow, so that you may not be wasted by the sword and by tortures. Since he is eager and intent on this, I thought it to your advantage to reveal it to you as a faithful friend. [?] Pray with him openly, but in your soul believe in God, who searches out hidden things, and you will not miss his eternal life." The invincible man was neither softened nor deceived by this. "Get away from me," he said, "[?] of lawlessness, get away." And with these words he left, and told the patrician privately nothing plain of what had been said, lest any thought of cowardice be born in him, but only, "A sentence of death has been issued against us for tomorrow." The patrician gave thanks to God for this, and having set his affairs in order, through Constantine he [roused] all who were with him to an all-night singing of hymns.

36. At dawn the ruler came out with an arrogant show of pomp and ordered only the leaders to come out from among the rest. So forty-two men came out, and he at once ordered the prison to be shut. He asked them how many years they had been in prison, and set going other idle talk, wanting to make them submit to his nonsense. But they answered that this was the seventh year, and, having set themselves boldly and with noble souls against his people's arguments from the divine Scripture, they were condemned to the road that leads to death. When they reached the Euphrates, on which their city of Samarra is built, the accursed man tried to shame Theodore Krateros, in the hope that by this at least he might persuade him to refuse death. "Theodore," he said, "how can you hope to go boldly through death to God, when, as you people say, you did not love his saving commandments? Otherwise you would not have left the priestly clergy, in which you were once enrolled, for the dress of a layman, nor would you now have filled your hands, once free of blood, with pollution and defilement again in wars." Without [?] or a moment's delay, Theodore said, "That is why I will not shrink from shedding my own blood, so that he may grant me his kingdom as ransom and [?] for my offenses, just as, if one of your servants ran away and came back again and performed the service you like, he would come into the place of pardon, not of ingratitude [?]." And at once he entered the stadium of the contest like an Olympic victor, and said to the patrician Constantine, driving away what seemed to be cowardice and fear smouldering in him, "Come now, soldier of Christ, since you were allotted to be preferred above all of us before the emperor on earth,

be the first also to [take] the crown of martyrdom." But the holy Constantine said, "Such an honor befits you rather, as one noble and strong; so you will have me following after you, if you first give [yourself] up to death [?]." So, having strengthened one another with words of encouragement, each went in order of his worldly rank to death by martyrdom, while all marvelled at the confident and noble spirit of their contest. But this was later. 37. At that time Emperor Theophilus, unable to bear the defeat and disgrace he had suffered from the Hagarenes, sent the patrician Theodosios, who was called Baboutzikos, to the king of Francia, asking for brave and numerous armies from there. For he judged that his own men were never defeated through weakness of hand or softness of soul, but that they always suffered this through running from battle, which is the same as saying treachery. And he would have put to the test, and come to know, the might and strength of the nations he was summoning (for the king had received the emperor's request for aid with delight), and the unfortunate Theophilus (he got this name from being defeated in war almost every time) would have campaigned against the Hagarenes again, had not Theodosios, whom he had sent, died first. For his death kept that army from coming to the capital, and the dysentery, gaining the upper hand over the emperor, brought him close to death rather than to taking up arms. 38. It is time to bring the affairs of Theophobos into the open and make them clear to all. From the cause already mentioned, the plan to make war on the Hagarenes at night, and also from the secret conversation held at night with the Saracens, as we said, and from other quarters as well, charges of treason sprang up against him and grew, making the man suspect [?] and feared. And since he could not hold out against them, knowing that Theophilus was easily deceived, he took flight to Amastris (this is a city of Pontus), together with children and women and some select men. A fleet was at once launched against him, and a fierce war was prepared as against an open enemy of the emperor; the commander of this fleet was the droungarios of the Watch, called Ooryphas. But Theophobos, taking the fear of God to heart, said that it was not right for a Christian to rejoice in the blood of faithful men. So he yielded to the emperor, lured by oaths, and was brought to him, trusting in the oaths. But Theophilus counted the oaths as nothing, and for the time being put him in a prison under guard at the Boukoleon, ordering that he be guarded. Then one day, when he knew that he himself was already departing this life and breathing his last, he ordered on his own authority that he be beheaded at night, as a kind of [?]

bitter and grievous funeral offering for himself, and that his head be brought to him. When it had been brought as ordered, he took its nose in his own hand and said, "Now neither are you Theophobos, nor am I Theophilus." There are some who attribute Theophobos's death to Ooryphas and not to the emperor, saying that as soon as Theophobos trusted him, he secretly inflicted capital punishment on him by night. From this it has been rumored among the Persians to this day that Theophobos will not see death but lives on in incorruption, because his death took place in secret and not openly. 39. At the same time the Cretans set out with their whole fleet, ravaging the coastland of the Thrakesioi and taking captives. Their daring exploits and stratagems went so far that they attempted not only to overrun the shore, but also to go with drawn sword against those who dwell on the mountain called Latros and embrace the solitary life, and to make everything there easy plunder. But Constantine Kontomytes, who was then administering this theme, when they had gone out onto the mainland, slaughtered them like dolphins and with a brave hand consigned them all to oblivion. And in the fourth [?] year of his reign, in the month of October, in the eighth indiction, the Roman fleet was defeated in a sea battle at the island of Thasos and perished utterly. And thereafter the army of the Ishmaelites did not cease plundering the Cyclades islands, and indeed all the others too. And again in Abasgia, Theophobos and Theodora's brother Bardas, who had been sent with a strong army, met with disaster, and very few returned from there. Droughts too, and again extraordinary winters, and in general irregularities and imbalances in the air, afflicted the earth and those on it; and from these came food shortages and famines and the shaking of the earth by earthquakes, so that there was no time when these did not occur throughout every day of his reign. 40. When he had emptied the whole substance of his body through diarrhea and wasting, so that his soul could no longer stay [in it] but sought to fly away and depart, he feared for his son and his wife. He gathered everyone together in the Magnaura [?], and when he had been lifted from his bed with difficulty and raised up by his attendants, he drew a deep breath with a groan and said, "Another man, [?] in such a disease and [?] the flower of youth, would lament [?] and such great happiness, which the envy that has existed from the beginning, terribly malicious, now eyes with jealousy and is removing me from among men. But I, foreseeing the widowhood of my wife and the misfortune and orphanhood of my son, and besides the loss of servants brought up in good ways and services, and of my senate and council, weep, O [?] [?]

[?], and I mourn that I am leaving you, gentle and mild as you are, for a life I do not know whither I go, and exchanging glory for one in which I do not know at all what will meet me. But remember, for the time being, my tongue, which you will hear no longer, and which at times was bitter for the sake of what was fitting and advantageous; and store up the goodwill toward me after my death and let it pass on to my son and my wife, keeping this above all in mind: as each man behaves toward his neighbor, so will it befall him in the future." As the imperial tongue charmed and soothed everyone with such words, there was no one who was not in tears, nor could one estimate the groaning and [?] that went up from those present.

41. Having lived a little longer, he departed this life on the twentieth of January, after holding power for twelve years and three months. Throughout his whole life he loathed those who held to the orthodox faith, and unsparingly brought every kind of storm upon them at every hour and season. For this reason he carried, like an inheritance, the name "the unfortunate" from everyone, since he never set up a trophy over the enemy that was worthy of an emperor and deserving of praise, nor was he able to make good his earlier defeat, although he waged eighteen wars against the enemy in his whole life, engaged them that many times, and went into battles that were not ignoble. But, leaving him here, having ended his life in this way, we shall move on to his remaining buildings near the palace, which are most noteworthy and deserve to be remembered.

42. As soon as you enter from the church of the Lord, you will find them facing you. For the Karianos, which bears this name because from its steps of Karian stone it has something like a broad river, and which today serves as the wardrobe where the silk robes are stored, is the work of his care. And not only this, but also its neighbor with the gilded roof, the Triconch, which takes its name from its shape: for it rises on three conches, one built on the east, which is supported by four Roman columns, and two transverse ones, I mean on the north and the south. The western part of the hall is held up by two columns and gives exit through three doors. Of these the middle one is made of silver, and those on either side of it of burnished bronze. The exit leads out into the so-called Sigma, which takes its name from its likeness to the letter, and which has a beauty on its walls equal and similar to that of the Triconch; for both this and that are revetted with Lakarian marble of every color. But

this one has a solid and splendid roof, since it rests on fifteen columns of Dokimian stone. Going down by [?] to its foundation, you will find a structure of the same shape and likeness, supported by nineteen columns and with its walkway paved with peperate stone. Near this walkway, somewhat further in and more to the east, the builder raised the Tetraseron, it too divided into three conches after the pattern of the Triconch above it. It took in one conch to the east, and of the other two, one to the west and the other to the south. The northern part, separated off by two columns of genuine peperate stone, contains the Mysterion; so this chamber is named. Like caves, it echoes and sends back the sound unimpaired to those [speaking]: if someone goes up to the wall of the eastern or the western conch and says something in secret and to himself, another person standing diametrically opposite, if he puts his ear to the wall, will hear for himself the voice that spoke in secret. Such is [?]

43. To this hall was attached, and built together with it, the peristyle of the Sigma, which we mentioned earlier. From this an open-air space spreads out, with a bronze basin in the middle whose lip is crowned with silver; having a pine cone of gold [?], it is named the Mystic Basin of the Triconch, taking its name from the Mysterion built nearby and from the triconch hall. Near it also stand steps of white Proconnesian marble, and in the middle of these steps is a marble tribune [?], supported by two slender columns. There, along the side of the Sigma facing its breadth, two bronze lion-mouths were also fixed. These poured out water and filled the whole hollow of the Sigma with the stream, giving no small delight. And at the time of receptions [?] the basin, filled with pistachios and almonds, and pine nuts as well, with spiced wine flowing out of the pine cone, mixed for and offered delight to all of those standing there who wished it: to all of the stage performers without exception, but especially to those who sing with instruments and [?]. On the steps stood the whole deme and the citizen body, together with the regiments from across the water [?], filling up the imperial ranks; in their midst, namely at the marble tribune mentioned above, they had, if they happened to be present, the domestic of the scholae with the exkoubitos and the two demarchs, of the Greens and of the Blues, the demarch of the Blues standing next to the domestic and that of the Greens next to the exkoubitos. But if the domestic and the exkoubitos sometimes happened not to be present, then for the time being the

…having their demarchs. The emperor oversaw all of this, filled with every delight and seated on a jewelled golden throne. As the books of ceremonial and imperial protocol prescribe, he did not rise until he had watched those leaps and civic dances to his heart's content. These things were built for Theophilus in this way and for this purpose. His love for them was so great that he even carried out his usual business and his daily processions in the Triconch itself. Facing its silver doors stands a canopy raised on four columns of Thessalian stone, that is, green stone. Opposite this and in front of it, near the steps already mentioned, on the western side of the Sigma, Theophilus built triclinia attached to it. The lower one is named the Pyxites. The other, the upper one, has no name, and it was allotted as the residence of the imperial clergy. Verses are carved on the side of this Pyxites, the work of an asekretis named Stephen and known as the Capetolite. Others, engraved around the circuit of the Sigma, are by the ecumenical teacher, who was called Ignatius. On the left side, toward the east of the Sigma, another triclinium is attached. It is called the Eros, and it served him as an armoury. So you would see nothing in it but painted shields and weapons of every kind, with the walls decorated with them, as is fitting. These are the buildings one can see erected there from the Triconch itself toward the west. On the eastern side you would see the triclinium called the Pearl. Theophilus built it from the foundations. It supports its roof on eight rose-mottled columns, its walls are decorated with animals of every kind, and its floor is paved entirely with Proconnesian stone and inlaid marble. You would also see its bedchamber. Four Bathyinian columns hold up the gold-studded circle of its ceiling, and four Thessalian columns raise and support its porticoes on the eastern and southern sides. Its walls and floor are splendidly laid like those of the Pearl. Theophilus lived in this bedchamber from the spring equinox to the autumn equinox, and then again [?]. When the winter solstice drew near, he moved to the other bedchamber, by the Carian triclinium, which he also built, because of the stronger and more violent south winds. It can now be seen as the lodging of the papias. No less will you see the sun terrace he built there facing north. From it one could see the old polo ground, which was there at that time, where … [Apparatus: καθ’] μεθ’ P. ἐνεστηκώς] ὃ P. ⁸¹ ἰσημερίας: μετοπωρινῆς P.]

…and the New Church was built, along with the two fountains and the middle garden, the work of Basil, the emperor of blessed memory. These are his buildings on the eastern side. To the south, he first extended the sun terraces themselves, as we said before, and laid out the present gardens. Then he added cubicula: the one called the Kamilas, a second cubiculum next to it, and a third next to that in turn, which is now the Augusta's wardrobe. The Kamilas raises its gold-studded ceiling on six columns of Thessalian stone, that is, green stone. The lower parts of its walls are lined with similar slabs. The upper parts bear figures in gold-gleaming mosaic gathering fruit, and the floor is of Proconnesian stone. Built together with it is a chapel with two sanctuaries, one dedicated to the all-holy Lady, the Theotokos, and the other to the archangel Michael. Beneath it is a mesopaton. Its view looks through a marble lattice toward the Chrysotriklinos, and Constantine Porphyrogenitus, the Christ-loving emperor, set it apart as a library. Its dining room has walls made bright with Bathyinian stones and a floor laid entirely in inlaid marble of various colours. The second cubiculum after the Kamilas has a ceiling like the first and is supported on four Docimian columns. Its floor is paved with Proconnesian stone. As before, the upper part of the walls is entirely adorned with golden mosaic, and the rest is filled with trees and ornaments in green mosaic. The space beneath it, also called the Mesopatos, serves as quarters for the kartzimades entrusted with the women's apartments. The third, after the Kamilas, now serves as the Augusta's wardrobe. Its ceiling is like the others and its floor is paved with white Proconnesian stone. All its walls were adorned with images later, not at that time, by his son Michael. Joined and attached to this is a ground-floor hall whose roof rests on seven Carian columns, five to the south and two to the east. It is enclosed by two walls, adorned with slabs of Roman, Peganousian and Carian marble, and also of green Thessalian river stone. It is called the Musikos because of the precise cutting of its marbles, and for the same reason its smooth floor is fitted together from stones of various shapes and of various beautiful kinds. If you saw it you would say it was a meadow teeming with all kinds of flowers. On its western side a cubiculum is joined to it, alike in every way in the beauty of its marbles. Five Carian columns bear its roof, three to the south and two to the west. Another lies at its foot, divided into two

rooms and adjoining the Augusta's bedchamber. There Leo, the Christ-loving emperor, built a chapel of Saint Anna. Its roof also rises on four Bathyinian columns, its floor is of white Proconnesian stone, and its walls are faced with Bathyinian slabs. This one adjoins the Augusta's bedchamber, as we said. But the one west of the Musikos has a staircase going down into the bedchamber already mentioned, and its entrance is likewise from there. It also leads to the new bedchamber and triclinium that Basil, the emperor of blessed memory, built, and to the portico of the fifth cubiculum, in which Basil, the emperor of blessed memory, founded the chapel of Saint Paul. [The text repeats a line here, garbled: "…and it also leads to the new …" [?]]

44. These, then, are the buildings Theophilus raised in the palace to the north and south. We record them in this history because we do not want his works, whatever they may have been, to be forgotten, so that his disposition in life may be understood. He also adorned the triclinia with golden mosaic, both the one called the Lausiakos and also that of Justinian. He brought a balustrade [?] from the palaces of the usurper Basiliscus and set it around the Lausiakos. He also built another triclinium with four stately and splendid cubicula. Two of these lie toward the mesopaton of the second cubiculum after the Kamilas, with gilded ceilings resting on four arches, toward the Porphyra [?]. The Porphyra is so called because from of old the empress distributed purple there to the noblewomen at the time of the Brumalia. The other two lie toward the Lausiakos and also have a view onto it. He paved their floors with Proconnesian stone and decorated their walls with paint rather than marble, but they were nevertheless destroyed by fire. Thecla, his eldest daughter, built from nothing the very beautiful cubiculum at Blachernae, where the chapel of Thecla the Protomartyr stands. There she ended her life, bedridden.

…he left as guardians and trustees of [?]: Theoctistus the eunuch, who was then keeper of the inkstand and logothete of the drome; the patrician [?], the Augusta's brother; and Manuel the magister, of Armenian descent, who was the empress's uncle on her father's side. Public affairs were thus settled, and for a time matters were well directed. The veneration of the holy icons was also about to be renewed and to return to its ancient honour. Then Manuel was struck by a terrible and grievous illness. Monks of the Stoudios flocked to him, for he had no small faith in them. They promised that he would regain his health easily and quickly if only he himself would embrace the veneration of the holy icons and persuade the rulers to decree it everywhere. Many of the God-bearing Fathers from the other mountains were also dear to him, for he had come to know them when he was strategos of the Armeniakon. They too visited him and urged the same, and they persuaded him at last to think rightly and to promise them what they desired, if only he recovered. And so it happened, through their prayer and earnest pleading with God. Once he was free of the illness, the monks did not let their zeal for the matter slacken. They kept urging him to remember his promises to God, and so they filled him with divine zeal. He shared the plan with his fellow guardians and persuaded them that it would be good to give affairs a right beginning. Having brought them round to his own wishes, he went in to Theodora and discussed the matter with her. She was devoted to God and truly an empress. When she heard about orthodoxy, she said: "I have always longed for this and never stopped thinking about it. But until today the crowd of senators and officials devoted to this heresy has prevented it. So have the metropolitans who champion the Church, and above all the patriarch. My husband had only a small root of this heresy from his parents, but the patriarch made it grow and become firmer through his suggestions and constant exhortations. He drove him to the grievous outrages and tortures that he devised against the saints day after day. That wretch became the trainer and teacher of such evils." They replied: "Then, Lady, since you think this way and plan what is best, what prevents you from putting it into action and ordering this public festival to be carried out?" At once she summoned the droungarios of the Watch, who was Constantine, father of the patrician Thomas who later became logothete of the drome. Through him she informed the patriarch that [?] [Apparatus: ⁸³ ὑποθεῖναι; cf. I 19.]

for unless this happens, you will see neither me following you nor the veneration and dedication of the holy icons, nor even the restoration of the Church."

5. With that she ended her speech. The orthodox Church and its leader Methodius said: "Lady, we cannot deny that what you ask is just. It is right to repay benefactors and rulers generously with fitting favours, when it is not merely a hand that rules [?] but a mind that loves God. But we are not able, as God's justice is, to deliver one who has already passed to another life, for that would be to imagine things beyond us. We are able indeed, since God has entrusted us with the keys of heaven, to open them to all who wish. But we can do so for those still living out this life, before they depart elsewhere, and sometimes also for those who are departing, when their faults are small and repentance was present. Those who have already gone with evil hopes, and whose condemnation is all too plain [?], are a different matter. We cannot cancel their reckoning."

6. Then the empress spoke, whether truly or for some other reason, warmed by love for her husband. We ourselves believe it was the truth. She assured that sacred company on oath that at the time of his departure she had wept bitterly, lamented and bewailed everything. She had described what would follow for them: "we would be hated in so great a city for such a heresy; prayers would be denied us, curses would multiply, the people would rise up." Then repentance for the heresy came over him. "At once he asked for [?] the icons and kissed them with a fervent soul as I placed them in his hands, and he gave up his spirit to the angels who were leading him away." They heard what she said and respected the Augusta's character, for she loved Christ if anyone ever did. At the same time they wanted the holy icons to be honoured. So by common vote and judgment they declared that, if things were as she said, he would find pardon with God for this sin, and they at once gave the empress a written guarantee of this. On these terms, having received [?] and having given the most holy Methodius the honour of the high priesthood, on the first Sunday of the holy Fast they held an all-night hymn service with the empress herself in the sacred shrine of our all-holy Lady, the Theotokos, at Blachernae. At dawn they went in procession with a litany to the great shrine of God's Word. The Church took back its adornment once more, and the holy mysteries were celebrated in purity. So the orthodox Church advanced. [Apparatus, largely illegible: ⁸⁵ … οἱ τῆς Θεοῦ δίκης margin … [?]]

…like an eagle, in the words of Scripture. All the heretics throughout the world under the sun were deposed, and their chief priest as well. This was John, whom the pious called Jannes because of his impiety. He was no incomer or foreigner but a native, an offspring of this queen of cities, for we have heard that a bramble can grow even in a vine. Nor was he from an obscure family. He came from a very noble line, the one called the Morocharzamioi.

7. To set out his story as well: he had long been hegoumen of the monastery of the martyrs Sergius and Bacchus in the quarter of Hormisdas, and he was counted among the imperial clergy. Michael the Stammerer held him in exceptional favour, either simply because he shared his heresy or because he had earned some reputation for outstanding learning. In any case, he was favoured and was appointed tutor to Theophilus. When Theophilus took the reins of empire, he first honoured him as synkellos and later made him patriarch of Constantinople, because John told him things in advance through bowl divination and sorcery. The sorcery went like this. Once a faithless and cruel nation, led by three commanders, was overrunning and plundering Roman territory. Naturally Theophilus and all his subjects were despondent. John advised him to put away his despondency and be filled with confidence and joy, if only he would follow his advice. His advice was this. Among the bronze statues set up on the euripus of the Hippodrome, there was said to be a statue with three heads, which through a kind of talismanic correspondence he linked to the leaders of the nation. So he ordered huge iron hammers to be made, as many as there were heads, and put into the hands of three men of outstanding strength. At a certain hour of the night they were to stand close to the statue, holding the hammers raised. When he gave the order, they were to bring them down all together with overwhelming force, so as to cut off the heads with a single stroke and blow. Theophilus was delighted and amazed by these words and ordered the plan carried out. So, deep in the night, they were there: the men holding the hammers, and John hiding himself in lay clothing so that he would not be recognized. Muttering the talismanic words to himself, John transferred the power of the leaders into the statue, or rather cast down, by the power of the [?] words, the power that had been in the statue before. Then he ordered each man to strike vigorously and hard. Two of them struck very powerful blows and cut off two of the statue's heads. But the third, striking more weakly [?]… [Apparatus: καὶ] μετὰ τ … ⁸⁸ κελεύσαιεν P.]

…[?] he made the blow [lighter?], so that it only bent the head a little and did not cut it clean off the body. What happened to the leaders followed from this. A fierce quarrel broke out among them, and civil strife, and two of the leaders fell at the hands of the third and were beheaded. Only the third was saved, and he did not come through unharmed. So the nation was brought to nothing and set off again for its own lands in flight and disaster. But that is enough about the sorcery.

8. This sorcerer had a brother in the flesh named Arsaber, who held the rank of patrician, an honour given him by Theophilus. He owned a suburban estate on the left as one sails out into the Euxine, at the monastery of Saint Phocas [?]. It had very large buildings, costly porticoes, a bath, and cisterns as well. The patriarch often stayed there, and he is said to have built an underground dwelling there like the cave of Trophonius. Behind the door, as it opened, there was a small gate close at hand that led anyone who wished down a good many steps to it. That was his wicked workshop. There, at some times, women were kept for him as chamber-companions, nuns and other women whose beauty was still unspoiled, and he debauched himself with them. At other times divinations were performed there by inspecting livers, by gazing into basins, by sorcery and by calling up the dead, and he used these women as his partners and helpers. As a result he often managed, with the help of demons, to foretell things that came true, not only to Theophilus but also to others who thought as he did. Long afterwards his brother sold this foul dwelling to Basil, who was then parakoimomenos, and it was turned into a holy monastery. This happened not only to that building but to the rest of the property, since it belonged to him, and the monastery of the holy great martyr was rebuilt from its foundations.

9. At that time, as has been said, he and his whole band had been deposed, but they did not try to pass their lives quietly. They went on behaving insolently against the holy icons. After his deposition he was exiled to a monastery. There an icon was painted on the ceiling, and it seemed to gaze steadily at him. He could not bear to see it looking down on him, so he ordered a servant to deface it and gouge out its eyes, saying only, "I cannot bear to look at its form." The empress heard of this, and he was given the punishment and correction he deserved with the lash.

10. Even so he was not content to love quiet. They tried to fasten a charge on Methodius, who is among the saints, a charge of seducing a woman who had an only son. (This was Metrophanes, who not long afterwards became the head of the church of Smyrna.) They bought her with plenty of gold and also promised her more if only she would agree with them, and they brought many accusations to the empress and to her son's guardians. At once a tribunal and court full of dread was convened, made up of civil officials

Michael, son of Theophilus.

…and churchmen. None of the pious was absent, none of the impious, none of those who had taken up the monastic life, nor anyone else who could hear or speak. Some were drawn there by a kind of shame, downcast at how strange the slander was. Others were drawn by the pleasure of applauding and gloating, out of their lack of self-control. The accusers were brought forward, and the woman with them as proof of what was being said. But as soon as the woman was presented, he did not hold back in the least. He asked her in the hearing of all, "How are you, lady?" (for he had known her for a long time because of her virtue), and how this person and that person were, asking about her husband and her relatives. That was how artless he was. His accusers grew all the bolder and exulted with pleasure. They pressed the charge further and thought that they had now given clear proof. When at last he understood what the charge was, he burned with zeal, so that the cause of the Church and of Christ would not be put at risk on his account. He judged that there is one time for modesty and another for reserve and dignity. So he rose a little from his throne, gathered up his robe [?], and showed his private parts [?] bare. They had withered by a miracle and not by any human means, and as he showed them he told the story of the miracle. Long before, when he was in elder Rome and his passions were still vigorous and at their height, a desire burned in him more fiercely than any ordinary surge of passion. He was in danger and unable to overcome it, so he stretched out his hands toward the church of Peter, the chief of the apostles, and begged persistently for some help and aid. Late at night, worn out by his prayer, he lay down to sleep, and the apostle appeared to him. Peter touched that part, quenched the surges of passion, and said only this: "You are now set free from the domination of the passions, Methodius." With this he convinced that great assembly and covered the enemies of the truth with shame. The magistros Manuel, however, did not think the accusations should be dismissed on these grounds alone. He threatened the woman that he would surely take her life unless she told the whole truth. At once she exposed the whole plot and made it plain. She said that she had been bought for such and such an amount of gold, and "It is still in one of my chests, just as it was given to me, sealed and kept under their seal." They sent at once and found the gold in the chest, as the woman had said, and brought it in. Through the patriarch's compassion and his pleading with the rulers, the accusers received pardon, not the punishments and tortures they deserved. Their only penalty and punishment was that every year, at the feast of Orthodoxy, they had to walk with torches from the venerable shrine of the Mother of God at Blachernae to the divine and renowned church of Wisdom, and hear with their own ears the anathema due to them for their hatred of the holy icons. This was observed for a long time and was kept up until the end of their lives. And this heresy, which had grown to a great extent, [?]

…had such an end from God. The divine images of the holy icons were restored. We do not worship them as divine or depict them as gods. Rather, they relatively and reverently carry our honour through themselves to their prototypes.

11. While celebrating this feast, Theodora once held a banquet at her own expense for the whole body of the Church together, in the palace of Karianos, which, as we said earlier, Theophilus built for his daughters. Every priest and confessor was there. Among them were Theophanes of Smyrna and his brother Theodore. When the banquet was past its height and the sweetmeats and cakes had been set out, the empress kept gazing at the letters on the Fathers' foreheads, reading them and sighing. Somehow, as if by agreement, the two of them looked back at her and saw her gazing at them. So they asked, "Lady, what is the reason you look at us so intently?" She said she marvelled, from the letters, at their endurance, and at the cruelty of the man who had done this to them. The blessed Theophanes was not at all cautious and gave no thought to the assurances given earlier. "For this writing," he said, "I will bring a very clear case against your husband, the emperor, before God's impartial tribunal." This grieved the empress deeply, and in tears she said, "Is this your promise, and your written declarations that you had not only forgiven him but would also [?]…?" "No," said the patriarch, rising at once together with the rest of the priests, "no. What we have promised will certainly hold firm, and the rashness of these men counts for nothing." In this way the matter was silenced, and the customs of the Church [?]

12. Another heresy also appeared, the so-called heresy of the Zelikes, together with its leader [?], named Zelix, who held the rank of first among the asekretai. It was healed and brought over to true religion in an imperial procession. Those who belonged to it were judged to need only the chrism. They were given new baptismal robes and garments and received into full membership with great splendour.

13. The ruler of Bulgaria (this was Bogoris) grew bolder when he heard that a woman held the empire. So he sent envoys to her, saying that he would break the treaties and march against the land of the Romans. She, however, had nothing womanly or unmanly in her thinking, and sent him this message: "You will find me campaigning against you too. I hope to defeat you. But if not, and you defeat me and so get the better of me,
…the victory will be plain for all to see: it was [?] a woman you beat, and not a man." For this reason he stayed quiet and dared no reckless act, and he renewed the bonds of friendship [?]

14. Theodora made a search and a long inquiry, whether because of certain dreams and a vision or for some other reason, about a monk named Theodore, surnamed Kouphares, who had been taken captive long before. She approached the ruler of Bulgaria about him and asked him by letter to search for the man and ransom him for her at whatever price he wished. He in turn took this as an opportunity to make a request about his own sister, who had at some time been [captured?] by the Romans and was now held in the emperor's [palace?]. She had been brought over to the faith and taught letters during her captivity, and she greatly admired the order of the Christians and their reverence and [?] toward the divine, as is fitting. When she was allowed to return to her brother, she never stopped extolling the faith, urging him on and sowing the seeds of faith in him. He had been taught a little by the Kouphares mentioned above and instructed in the mysteries. So he sent Kouphares back and received his own sister in exchange. Yet he remained what he had been, held fast by unbelief and honouring his own religion. Then a plague sent by God struck him. It was a famine, since the coarser and more earthly kind of people are, it seems, more readily taught a different lesson in this way. It besieged and wasted his land. This forced him to call for protection from these evils on the God whom Theodore and his own sister had often praised and worshipped, as was natural. When they were delivered from these evils, he turned to true religion. He was found worthy of the bath of rebirth and was named Michael, after the emperor, by the archbishop sent to him from the queen of cities.

15. They say something like the following also happened. The ruler Bogoris had a fierce passion for hunting, and he wished to have hunting scenes painted in one of his houses, where he constantly spent time, so that he could enjoy this delight of the eyes by night and by day. When this desire came over him, he sent for one of our Roman painters, a monk named Methodius. As the man stood before him, by some divine providence Bogoris did not order him to paint the slaughter of men in war, or of [?] and wild beasts. He told him to paint whatever he wished, saying only that he wanted those who saw it to be struck with fear by the sight and at the same time moved to [amazement?] by the painting. The painter knew of nothing else that could inspire fear except the second coming of God,

…so he painted that there. On one side the righteous were receiving the prizes for their labours. On the other the sinners were reaping the fruits of the lives they had led and were being violently driven off and sent away to the punishment threatened against them. When the painting was finished and Bogoris saw it, the fear of God was conceived in him through these images. He was instructed in our divine mysteries and received divine baptism in the dead of night. When this became known, his whole nation rose up against him. With only a few men he defeated them, carrying the image of the divine cross in his bosom. He made the rest of them Christians, no longer in secret but openly in every respect, and they themselves were willing. After his conversion to true religion, he wrote to the empress about land, since he was hard pressed by the size of his people. He asked her rather freely, since they were now one and no longer two, bound together by faith and unbreakable friendship. He promised to submit himself and to make a peace that would be everlasting and would never fail. She received his request kindly and gave him the land, deserted at that time, from Sidera, which was then the border between the Romans and the Bulgarians, as far as Debeltos, which they call Zagora. In this way all Bulgaria was transformed and brought to true religion, since God called them to knowledge of himself. So from small sparks and blows [?], they were granted the land of the Romans as a kind of second promised land, and they bound themselves to an unbreakable communion.

16. Affairs in the West, then, stood splendidly and were talked of everywhere. She was delighted at this and was eager to set up even greater trophies. So she tried to bring the Paulicians in the East over to true religion as she wished, or else to wipe them out and remove them from among men. This filled our land with many evils. She sent some of those in authority (those sent were said to be the son of Argyros, the son of Doux, and Soudales), and they hung some on the stake, put others to the sword, and gave others to the depths of the sea. The people who perished in this way were counted at about a hundred thousand, and their property was carried off and brought into the imperial treasury. Now the strategos of the Anatolikon theme (this was Theodotos Melissenos) had a man on his staff named Karbeas, who held the office of protomandator. He boasted and took pride in the faith of these Paulicians. When he heard that his own father had been hung on the stake, he thought it beyond all horror. He put his affairs in order and fled, with five thousand others who shared this heresy, to the emir who ruled Melitene at that time, and from there they went on to the caliph. They were received with great honour, and they gave and received pledges of security in turn.

Not long afterwards they went out against the land of the Romans to win trophies. Since they had grown into a great multitude, they set about founding cities for themselves: one called Argaous and another, Amara. Then many more who were caught up in the same wickedness flowed in, and they began to found yet another city, which they named Tephrike. They set out from these cities, and many joined together: the emir of Melitene, whom most people called Ambros, garbling the letters of his name somehow; Ali of Tarsus; and this wretched Karbeas as well. They never stopped ravaging the land of the Romans. But Ali was sent to rule a certain region of the Armenians and lost his life there sooner than he wished, together with his ill-fated army. Amer, out of rivalry, fell into civil war with his co-ruler, who was called Skleros, and was being worn down, and thought that he should fight Skleros rather than anyone else. Their strife grew so great, and they campaigned against each other so much, that their strength fell from about fifty thousand and a little more to barely ten thousand. When he had got the better of his enemies, he was again led on by his own boldness and decided to take up arms against the Romans, joining forces with Karbeas. Petronas marched out against them. At that time he was in charge of the office of domestic. In name it had been given to Bardas to hold, but since Bardas was obliged to devote himself to his duties as guardian, he asked his brother, who was strategos of the Thrakesians, to hold and manage it in practice.

17. The emperor Michael too had just passed the age of boyhood and was hastening toward manhood, and he wanted to charge out against the Ishmaelites and march against them, and he always had this desire. But while planning this, he somehow decided to begin with domestic affairs first, which he ought not to have done. This did not come from himself or from his own idea, but from the judgement and advice of his guardian Bardas. The history will show how and why this happened. For the body of history is truly somehow mute and empty when it is deprived of the causes of events. Where time has kept us from finding out the facts properly, lovers of learning will surely forgive those who want to write what is true and not what is invented, for whom this difficulty is no small matter. But where the cause is known, it must be shown and made clear to readers, since their benefit comes from this and from nothing else.

18. A desire for the throne arose in this Bardas, and no mean one. It was not a desire like other men's, which grows at one moment and at another is cut short by the promptings of reason. It was hard to resist and hard to change. Or rather, to take the story further back, a disagreement arose between Manuel and Theoctistus [?]. Both of them were guardians and lived [?]

…in the palace. The disagreement even led to charges of treason, and things were soon being whispered against Manuel in secret. Manuel feared this. He saw that the envy against him was invincible and hard to fight, and he thought he should cut it off and put an end to it, if only he got further away from the palace. So he went down to his house by the cistern of Aspar. He later turned it into a monastery, and his remains were laid there. He came in from there each time to share in the business of the palace. Bardas had thus shaken him off, not by himself but through Theoctistus, or, so to speak, had unloaded him. Now that fortune had become his partner in what he was striving for, he planned to accomplish the whole thing no longer through another but by himself. First he would bring down Theoctistus, so that he would not have him as an obstacle to his advance. At the same time he would brush off and get rid of the great reproach about his daughter-in-law, for Theoctistus reproached him about it constantly.

19. The emperor Michael had a tutor who was ill-bred and far from having noble manners. The emperor asked Theoctistus and his mother to raise this man above the imperial dignities and award him greater honour. Theoctistus would not agree to this. He did not want to indulge the emperor's whims, and said that the affairs of the empire had to be managed worthily and not unworthily. Bardas took this tutor as his wicked tool and never stopped sowing tares about the man in the tutor's soul and in the emperor's. Among many other things, he said this about the public administration: "It is not being well managed. What is more, the empire was left to you as an inheritance, yet this man is putting it out of your reach. He is planning a marriage with your mother or one of her daughters, and to put out the eyes [?] of you, her son." He drove these words like arrows into the emperor's heart and stirred him up, and he said that wise and very swift counsel was needed to stop these things from happening. They met many times about this matter, and they agreed on one decision and declared it: Theoctistus was to be removed by assassination or by exile. This was settled, and he hurried to carry out what they had resolved. The plan was this. When Theoctistus was about to go out to the Lausiakos after handling the petitions, the emperor would follow a little behind and simply shout to the praepositi, "Seize him!" At that time Bardas was sitting in the Lausiakos. As Theoctistus came out, he saw Michael's signal running ahead and getting there before him, and he decided to save himself by flight. He fled toward the Hippodrome, by the offices of the asekretai, since the lodging of the asekretai was there at that time. But he was one man seized by many, and he was forced to stay instead of fleeing; and

…Bardas drew his sword with his own hand and threatened to fend off anyone who might try to stop him, [?] toward the murder of those under someone's hand. But no one dared to touch Theoktistos at that moment. Instead he was led off to the Skyla, to be held in custody for the time being until they should pronounce on his case. But they resolved that he must not live, both for fear of the Augusta and so that he would not be released too quickly. So they sent one of the Hetaireia against him, brandishing a bare sword. When Theoktistos saw the man coming at him sword in hand, he crept under the bench, hoping to escape his grip. But before he knew it he was struck in the belly and given over to death, and his entrails poured out. It was then that Manuel, as though seized by prophetic frenzy, is said to have told Bardas plainly: "You bared your sword against Theoktistos alone, but you bow your own neck to slaughter every day." 20. So Theoktistos met the end of his life in this way. After his murder Bardas took over the charge and the dignity of the kanikleios. When Theodora learned of these things, she came running [?], weeping and lamenting loudly, and filled the palace with her wailing. She called down curses on both of them, saying: "O shameless and utterly foul beasts! You, ungrateful offspring, why have you repaid your second father with evil for good? And you, envious and wicked demon", and here she addressed her brother in tragic lament, "[why have you defiled?] my reign, which was kept pure and unstained? There is a God who watches over such outrages, and he will surely deliver you both to no other death than one like this, a murderous one." At the same time she spread out her hands and spoke almost like a prophet: "May I see it fall upon them, Lord, may I see the vengeance for this man!" From then on they could not bear her constant curses and reproaches, and Bardas was also pressing on along the road toward his own goal. So they resolved to push her out of the palace as well, and from then on to proceed openly to whatever they saw fit. She detected this, for she was able to see and to guess what was coming, but she did not think she ought to resist, since she wished to avoid the murder of men and harm to her own people. The wealth, however, that had been stored up until then, which is still treasured in the palace today [?], she decided to make known to the senate, both to restrain her son from unsparing expense and to proclaim her own virtue. Standing where all could hear, she cried out that one thousand and ninety centenaria of gold were laid up in the imperial treasury, and about three [?] of silver. Part of this, she said, her husband had amassed and procured, and the rest she herself had kept from being spent, since she had no love for squandering and luxury. 21. Yet great as the imperial treasure was, it came to absolutely nothing through Michael's folly and ill-timed lavishness. He delighted in horse races if anyone ever did, and he did not even refuse to drive a chariot himself (oh, how humbled the empire of the

Romans was at that time!). He sponsored at holy baptism the children of those who played and drove chariots with him, and so emptied the imperial wealth, granting each of them fifty, or forty, or at the very least thirty pounds of gold. Once there was a certain patrician called Himerios the Pig, so named because of the wildness of his face. He used to talk obscenely at table, and he let loose a noise from his profane belly right in the face of the emperor and his fellow diners, so loud that the blast put out the lamp that lit them. For the marvel of such a wonder Michael gave him a hundred pounds of gold. On another occasion he received from the holy font the son of Cheilas, who drove chariots with him, and likewise gave him a hundred pounds of gold. In this way he spent the public funds on nothing that was needed. Being a terrible lover of horse racing, he squandered that great wealth in a short time on such theatrical and lawless pursuits. Then the time came for the distribution of the imperial donatives, and there was no money with which to reward the armies that hold off the enemy's battle lines. So he melted down that golden and much-celebrated plane tree, the two golden lions, the two griffins of solid hammered gold, the organ of solid gold, and other works of the imperial display as well, weighing no less than two hundred centenaria, and gave them to the imperial treasury to be struck into coin. Toward the end, for lack of money, he also handed over to be coined certain imperial and Augustal robes, and robes of the senate too, some of solid gold and some woven with gold, which were kept in the eidikon. But before they could be melted down he departed from among men. Basil of blessed memory, when he took the empire, found them still undamaged and recovered them, and ordered what is now called the senzaton [?] to be struck. Of all that great wealth he found nothing else but three centenaria of gold and nine sacks of miliaresia. [?] He made this public and showed it to all, and lamented before the senate the means with which he would have to administer the state. 22. But these things happened as time went on. At that time Theodora was in the habit of visiting the holy church at Blachernae quite often, both to offer prayers to God and to use the bath. Once, when she arrived there late, Michael and Bardas sent Petronas, her brother, and had her tonsured together with her daughters. For the time being they confined them in the palace of Karianos. Later, sending not once but [?] times, they took away the wealth the women had and let them live in a common, private manner, not as royalty. Theodora departed from this life not long after, and [?] Basil of blessed memory sent her body and her daughters

to their grandmother's monastery, which is called Ta Gastria, to live there and spend their lives in holiness. So she [?], leaving her son a name that was not wicked, as those others did, but good and venerable. The book before this one has shown where and from whom she sprang, how she came to the palace, and how many daughters were born of her womb. This book will show the rest of her kin. There were, then, two brothers on the male side: Petronas, at that time general of the Thrakesion and a patrician, and Bardas, already mentioned. Bardas had once been caught by Theophilos in some improper act, and while the customary procession was held up he was flogged at the Horologion with sixty lashes. There were three sisters: one bearing the auspicious name Kalomaria, then Sophia and Irene. Sophia was given in marriage to Constantine Babutzikos, Kalomaria to Arsaber, then a patrician and later a magistros, [and Irene] to the brother of Irene, the mother of Photios, who afterwards took over the patriarchal throne. With him she bore two sons, Stephen the magistros and his brother Bardas, also a magistros, [father?] of the patrician Constantine, general of Sicily and son-in-law of Kontomytes (it was from him that he too received the surname Kontomytes). Through them she kept up her kinship with the patriarch Photios, for both these magistroi were his first cousins. This mother of the men just named, when she lost her first husband by death, did not choose to take a second and live in vain [?]. She lived as a widow with her sister in the palace, dressed in a squalid and humble garment. Moreover [?], taking the eparch by the hand, and bringing along not only the teichiotes but also the [count?] of the Noumera, at every new moon she walked on foot through the Scholai to those held in the prisons of the Chalke, the Praetorium and the Noumera. She [asked?] why each had been locked up, and [freed?] some by appealing to her sister, and she supplied each of the prisoners with a gift and with alms that were not small. So much for affairs in the women's quarters. 23. Bardas was the sole guardian and administrator of the empire, and was loved above all others as a relative of the emperor. For this reason he received the dignity of kouropalates, as a sort of prize for the affair of his sister. As has been said, he campaigned with Michael against the Ishmaelites and Amer, Michael having just passed from beardless youth to manhood in strength of body and hand. When they [invaded] the enemy's land, they came to a city called Samosata, which was heavy with power and strength, and tried to besiege it. But without realizing it they were raising their hand not against Theodora but against wily men. It was the third day of their siege, the first and lordly day of the week, and they were about to celebrate the bloodless mystery so that they might

partake of the holy mysteries. Suddenly, whether because they were celebrating them without posting a guard, or because in their inexperience they held the city in contempt, as though no one would dare raise a hand against the emperor of the Romans, at the very hour when they were about to partake of the divine mysteries, the enemy sprang out of the city on every side with their weapons. There was not a Roman to be seen who was not running away. Michael himself was seen barely managing to mount his horse and fleeing, not fighting in front. He escaped only with great difficulty, leaving behind his very tents and all the attendants who were with them. They say that the Karbeas mentioned earlier, the one who built Tephrike, distinguished himself there. He wrought great slaughter not only among the common people, but also took alive some of the great generals: the [?] tzangotoubos Abessalom, the palatinos, and other lieutenant generals and tourmarchs, up to a hundred of them. After the fighting had passed, these generals were kept in custody. They sent home for money and gave Karbeas a considerable sum, asking to be ransomed. When Karbeas had it in hand, he at once asked Seon whether he felt erotic desire for sexual pleasure and whether his body was subject to passionate stirrings. Seon said no and denied experiencing anything of the kind. Then Karbeas asked Abessalom the same thing. Abessalom saw through his wickedness and depravity, or perhaps he was telling the truth, and said that he did experience this and was subject to such stirrings. To him Karbeas said, "You are ransomed from your bonds," and released him at once. But to Seon he said, "God does not wish you to be released from custody," and at the same time he gave him back the ransom that had been paid for him and shut him up in prison until he breathed his last. 24. When a second year had now passed and Michael heard that thirty thousand men were marching against the Romans, he wanted to make up for his defeat. He gathered Thracians and Macedonians, up to forty thousand of them, and eagerly set out against Amer. He encamped on a grassy plain called Kelarion. Just then Amer, outgeneraling him, left the beaten road and went farther on, hurrying toward Chonarion. Meanwhile he drew closer, came to grips and joined battle, and forced the emperor to flee headlong instead of standing his ground. The emperor tried to flee while his horses were still at full speed, but supposed he was not being cut off [?]. It was high noon, and the blazing sun was causing no little [heat?]. They were forced to climb a mountainous place called Anzes, hard to reach and difficult to cross because of its rough stones. There the emperor, in his flight, made camp. Amer followed close on his heels and surrounded him, wanting to take him as if in a net. He would have taken him captive by the spear, but the strength of the imperial tagmata, fighting back stoutly, and the steep, high ground of the place saved them for a while. There, as

they struggled in danger of their lives and were afraid, Michael pressed Manuel to tell him a [plan?] that would save them both. Manuel advised the emperor to take off whatever still made him recognizable as emperor and to put on ordinary dress. Then, with picked men of outstanding strength, he should break through the enemy phalanx and get clear of them openly [?]. Michael asked again how the crowd and the army that remained might be saved. Manuel said, "May you, emperor, be kept safe and unharmed. God will take care of them. It is not the same thing for an emperor to become a captive of the enemy as for any ordinary Roman." So the emperor changed his clothes, kept close to Manuel, and hurried to follow him as he and others broke through the phalanx. But when they reached the point of danger, near the enemy's line, fear robbed the emperor of strength and nerve, and he chose to stay behind rather than run ahead. Manuel cut through the phalanx and came out safe, but could not see the emperor, so he ran back again, fearing that the emperor was in danger.
