When there were further clashes and many Saracens were slain, Amer decided to move farther off in search of water and fodder, and sounded a recall. Then Michael, given a respite, barely got away from there in safety and returned to the capital. 25. Barely had a second year passed when Amer campaigned again with forty thousand troops. With no one to stop him, he plundered and enslaved both the Armeniakon and Amisos by the sea. It was then that he is said to have behaved just like that foolish Xerxes and ordered the sea to be beaten with rods, because it did not lie farther off, but caught him close at hand as he plundered and so held him back. The emperor [?], vexed and distressed at this, ordered Petronas, the empress's brother, who held command of the Thrakesioi, to take the Roman forces with all his strength and march against Amer, and not to let him go on plundering the land of the Romans much longer. At that time the son of Bardas, named Antigonus, commanded one of the imperial tagmata, the Scholai, though he was still a mere boy of about nine or ten. This amazes me: how Bardas, who laid claim to shrewdness and wisdom, as they say, and who swallowed up and took over everything for himself, did not entrust such a command to someone else at a dangerous and difficult time. In the meantime, however, he gave his brother the semblance of that command. When Petronas heard the imperial letters arming him against the enemy and urging him to act bravely, he was shaken. Deliberating how matters might turn out well, he stayed at the Holy Mountain near Ephesus, either to excuse himself or to beg for help from above. While he was staying there, a report ran ahead like a messenger

and announced that the famous monk John was coming of his own accord. He was a tall man who always went barefoot and lived on Latros. That age admired him for his life of stillness, since he never left his cell. When the patrician heard that the man was somewhere nearby, riding a little donkey, he ran to meet the monk and clasped his feet. Without delay the monk said, "Go against the Saracens, obey the imperial letters, go! For you will have God to rescue you and go before you, if only you have John, whom he loved, written clearly on everyone's shields in place of any other amulet." And he added, "I have made this journey here for no other reason than this." Armed by his prayers, Petronas caught up with Amer and his whole army at a place called Poson, which is naturally protected by rocks and cliffs. Beside it flows a river called the Lalakaon, running from north to south, and nearby lies a meadow called Gyris in the country speech. Petronas learned that Amer was encamped there and did everything he could to make the place impassable and inescapable. He at once sent the generals of the Armeniakoi, the Boukellarioi, Koloneia and Paphlagonia to hold the northern side, and the generals of the Anatolikoi, the Opsikion and Cappadocia, together with the kleisourarchs of Seleukeia and Charsianon, to hold the southern side. He himself took the western side, with the four imperial tagmata and the generals of Thrace and Macedonia (for when the Bulgarians were at peace it was the custom for these to share the dangers of the eastern forces and campaign with them), and he also had the theme of the Thrakesioi with him. When Amer heard that he was guarded on every side in this way and shut in by the Romans like a wild beast, he decided he must take the omens. He summoned one of the captives and asked the names of the place, the meadow and the river. The captive, mispronouncing slightly, said "Ptoson" instead of "Poson", and Amer explained that this signified his own fall. He took the river to mean "harm to the people", and from the coincidence of the meadow's name, Gyris, he concluded that they would be terribly turned about by the Romans. "Nevertheless," he said, "we must not shrink back, but rouse ourselves and play the man in tomorrow's battle." At once he ordered everyone to arm and to show their swords freshly polished, as if newly made. When the day was just dawning and gave him a respite [?] to consider how he might get the better of the Romans, he decided to seek a way out against those guarding the north. But the badness of the ground and the courage of the generals posted there met him and stopped him, so he was forced to make his push to the south. When [?]

he found the enemy line there just the same, he decided [?], drawn by the ground (for it was smooth and easy to approach), to advance in that direction rather than the others, and he saw Petronas encamped there on guard. With a din and a shout he leapt upon the enemy, but he found that the Romans did not give way at all. They were stronger than his own men, striking back manfully and resisting vigorously. So he drew back a little, collected himself, and attacked again in force, trying to win himself a way out and a passage through. But again they did not give way. They met him, closed ranks and turned him back, and forced him to keep doing this [?]. Then he saw the troops posted in the northern and southern parts rising up on every side and leaping out from all directions. Already despairing of escape, and struck in mind as if by a thunderbolt, he charged against the swords, not holding back from the foremost [?]. There he received a mortal blow and fell heavily, and not one of his men escaped anywhere. When they heard that his son had fled somewhere with a detachment, the kleisourarch of Charsianon overtook him not far off, overpowered him and his troops, and brought him and handed him over to the general Petronas. So Petronas set up trophies over Amer, and from then on he held the monk in great reverence and honor, calling him another prophet. He entrusted the care of his soul to him and rode into the capital bringing him along, rightly praising the man's virtue as divine before the emperor and Bardas. Petronas no longer merely played the part of domestic, but received the office itself from the emperor. The monk, having learned from God of his departure to God, told Petronas that he was soon to depart. "And where do you mean to leave me, your lamb, when you go away, my shepherd and my beloved?" asked Petronas in tears. "In this life? But I fear I may slip back into my former fall, and my last state will be no better than my first." "Do you want to follow me, then?" said the monk. And Petronas said, "Yes, Father, gladly." And indeed, as soon as he returned home, he too was struck by illness. He sent word to the abba of what was happening and received word back: "You will be with me shortly, as you asked." A few days later the monk was called to God, and Petronas at once followed him gloriously, as if by agreement. Their departures from this world came so close together that, short as the interval was, neither heard of the other's death. Manuel had met a similar end of life before this, overcome by an illness. 26. Bardas too kept advancing and continually exchanged one honor from the emperor for another, as some proud and ambitious youth changes his various [garments?] for his pleasure

[?]-las. So he moved on and rose to the glory and honor of Caesar, since Michael was not so excited by any other affair of state as by theaters and horse races. And what was worse, he was not content just to be a spectator, if he even had the leisure for that. Instead the emperor of the Romans drove chariots himself, and so became a spectacle, a plaything and a laughingstock to everyone. In this way Bardas acted as guardian to his nephew, and it seems he did not even want to live unless he could win over this slavish creature. For the time being, though, he ran affairs of state himself and set his sights on the throne, meaning to seize it when the moment was right. But that was being stored up for the future. At that time he took care of secular learning, which over so long a period had dwindled away and come to nothing at all through the boorishness and ignorance of those who had ruled. He set up schools of the mathematical sciences at the Magnaura and was eager and ambitious to make learning flourish and grow young again. This was the finest and most celebrated of his deeds, yet somehow it could not wash away the stains that otherwise clung to him. At the head of this school, expounding philosophy, was the great Leo the Philosopher. He was related to the patriarch John as his cousin, and he had held the throne of Thessalonica. Since he was now without office after his deposition, he was promoted to this school, and he drove ignorance far away and turned it back. 27. It is worth not passing over how so great a man came to the notice of the ruler of that time. This was Theophilus, Michael's begetter and father. Leo had trained himself to the highest knowledge of the sciences and had progressed through all of them: philosophy and its sisters, by which I mean arithmetic, geometry and astronomy, [?] and also much-celebrated music. He reached the summit of them as no one else had of any of them, through great diligence, a quiet life and greatness of nature. Living in a humble lodging, like an inn, he taught those who came to him, instructing them in whatever science they wished. As time went by and not a few of his students were making progress in the sciences, it happened that one of his pupils, a young man who had just completed the science of geometry, became secretary to a man of the rank of general, and to get ahead in life he was content to follow him. When he was with him on campaign, he was captured by the Hagarenes, I do not know how, and because of his youth he was given as a slave to one of their nobles. At that time the man called Mamun was amermoumnes of the Ishmaelites. He devoted himself to other Greek studies and especially did not neglect geometry. Once, when the master who owned the young man spoke about the zeal

of the amermoumnes and his devotion to the sciences, and was also talking about geometry, the young man said that he wanted to hear him and his teachers, since he himself had some knowledge of geometry. When the amermoumnes learned this, he summoned him with great delight and asked the captive whether he had knowledge of that science. When he said yes, the barbarian, still not believing his words, said there were no others under heaven [to compare] with his own teachers [?]. When the young man said he wanted to hear them and their teaching, they came forward at once and began it. They drew triangles and squares and brought out the rules of Euclid. What they taught, they taught confidently and expertly, saying that this figure had this name and that one that name. But the cause and the reason, why it is so and why it has that name, they could not give properly at all [?], since what they had was ignorance, not some difficulty of language. When the young man saw them exulting and proud over drawing the figures, he said: "Why, gentlemen, [?] when the force of the explanation lies in the reasoning and the fact, and in the 'why', do you state only that things are so, pass over their reasons as unnecessary, and bring the one being taught to the same place as someone who has learned nothing and knows nothing about these things?" They were at a loss and urged him to explain the causes and teach them. When they heard him interpreting them and stating them clearly, saying "this has the stated name and [?] for these reasons, and that one for this reason," their minds were opened at once and they understood what was said. Then, seized [with wonder], they asked how many such experts Byzantium nurtured. He said many, and counted himself among the band of learners, not of teachers. So they asked him in turn about his teacher, whether he was still numbered among the living and was above the earth. He said, "He is above the earth," and praised his virtue to the skies, saying that he lived without possessions, unknown to most, though shining in wisdom. At once Mamun wrote a letter to him to this effect: "From the fruit we have recognized the tree, and from the student the teacher. Since you, though so great in the knowledge of things that exist, are unknown to your fellow citizens because of your virtue and the depth of your knowledge, and have not yet reaped the fruits of your wisdom and knowledge, since you have not been thought worthy of honor by them, do not disdain to come to us and share your teaching with us. For if this happens, the whole race of the Saracens will bow their necks to you,

and you will be honored with wealth and gifts such as no one has ever received [?]." He gave the letter to the young man, treated him kindly with gifts, and ordered him to go to the teacher. He promised him honors and gifts at once, and also, if he wished, a return home, if only he could persuade Leo to leave the land of the Romans. When the young man reached the Queen City and stood face to face with his teacher, the sight of him stirred him up and, as it were, warmed him, so that he could not help weeping, and he drenched with tears not only his cheeks but his neck and chest. At first the teacher was bewildered by what was happening, not knowing who he was or why he was doing this. For his appearance, changed by time and the hardships of captivity, made the young man seem someone other than the one he had known. But when he gradually made himself known, giving his name and what he had studied, and adding the story of his captivity and the reason for his release and arrival, and at the same time putting the letter into his hands, then together they played out the tragedy and lament. However, Leo reckoned that a letter from the enemy was not without danger if he were ever caught with it, so he went to the logothete (this was Theoctistus, who later fell victim to Bardas), told him everything about the captive and student, and at the same time gave him the amermoumnes' letter. This was how this man came to be known to the emperor and to enjoy his favor. So the student and this letter brought Leo's wisdom, which until then had been in a corner, out into the open air, and led him out of that meanness and poverty. For the logothete showed the letter to Theophilus, and the emperor himself summoned Leo; he was enriched and urged by the emperor to teach publicly in the church of the Forty Saints. Not long afterward, when Mamun realized that the philosopher did not want to exchange his own land for a foreign one, he set out in a letter difficult problems in geometry and astronomy and some other hard chapters, and asked to receive their solutions. Leo explained each one properly and set out their solutions, and to them he added some predictions in order to astonish him. When the amermoumnes took them in his hands, he was deeply wounded with longing for him and cried aloud, admiring the man exceedingly for his philosophy and his science. So at once he sent a letter, not to Leo but to Theophilus, to this effect: "I wished to come to you myself, fulfilling the role of friend and student. But since the rule entrusted to me by God and the great people under my hand and authority do not allow this, I ask you to send me, for a short time, the man you have who is famous for philosophy and the other sciences,

and to persuade him to stay with me, sharing his knowledge and virtue by teaching me, since I am so passionately devoted to them. Surely there will be no delay because I do not speak your language and am a stranger to your faith. Rather, because the one asking is such a man, the request will be granted among fair and good friends. In return for this, twenty centenaria of gold will be paid to you, together with peace and treaties everlasting and unending." With such offers he pressed for Leo's presence and arrival. But Theophilus answered him. Considering it unreasonable to give one's own good to others and to make available to the nations the knowledge of things that exist, through which the race of the Romans is admired and honored by all, he did not consent to his request. Instead he held Leo in still greater honor, and ordered John, who was then laying claim to the patriarchal throne, to ordain him to the metropolis of Thessalonica, both because he was full of wisdom and because he was related to John by kinship. 28. After his ordination he came to Thessalonica, and everyone revered and honored his virtue. But they honored him still more brilliantly for a reason the account will now show. At that time the land appeared so barren and childless in bringing forth crops that death itself was pressing upon them. Seeing this and moved by pity and compassion, he urged them neither to despair nor to perish along with their misfortunes, if only they wished to receive the help of God and of himself. At a certain time, which he learned from astronomy, when through the risings and phases of certain stars some emanation and influence comes upon earthly things, the seeds were sown in the earth and committed to its bosom. From them there came such fertility and abundance of fruit, when spring arrived and summer came, that it was enough for them for many years to come. Surely it was God who brought forth the abundant harvest, yielding to the litanies and supplications of those in distress, and not that man's vain labor in such matters. In any case, this increased the Thessalonians' affection for the man still further and roused their love, so that [?]. 29. Many marveled at his wisdom and at how he had reached the summit of all the sciences. He is said to have told one of his intimates that he had mastered grammar and poetry while living in Constantinople, but [rhetoric?] and philosophy and the study of numbers [?] when he was on the island of Andros. There he met a wise man and received from him only the first principles and some lessons. Since he did not find as much as he wanted, he went around the mainland, [visiting monasteries?], seeking out and acquiring the books stored there, and studying them [more diligently?] on the mountain peaks. In this way he climbed to the height of knowledge. Then, having had his fill of learning, he returned to the Queen City, sowing the seeds of

the sciences in the minds of those who were willing. But all that was earlier. Now, after three years (that was how long he held the throne), he was again without office following his deposition, and he headed the school of philosophy at the Magnaura. His student Theodore presided over the school of geometry, Theodegius over that of astronomy, and Cometas over grammar, which renders words into proper Greek. Bardas supplied them generously and often visited them out of love of learning. He encouraged the talents of the students, and within the proper time, as if giving wings to their studies, he made them grow wings and advance. 30. Bardas also continually gave himself up to the contests of the hippodrome, eager to be thought a devotee of this inclination. He might have won good repute among many, once time had covered over what had happened [?]. But because he again stirred up and threw into confusion the affairs of the Church, and instead of calm became the cause of strife and ruinous afflictions for her, he fittingly earned not the better reputation but the opposite. For Methodius had just departed this life, having held the throne of Constantinople for only four years, and they raised to the patriarchal throne Ignatius, a monk and hegumen of the monastery of Satyrus, grandson of the emperor Nicephorus and son of Michael, a man attested for his piety and every virtue, and entrusted him with the helm of the whole world. After some years Ignatius barred Bardas from the church, because he had unreasonably and without cause cast off his own wife and was having relations with his daughter-in-law; for Ignatius would not neglect the divine canons. But the penalty he had imposed on Bardas by sending him out of the church, Bardas exacted from him in turn. To pass over the hunger and thirst, the man's being stretched out on the ground and beaten with rods, and the savage blows all over his body, I will tell only this one thing and then go on to what follows in the history. 31. Bardas handed Ignatius over to custody, harsh and cruel custody. It was in the precinct of the Holy Apostles, not the great and venerable church, but where the tombs are said to be and are. There they shut him up in a certain tomb of Copronymus, in frost and ice, "more naked than a pestle," as the proverb goes, and setting him up high, they forced him to suffer the effects of frost and winter. These were dysentery, the discharge of the inner organs through the belly from the extreme cold, and from this a bitter death. He would have died from the cruelty and savagery of his guards (these were John Gorgonites, Nicholas Scoutelops and Theodore Moros), had not someone moved by pity (this was Constantine the Armenian), while they were away at their meal, brought the man down from there and [?]

a little, and also eased his suffering for a while with bread and some small comfort. When the punishment seemed enough to him, Bardas exiled the man to the island of Mytilene. But some of the bishops objected. They appealed to justice, which had long since gone far away and departed, and they threatened that if anything happened they would not accept another patriarch but would break away from the Church. Fearing the turmoil this would cause, he decided to get round them too by deceit. He summoned each of them privately and in secret and promised and offered him no small or humble thing, if only he would desert Ignatius, but the throne of Constantinople itself. When they all [accepted?], overcome by the prospect of glory, and none of them spoke against it for the sake of what was good and lawful, then, yes then, he suggested that the emperor would fulfill the promises, but that they should preserve decorum and dignity and, as soon as they were called to him, should not accept what was offered, "so that he too," he said, "may admire your virtue." So, calling each of them to Michael not together but individually and alone, he persuaded them not to leap at the honor straight away. And these men, merely by being offered it and refusing, made examples of themselves without realizing it. For they fell from virtue, conquered by love of glory, and then failed to gain the glory, because they had betrayed Ignatius not honorably but treacherously. 32. So, since these too, being only men, [wavered?] and were deceived in this way, he gave the throne of Constantinople to Photius, a man known for his wisdom, but belonging to the secular order and holding the dignity of protasecretis. [?] To make their position stronger, they summoned legates who had been sent from Rome on other pretexts (namely against the Iconoclasts), arranged for them to act against Ignatius as the moment required, sat in council, and in the precinct of the divine Apostles subjected him to a public deposition [?]. When they recalled him from exile, they battered his face and [?] teeth with their fists [?] all darkness against the priests, wickedly [?], and a second like him has not yet appeared among those on earth. But as for all the other outrages he committed against all the priests, handing them over daily to prisons, exiles and the most savage punishments to make them enter into communion with [him?], they are many, and all time would not be enough to tell their tragic story. 33. After this the incursion of the Rus' began to ravage the lands of the Romans (they are a Scythian people, savage and boorish). They burned the Pontus [?], though not the Euxine, and surrounded the city itself, at the time when Mi-

chael was on campaign against the Ishmaelites. However, they were then filled with divine wrath, after Photius, who held the helm of the Church, had propitiated the Deity, and they went off home. Not long afterward an embassy of theirs came to the Queen City, begging to be allowed to partake of divine baptism, and this was done. 34. On one side, then, their incursion was doing harm. On another, the fleet of Crete put to sea with as many as twenty koumbaria, seven galleys and some satourai, and was plundering and enslaving, now going around the Cyclades islands, now the whole coastline as far as Proconnesus. On yet another, continual earthquakes did damage and threw things to the ground. Once, on the day when the Ascension of our Lord and Savior is celebrated, they leveled the southern third of the Exakionion, with fine churches and splendid houses. Another time they shook down statues: the Victory set up at the Golden Gate of the city, and those standing firmly in the Deuteron near St Anne's. Seeing the latter fallen, Leo the mathematician said that it clearly threatened the fall of the man second to the emperor. It would take long to tell of the disappearance of rivers and springs and of other calamities that happened in Isauria and in every region. 35. The reigning emperor put all these things in second place and was wholly absorbed in horse races at the church of St Mamas built on the Euxine. And once... but first I will describe a certain custom that would in an instant make known and reveal to the emperor, by beacon, any Saracen expedition against us. There is a fort and stronghold near Tarsus in Cilicia, bordering on it, called Loulon. As soon as the men stationed to guard it saw the enemy setting out, they signaled with a beacon to those on Mount Argaeus, they in turn to those on Isamus, they to those on Aegilum, and these to those on the hill of Mamas. Then Cyrizus took up the signal, and from it Mocilus, and from this the hill of St Auxentius made it plain within a short time to those assigned to this duty [?] in the Great Palace, on the terrace of the Pharos. Once, then, Michael was about to race at the church of the martyr Mamas mentioned above and had given the signal for the race to begin. When, in the evening, the beacon from the Pharos announced the incursion of the nations through the [pappias?], the emperor fell into as much agitation and fear that his chariot-driving would be ignored by the spectators because of this news as another man would feel whose life was in danger and who was rather struggling to keep the enemy from coming near. That was how he made a spectacle of himself without shame. Therefore, so that none of his contests

[?] … might be abandoned, and so that nothing else distressing arriving from there might make the spectators less attentive, he ordered the beacons nearest the city to operate no longer, and such matters to be buried in deep silence and long oblivion. 36. And at another time again (so that the man's lack of breeding and his folly may become still clearer), he himself was driving a chariot and was about to burst out of the starting gate. He was driving for the Blues; for the Greens drove the logothete Constantine, father of the patrician Thomas, who also became logothete of the drome; for the Whites, Cheilas; and for the Reds, Krasas. Nor was the protasekretis free to sit idle, any more than the protonotarios of the drome: one was scorekeeper for the Blues, the other for the Greens. So while they were standing on their chariots, wearing charioteers' dress, news came that the Emir Amer was terribly overrunning and ravaging the Thrakesion theme and was approaching Malagina, and that disaster was expected at any moment. At this the protonotarios grew grim, and he reported dejectedly the reply from the domestic of the schools, holding the letters in his hands and showing them. Michael said: “You there, what [?] makes you try to talk to me about such things during this vital contest? This is my only concern: whether [?] the middle chariot on the left …”

37. And this was not the only desire, or passion if you prefer, that held him captive. Nor was he free of other, more unseemly ones. Instead, [?] pursuing them without measure, he fell far short of what was fitting, and above all of imperial dignity. [P. 124] Once, on the road, he met a poor woman whose son he had sponsored at baptism. She was coming from the bath and carrying her jug in her hands. He leapt down from his horse and sent the members of the senate who were following him off to the palace there. Then he took along some dissolute little fellows of his inner circle and went off with the woman, taking the jug out of her hands, and said: “Come now, woman, don't be afraid. Receive me in your house. I have a craving for a bran loaf and some fresh cheese.” For I must quote his own words. The woman was struck dumb by the strangeness of the sight and was at a loss for everything, having neither a table nor anything to set it with. Michael, quicker than it takes to tell, turned around and took the towel she was carrying from the bath, still [?] damp, and used it instead of the fine linen that is spread on a table. Then he took the woman's key and was everything himself: emperor, table-setter, cook and guest. He took out what that poor chest held, feasted with her and dined with her, claiming that he was imitating my Christ and God. From there he walked back to the palace, accusing the earlier emperors of great foolishness, pretension and pride. Those who heard of this nonsense

said: “It was not by indulging in such luxury and playing such games that you should have done this and condemned our pride, but by fighting in the front line, going short of necessities, and being the table-companion and lover of soldiers, not of [?] and worthless little women.” All these things made Michael hated and stirred up God's most just wrath. 38. What was worse still was the band he kept with him. They were like satyrs, unrestrained in every kind of obscenity, and one might well call them devotees of Dionysus. He treated them with honor and respect while scorning divine things. He put gold-embroidered priestly vestments and omophoria on them and in general forced them to perform the holy rites indecently and impurely. He called their leader, a man named Gryllos, patriarch, and the remaining eleven he called metropolitans of the [?] and illustrious sees. Unless he himself shared with them, [P. 125] he did not even think it worth being emperor, which is why he was called, and is still named, the bishop of Colonea. Since they had to sing and celebrate the mysteries, they performed the hymns on the kithara. Now they played softly and clearly, imitating the secret prayers; now they played with unrestrained and piercing force, imitating, forsooth, the priests' exclamations. They also filled golden vessels set with pearls with vinegar and mustard and gave them to whomever they pleased to partake, mocking the immaculate mysteries in this way. This Gryllos would ride on an ass when he made public processions, and he delighted in having such a band following him. Once he happened to meet the blessed patriarch Ignatius in procession during the church litany, followed by the priestly clergy. When Gryllos saw him, he gladly seized the opportunity: he struck up the strumming, hitched up his phelonion, and with his fellow initiates struck their kitharas more vigorously, pelting those holy men with abuse and the most shameful words. Michael also once summoned his mother Theodora, who was still alive and living in the palace, to be blessed by him, pretending that this man was the blessed Ignatius. The most holy woman came out with piety and reverence and threw herself to the ground asking for a prayer, for he was not recognized for the moment, since he hid his beard as best he could. At once he let off a noise full of stench and unseemly words, and so called down on themselves her curses and those of the more pious. She also prophesied the future and made it clear to Michael that he had fallen outside God's providence and protection. 39. But a man who had turned aside from the straight path and abandoned virtue could not be called back and set on the blessed road. So the evils were no longer far off. Rather, those who caused and devised such things [?] brought them near to themselves. And first [?] … woman and [?] …

Bardas brought these things upon himself, or rather Theoktistos the kanikleios did so before him. Perhaps they both wholly gratified Michael with one accord and failed, as his guardians should have tried to do, to restrain him from more wicked teachings. Or perhaps one restrained him while the other, not of the same mind, did not join in restraining him out of rivalry but rather gave him free rein, as we too have seen such people [P. 126] in our own times. Either way, they brought evils upon themselves. Theoktistos, as has been said, was in the end slaughtered, and before that he had failed in the tasks he undertook. Although he was often chosen to command many armies and set out against many enemies, both then and before, he never once returned victorious or even prevailed over the enemy at all. Instead, he was defeated and delivered his armies to total destruction. I do not know whether this was because he lacked judgment and reason and had no experience of feats of war, or because he had never practiced these things, or because of some other, greater cause beyond us, or the one just mentioned. For once, after two solar eclipses had occurred, he was chosen as general against the Abasgians and unhappily met with divine wrath. Some of his men were shipwrecked and lost their lives, while those who landed on dry ground shared their misfortune. That is how this army perished. Not long after, he again went to war more rashly and lost more than forty thousand men. And once more he campaigned against the Arabs in Crete and came back having achieved nothing, leaving many of his men behind there because he had taken to flight and got away from the island in a hurry. But that was earlier. 40. Now clear signs, the appearance of comets and visions in dreams, revealed to Bardas the terrible things to come. This did not happen at all by chance or through some other irrational force, but by the providence of Him who does not seek the death of the sinner so much as his conversion. In his sleep he dreamed that he went with Michael to the shrine of God named Sophia, in a public festival and procession [?]. When they arrived and were in the middle of the church, two figures in white appeared, angelic in form. When they went further on, they saw nothing else except an old man seated on the throne, whom they suspected to be Peter, the chief of the apostles, and at his feet the blessed Ignatius, rolling on the ground and begging to see vengeance for the terrible things he had suffered at their hands. The old man, as one who shared his suffering, said he would grant it before long. To one of those standing by (two figures clothed in gold [P. 127] appeared beside him) he gave a sword of no great size and said: “Come, [Apparatus: ἐριθείας] ἐρεριθείας G?, ἐρεσχελίας in the margin; ναυαγίῳ] perhaps ναυαγίᾳ; δὲ] μὲν P; ἐπὶ] περὶ P.]

take this. Set this one in the place of those on the left and cut the God-detested man limb from limb.” By this he meant the Caesar. “But the other, the child of impiety,” meaning the emperor, “enroll among those on the right, and tell him to expect a similar punishment.” So the dream ended. What follows was waking reality, not a dream. Bardas was just then arming with Michael in full force against the Cretans. He went to the church of our most holy Lady the Theotokos, which is called the Hodegoi, and entered with candles to perform the farewell service. As he was approaching the sanctuary, his cloak suddenly slipped from his shoulders, which made him sense that even stranger dangers lay ahead. One day before he was to leave the city, whether of his own accord or driven by what was coming, he gathered his friends together, and after dining with them he urged them to remember his friendship and handed out legacies, as if he were already departing this life. But these things had to reach their end. When they set out against Crete and entered the theme of the Thrakesians at a place called Kepoi, their attendants went ahead and pitched the tents, competing eagerly with each other. There, whether by providence or simply through ignorance, they spread out Michael's tent on a flat and level site, but the Caesar's on a hill rising above the ground. Those who were denouncing the Caesar to Michael seized on this as a godsend and an unexpected gain. They made accusations about it and stitched together plots against him. But the Caesar's superior power troubled them and made them somewhat hesitant about the attempt. For Antigonos, the domestic of the schools, obeyed him rather than the emperor, as his son, and was led by him, and so did the other generals. And the logothete of the drome, a man called Symbatios, who was the Caesar's son-in-law through his daughter, was bound to share his views without question. But Symbatios had been secretly won over and was in fact going to bring about his father-in-law's murder. When the plan was ready, the ambush prepared and those who were to carry out the deed in position, Symbatios and no one else had arranged the signal. As soon as he came out after reading the reports, he gave the sign by tracing a cross on his face. But again there were [P. 128] delays and loss of nerve, because the Caesar's retinue was standing [?] around him and facing them. Michael was afraid of being found out and drawing the sword upon himself, so he encouraged the men through a trusted agent and emboldened them with promises and honors. Even so, the Caesar would have got past the danger and escaped murder, since the men were struck with fear and overcome by despondency. But Michael again sent a message to Basil (who was

parakoimomenos) telling him that the crisis stood on a razor's edge, that he had given up on his life, and that he was arming himself for [?]. When Basil heard this, he feared for the emperor. He persuaded the men to cast off their fear, and by crying, “Oh, for courage and a daring soul!” he suddenly gave them wings and made them leap into the fight. When Bardas saw them all at once with swords drawn, he was terror-stricken. He knew it meant death and threw himself at the emperor's feet. But there was no escape. They [?] dragged him away from there and cut him limb from limb, on the twenty-first of April, in the fourteenth indiction. Then they hung his genitals on a pole and paraded them as an example and a trophy. A great uproar and confusion broke out, and Michael could be seen almost running for his life. But the droungarios of the watch, who was Constantine, rushed into the midst and dispersed the great din. He showered the emperor with acclamations and drew up troops against those who were rising up. So Bardas departed from among men, and so the army against the Cretans was disbanded, and the emperor returned to Byzantium. 41–42. Another sign had also been given to Bardas two or even three days before. For Theodora [?], whether divinely inspired or because she had overheard one of those involved in the plot, sent him, as a riddle, a very beautiful garment embroidered with golden partridges, but one that did not match his height and fell far short of it. The choice of partridges rather than some other birds for the weaving, and the shortness of the garment, foretold that he would fall into a trap sooner than he should. 43. The emperor, then, returned. Since he had not been blessed with a son, he adopted Basil and honored him with the rank of magistros. [P. 129] As time went on, Michael was incapable of managing public affairs and recognized his own simplicity. At the same time he heard that the senate was plotting an uprising and rebellion because the affairs of the Romans were being badly managed. So he placed the much-coveted diadem on Basil's head and proclaimed and acclaimed him emperor on the day of Pentecost, the twenty-sixth of May, in the fourteenth indiction, in the Great Church named the Wisdom of God. Who this Basil was, where he came from and how he came to the ruler's notice, the history devoted to him will [?] tell. For now, having been granted imperial glory, he held to the business of ruling. He kept away from the daily contests and horse races and from the obscenities surrounding the most shameful Gryllos, the false patriarch, in which Michael indulged so unseasonably. Many have said that one can have one's fill of all things, both shameful and natural, and experience of them is the teacher [?]. But Michael, who was then ruling, could never get his fill of horse races, or of his other bouts of drinking unmixed wine and [?], as they say. Trying to prevent [Apparatus: γάρ] μὲν P; ἐνυφάναι] ἀνυφάναι P.]

this, Basil also tried to draw him further away from such things. Now he used exhortations; now he set before him the hatred of the citizens, the curses of the priests and the uprisings of the senate, painting them, as it were, before his eyes. Without realizing it, he made himself the object of envy, and the adopted son came to be regarded not as a friend but as a hated enemy. Not long afterwards, Michael brought in another man, who was then serving as a rower on the imperial dromon. He was called Basiliskianos, and he was the brother of that Kapnogenes who was twice granted the rank of eparch. Michael clothed him in purple, set the diadem on his head, and put the imperial insignia on his shoes. Then he led him out to the senate, holding him by the hand, and said to the assembly: “Men, I ought long ago to have brought this man into this conspicuous adornment. First, he has a figure worthy of rule; and second, the crown suits him naturally. Everything fits him for the dignity.” And he added: “How much better it would have been for me to make this man emperor rather than Basil. I regret having made him emperor.” This was the beginning of his downfall. When it echoed around everyone, they were astonished and seized with great speechlessness that, like the mythical Giants, he was producing sown emperors every day. [P. 130] From then on the hatred toward Basil grew, and became fiercer according to the man's nature. The kindling and cause of it was that Basil wanted neither to be corrupted along with them nor to be drawn into their licentious designs. For Michael often ran aground in such folly through heavy drinking and drunkenness that while drunk [?] he would order terrible things, beyond terrible: he commanded that one man's ears be cut off, another's nose, another's head. If some, moved by pity, had not ignored these orders and put them off until the next day, awaiting the man's recovery and change of mind, which did in fact happen, everyone who stayed with him and endured him would have perished. Basil too very nearly perished, having more than once become the plaything of his drunken violence. But he endured and stayed on, hoping for some change of heart in the man and humbling himself [?]. But Michael, like a chariot wheel bent from his earliest youth, could never recover his original straightness, whatever happened. So he stitched together a greater plot against Basil. The plan was that during a hunt one of the shield-bearers should throw his spear, ostensibly at the quarry but in fact at Basil. The very man who was ordered to do this and threw the spear confessed it at the time of his death, making it clear and credible. The man who had been ordered did throw the spear, but he missed. And so Basil was saved, having come very close to death, by God who trampled death down. When these things became known and evident to all, they sharpened the sword against Michael. So that they might not see Basil slaughtered as well, as shortly before

the Caesar had been, and before him Theoktistos, Michael was slaughtered by the men of the emperor's bedchamber. Whether this was by the counsel of the senate or by the decision of those who loved Basil (for death had been threatened against them too) [is uncertain]. It took place in the palace of the holy great martyr Mamas, on the twenty-fourth of September, in the first indiction, in the year six thousand three hundred [P. 131] and seventy-six, at the third hour of the night. He had reigned fourteen years with his mother Theodora, eleven as sole ruler, and one year and three months afterwards with Basil. 44. [?] all the stage and theatrical things, but it is also worth remembering the praiseworthy [?] of the offerings he brought to the famous church of the Wisdom of God, a work executed with loving care and praiseworthy for its munificence. For none of the ancient sacred treasures, nor any of those crafted for churches since mankind came to be, equals his paten in size, nor has such comeliness and beauty bloomed on any work ever made, since everything beautiful and precious came together in it. The chalice too matched it very well. Nor is the circle made by him for lighting, which they call a polykandelon, inferior to any of the [?] others. It too was made entirely of gold, weighing sixty pounds, and it far surpasses the rest, which yield it first place and reverence.

HISTORICAL NARRATIVE OF THE LIFE AND DEEDS OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS EMPEROR BASIL, WHICH CONSTANTINE, EMPEROR OF THE ROMANS IN GOD, HIS GRANDSON, DILIGENTLY COLLECTED FROM VARIOUS ACCOUNTS AND ENTRUSTED TO THE [?] PRESENT WRITER. [P. 132] 1. For a long time I have had the eagerness and desire to implant experience of affairs and knowledge in the minds of the more studious [?] through the ever-memorable

[?] …and immortal mouth of history, and I wished, if I were able, to record the whole span of the Roman empire at Byzantium: the more noteworthy deeds of the emperors, of the officials, generals and lieutenants under them, and of individuals one by one. But the task required much time, constant labour, plenty of books and freedom from public affairs, and we had none of these. So I was forced to settle for the second-best course. For the present, I will narrate from beginning to very end the deeds and the whole conduct of a single emperor. He raised the power of the empire to great heights, his very name spoke of kingship, and he was a great benefit to the Roman state and its affairs. I do this so that later generations may know the first source and root of an imperial stock that has lasted a long time, and so that his descendants may have, set up in their own house, a rule, a statue and an archetype of virtue to imitate. And if more years of life are measured out to us, if we are granted some small respite from illness, and if nothing from outside stands in the way, perhaps we shall go on to add the whole history of his line down to our own time.

2. This emperor Basil, then, whom the present account undertakes to describe, came from the land of Macedonia, but his family descended from the Armenian nation of the Arsacids. The ancient Arsaces, who ruled the Parthians, rose to great glory and virtue. Because of this, a law was established for later generations: neither the Parthians nor the Armenians, nor indeed the Medes, were to be ruled by anyone except a member of the family of Arsaces and his descendants. While these nations were ruled by this line, the ruler of the Armenians at one point departed from among men, and strife arose over the kingship and the succession. Artabanus and Cleienes, who had not only been driven from their ancestral rule but were also in danger of their lives, came to this imperial city of Constantinople. At that time the Roman empire was governed by Leo the Great, the father-in-law of Zeno. He received the men, treated them with a kindness worthy of their noble birth, and assigned them a fitting residence and livelihood in the imperial city. The man who then ruled the Persian realm learned that they had fled their homeland, taken refuge in this imperial city and been kindly received by its rulers. He summoned them by letter, promising, as if out of goodwill, to install them in their ancestral rule, while in fact he was seeking to bring their nation under his own control. They received the letter, but while they were still considering what to do, the matter was disclosed by one of those who

served them to the emperor, and the letter was handed over. The emperor saw that the Persian was summoning them not so much to put them in power as to make their nation subject to himself, which benefited neither the men summoned nor the affairs of the Romans. So measures were taken to keep the Persians' plan from succeeding. The emperor cut off any easy chance of flight under a respectable pretext, as if to give them more room and greater freedom: they were moved, with their wives and children, to Nike, a city in Macedonia (for these too had later slipped away to join them). As time went on and the Saracens grew more powerful, the caliph of that day made a similar attempt on the descendants of the earlier Arsacids, summoning them by letter, supposedly to their ancestral authority and rule. This plot too was detected by Heraclius, the emperor at the time, and the letters were handed over to him. He recognized that the summons had been issued not out of goodwill toward them but to serve the schemers' own ambitions for power. The Saracens hoped that if they had these men on their side, they could easily win over the nation through its old loyalty to Arsaces. For this reason the emperor again moved them to Philippi, another of the cities of Macedonia, for greater security. Later he moved them from there to Adrianople, a more splendid city and a better situation. The place suited them well. Forming as it were a separate clan and tribe, they grew numerous and prosperous, preserving their ancestral nobility and keeping their lineage unmixed. 3. Some time later, when Constantine reigned with his mother Irene, a certain Maiktes, who was also of the blood of Arsaces, came to this renowned city of Constantinople on some embassy or business. By chance he met a man of his own race named Leo. From the man's outward bearing and the distinctive style of his dress, he recognized that he was not some ordinary, lowly person but noble and distinguished. He fell into conversation with him and found his speech familiar and native to him. When he learned Leo's lineage, he chose to live with him, preferring the other man's house to his own because of his virtue. Gladly accepting an alliance with him, he married one of his daughters. From this couple came the father of the man under discussion. He was well brought up, and after a praiseworthy upbringing he reached manhood. He excelled in bodily vigour and strength and was adorned with every kind of virtue, so that many wished to make him their kin by marriage. There was a noble and modest woman living in Adrianople whose husband had died and who was passing her widowhood chastely (for a report

that was by no means faint went around that she was related to Constantine the Great). He thought her more worthy of honour than the others among whom he lived, and so he married her daughter, who was outstanding in noble birth and bodily beauty and adorned with modesty. From them sprang this imperial root, Basil. On his father's side he descended from Arsaces, as has been said. His mother took pride in her kinship with Constantine the Great and, on the other side, boasted the splendour of Alexander. Born of such parents, Basil showed from the very start many signs of his later glory. When his hair first grew, a scarlet band was seen around his head, and purple dyes appeared about his swaddling clothes. 4. Until then the family of the descendants of Arsaces had remained a separate clan, as it were, living in Adrianople, even though it often mixed with the local people through intermarriage. Then Krum, the ruler of the Bulgars, broke his treaties with the Romans and laid siege to Adrianople. After a long siege, lack of supplies forced the city to surrender, and he carried off all its inhabitants to Bulgaria, together with Manuel, the archbishop of the city. Among the others, Basil's parents, who still had him in swaddling clothes, were taken away to the land of the Bulgars. There that wondrous archbishop and the people with him kept their Christian faith unadulterated and brought many of the Bulgars to the true faith of Christ (for that nation had not yet been converted to piety). In many places they sowed the seeds of Christian teaching, drawing the Scythians away from pagan error and leading them to the light of the knowledge of God. Mutragon, Krum's successor, was angered at them for this. He tried to persuade them to renounce Christ, and when he could not, he tortured the most holy Manuel and many others who were shown to be involved, and sent them to a martyr's death. So it happened that many of Basil's relatives won the glory of martyrdom, and he too had a share in that honour. When God was at last visiting his people and arranging their departure (for the ruler of the Bulgars, unable to hold out for long against the Roman forces, was again inclining toward submission), the Christian people who were about to be released to their homes were gathered before the ruler. He saw the boy Basil, noble in appearance, smiling charmingly and skipping about. He drew him to himself and gave him an apple of wonderful size. The boy leaned simply and boldly on the ruler's knees and, with his unaffected manner, [?] his own nobility

5. But to cut short what came between: by God's providence the whole Christian people who had been carried off as captives went home. Basil's parents went with them, bringing along their beloved child. And while he was still very young, something wondrous happened to him that pointed to his future fortune, and I think it would be wrong to pass it over in silence. At harvest time his parents went out to their own field to oversee the reapers and urge them to work hard. As the day wore on toward mid-morning and the sun was already burning more fiercely with its midday rays, they bound together ears of grain to make a sort of tent and laid the child in it to sleep, so that the heat of the sun would not harm him. While they were busy with the reapers, an eagle swooped down, perched above him, and shaded the child with its outspread wings. Those who saw it cried out that the eagle might do the child some harm, and the mother, loving and devoted to her child, ran to him at once. She saw the eagle shading the child with its wings. It was not even startled at her approach, but gazed at her pleasantly, as it were. On the spur of the moment she could think of nothing better to do than throw a stone at it, and so the eagle flew up and seemed to go away. But when she went back to her husband and the workers, the eagle was there again in the same posture, shading the child. Again the onlookers cried out, the mother ran to the child, the eagle was driven off by a thrown stone, and the mother went back to the workers. Providence wished to show more plainly that this was happening not by chance but by divine foreknowledge, and so the same thing happened a third time: the eagle over the child, the onlookers shouting, the mother rushing at the eagle, and the eagle leaving only under force and with reluctance. In this way God always lays down, far in advance, signs and tokens of great things to come. This happened to him more than a few times as he grew older; he was often found asleep in the shade of an eagle. But at that time people thought almost nothing of it. Until his virtues became evident, even great portents went unheeded and unnoticed, since no one could imagine how such a thing could ever come to pass in a plain and common household. However, lingering longer on these matters might seem close to flattery, and we might be thought

to be filling the history with them for lack of good things to say about him. So we shall pass over everything of this kind and from his childhood, and eagerly carry the account forward, rejecting greed for praise as something itself unworthy of praise. 6. The boy, then, was brought up by his father. His father guided him in what to do and explained what to say, and was his teacher and trainer in everything earnest and praiseworthy. He needed no half-human Chiron, as Achilles did, nor any lawgiver like Lycurgus or Solon, nor any foreign upbringing abroad. Under his father alone he was trained in the finest of good things: holiness and piety toward God, respect and obedience toward his parents, deference to his elders, guileless goodwill toward his peers and kinsmen, submission to the powerful and compassion for the poor. He shone conspicuously in all the virtues, showing himself temperate and brave from youth. He loved and especially honoured equality [?], and in nothing did he exalt himself over those humbler than he. As a result, everyone wished him well, and all found him dear and lovable. 7. When he had left childhood behind and reached adolescence, and it was time for him to take up more manly pursuits, the father who begot him departed this life for the world beyond. Grief and lamentation, naturally, overran the house. His mother was widowed and this most excellent youth orphaned, and sorrows and afflictions followed. A swarm of worries about their livelihood poured in as well, for at once the whole care of the household and the support of his mother and siblings fell on him. The income from farming seemed small and ignoble to him, so he planned to go to the imperial city and display his own virtue. In this way he could provide what was needed for himself and his family and show that his protection and foresight were of great benefit to them. For he knew that in great cities, and especially in imperial ones, able natures win esteem, and those who excel others in anything are noticed and rise to more brilliant fortune. In obscure and humble cities, on the other hand, as in village life, virtues are dimmed and waste away; because they are neither displayed nor admired, they fade and wither of themselves. For these reasons the journey to the imperial city seemed advantageous and expedient to him. But his longing for his mother held him back and restrained him, along with his wish to lighten

her hardships. She herself especially pressed her hope that he would care for her in her old age, and [?] demanded his help and service close at hand in what was due to her. 8. But the divine plan had to prevail, and he had to rise step by step along the road to what he had been destined for. So visions in dreams persuaded his mother to let him go and give way to his eagerness for the city. Indeed, they led her to urge and exhort him herself to go to the imperial city and display the meadow of his soul and the excellences of his noble spirit. Once his mother dreamed that she saw a very great plant spring up from her, as Cyrus's mother saw the vine. It stood over her house, covered in flowers and heavy with fruit. Its great trunk was golden from the ground up, and its branches and leaves were golden too. She told this to an acquaintance who was thought to be skilled in such matters, and was told that it meant her son would rise to brilliant and great fortune. Again, a short time later, she saw in her sleep an old man with fire coming from his mouth, who said to her plainly: "Your beloved son Basil will be entrusted by God with the scepter of the empire of the Romans, and you must urge him to go to Constantinople." Overjoyed at this glad news and filled with delight, she bowed down before the old man and said to him: "Who are you, my lord, who did not disdain to appear to your handmaid but brought me such joyful good tidings?" He said, "I am Elijah the Tishbite," and vanished from her sight. When she woke, these auspicious visions, or rather divine revelations, gave her wings, as it were, and kindled her spirit. She eagerly urged her son on and sent him off to the imperial city. As a mother she admonished and exhorted him to keep the fear of God in his soul at all times. He must always remember that the eye of Providence watches over his every deed and thought, and must pursue nothing unworthy of such oversight. Instead he must display his own virtues by fitting conduct and never disgrace the nobility of his ancestors. 9. So he set out from Macedonia in Thrace and journeyed to this queen of all cities, wishing to attach himself to one of the powerful and distinguished men and to enter his service. He covered the distance between and reached the Golden Gate of the imperial city. He passed through it as the day was already declining and came to the monastery of the holy martyr Diomedes, which happened to be nearby. Worn out from the journey, he lay down somewhere there in front of the gate, on the steps,

carelessly just as he was [?], and rested. About the first watch of the night, the martyr Diomedes appeared in a dream to the abbot of the monastery. He ordered him to go out to the monastery gate and call out the name Basil, and to bring whoever answered his call into the monastery. There he was to treat him with care, giving him food, shelter, clothing and whatever else he might need. For the man had been anointed emperor by God, and he would one day rebuild and enlarge this monastery. But the abbot thought the vision a mere fancy, an empty figment of the mind. He paid it no heed and went back to sleep. A second time he saw and heard the same things. Still sluggish and drowsy, it seems, he did not get up, and so he saw the martyr a third time. Now the martyr was no longer urging him gently and cheerfully, but threatening him fiercely and seeming to make ready to whip him unless he quickly did as he was told. Then at last, as if coming to his senses and shaking off from his eyes that sleep which is neighbour to death, he went to the gate and, as the martyr had commanded, called out the name: "Basil!" At once Basil answered: "Here I am, lord. What do you command your servant?" The abbot brought him inside the monastery, dirty and unkempt as he was and badly sunburnt on his face, gave him the care and attention he needed, and showed him every kindness. Then he advised him to keep the secret to himself and tell no one, because it was dangerous, and revealed to him the martyr's prophecy, making him promise to remember it once it had come true. Basil seemed to think the matter beyond him and would not even accept it. Instead he asked the abbot to place him in a household and give him into the service of one of the more prominent men, and the abbot eagerly set about doing this. There was a relative of the emperor Michael and of the Caesar Bardas who was on familiar terms with the monastery and often visited it as a friend. People called him by the diminutive Theophilitzes, and his nickname was "the Pupil." The abbot recommended Basil to him. This little Theophilus happened to be proud in spirit and fond of grandeur. He was eager to have around him noble men, handsome and well built, and especially men outstanding in courage and bodily strength, and he prided himself and gave himself airs because of them. One could see them at once, dressed in silk garments and splendid in the rest of their attire. Theophilus enrolled the newly arrived young Basil among them, and since Basil seemed far to surpass the rest in bodily strength and courage of soul, he made him his protostrator. Day by day Theophilus loved him more and admired him for his excellent qualities. For Basil showed himself bold in action, intelligent in mind, and quick and capable at carrying out every command.

10. His mother was constantly lamenting over him. Because she had not yet learned how his journey had gone, she was downcast and distressed, and again in her sleep she saw a great plant [?]. When she woke, that same day she told the vision to one of the pious women, who, like the famous Anna, did not leave the holy church night or day but gave herself to prayer and fasting. This woman urged her to take heart about her son. She interpreted what had been seen and declared firmly that it meant “your son will become emperor of the Romans.” [?] From then on the mother was no longer troubled or distressed about him. She fed on these hopes and, waiting for help from above, [?].

11. At that time it happened that Basil's master Theophilos was sent to the Peloponnese on some public business by the reigning emperor Michael and by Bardas the Caesar. Basil was with him, assisting in the duties assigned to him. When Theophilos reached Patras in Achaea, he went into the church of Andrew, the first-called Apostle, to pray. Basil was busy with his own duties, it seems, and did not go in with him. Later he too came to the church alone to pay the Apostle the reverence he owed him. A monk lived there and spent most of his time in the Apostle's church. When he saw Theophilos come in, he did not rise, did not pray for him and did not even think him worth a word. He paid no respect to Theophilos's escort and splendour, as one would have expected. But later, when Basil came in, the monk rose as though for one of his betters and offered him the acclamation customarily given to emperors. Some of the people present saw and heard this and reported it to a noble and very wealthy woman of that region, who was called Danelis after her husband. She knew from experience that the monk had been granted the gift of foresight, so she did not ignore the report. She summoned the monk and went over the matter with him reproachfully. “I have been known to you for so long, spiritual Father,” she said, “and you certainly know that I stand above most people and am foremost and preeminent among those in this land. Yet you have never risen when you saw me or prayed for me, and you have not shown such honour to my son or my grandson either. How is it, then, that now you saw a lowly foreigner, unknown to most people, and you rose and honoured him like an emperor?” That pious monk [?]

answered her: “I did not see the man as one of the ordinary people, as you say. I saw him as a great emperor of the Romans, anointed by Christ, and so I rose and acclaimed him. For those whom God has honoured are surely owed honour from men as well.” Basil's master stayed in that region for some time and completed the public business entrusted to him. When he was about to return to the capital, Basil happened to fall ill and was left behind there. He received proper care and after some time recovered from the illness, and he too began preparing for the journey back. Then the woman Danelis, whom we mentioned before, summoned him and welcomed him with many great gifts. She did this very prudently and wisely, as though sowing seed in good soil so that she might reap it back many times over at the right time. She gave him a good deal of gold, thirty slaves to serve him, and great wealth in clothing and goods of various kinds. For the present she asked nothing else from him than that he enter into a bond of spiritual brotherhood with her son John. Basil declined the request as being too far above him, since the woman seemed so distinguished and he himself so obviously humble. But when she pressed him further, he agreed. Then, as if she had grown bolder, she said to him openly: “God has [?] you … in abundance all those belonging to you [?]; as in virtues, so also in possessions and in [?]

12. One day Antigonos, patrician and domestic of the schools, gave a banquet in the imperial residences by the courtyard next to the palace [?]. He prepared it lavishly and made his own father Bardas both host and guest of honour. The Caesar went to the feast and took with him the leading members of the senate, his relatives and his close associates. He also brought along his friends from Bulgaria, who at that time were staying in the capital, as was usual. Basil's master Theophilos was at the banquet too, since he was also a relative of the Caesar. So was the patrician Constantine, who was the father of the patrician who in our own day is logothete of the drome, a man supreme in philosophy and conspicuously incorruptible.

[?] The Bulgarians are always rather conceited and boastful. At that time they happened to have with them a Bulgarian who prided himself on his bodily strength and was a superb wrestler. Hardly any of his opponents had ever thrown him. They were unbearably proud of him and boasted beyond all measure. As the drinking went on and merriment danced around the table, little Theophilos said to the Caesar: “Master, I have a man who will wrestle this famous Bulgarian, if you order it. It is the greatest disgrace to the Romans, and no one will be able to endure their boasting, if this man goes back to Bulgaria undefeated.” The Caesar ordered the match to take place. The patrician Constantine, mentioned above, was very friendly toward Basil, since he too was of Armenian descent. He saw that the floor where they were to fight was damp and feared that Basil might slip. So he asked the Caesar to order sawdust scattered on the floor. When this had been done, Basil grappled with the Bulgarian. He quickly squeezed him and bound him tight, then lifted him up as easily as a light, lifeless bundle of hay or a dry, light fleece of wool, and threw him over the table. After this there was no one present who did not praise Basil and marvel at him. The Bulgarians too were astonished at his superior ease and strength and stood speechless. From that day Basil's fame began to spread more widely through the whole city. He was on everyone's lips and had become a man people admired.

13. Emperor Michael had a horse that was unruly and undisciplined, stiff-necked and wild, but in other respects noble and fine, and great and wonderful in size, beauty and speed. If it ever slipped its halter or got loose some other way, it was very hard to get back in hand and gave the grooms a great deal of trouble. Once the emperor went out hunting on this horse and struck a hare with a club with his own hand. In his delight he at once leapt down from the horse to kill the hare. The horse was left loose and bolted. Many people ran after it, and the officials of the stable, the manglavitai and others around them joined the chase, but no one could catch it. The emperor grew so angry that he ordered the horse's hind legs to be hamstrung if it was caught. Bardas the Caesar, who was present, begged the emperor not to waste the many good qualities of such a horse over a single fault. Basil, who was there with his master, said to him: “If I ride up alongside the emperor's horse and leap from my own horse onto it, will the emperor not be angry with me because it is

decked with imperial trappings?” The emperor was told of this and ordered it done, and Basil did it readily and skilfully. When the emperor saw this, he loved Basil's skill, which was joined with courage, and his intelligence. He at once took him from Theophilitzes and enrolled him among the imperial grooms. He paid attention to him and loved him, because he saw that Basil far excelled the others in everything. And so, since Basil often showed his abilities before him, he promoted him to the rank of protostrator.

14. After this a hunt was announced at the place called Philopation. The protostrator rode on horseback ahead of the emperor, as was customary, and carried on his belt the imperial mace, which custom calls the vardoukion. As those taking part in the hunt raised a din, an enormous wolf burst out of the woods. Almost everyone was terrified and thrown into confusion. Basil charged at it and hurled the imperial vardoukion from behind. It struck the beast in the middle of the head and split it in two. The Caesar was riding behind the emperor as usual and saw what happened. He said to some of the intimates and acquaintances who were with him: “I think this man is going to be the ruin of our whole family.” He drew this conclusion from Basil's success and good fortune in everything and from the affection the emperor had for him because of it. Moreover, they say the Caesar had heard the same from Leo, who at that time was foremost in every kind of learning. The Caesar often questioned the man about these matters. First Leo told him: “I find that your family will be ruined by a certain [?].” Later, as Basil was coming into prominence, Leo pointed him out to the Caesar with his finger and said: “This is the one [?] who is to be your successor.” From then on the Caesar always suspected Basil and lay in wait for him. Yet he could not undo anything that the divine will had already ratified, for what is fated is not so much unexpected as always inescapable. These things have perhaps been told by way of a digression, but they are not beside the subject.

15. The emperor was fond of hunting. A little later he crossed over again to the place called Armamentareas for a hunt and a short tour. A meal [?] was prepared privately, and the emperor sat at table with his mother Theodora, his relatives and the closer members of the senate. The protostrator was also invited at the emperor's order. When he sat down, the empress Theodora began to stare at him again and again, gazing at him and observing him and scrutinizing him more closely. She recognized certain signs on him and gradually fainted. Water had to be poured on her, and with the help of rose essence she

Book V: Basil the Macedonian

barely recovered her breath, while those present withdrew [?]. When she came to herself and her colour returned, her son the emperor asked her what had happened to her and why such a sudden faint had come over her. She could barely collect herself from the turmoil in her mind. She said: “My lord and my child, the man your father said would destroy our family is this man you call Basil. For this man has the signs that your father said the one who would succeed us would have. When I took in the whole matter and saw ruin as though it were before my eyes, I was shaken and fainted.” The emperor took away his mother's fear, calmed her and comforted her. “You have judged well [?], mother,” he said. “This man is an unlettered and very simple fellow. He has nothing but strength, like Samson of old, and nothing else. He is like some Anak or Nimrod raised up in our own days. So have no fear of him and harbour no evil suspicion.” And so on that occasion Basil, guarded by God, came safely through that wave.

16. At that time the emperor's parakoimomenos was the eunuch Damian, a patrician and a Slav by race. Out of devotion to his master he often spoke to the emperor about various people who were not managing affairs as they should. Above all he spoke about the emperor's uncle, Bardas the Caesar. He said that Bardas had drawn most of the power to himself and often went beyond what was proper. And so Damian overturned some of the Caesar's arrangements by showing the emperor that matters actually stood otherwise. For this reason the Caesar, urged on by his close friends and loyal advisers and counsellors, plotted against Damian. He spread many slanders about him to the emperor and framed the charges plausibly. In this way he changed the emperor's mind and turned him from his goodwill toward Damian, until he persuaded him to remove Damian from his office. After Damian was driven out, the office stood vacant for some time. But when Providence drives events toward [?], prudence achieves nothing and cunning is caught in its own tricks. For the Caesar and many others were putting it about that this man or that would be promoted to the office, and were secretly working for it. Then, against all their hopes and after a long time, the emperor appointed Basil parakoimomenos. He also honoured him with the rank of patrician and married him to a wife who surpassed almost all noblewomen in bodily beauty, loveliness and decorum. She was the daughter of Inger, a man everyone spoke of at that time for his nobility and wisdom. When this had happened, and

the emperor's love for Basil grew day by day, the Caesar saw it and was stung by envy. He dreaded what was to come and often abused and blamed those who had advised and urged him to slander Damian. He called them fools and bad counsellors. “I was wrong to listen to them,” he said. “I drove out a fox and brought in a lion in its place, to [?] and devour all of us.” Soon afterwards Emperor Michael set out on campaign against Crete with his uncle Bardas the Caesar. The Caesar was handling affairs more arrogantly and issuing his orders more imperiously, and frequent, unceasing slanders against him began to be reported to Emperor Michael every day. They came to Kepoi, a place on the coast of the Thrakesians near the Maeander. There, whether by chance or by design, the emperor's pavilion (or kortē) was pitched on a low, level spot, while the Caesar's was on a high and conspicuous one. Those who had long resented and hated the Caesar seized on this as a plausible pretext and [made] many [accusations] against him. They said that he was already behaving insolently and openly insulting the emperor. Not content with everything else, they said, he was eager to outdo the emperor even in this, so that the emperor's tent would look low and humble while his own was conspicuous and lofty. The emperor was persuaded by them and moved to plot against Bardas and to consider how to do away with him. He could not openly say or declare anything against him, because Bardas was almost his equal in rank and a partner in his rule. Everyone also feared Bardas's faction of associates and his party. All the officials and generals were attached to him and looked to him rather than to the emperor, since he paid closer attention to affairs and arranged each matter as seemed best. Above all, his son Antigonos, proconsul and patrician, was at that time domestic of the imperial schools. Still, the emperor had many who shared his plan and promised to carry out the killing. At dawn, as usual, the Caesar came to the emperor's tent so that they could discuss the business at hand, even though evil omens had appeared to him. The emperor thought this was the right moment to do away with him. With a nod he signalled to the patrician Symbatios, the logothete of the drome, to go out and bring in the men who were to kill Bardas. Symbatios was the Caesar's son-in-law, married to his daughter, and he was party to the emperor's plot against him. He went out and made the agreed signal, which was to seal his own [?] with the sign of the cross. But since

[?] “the uncle and Caesar.” 69 “of the” omitted in P. 70 “and” omitted in P. 71 Perhaps “they make many slanders against him,” or “they put forward many [charges]” [?]. 73 “which was the sign of the cross” omitted in P.

the men were perhaps faint-hearted, they lost their nerve. Standing at the very edge of the terrible deed, they grew dizzy at how great an act it was, and time was being lost. The emperor did not know what to do. Through one of the palace chamberlains he learned that they had cowered in fear and were putting off the attempt, a deed that truly called for a daring mind and a brave, bold spirit. He sent a trusted member of his household to Basil, the patrician and parakoimomenos, and fearfully told him: “If you do not quickly put heart into the men made ready for the deed and urge them to set to work at once, I know for certain that he will kill me immediately. It is impossible that what I have plotted against him will escape his notice, and then it will be you who appear to be my murderers and slayers.” When Basil heard this, he was in anguish lest something happen to the emperor. He quickly made the cowards bold and the trembling confident, and stirred them up to carry out the emperor's will. As though filled with fury, they suddenly burst into the emperor's tent. The Caesar realized that the rush was aimed at him, as indeed it was, and he leapt up and clung to the emperor's feet.
