The assassins dragged him from there and slaughtered him before the emperor's feet. It was the twenty-first day of the month of April, in the fourteenth indiction. The emperor at once broke off the campaign and returned to the capital.

18. Providence was skilfully leading Basil toward what it intended. Immediately after the return from the campaign, the emperor adopted him as his son, for he had no children of his own at all, and honoured him with the most splendid rank of magistros. At this the logothete Symbatios was bursting with envy. He could not bear to watch the man he envied making no small advance every day. He resigned the post he had held until then, saying he could not live in the capital, and asked for the command of the Ionians, that is, the Thrakesians. The emperor granted his request and appointed him strategos of that theme. A short time passed, and affairs were shaking dangerously. The government was tottering and looking for someone to take charge, because the emperor was occupied with other things rather than knowing how to handle affairs as he should. Before, much of this had gone unnoticed, because the Caesar, as partner in rule, had always handled urgent matters, and the affairs of state and the whole burden of secular administration had rested almost entirely on him. [?] There were outcries and grumbling against the emperor from the senate, from the citizen body and from almost everyone in the administration who handled public affairs, and also from the armies

[?] and of the whole populace of the city. When the emperor learned of this through his closest associates, he came to his senses a little, if only briefly. He recognized not only his own neglect and indolence in public affairs but also his unfitness and simplicity, and, fearing an uprising or revolt by the people, he decided to take on a partner in affairs and in power. Not long before he had adopted Basil as his son, and he knew that Basil surpassed most men not only in courage but also in understanding, and was able to make up for his own shortcomings in steering the ship of the world. With divine Providence also guiding him to this, he settled his mind on [?] Basil emperor. And so, with God lending a hand to the plan and to the deed, on the very day of holy Pentecost, when the Paraclete came from the Father to the disciples of Christ our God, in the renowned church named after the Wisdom of God, Basil was crowned with the imperial crown: by the hand of Michael, who was then reigning, but by the vote and judgment of Christ, who reigns forever. It was the twenty-sixth of the month of May, in the fourteenth indiction by the Roman reckoning.

When Symbatios, who was then in command of the theme assigned to him, learned what had happened, he could not, being human, bear the envy that consumed him. Finding a partner in his madness in the patrician Peganes, who commanded the theme of Opsikion, they turned their eyes toward rebellion and resolved in their recklessness to raise [?]. Persuading the troops under them as well, they put their plans into action. They acclaimed Michael as emperor, so that they might win over the masses by this and not seem to be lifting the heel of rebellion against the sovereign, while they reviled Basil and heaped countless insults upon him. Swaggering in this madness through the summer season, they burned many estates belonging to the magnates of the capital, and seized in the harbors and burned not a few ships of those sailing to the imperial city. But when winter came, they broke up, as the partners in their venture slipped away secretly, a few at a time. Seeing this, the leaders of the drama tried to find safety in flight. Symbatios took refuge in the fortress called Plate Petra, and Peganes held Kotyaeion. But they gained nothing from this scheme, for they were captured by the emperor's forces and brought to him in chains. They found him staying at the palace of Saint Mamas. When he saw them, he reproached and reviled them at length for their madness and disorder, first punished them with a sound flogging, and then handed them over to the

penalties of the law. Symbatios was deprived of both eyes and one hand and sent into exile; Peganes too had his eyes put out and his nose slit with a sword, and he too was sent into exile. Yet when the noble emperor Basil received sole power, he recalled them from banishment and honored them with the gifts they had held before the revolt. He showed not a trace of resentment toward them, often had them share his table, consoled them with words, and by doing them good in deed made it easier for them to bear the misfortune their folly had brought on them.

19. But that came later. At that time the prediction and prophecy made three hundred and fifty years earlier by Isaac, the most clear-sighted of priests and monks, was fulfilled. He too was descended from the Arsacids, and he learned through a vision that after that span of time one of the descendants of Arsaces would ascend to the scepter of the Roman empire. The event answered the prayers of those in high office, of the whole people, of the army and its generals, and of all the multitudes under Roman rule in every land and city. For all prayed that a man should take charge of affairs who had himself experienced a humbler lot, and who knew the blows dealt to the poor by the powerful, the unjust seizures they suffered at their hands, the virtual uprooting of the humbler folk, and their enslavement by their own countrymen. All these things had flourished under Michael's reign, because the emperor was more occupied with other matters than willing to attend to such things.

20. Or rather, since I have come to this point in my account, I think I should pause the history of the emperor Basil for a little and, going back, show as briefly as possible what kind of life the emperor Michael led, what sort of pursuits he enjoyed, and on what he squandered his time, all his energy, and the public funds. Thus anyone who wishes may reason from this and know that it was clearly a divine decree that called Basil to rule (for affairs could not have stood as they then were), and that afterwards Michael himself whetted the swords against himself, sharpened the hands of those who killed him, and provoked them to his own slaughter. So far had he strayed from what was fitting, so wildly had he given himself over in frenzy to every lawless deed, so thoroughly had he made a mockery of divine things and outraged the laws of the state and of nature alike. He gathered about him an impious troupe of lewd, foul, and utterly wicked men, dishonored the dignity of imperial majesty, and the wretch spent his days in revels, drunkenness, lewd loves, and shameful stories, and also among charioteers, horses, and chariots, and the madness and derangement that comes of them,

and he poured out the public funds unsparingly on such men. And the most outrageous thing of all: he mocked and jeered at the very symbols of our faith. He set up mimes and buffoons from his own circle as counterfeits of the venerable priests, and made these sacred things an object of derision, mockery, and laughter. I will relate a few of these things, not many, so that from the few you may know also the [?]

21. That he was a chariot driver and charioteer, sitting on the chariot behind the horses in charioteer's dress and competing with his rivals around the turns of the racecourse, both inside the imperial city and the palace and outside it at the imperial residence by the church of the martyr Mamas; that he spent vast sums on these things, so that the soldiers' funds became show money and the wealth of the Romans was poured out from the battle lines onto stage dances and idle chatter; that the imperial treasures were carried off prodigally and in floods on lewd and lawless revels and dissolute loves—all this I think I shall pass over, since it is well known and plain to all. But how he made sport of divine things, naming one of the foul and lewd effeminates in his company patriarch and appointing eleven others of them as metropolitans, with himself making up the number twelve—this I will relate. He bestowed the title of patriarch on that accursed and most abominable Gryllos, adorned him with a gold-embroidered and resplendent archiepiscopal robe, and placed an omophorion on him. As has been said, he decked out eleven others from that same council of like-minded men in the rank of metropolitans, and named himself the twelfth, archbishop of Koloneia. He gave each of them a lyre to carry under his priestly vestments and ordered them to play them underneath. In this way, mocking and making a dance of it with them, he performed the sacred rite and liturgy, as it were—the most abominable among the utterly abominable, the accursed among the profane. When a supposedly mystical prayer was being said, the lyres had to play softly beneath; when the time called for a priestly exclamation or the people's response, the lyres had to be struck loudly with the plectrum and ring out, so that their melody could be heard far off. Then they took the sacred vessels, made of silver and gold and adorned with precious stones and gleaming pearls, which had often served in the divine mysteries, put mustard and vinegar into them, and so gave communion to their like, amid much laughter, filthy words, and abominable and disgusting gestures. So much for that.

22. Once, when the most holy patriarch Ignatius, with his whole ecclesiastical escort and order, was going out in a litany procession before the city and making his way to a certain holy

church with the customary sacred chanting and ceremony, it happened that the impious Gryllos, the emperor's patriarch, wearing priestly vestments and riding on a donkey, came toward them from the opposite direction with his still more impious metropolitans and all his theatrical and satyric troupe and company, chanting and singing, stage-fashion, things that suited their deeds. When they came near, they hoisted their phelonia onto their shoulders, struck their lyres more vigorously, sang lewd words and songs in counterpoint to the tune of the sacred chant, leaping like Pan and the satyrs and clashing cymbals, and, sneering at the priests and the high priest as their rivals, they carried through their diabolical dance and procession. When the holy high priest inquired and learned who they were, by whom they had been assembled, and for what purpose, he groaned deeply and wept over their ringleader and the one responsible. With tears he besought God to stop such blasphemy and outrage and to scatter the impious [?], so that holy things might not be profaned nor the mysteries and sacred rites be held up to ridicule. Then, keeping to the hymn in hand, he continued on his way.

23. On another occasion the senseless and deranged emperor staged something like this, to belittle the celebrated patriarch Ignatius and to make a fool of his own mother. He sat on the imperial throne in the resplendent Chrysotriklinos and seated the most shameful Gryllos, in his archiepiscopal vestments, very close beside him, as if in the person of the true patriarch, and paid him the honor fitting a high priest of God. He had him hide his abominable beard with the covering on his head, and then sent word to his own mother through one of the chamberlains: "The most holy patriarch Ignatius is sitting here with me. If you wish to receive his blessing, come and receive it along with me." She, being a pious and God-loving woman with great longing and fervent faith toward the most holy Ignatius, hurried out eagerly as soon as she heard. Out of reverence she could not even look at him directly, and being free of all malice and suspicion and suspecting nothing wrong, she fell at the feet, as she thought, of that holy high priest and begged him to pray for her. But that utterly foul man rose a little from his seat, turned his back to her, let out an asinine noise from his loathsome bowels, and said to her: "So that you may not say, lady, that we did not deem you worthy even of this." The emperor burst out laughing, and the utterly profane fellow himself laughed enormously, and they babbled a great deal, or rather raved most senselessly in their deranged minds. Then the empress realized the fabrication and deception,

and, groaning deeply over what was happening and hurling many curses at her son, she finally said to him: "See, wicked child, God has withdrawn his hand from you, and you have been given a depraved mind to do what is not fitting." Having said this, she withdrew lamenting and wailing and tearing out her hair. Such were the youthful exploits of the noble emperor, and such his piety and reverence toward divine things and holy men.

24. Since such things, and many worse, were done by him every day throughout his reign, and since even after taking Basil as partner and raising him up he kept on with the same behavior, Basil, seeing and hearing this, was deeply distressed and grieved and despaired of his own life. Wishing to bring every possible help and to leave nothing undone that seemed to lead to amendment, he first tried through others to turn him from such things and bring him back to what was proper. Then he once took courage and himself, with a well-meaning mind and intent, admonished the emperor, to draw him away, if possible, from such impieties. He spoke to him in a humble and submissive manner, as follows: "It is right, my lord and emperor, that I, who have enjoyed so many benefits and gifts from you, should propose what is needful, suggest what is best, and remind you of what is profitable and salutary. We are hated, know it, my lord, we are hated" (he included himself so as not to give offense, though he had no share in any of these improprieties) "by the whole city and by the senate, and we have come to be accursed by the high priests of God, and all slander and revile us. And even if we count what comes from men as nothing, we must at least dread God's indignation and fear lest we experience his anger and wrath." But in saying this he was sowing on rocks, talking to the seashore, and, as it were, trying to wash an Ethiopian white. So indelible had wickedness become in him, and so deaf was he to every saving word, stopping his ears like an asp against charms. Not only did he not change for the better; he now even hated Basil and turned away from him, and with his companions in revelry and orgy he slandered and sneered at these words, hinting at his estrangement from him and then showing it more plainly. When those foul and accursed men perceived this, they bestirred themselves and lined up against Basil and plausibly devised slanders, calling his dignity arrogance, naming his abstention from pleasures ill will, and his refusal to sin with them contempt. "For how," they said, "could he love you, who does not delight in what you delight in, nor joins in eagerly providing you with the things that please [?]

26. Yet it was not only the gentle, care-loosing, luxurious, slack, soft, and unhinged side of drunkenness that he had taken from Dionysus, giver of joy, whom he fancied himself imitating and strove to imitate. He also had, like that same god in his aspect as Raw-Eater, something of the Furies and the Titans, and many a comic night-long revel ended in a tragedy of disasters. For, crazed by drink and lawlessly carried away by his good fortune, he ran aground on every kind of impiety. When he was wholly given over to unmixed wine and drunkenness and had completely lost his wits, he turned to murders and to strange punishments and slaughters of innocent men, and commanded his servants: "Take so-and-so and so-and-so and hand them over to the executioner; gouge out this man's eyes; cut off that man's hands and feet. Let this one be beheaded, and let that one be burned alive." The servants took them, but knowing that he was out of his mind when he pronounced these sentences, they kept them in custody and did not subject them to the punishments. Often, however, if it happened to be someone they disliked and hated, they made use of the imperial command and punished the innocent man as though condemned. Then that miserable wretch, not even knowing where he was, was laid on the imperial couch by the chamberlains and surrendered like a slave to sleep, the neighbor of death. At dawn, when sleep had barely dispersed the wine fumes and that thick fog from his brain, he would wake remembering nothing of the evening, and often asked for some of those whom he had condemned in his drunkenness and handed over to death. When he learned from the guards and servants what he had decreed against them the evening before, he repented and groaned. Sometimes those he sought were found; at other times his repentance for his unholy deeds was useless to him, because those handed over had been killed. Then, when evening came again and the drinking with those accursed men pressed recklessly on far into the night, in deeds and words, he fell into the same state again. Who, hearing and seeing these things, even if he had a heart of stone or were utterly without feeling, would not have been moved to anger and burned at last to avenge those who were perishing without cause? I think not even David, the meekest of all men, would have tolerated such drunken outrage from this scum; for forbearance here is reckoned folly and callousness, not long-suffering.

27. Now that nearly all the stored-up funds had run out, spent on such things, it had become inevitable that all those in high office would be openly slaughtered and their property confiscated, so that the emperor might have the means to lavish gifts on charioteers, prostitutes, and lewd men. For nine hundred and seventy kentenaria of coined [?]

…of gold, apart from silver, both unminted and coined, which his father Theophilus had left stored in the imperial treasury; and further, his mother Theodora had added thirty more, completing the sum of a thousand centenaria. Yet in not even fourteen full years from the time he received power over everything, he squandered and spent it all, so that after his death nothing was found except three centenaria and no more. And how could it not run out, even if it had flowed in from rivers, when it was scattered so wantonly and prodigally? Once, when he stood sponsor at the font for the child of a charioteer called Cheilas, he presented him with a whole centenarium. And then there was the patrician Himerius, whom the emperor himself called Choirus (“Pig”) because of the wildness of his looks [?], though he deserved the name rather for the swinish and filthy character of his life. This man was once talking obscenely in the emperor's presence and indulging in the buffooneries of the stage, and, being utterly shameless and shrinking from nothing disgraceful, let loose from his foul belly an unbridled noise, so heavy and violently gusting that it even put out the lamp that was burning. For this the emperor honored him with a gift of fifty pounds, as though he had accomplished some labor of Hercules. His gifts to others like him were just as excessive. Had he lavished such sums so readily on soldiers, champions and heroes, or on men distinguished in some other good thing, one would have taken them as signs of magnanimity, liberality and a generous character. But since they were senselessly squandered on mimes, charioteers, dancers, buffoons, flatterers and men full of every abomination, while not even an obol went to anything worthwhile, one would surely reckon them proofs of prodigality, drunken madness and folly. And when these funds were already running out, it became necessary, as has been said, for churches to be plundered, holy houses to be despoiled, and all who possessed more than others to be put to death and slaughtered for their money. For all these reasons the most eminent of those in office and the sensible part of the senate conspired together, and through the soldiers who guard the emperors' bedchamber they did away with him in the palace of the holy martyr Mamas, as he passed insensibly from sleep into death because of his excessive drunkenness. For just as people kill scorpions and vipers as soon as they see them, before they can strike, because of the malice inherent in them, so too those who foresee danger from venomous and murderous men hasten to kill them before they can strike and destroy. So this man, having lived in this way, shamefully and ruinously both for himself and for the state, met an end to match, worthy of the life he had led.
