40. [P. 159] 28. Basil, who until then had held second place in it, was at once promoted to the rule of all. Sought by the honorable senate, the lower orders, the whole army and the city populace, and before all this by suppliant prayers, Basil was proclaimed autocrator. As soon as he came to the rule of all, he dedicated both himself and the reins of power to God, praying in these very words: “Christ, King, having received the kingship by your judgment, I dedicate both it and myself to you.” He immediately summoned the leaders of the senate and those foremost in rank, and with them he opened the treasury of the imperial palace; and out of all that great quantity of money nothing was found except three centenaria and no more, as I have already said a little earlier. The emperor then asked for the register of expenditure, and found it with an old eunuch, the protospatharius Basil. Having learned where the money had gone, he put the matter to the leading men for counsel. Their verdict, harmonious and unanimous, was that those who had wrongly received the money should return it to the public treasury. But the emperor, softening this excessive justice, ordered each of them to return half of what he had received to the imperial treasury. So it came about that those men, though unworthy of any largesse, still kept no small part of the gift, while three hundred centenaria were brought into the imperial treasury, from which the emperor began to meet urgent needs and to govern as he ought. 29. On the very day Basil came to sole rule, as if God were showing that Roman affairs were changing for the better, it happened that news of many victories reached this imperial city, and the rescue of a multitude of Christian captives was announced. So the emperor went in procession to the great church of God named after his Wisdom, and gave thanks to him for everything together; and on his return he celebrated the consulship and distributed much money to his subjects, not from public funds (for there were none) but from his own, which he had possessed before. His consort, the empress Eudocia, together with their sons Constantine and Leo, also celebrated the consulship and gave the citizens much money from her own resources. Although the emperor was at that time still short of money, as has been said, later on an ample abundance of other money came to him. This was partly because God, on account of his mercy toward the poor and his justice, was pleased to let many treasures hidden under the earth come to light in his days, and partly from the gold found in the Eidikon. The previous emperor Michael had melted down the finest works of art for this, I mean the so-called golden plane tree, the two griffins of solid gold, and the two hammered gold

[?] the organ of solid gold, and various other works of gold plate for the table, and the imperial and augustal robes and the garments belonging to the great dignitaries, all of them woven with gold [?]. All these he had melted down and meant to spend on his own pleasures; but since he was snatched away first, the gold that was found [?] stamped proved useful in every way to the emperor. For, as the saying goes, “There is need of money, and without it nothing needful can be done.” But this happened later. 30. At that time, since Providence had raised Basil to sit at the helm of government, he immediately strove from the very starting line, as they say, to show himself worthy of the greatness of his office. He stayed awake at night and deliberated by day, turning over every thought and weighing every plan, so that he might be the cause of some good to all his subjects and so that affairs might undergo a great and manifest change for the better. First, he chose the best men of all with the greatest care [?] and appointed them to the offices. For these men, both by their own nature, since they were the best, and because of the emperor's close oversight, the first task and endeavor before all others was to keep their own hands clean of every kind of gain; next, to honor justice above all virtues and to make equity prevail everywhere; to see that the poor were not oppressed by the rich and that no one was unjustly subjected to any penalty, but to rescue the poor and needy from the hand of those stronger than they; and little by little to revive people whom he knew to be fainting and failing because of what had gone before, and, restoring their strength, to strive to bring everyone back to their former prosperity. Because of their inclination to the better from the outset (for such indeed were the men chosen), and because of the ruler's zeal in these matters [P. 161] and his vigilant watch in every direction, they eagerly vied to outdo one another in everything that was needed. So all injustice was at once driven out from everywhere, justice spoke freely, and the hands that had once reached out after other people's property, more numerous than those of Briareus, seemed numbed, as though paralyzed. And the weak

…each could work his own plot of land without fear and enjoy the fruit of his own vineyard, and no one dared to take another's ancestral olive and fig tree into his own power, but each rested in their accustomed, ancestral shade. Such, then, was the pious emperor's conduct toward all the people under his hand in the lands, places and cities of his dominion. But if some knot of wickedness, as it were, had grown hard and firm in one of the local officials, so that it could not be changed or entirely cut out, then through the emperor

himself it was either changed or [?] received its cure in some way. For this most excellent man, determined to root out injustice entirely from every quarter, issued decrees everywhere and sent them out to every province. By these every payment that until then had seemed reasonable because of a wicked custom of long standing was abolished and cut off, and all equality before the law and all justice seemed to return to life as if from some exile abroad, and to dwell among men. 31. He also took men suited to judging, attested as having sufficient learning and as being, in disposition and choice, pious and incorruptible. He raised and lifted them above the ranks of lower grade, welcomed them with annual salaries and the provision of other allowances and honors, and installed them in almost every street and every holy residence. In particular there was the building called the Chalke, which of old had been most splendid and admirable, but through time and the negligence of rulers, and perhaps also through some fires, had fallen apart in many places, and its roof had suffered. He himself, at the cost of labor and expense [?], cleared it, restored it and made it a public court, more august than the Areopagus and the Heliaea. Nor did he provide that those who said they had been wronged [P. 162] should obtain justice only through the selection and appointment of judges; he also provided daily food for those who from time to time were forced to come to the capital because of violence from the more powerful. For fearing that, for lack of necessities, some might often leave the city before their case reached its conclusion, he set aside a sufficient revenue from which plaintiffs were maintained until they received the judge's verdict. And these were not the only measures he devised for the utter destruction of injustice: he also devoted himself to this task. Whenever he happened to be free from campaigns and from dealing with embassies from every quarter, he would go down from the palace and sit in the place called the Genikon, so named, it seems, because people run together to it from every quarter. There, with great labor and constant care, he examined those who had been wronged by the collectors of public taxes, as often happens because of the size of the empire, and who took refuge in that tribunal as in a common prytaneum and laid their complaints before it. In this way he came to the aid of the wronged, and through lawful punishment he stopped the wrongdoers from daring to do such things any longer. Some time later, it is said, he once went down to this place to vindicate the wronged; and when there happened to be no one bringing a complaint, he suspected that certain people were preventing others from coming in to him, and sent his bodyguards

[?] to search many parts of the city to see whether anyone had a complaint against anyone. When they came back and said they had found no one anywhere complaining against anyone, they say that noble man wept for joy and so gave thanks to God. He saw, too, that wicked people found an opportunity for wrongdoing in the fact that the ancients, for brevity's sake, had used fractions of numbers, such as halves, sixths or twelfths, in the records of tax collection. Wishing to remove this pretext as well from those who wanted to do wrong, he decreed that the tax registers should be written in plain letters, which even country people can read, with the figures for the amount written out in full and clearly. He met the cost of this from his own resources, for the paper, the writing and the scribes, so that the poor might not be wronged. Such and so great is this proof of his care for his subjects, and of his wish that no one should be wronged by anyone. [P. 163] Such, then, was he in civil and public affairs. 32. Nor did he wish to seem to neglect the churches of God. (For since they too are contained, as it were, in the ship of the world, they too fall under the ruler's providence, and his all the more, since he loved God and had great reverence for divine things.) He saw that the churches too were in a kind of tossing and turmoil, because they had shared in the common ruin under his predecessor: their lawful head had been driven from his own see and flock, and another had been brought in in his place. He did not neglect these matters either, but by means of a general synod and assembly of God's high priests from every quarter he stilled the storm in the churches as far as possible. He confirmed the holy seventh synod held before this, consigned the remaining iconoclast heretics to anathema, and canonically restored to the Church her true Bridegroom and to the children their Father, while ordering the one who had been brought in in his place to remain in retirement until the Lord should take him to himself. Thus well and finely he set the affairs of the Church in order, and by his own zeal and forethought [brought] it too such calm as was possible.

33. He also found that the civil laws were full of obscurity and confusion, because good and bad were mixed together, I mean because laws that had been repealed and laws still in force were recorded together without distinction. These too he corrected suitably, as was fitting and possible: he removed the useless repealed laws, cleared up the mass of valid ones, and gathered the former boundless mass into chapters, as in a synopsis, so that it could easily be remembered. 34. But since envy always springs up alongside good things,

as worms do above all in the sweetest woods, and since the wicked demons, envying worldly prosperity and plenty, try through wicked men to disturb the course of good things, a plot was devised against him too by such men: Symbatius and George, with a band of abominable and impious men, armed themselves even for murder. But God would by no means permit or allow wickedness to recover so quickly from its defeat and drive good order and justice from the earth, and their wickedness [P. 164] was exposed by one of the conspirators. Proofs followed, and the extreme penalty of the laws hung over them, that is, confiscation and the loss of all their possessions, and the loss of life itself as well. But the noble emperor's clemency limited the punishment for the time being to the putting out of the eyes of the ringleaders of the wicked plot. He would have moderated the penalty still further, had he not known that extreme clemency toward these men would encourage others to imitate them, and that he would then be forced into an even heavier retribution. So by this penalty he gave them time for repentance and brought the rest of the wicked to their senses. And wishing to check still further the impulses of those who unjustly sought another's death, and to take away all their hope, he raised to imperial rank the eldest of his sons, Constantine and Leo, who were already being brought up and educated in royal fashion and shone in every virtue fit for rule. In this way he was, as it were, putting down more and stronger roots for his rule, and [?] the noble shoots of the empire upon it.

35. But since I have reached this part of the narrative, I wish now to speak about his other children as well, and how he made pious provision for each of them. For like the pious and blessed men of old, or rather even beyond them, God showed him to be the father of many fine children. After some time, then, he also gave a share of the crown to Alexander, his third son. The youngest of them, Stephen, he offered to God as Abraham offered Isaac, and enrolled him in the Church of God [?]. His female offspring, equal in number to the male, he consecrated in the holy convent of the all-praised martyr Euphemia, and dedicated them to God as an acceptable gift and offering, adorning them in habit and dress like the virgins who are betrothed, pure and undefiled, to the immortal Bridegroom, Christ. Although these things happened later, let them be set down here together, joined in the narrative as they are joined by nature to the four brothers. 36. When, then, his household affairs were in good order, in keeping with a pious and God-pleasing purpose, and his fervent concern for the whole state was calling him to campaigns beyond the frontiers

as well, so that by his own toils, courage and nobility he might extend the borders of the empire and push the enemy back [P. 165] and drive them farther off, he did not neglect these matters either. First, the military rolls had dwindled because the allowances and imperial rations given to the soldiers had been cut back [?]; these he refilled by levying and selecting new men, and he strengthened them by supplying and providing what was needed. Then he trained them in tactical exercises, made them experienced in the struggle of war through continual toil, and accustomed them to pay the greatest attention to good order and to care about obedience; and so, with them, he campaigned against the barbarians on behalf of his fellow countrymen, kinsmen and subjects. For he knew that no one can know even one of the mechanical and common crafts before learning it, and that no one has ever succeeded without a teacher even as a shoemaker, let alone in one of the more serious arts. And if anyone who wished could know the science or art of war without learning and sufficient experience, then those who labored long over this subject in their tactical treatises had no sense but were talking nonsense, and so were the greatest emperors and generals, who set up many trophies over many enemies, and none of whom ever dared to throw an untaught and untrained army against an enemy battle line. But it is impossible for one who has not learned to know, or for one who has not practiced and trained to fight. For this reason this noble man first trained and equipped the military units, mixed the newly levied troops with the old, and with fitting provisions and gifts strengthened [?] their sinews and braced their right hands; and so, with them, he attacked the enemy, set up many trophies and won countless victories. I will relate these briefly. 37. When he had found leisure to set the city in order and had had time for affairs of state, as spring began to shine he took up arms and [?] with the military rolls, believing that a true ruler ought to face danger ahead of his own people and willingly take on toils and hardships so that all his subjects might live without fear. At that time the leader of Tephrike [P. 166], whom they called Chrysocheir, being reputed to excel in courage and intelligence, was greatly troubling the land and people of the Romans; every day he took many of the country people captive, and he was proud and arrogant. So the emperor marched out against him and the city under his rule. That haughty and bold man, faced with the bravery of the advancing army and the intelligence and courage of its

…ruler did not dare to resist him openly. Instead he withdrew, having decided only to guard and fortify his own city. So the emperor advanced, with no one at all to stop him, plundering, ravaging, cutting down and burning all the lands and townships under Chrysocheir, and gathering endless booty and captives. He also attacked the city of Tephrike itself and tried to take it by skirmishing and a siege of no great length. But he saw that it was well secured and hard to capture, because of the strength of its walls, the great number of barbarians in it and its plentiful supplies. Besides, in a very short time the great size of his army had stripped everything outside the city, and the provisions were nearly used up. So he gave up any lengthy persistence in the siege. He sacked the fortresses around it, Abara, Spathe and some others, moved his whole army away from there unharmed, and returned, as has been said, with abundant spoils and slaves. 38. When the other city of the Ishmaelites, which they call Taranta, saw the great slaughter of the people in Tephrike, it sent envoys asking to obtain peace and to be enrolled among the allies. The most mighty emperor showed as much gentleness toward those who submitted as he showed courage toward those who opposed him. He gave way to the embassy and granted peace to those who asked for it, and from then on he had them as allies instead of enemies. After this many others came over to him, among them a certain Armenian, Kourtikios, who then held Lokana and constantly harassed the frontiers of the Roman realm. He fled to the emperor and submitted his city, his arms and his people to him, for he admired the emperor's mildness joined with courage and with power…

39. While the enemy kept their minds fixed on him, watching which way he would turn so that they too could join forces wherever there was pressure, he sent a raiding party of picked warriors against the place called Zapetra. They hurried through the narrow parts of the road, fell upon the city itself and took it at the first assault. They slaughtered many in it, seized many captives and much booty, and brought out men who had long been held in its prison. Then they burned the lands lying beyond, sacked Samosata, and in the same rush crossed the Euphrates. There was no one at all to stop them, because the enemy were encamped opposite the emperor. After taking many captives and spoils, they returned to the emperor. He was still staying by the river Zarnouch, where Keramision is. He seemed to be idle there, but in fact he was most wisely accomplishing such things through his subordinates. 40. Setting out from there, the emperor, with his whole army,

took the road leading toward Melitene. When he reached the banks of the Euphrates, he saw it flooding and spreading out like a sea in the summer season. He thought it ignoble, and unworthy of the power he had with him, to sit waiting for a crossing until the river fell. So he decided to span it with a bridge, and eagerly made everything ready for the work. He wanted to ease his soldiers' toil and persuade them to bear their labors readily. At the same time he wanted to wear himself out in labors he chose, so that if labors he had not chosen should often befall him, he would not find them strange or be unused to them. So he joined the soldiers in the work very eagerly, carrying the heaviest loads on his own shoulders to the bridge. One could then see three soldiers together barely managing to carry a load as large as the one the emperor carried with ease. Having crossed the Euphrates in this way, he at once sacked the fortress called Rhapsakion. Separately he ordered the Chaldians and Koloneians to overrun the land between the Euphrates and the Arsinos. Through them he took much booty and many captives, and he sacked the fortresses of Kourtikios, Chachon, Amer, the one called Mourinix, and Abdela. He himself attacked Melitene, which at that time was full of brave men and held a great multitude of barbarians. They came out to meet him before the city with barbarian war cries and snorting defiance. But he showed his own valor, so that not only his own men but even the enemy were plainly amazed at his courage and skill. He engaged the enemy prudently and with youthful vigor alike. He showed himself noble in hand-to-hand fighting and outstanding in daring, and was seen to be bold and undaunted in the face of danger. He was the first to rout the men drawn up against him, with great slaughter. Then his men, each against the foes before him, pursued them and cut them down all the way to the city. As a result the plain before the city was strewn with many corpses and the water before the wall was mixed with blood. Many were taken alive, and others deserted of their own accord out of fear. The rest were shut up in the city and completely prevented from coming out again. The emperor intended at this point to set up engines, send for every kind of siege equipment, and show deeds of daring and nobility in assaulting the walls. But he saw that the city was strong in its circuit of walls and hard to capture because of the great number of men defending it from the wall. He also learned from the deserters that it had a great abundance of provisions and did not fear a long siege. So he left there and attacked the land of the Manichaeans. He cut down its trees, set the houses on fire and destroyed everything in his path. He burned and razed their fortress called Argaous, and those of Koutakios, of Stephen, and Rhachat. Then

he treated all the people under him with great kindness and honored each of those who had distinguished themselves with prizes for valor. Then he returned to the imperial city with many spoils and crowns of victory. He entered through the Golden Gate, like the emperors of old in glorious Rome who celebrated their triumphs, and received the people's acclamations and praises for his victory. He went straight from the road, just as he was, to the great sanctuary of the Wisdom of God, to offer his prayers and due thanksgiving. There the patriarch of that time crowned him with the crown of victory, and he returned to the palace. 41. Once again the cares of government took hold of him. He gave suitable answers to embassies from various nations. He rejoiced for a short while with his children and his wife, and visited the holy and divine churches of the city and offered his prayers. Then he was occupied again, as usual, with the administration of the state and with lawsuits, showing care and sleepless forethought for his subjects. Yet he did not stop going every day into the holy and divine church and beseeching the Lord. He put forward the chief commander Michael and the prophet Elijah as his mediators with God, praying that he might not depart this life before he saw the destruction of Chrysocheir and planted three arrows in his abominable head. And this did happen later. In the following year the Chrysocheir mentioned above invaded the lands of the Romans and plundered them, and the emperor, as usual, sent the Domestic of the Schools against him. The Domestic set out, taking the whole Roman army with him. Since he was afraid to oppose Chrysocheir openly, face to face, the Roman forces for the time followed him at some distance. They checked his separate raids and did not let his men scatter over the country without fear. So the barbarian, accomplishing some things and failing in others, and with the season now calling him home, began to think of going back. As he was returning to his own land with abundant booty, the Domestic of the Schools detached two of his generals, those of Charsianon and of the Armeniakon, each with his own force. They were to accompany and follow Chrysocheir as far as Bathyrrhyax. From there, if he sent an army against Roman territory, they were to report this to the Domestic. But if he went straight back without turning aside and slipped into his own lair, they were to let him go and return to the Domestic. 42. In the evening the barbarian army reached the place called Bathyrrhyax and camped below at the foot of the mountain. The Roman generals occupied the heights above it and watched for what would happen. Then a quarrel arose about who held first place, a rivalry among the soldiers of the two themes and

the taxiarchs and company commanders. The men of Charsianon claimed for themselves the highest distinction in strength and valor, while the Armeniakoi, for their part, would not allow them to take first place in courage in war. As the rivalry went further and their spirits grew heated, the leading men of the Armeniakon contingent are said to have spoken thus: "Why do we each boast in vain words and brag to no purpose, when we can show by deeds the valor we are disputing? The enemy are not far off. It is possible for the bravest to be revealed in action, and for the better men to be judged by their courage in hand-to-hand fighting." The generals heard such words and saw the army's eagerness and zeal for valor. They also considered the advantage of the terrain: they would be attacking from higher ground against men encamped on the plain. So they divided the force in two. It was decided that the picked part of it, up to six hundred men, would attack the barbarian army together with the generals themselves. The rest of the Roman force, which was small enough to be counted easily, they gathered somewhere up on the heights to give the impression of a great multitude. They gave these men a signal for the right moment: when the first group attacked the enemy, they too were to raise a terrifying shout with a mighty war cry and trumpets, with the mountains themselves echoing. The first group then put on their full armor and secretly by night approached the enemy camp. Before dawn, when the sun had not yet fully passed through the hemisphere beneath the earth, they raised a loud battle hymn, shouted together, "The Cross has conquered!" and fell upon the enemy, while the rest shouted with them from the mountain. At once the barbarians were struck with terror by this unexpected attack. They had no chance to form up or to see how large the attacking multitude was, nor could they see any other means of saving themselves on the spot, so they rushed to flight. Surely it was the emperor's persistent prayer that terrified them and drove them to destruction. The pursuing Romans kept calling out to the generals who were not there, to the tagmata and to the Domestic of the Schools, as had been arranged, and the fugitives were driven into even greater fear and confusion. So the pursuit went on for thirty miles, and the ground in between was strewn with countless dead. 43. At that time, it is said, that shameless and bold Chrysocheir was fleeing with a few of his men, and a certain Roman nicknamed Poulades was pursuing him. This man had once been a captive at Tephrike, and because he was witty and charming he had become a close acquaintance of Chrysocheir. When the barbarian saw him pursuing with such fervor and eagerness, he turned and said, "What harm have I done you, wretched Poulades, that you pursue me so madly, eager to kill me?"

He answered briefly: "I trust in God, patron, that I will repay you today for your kindnesses, and that is why I am pursuing you." The one went on ahead, as if his wits had been struck by God, desperate and cowardly, while the other followed with daring and youthful courage. Then the man being pursued came upon a deep ditch. His horse was afraid to leap it and buckled at the knees. While Chrysocheir's attention was on the ditch, Poulades struck him in the side with a lance. At once, reeling from the pain, he slid off his horse. One of his men, whose surname was Diakonitzes, threw himself from his own horse to tend his fallen master. He laid his master's head on his own knees and lamented what had happened. Meanwhile others came up to join Poulades. They leapt from their horses and cut off the head of Chrysocheir, who was already fainting and dying, and they counted Diakonitzes among the rest of the prisoners. So the enemy were defeated beyond all expectation and the Christians' pride was exalted, and Chrysocheir's head was swiftly sent to the emperor with the messengers of the joyful news. At that time he happened to be staying at the place called Petrion, where the convent in which his own daughters lived was located. When the head was brought to him, he remembered his prayers and with tears lifted the eye of his mind to the one who does the will of those who call upon him. He ordered a bow and arrows to be brought, quickly drew the string, and in plain view [?] shot three arrows at that murderous head, and did not miss even once. He thought this a fitting expiatory offering of the impious man, in return for the many tens of thousands he had destroyed in the many years of his rule. So the affairs of Chrysocheir and the power of Tephrike, which was flourishing at that time, came to such an end through the help of God, who was moved by the many supplications of Basil, who reigned piously. 44. Now the celebrated patriarch Ignatius had recently ended his life in holiness and in a manner pleasing to God. Rich in old age, surrounded by his virtues like a bodyguard, and called blessed by all, he exchanged the present life for a better one. Then the emperor rightly gave the Church back to the man who earlier had seemed to lay claim to it wrongly, and he lawfully and canonically installed the most wise Photius on the vacant throne of the queen of cities. Even before this he had never stopped treating Photius kindly and honoring him for his wisdom and virtue of every kind. Even though he had removed him from the throne, because he wished to put nothing ahead of justice, he still did everything he could to console him. So he gave him lodging in the palace and appointed him tutor and

teacher of his own children. In this way, as far as he was able, he let no one remain in distress. He treated everyone graciously and gently and did not neglect to console them in whatever way he could. 45. But although he was so fatherly and caring toward his subjects, he still had people who hated him, or rather who envied him and plotted against his life. The man called Kourkouas, who had apparently grown insolent through wealth and luxury, lusted after tyranny. He gathered a crowd of like-minded men as fellow conspirators and looked for a chance to attack. But one of the conspirators revealed the plot to the emperor in advance, and the wicked men were handed over to the laws. Yet again the noble emperor's love of mankind broke the severity of the laws and moderated the penalties. The ringleader had his eyes put out, while the rest were chastised humanely, with blows to the body and the shaving of their hair. So these men were brought back to order in a fatherly rather than a despotic way. 46. But his concern for the whole state, and the trophies still to be won, did not let him sleep. First there was the very strong fortress called Loulon, which was of the greatest use to the Roman realm. Through earlier excessive negligence and disregard of what was beneficial, it had been taken by the Hagarenes together with its garrison, and they had fortified it and held it because of the security its site offered. The emperor, by his own intelligence and care and by lavish gifts, applying both persuasion and force, removed it from barbarian control and brought it back under the former authority of the Romans. After this the fortress of Melouos also came over to him of its own accord and proclaimed the emperor its master. At that time he also sacked, through his generals, the city of the Manichaeans called Katabatala. But success won through others did not please him as much as it grieved him that the trophies were not being set up through his own toils and dangers. So he set out again, this time taking with him Constantine, the eldest of his sons. He wanted to give him, like a noble whelp, a taste of the enemy's blood, and to be his teacher himself in tactics and in bold presence of mind in danger. With him he set out against Syria. He reached Caesarea by Argaeus, the first city of the Cappadocians, and drew up the select troops under him in tactical order. He detached a body of them and sent them ahead as scouts and forerunners, while he himself followed behind with the heavy force. In this way the most vigorous part would lead like a sword in action, while the still sturdier force pressed on behind. These men swiftly passed through deserted country and

sacked the fortresses of Psilokastellon and Paramokastellon, enslaving those they caught in them. The inhabitants of the fortress called Phalakrou were struck with fear of the approaching force and went over to the emperor of their own accord. Abdallah, son of Amr, the emir of Anazarbos, had been barbarously bold while the emperor was far away. But now he sought safety in flight with the band of the Melitenians, thinking that his only sufficient security was to escape notice wherever on earth he had hidden himself. In the destruction caused by this campaign, Kaisou, also called Katasama, and Rhobam, also called Endelechone, were sacked, and at the same time Andalou and the place called Eremosykaia. At this time too, Semas, son of Tael, who held the rugged country of the Taurus and harassed the Roman frontiers with raids, fled to the emperor. 47. If we report such great deeds briefly and plainly, as if in passing, let no one be surprised, and let no one find fault. The narrative seems to imitate the speed of those deeds, and that is why it is so simple and rapid: those places were taken then, and the deeds completed, faster than they are now reported. Besides, much time has flowed by in between and the silence since then has, so to speak, dimmed the details of these deeds. We cannot know or report the formations of the battle lines, the approaches of the attacks, the extending and closing of the phalanxes, or the timely use of stratagems. So it is not possible to dwell on particulars and linger over them lovingly, which is how a narrative is filled out. As for things whose credibility rests on no witness, even if they are often told, we do not want to accept them without examination, lest we seem to ascribe to the emperor a made-up account of things that never happened. This is all the more so because, even while he was alive, he plainly did not welcome flattering words that crept in to please him. We are neither able nor at leisure to commit to writing even what everyone agrees on; we would hardly lengthen our account with matters that are doubtful. But let the account pull back and return to the path of the original narrative. 48. After this, then, the emperor crossed the river called Onopniktes and the Saros with his army and came to Koukousos. He burned the thickets there and made the impassable country passable by cutting down the trees, and so overcame the ambushes hidden in them. He reached Kallipolis and Padasia, and then, travelling along difficult roads, he dismounted and went through the narrow parts of the road on foot, encouraging the weaker men under him by his own toil. Then he attacked Germanikeia. All opposition at once gave way and shut itself up within the walls, and none of the enemy dared to come to blows, so everything around the city with fire

[?] and the fine places in front of the city, turning them into a plain of desolation, he arrived at Adata. The people of that city did not dare to fight in the open. They gathered inside the walls and resolved to endure the siege. So he [?] plundered the land in front of the city, sacked the nearby small town they called Geron and let it be looted, and once the spoils had made his soldiers keener for hard work, he attacked the walls themselves and brought his siege engines into play. Because of the weight of the army around him he had no small hope of taking the city by storm. But he saw that those inside bore what befell them without fear and were not troubled by the almost certain ruin of their homeland, so he asked what they were trusting in, since they seemed to take so little account of him. He learned from one of the inhabitants that they had received full assurance from one of their holy men, who knew it either by some more divine knowledge or by a scientific method, that it was fated for this city to be taken not by you who are now besieging them, but by another of your kin, called Constantine; and that was why they were not dismayed by what befell them. Basil then pointed out his son, told him that this was the boy's name, and said that their oracle would not fail at all if the city were taken now. But the man interpreted it otherwise. He said that this was not the Constantine who was to lay their city waste, but another one, a long time afterwards, from among your descendants. At this Basil grew angry, as it were, and wanting to prove by deed that the saying was empty talk, he pressed the siege harder and worked his engines more vigorously. But for all his toil he saw that his efforts made no progress and that he could rest on no secure hope. He also considered the hardship of his troops camped in the open in icy country, and reckoning that saving his own men was better than capturing the enemy, he judged it best to withdraw before winter. So much for that. But we, who after so long a time have seen that prediction fulfilled, cannot help wondering how those barbarians, who were by no means upright in their way of life or their worship, could have such exact knowledge and grasp of the truth. For though he could not take the city then, now in our own times Constantine, the scion of the purple, son of Leo the most wise and grandson of that emperor, has won this distinction and is credited with the achievement of utterly destroying the inhabitants of Adata. So it was, as Homer says, that “it is a good thing for a son to be left behind by a man who has perished,” so that the son might stand out plainly as the avenger of those who had dared to act insolently against his grandfather's power. But let the narrative now run back along its track and set out what followed.

41. Then the emperor, having loaded his army with many captives and much booty, ordered the captives to be put to the sword so as to lighten the burden, because the road was long and hard going. He then turned his thoughts to the return journey, leaving the descendants of Hagar in great fear of him. Still, he expected some attack in the narrow passes of that country, for he knew that “I would never have expected it” is a bad thing for a general to say. So he set ambushes at the key points and took alive many of those who thought they would be the ones doing the capturing. When Abdelomel, who ruled those parts, saw this, he sent envoys asking for safety and peace. He promised to become a loyal servant and offered to submit and hand over the forts and places under his control. The emperor accepted his plea and granted what he asked, and from then on he had him as a willing ally against his own people. From there the emperor crossed Mount Argaeus again and reached Caesarea, where he received reports of victories from Koloneia and Loulon. Proof of these followed in the form of a multitude of spoils and captives, which came from the forts of Tarsus and from the Manichaean cities. There too he ordered a very large crowd of Kurds who had been brought to him to be slaughtered, since they were of almost no use, and as the army was already overloaded he did not want to have these as a troublesome encumbrance as well. On his way back the emperor came to Medaeum. There he handed out honors to his men, promoting each in proportion to his own valor and treating them with kindness. Then he released them to winter quarters and went on his way. On reaching the imperial city, he received the crown of victory from the patriarch according to the former custom, and the acclamations of victory from the people. 50. Tephrike had by now withered away and been utterly extinguished, but the strength of the Tarsians began to sprout and grow, and once again the outermost Roman frontiers were constantly under pressure from them. At that time that Andrew of Scythian origin often fought bravely against them. With the forces at his disposal he killed or captured many of those who rode out to forage and became cut off from the main army. Since he gave ample proof of courage and intelligence every day, the emperor promoted him to the rank of patrician and to the command of the Scholae. Then, with greater authority and power, he fought many pitched battles against the men of Melitene and of Tarsus, and won. Once the emir of Tarsus wrote him a letter full of blasphemy and madness against our Lord and God Jesus Christ and his most holy Mother. It said: “I shall see what good the son of Mary will do you, and she who bore him,

[Textual notes:] [?] A. “forts”]: “places” P. “surrender” (variant spelling) A. “from” AP. “were pressed” omitted in A. “by” A. “and to the command of the Scholae” omitted in A. “against … those” [?] A. “and won” omitted in A. “blasphemous” A.

when I march against you with a strong force.” Andrew took the abusive letter and, weeping many tears, laid it before the icon of the Mother of God, who was holding the Son in her arms. He said: “Behold, O Mother of the Word and God, and you who are from the Father before the ages and from the Mother in time, how this barbarian and braggart, the new Sennacherib, has reviled and raged against your chosen people. Become the helper and defender of your servants, and let all the nations know the might of your power.” After praying these words to God with a contrite heart and many tears, he set out with the Roman forces against Tarsus. When he reached the place called Podandos, where the river of the same name flows, he found the barbarian army drawn up against him. This noble man attacked with trust in God and with his whole army, which he had first stirred up for the contest with words of encouragement. He himself displayed many feats of intelligence and courage, and his lieutenant generals, taxiarchs and captains and the whole host fought bravely, so the mass of barbarians was routed with great slaughter. The emir himself fell first, along with all the flower of his army. A few of those at the camp and of those posted somewhere in the rear barely escaped the danger and got safely back to Tarsus. Andrew buried his own dead, but gathered the enemy's dead into one place and made a great mound of them, to stand as a monument for later generations too. Then he returned home with booty, spoils and many captives. He bore himself modestly in victory, treating it as God's work alone and ascribing to him the generalship and this great triumph. For that reason he feared that greed for victory and the desire for more might, as often happens, bring the jealousy of Nemesis to spoil what had already been achieved, and so he held back from advancing further. He reported his achievements to the emperor, but the envy of his peers kept him from receiving rewards worthy of his deeds. They constantly spread rumors and got to the emperor's ears first, slandering the man as having deliberately shirked and robbed the Romans of the capture of Tarsus. “For when God had given it into our hands,” they said, “if he had followed up the victory while the troops were emboldened by what they had achieved, [we would have taken it]. We lost it through the general's laziness.” These things were said so often that the emperor was won over (for even sensible men are often deceived when they are told what they like to hear). He removed Andrew from command for not fully following up his exploits against the enemy. In his place he appointed Kestas, called Styppiotes, to lead the tagmata and the whole army. This man promised to take Tarsus and foolishly imagined he would accomplish many other noble deeds. [Textual notes:] “to march against” [?]; “carrying” A; “addressing” P; [?] P; “to accomplish” P.

51. He at once took all the Roman forces and set out against Tarsus, and in doing so he showed that Andrew had been no shirker or coward, but a circumspect, prudent and excellent general. For Kestas considered the barbarians easy prey. He thought through none of the necessary measures in advance, set no ambushes, and planned nothing worthy of military experience and good judgment. Full of senseless pride and heedless boldness, he came near Tarsus, to the place called Chrysoboullon. The barbarians saw that he had taken no precautions: he had not occupied strong positions, had not put a palisade and ditch in front of his camp, and had done none of the other things that the reason and good sense of generals arrange beforehand. So they planned to steal the victory, and they attacked him at night while he was unprepared and off his guard. Given their difficulties and circumstances, the stratagem they used proved a clever one. Since the earlier defeat had left them few and easily counted, their weakness forced them to turn to cunning. They gathered many horses, tied dry hides to the horses' tails, and at a single signal let them loose into many parts of the Roman camp. Then they themselves, beating their drums, leapt from various directions into the middle of the camp with drawn swords. Panic and confusion fell on the Roman army. Horses and men were thrown into disorder together and collided with one another, and so it came about that the barbarians prevailed and caused boundless slaughter, most of the Romans being ingloriously trampled and crushed by their own side. Having won so unexpectedly and against all hope, and having cut the sinews of Roman power, the sons of Ishmael sang songs of triumph to the sound of drums and barbarian war cries. Such was the end of senseless generalship that envy awarded against the Romans, and such was the trophy that jealous Nemesis set up against the Romans who had been so fortunate before. 52. Such, then, was the state of affairs in the east during the pious reign of Basil. I now come to tell of affairs in the west. Like everything else, the affairs of the West had been badly neglected in the reign of Michael. Almost all of Italy that had been assigned to our New Rome, and most of Sicily, had been overrun by the neighboring power of the Carthaginians and made tributary to the barbarians. Moreover, the Scythians settled in Pannonia and Dalmatia and the lands beyond them, I mean the Croats, Serbs, Zachlumians, Terbouniotes, Kanalites, Diokletians and Rentanoi, had thrown off the Roman dominion that had held them from of old and had become self-governing and independent, [Textual notes:] Barberinus: “Chrysoboulon”; “in the many” P; “had become” (variant form) P.

ruled only by their own leaders. Most of them went further in their apostasy and even renounced divine baptism, so that they would have no pledge of friendship and subjection toward the Romans. 53. While the affairs of the West stood thus, in such anarchy and disorder, the Hagarenes of Carthage seized the opportunity and joined in the attack. They appointed as commanders Soldanos, Sambas and Kalphous, whom they believed far surpassed their fellows in wickedness and military experience, and they sent a fleet of thirty-six warships against Dalmatia. It captured various Dalmatian cities, such as Boutoma, Rhosa and Lower Dekatera. As things went the way the enemy wanted, they came also to the metropolis of that nation, which is called Ragusa, and besieged it for a considerable time. But they could not easily take it, because those inside fought fiercely, running, as the saying goes, for their lives. When the people of Ragusa had suffered for some time and been driven to the last extremity, necessity forced them to send envoys to the emperor. They were well aware that the ruler was preoccupied with other matters, yet they begged him to take pity and come to the aid of people in imminent danger of falling into the hands of those who deny Christ. The envoys had not yet reached the imperial city and were still dawdling on the way, when that worthless emperor departed from among men, and the imperial authority passed to Basil, the watchful and sober guardian of the common good. Even before this he had been deeply distressed and troubled about such matters. Now he listened carefully to the envoys and, regarding the sufferings of his fellow believers as his own wounds, set about preparing the forces to be sent to help the suppliants. He fitted out a fleet of a hundred ships and prepared everything properly. He chose a man who far excelled others in intelligence and experience, I mean the patrician Niketas, drungarios of the fleet, who was surnamed Ooryphas, and sent him like a fiery thunderbolt against the enemy. The Saracens from Africa who were besieging the city learned from deserters that the Ragusans had sent envoys to the emperor to ask for forces and an army against them. Partly because they despaired of taking the city quickly, and partly because they feared the help expected from the emperor, they raised the siege and left that region. They crossed over to Italy, to the part now called Lombardy, and sacked the fortress of Bari. They settled there and every day attacked those nearest, ventured against those further off, and kept seizing more, until they had mastered all Lombardy almost as far as once most glorious Rome itself. That is how matters stood.

54. The Croats, the Serbs and the rest of the peoples mentioned above saw the help the Romans had given to those in Dalmatia. They also learned of the clemency of the present emperor of the Romans, and of his justice and virtue in all things. They decided it was better to be governed well than to rule precariously out of rashness, and they made efforts to return to their former allegiance and be brought back under Roman rule. To this end they too sent envoys to the emperor, both those who had revolted while keeping the same faith and those who had deserted divine baptism entirely. They took the opportunity to remind him of their original subjection and of the services they had once rendered to the Romans, and they asked to be placed, they too, under the humane yoke of Roman authority and under its shepherd. The emperor heard their request as a reasonable one. Even before this he had been troubled and grieved about them, since no small part of his realm had been cut off and plundered. So he received and welcomed them graciously, as a loving father receives a son who foolishly rebelled and then repented and came back. He immediately sent priests back with them, along with an imperial official, so as to rescue them first of all from spiritual danger, restore them to their former faith, and free them from the errors they had fallen into through ignorance or folly. When this God-pleasing work was completed, and all had received divine baptism and returned to Roman submission, the emperor's dominion was made whole in this region. By the humane command of the ruler, all of them received rulers from among their own people and kinsmen to govern them. For he did not treat the offices of governing them as things for sale, so that he might set over them those who paid the most and who would then strip his subjects bare. Instead, he wisely decreed that they should be ruled by men whom they themselves chose and, as it were, elected, as chosen rulers obliged to keep a fatherly goodwill toward them. So much for that. 55. The barbarians who had crossed into Roman territory during that careless and indolent reign and had been driven back from Ragusa, as related above, were still lingering in Italy. They kept overrunning it and plundering it unsparingly, so that they had subdued as many as a hundred and fifty fortresses, some through betrayal and others by siege. When the emperor heard this he was deeply grieved. He lay awake over these cares, seeking how he might readily either rout the enemy completely or at least drive the hostile host out of Roman territory. As for the forces already sent for the sake of the Ragusans and the whole Dalmatian nation,

which, as we said earlier, were commanded by the patrician Niketas surnamed Ooryphas, he judged them no match for such a multitude of barbarians. This was especially because they would often need to fight inland, far from the sea, which seemed both unsuitable and impossible for a naval force. Nor did he think it worthwhile to send further forces from here, both because of the cost of the expedition and because the regions here needed them. After wise deliberation, he sent embassies to Louis, king of Francia, and to the pope of Rome, asking them to support the forces from here and to join them in battle against the Hagarenes who had settled in Bari. He also ordered the Slavic lands mentioned a little earlier to take part in the undertaking, crossing the Dalmatian sea by means of the people of Ragusa and their local ships. When all this had been done and a great force had been gathered, and since the Roman admiral also far excelled everyone in intelligence and courage, Bari was quickly taken. The fortress itself, the surrounding land and all the captives were recovered into Roman possession, and the land got back its own inhabitants. The king of Francia took that Soldanos and the Hagarene people under him and led them away to Capua, since he ruled that city, and Benevento as well. Such was the outcome of the emperor's first expedition in the West, and the imperial city was adorned with its spoils and its glory. 56. Since history often likes to vary its account with digressions and to delight the ears of its readers, we should also relate what took place between the king of Francia, Soldanos the emir of Africa, and the inhabitants of Capua and Benevento. For two years Soldanos lived with the king of Francia in Capua, and in all that time no one ever saw him laugh. The king promised a gift of gold to whoever caught him laughing. Then someone reported to the king that he had seen Soldanos, who had always been gloomy until then, laughing, and he brought witnesses to prove it. The king summoned Soldanos and asked him the reason for the change and for his laughter. He replied: “I saw a wagon and watched its wheels, how the part on top is brought low and the part below is raised up again. I took this as an image of the unstable and insecure happiness of men, and I laughed. I was thinking how we pride ourselves on things so insecure, and at the same time I thought it not impossible that I too, just as I have been brought low from on high, might be raised up again from the dust to greatness.” When the king heard this, he [?] and, judging him a wise man, began to allow him to speak freely and to share his company.

57 [?]. The Soldan, a cunning man with his share of Phoenician guile, decided to win his own safety by slandering each side to the other. The rulers of the fortresses of Capua and Benevento often came to visit him, both as a shrewd and wise man with the experience of old age and as one who had fallen from good fortune into bad. Pretending friendship toward them, he said that he wanted to reveal to them a secret plan of the king, but feared the danger of being found out as an informer. When they swore to keep what he told them undisclosed, he said: “The king intends to send all of you in iron chains to his own country of Francia, since otherwise his hold over your cities is not secure.” They did not yet altogether believe the information and asked for clearer proof. The Soldan then said something like this to the king in turn: “Your possession of these fortresses is not secure as long as their rulers remain here. If you want to be their master securely, send these men off to Francia in chains as quickly as possible.” Persuaded by these words, the king ordered chains to be forged at once, as though for some urgent need. The Soldan then saw the rulers again and said: “Do you still not believe what I told you? Go and look into what all the smiths are working on at the king's command. If you find chains and fetters, do not disbelieve what you have been told for the sake of your safety.” Finding that the barbarian had told the truth in this, the rulers no longer doubted the rest and looked for a way to take revenge on the king. Shortly afterwards, when he went out hunting, they shut the gates against him and would not let him back in. Unable to do anything about it at the time, he went back to his own country.

58. The Soldan then went to the rulers and asked for his reward for the information, which was permission to go home to his own country. They granted it. He reached Carthage and recovered his own rule. But he had not stopped being wicked, and he marched against Capua and Benevento, paying them back with this “thanks” for his rescue. They sent envoys to the king, but he dismissed them with insults, saying that he rejoiced at their destruction. The leaders of these fortresses then sent a messenger to the emperor. The emperor, being compassionate and humane, quickly sent the envoy back to tell them to expect help from him shortly. But the bearer of this message fell into enemy hands before he could deliver the reply to those who had sent him. The Soldan said to him: “If you do what I want, you will be spared and will receive gifts.” When the man agreed to do whatever he was ordered, the Soldan said: “I want you to stand

BOOK V. — BASIL THE MACEDONIAN.

outside the fortress and tell those inside: ‘I have carried out my mission and done everything I was ordered to do. But do not expect help from the emperor, for he did not listen to your plea.’” The man promised to say this, and he was sent with the Soldan's servants to say it to the people in the city. When he came near the wall, he asked for the leading men of the city to come and listen, and said: “Although my death is plain before me and the slaughter is at hand, I will not hide the truth. But I beg you and adjure you to repay this kindness to my children and my wife. For I, my lords, though I have now fallen into the hands of the enemy, did carry out my mission and delivered your embassy to the emperor of the Romans, and you may expect help from him shortly. So stand firm and do not lose heart [?]. The one who will rescue you is coming, even if he does not rescue me.” When the Soldan's servants heard this, they were furious at the deception and at once cut him down with their swords. But the Soldan feared the force he expected from the emperor, so he raised the siege and returned to his own country. From then on, the leaders of these fortresses remained loyal to the emperor and kept the fortresses in subjection to him.

59 [?]. At about that time another fleet of Hagarenes also came against Roman territory. But thanks to the emperor's constant prayers to God, his sensible orders and the proper handling of affairs, the victory went to the Romans, and the sons of Hagar suffered a shameful defeat. The emir of Tarsus, named Esman, fitted out a fleet of thirty very large ships, called koumbaria, and armed it against the fortress of Euripus. By imperial order the general of Hellas (this was Oeniates) had brought in from all over Hellas enough people to guard the fortress and had prepared suitable defenses on the walls. When the men in the fortress saw the ships approaching the walls and the barbarians trying to drive the defenders off the walls with constant volleys of arrows, they were filled with anger and fighting spirit and resisted bravely. With stone-throwing engines, crossbow-ballistae and stones thrown by hand they killed many of the barbarians every day. And not only that: when the wind was in their favor, they burned most of the ships with liquid fire. The barbarian was at a loss and disheartened. Knowing that many men will gladly die at the prospect of money [?], he set a great shield in front of the palisade, filled it with gold and said: “I give this as a prize and reward for valor, together with a hundred chosen virgins, to the man who is first to climb into the town and

win the victory for his countrymen.” When the people in the city saw this and understood what he intended, they encouraged one another with rousing words. Then, at a single signal, they opened the gates and charged bravely out against the barbarians. Many were killed. The emir himself received a mortal wound and fell, and the rest turned to flight. With their pursuers pressing on them, they were cut down all the way to the remaining ships, and there was great slaughter of the barbarians. The survivors manned a few of the ships and fled home in disgrace. Thanks to the emperor's prayers [?] and the valor of those who opposed him, he was clearly defeated and withdrew in disgrace.

No sooner had the cloud from Tarsus scattered than storms from Crete rose up again. Saet, the son of Apochaps, was emir of that island at the time, and he had as his associate a certain Photius, a warlike and energetic man. Twenty-seven koumbaria were built in Crete, together with a corresponding number of light raiders and fifty-oared vessels, which many people usually call saktourai and galleys. Setting out with these against Roman territory, they plundered the whole Aegean and often raided as far as Proconnesus on the Hellespont, enslaving and killing many. Then the patrician Nicetas mentioned earlier, who had been appointed commander of the Roman triremes, attacked this Cretan fleet. He fought a fierce battle with them and at once burned twenty of the Cretan vessels with liquid fire, and the barbarians on board were shared out among sword, fire and water. The rest, as many as escaped the danger at sea, saved themselves by flight.

61 [?]. Yet although the Cretans had been weakened in this way and had come home in misfortune, they were not content to keep quiet. They took up their seafaring once more, and with the Photius mentioned above as their admiral they harassed and plundered the regions farther from the capital, by which I mean the Peloponnese and the islands south of it. So Nicetas, the able commander of the Roman triremes (I mean Ooryphas), was sent against him too. He had a good voyage and reached the Peloponnese in a few days. He anchored in the harbor of Cenchreae and learned that the barbarians were ravaging the more westerly parts of the Peloponnese: Methone, Patras and the districts near Corinth. Then he made a shrewd and wise plan. He decided not to sail around the Peloponnese, rounding Cape Malea and covering a distance of a thousand miles, and so miss the right moment. Instead he set to work at once, just as he was: that very night, with many hands and much skill, he hauled the ships over dry land across the Isthmus of Corinth to the other side. And while the enemy had not yet heard anything

about this, he suddenly appeared before them. He threw their minds into confusion with fear, partly the fear left over from the earlier battle and partly the surprise of the attack, and he gave them no chance to form up or even to think of fighting back. He burned some of the enemy ships and sank others; some of the barbarians he killed with the sword and others he sent to the bottom of the sea. He also killed their leader and forced the rest to scatter across the peninsula. Later he rounded these up like fish in a net, took them captive [?], and subjected them to various punishments. Some he flayed alive, especially those who had renounced the baptism of Christ, saying that he was taking back from them what was not theirs. From others he cut strips of skin from the nape of the neck down to the ankles, with excruciating pain. Others he hoisted on cranes and then threw and thrust them down from the height into cauldrons full of pitch, saying that he was giving them a share in their own baptism, painful and dark. Having mocked them in this way and exacted punishments that matched their deeds, he struck no small fear into them of ever again campaigning against Roman territory.

62. In this way the winds from the south were scattered, and from then on the ship of the Roman state sailed on through calm waters. But from the West a terrible surge rose up again. The amermoumnes of Africa built sixty enormous ships and set out against Roman territory. He plundered the lands along the way and took many captives, and reached the islands of Cephalonia and Zacynthus. When the emperor heard this, he quickly roused himself to bring aid. He fitted out a great number of triremes, biremes and other fast ships and sent the commander of the naval forces (this was Nasar) with a strong force. Nasar set sail quickly, had favorable winds and reached Methone in a short time. But he was prevented from attacking the enemy quickly for the following reason. A good many of the rowers lost their nerve in the face of the danger and slipped away secretly a few at a time. Their desertion robbed the ships of the speed they needed, since they could no longer charge the enemy swiftly with the rush of oars, and he decided that he must not go against the enemy so poorly equipped. He reported what had happened to the emperor by courier. The emperor quickly sent men suited to the task, caught all the deserters alive and put them under guard. He then considered how he could keep his hands clean of the blood of his own people and yet put a proper fear into the rest of the rowers, so that the wrongdoing of these men would not be imitated elsewhere and most of them would not willingly play the coward and shirk their duty. He
