made a shrewd plan. He ordered the drungarius of the Watch to take thirty of the prisoners and criminals in the praetorium who had been sentenced to death under the law and to bring them out while it was still night. He was to smear their faces with soot and singe off the hair of their beards and heads, so as to remove anything by which they could be recognized. He was to make sure that no one at all dared speak to them or address them, setting death as the penalty for such boldness. They were to be flogged in the Hippodrome as the supposed ringleaders of the deserting sailors and then paraded through the city's marketplace with their arms tied behind their backs [?]. After that they were to be secured in stocks and sent to the Peloponnese, so that they would receive the punishment they deserved in the very place they were thought to have deserted from. John, general of the Peloponnese, known as the Cretan, was given the task of carrying this out. Following the imperial order, he had as many gibbets set up at Methone as there were prisoners sent, and he impaled the men who had been sent as ringleaders of the desertion. When the Roman fleet heard and saw this, they pitied those men as cowards and wretches, and they themselves were strengthened to face the danger. They put aside all softness and love of comfort and begged their commander to lead them against the enemy quickly.

63. Meanwhile the commander filled the gaps in his force with soldiers from the Peloponnese and Mardaites, took the general on as his colleague, and made ready to attack. The Saracens had by now concluded that the Roman fleet was thoroughly cowardly, because the time in between seemed to be passing to no purpose. They were leaving their ships with complete confidence and plundering the lands and islands nearby. Suddenly the Roman naval force came up close to them unseen, and at the general's signal it fell on the enemy without warning in the night. The enemy had no chance to form up or turn to resistance and were miserably slaughtered, and their ships were burned along with the marines and everyone else on board. The ships that escaped the danger of fire Nasar took and presented to the church of God at Methone as a thank offering, and he let the men under his command profit from the spoils and the surviving captives. He promptly reported this to the emperor and asked what he should do next and where he should turn. The emperor praised him for what he had done and ordered him to advance further.

64. Since the army was eager after its earlier successes, he crossed over to Sicily and Palermo. He attacked and plundered the cities there that paid tribute to the Hagarenes of Carthage, and he captured a great many cargo ships and other vessels, whose freight was abundant olive oil and many other valuable goods. So cheap, they

say, did oil become at that time as a result of this import that a litra sold for an obol. The same fleet then crossed over to Italy and joined the Roman infantry and cavalry forces. These were commanded by Procopius, the emperor's protovestiarios, and Leo, then general of Thrace and Macedonia, whom they called Apostyppes. Together they achieved much for the benefit of Roman rule. Nasar himself defeated the fleet that had again come out of Africa at the island called Stelai, and the fortresses held by the Hagarenes in Calabria and Longobardia were, with very few exceptions, all freed from barbarian hands and brought under Roman authority. Thus the naval force proved stronger than guile, envy and nemesis and returned to the emperor with many spoils and victor's crowns. It filled the whole citizen body with joy and gave the emperor many reasons for thanksgiving and praise to God.

65–66. The land forces, however, did not entirely escape envy. They performed brave and brilliant deeds, but because of a quarrel and rivalry that broke out in the middle of the fighting they lost the senior general. Leo had fallen out with Procopius. All the same, they engaged the enemy, and it so happened that Apostyppes, fighting on the right wing with the Thracians and Macedonians, got the better of the enemy and caused great slaughter, while Procopius, drawn up on the other wing with the Slavs and the Westerners, was hard pressed by the enemy. Because of their earlier rivalry his fellow general sent no help to the struggling wing, so Procopius's wing was completely routed, and he himself was killed in the pursuit when his horse fell with him. Since the battle ended this way, Leo wanted to do something else brilliant to cast a shadow over what had happened because of the quarrel. He took his own army, together with those of Procopius's men who had survived the rout, and attacked the fortress of Tarentum, which was still held by the Hagarenes. He took it by storm and enslaved the whole population. He let the soldiers profit amply from them and brought the emperor a great deal of spoil. But the emperor did not look on this with pleasure, nor did he reward Leo as a hero. When he investigated, he found that the fellow general had died because of the rivalry that had arisen during the battle itself, so he removed Leo from his command and sent him into exile at his own house, which was near Cotyaeum.

67. Apostyppes met with further misfortunes of this kind later on. Baianus the protostrator and Chamaretus the cubicularius, the closest of his intimates, plotted against him and drew up a written accusation against their own master for the emperor. In it they claimed that the death of the protovestiarios Procopius

had come about by the design of their master, and they added a charge of treason and other serious and damaging accusations. Chamaretus took this document to the capital and handed it to the emperor. When Apostyppes' sons, Bardas and David, learned of this, they murdered Baianus with their own hands, cutting him down mercilessly with their swords. Because of this crime and their fear of the emperor, they set out with their father to flee to Syria. When the emperor heard this, he sent Bartzapedon the manglabites in great haste to seize them and bring them to him. He caught up with them already in Cappadocia, pressing on hard along the road to Syria. He tried to arrest them in accordance with the imperial order, but they resisted and defended themselves as best they could. In the hand-to-hand fighting [?] and struggle that followed, the two sons of Apostyppes were killed. Apostyppes himself was taken and brought in chains to the emperor, who was staying at the imperial residences at Hieria at the time. By imperial order he was put on trial before Manuel the magistros, and one of his eyes was gouged out and one of his hands cut off, both because of the evidence against him and because he had tried to flee to the enemy. For the rest of his life he grew old in exile at Mesembria. So the career of Apostyppes, who was not a good man in other respects either, came to this end.

68. While the emperor's affairs in the West were being carried out by his subordinate generals, the Arabs of the south caught their breath and took heart again, thinking that he was idle, at leisure and careless. They decided to take up their seafaring once more. They built ships in Egypt and in the coastal cities of Syria and planned a campaign against the lands and seas subject to the Romans. But they decided that they should first look into the emperor's situation through spies, and they sent a man dressed as a Roman and speaking the Roman tongue to observe everything and report back to them. The emperor, however, was always alert in his care for the common good and prepared in advance whatever was needed. Since the ships being built in Syria had not escaped his notice either, he had more triremes built, gathered the naval forces in the capital and waited to see what would happen. In the meantime, so that the sailors would not grow unruly through idleness, he set them to work on building the church then going up in the imperial palace, dedicated to our Savior Jesus Christ, the Archangels and Elijah the Tishbite. As soon as the enemy fleet showed itself beyond the borders of Syria, they too were to be sent out to face it. So the spy came from Syria and saw the number of the ships and how the force stood ready for

…the dispatch, and once he had learned everything and made his estimates, he reported to those who had sent him. When they heard that the emperor was far better prepared than they had expected, they cowered, welcomed peace and quiet, and gave up their eagerness to sail out. The naval force, however, stayed in the capital, still busy with the task already described. 69. Meanwhile the barbarians in Carthage, because of their earlier defeats, feared that the Roman fleet might next try to cross over against their own country. So they too built a considerable number of ships. When spring had passed and they learned that no force had come down from the emperor, they supposed that the emperor's army was taken up with other wars, and they made bold to campaign against Sicily. They came to its chief city, Syracuse, I mean, laid siege to it, and plundered and ravaged the country and the suburbs around it. When the general of Sicily made this known to the emperor, the force that had been made ready against Syria was immediately sent to Sicily, under an admiral named Hadrian, who happened at that time to command the navy. He set out from the capital, but he was not blessed with suitable and favourable winds, and he barely got as far as the Peloponnese. At Monemvasia he anchored the ships in the harbour called Hierax, “the Hawk,” and waited for a following wind. He was rather sluggish, it seems, and lacked the fervour of spirit to venture out against contrary winds and to press on toward his goal by rowing in the calms between them. While he wasted a long time in that harbour, the Hagarenes pressed the siege more fiercely, setting every engine in motion and hurrying to achieve their aim before help could reach the besieged. And so it came about that the city was taken by storm. There was great slaughter of those who had been posted to defend it, the whole population of the town was enslaved, and its wealth became spoil for the enemy. The city was razed, its holy churches were given to the flames, and the city that until then had been illustrious and splendid, and had often overthrown many Greek and barbarian armies that came against it, became a ruin. 70. News of what had happened reached Hadrian in the following way. There is a place in the Peloponnese, not far from Monemvasia, where the Roman fleet was encamped, called Helos (“Marsh”). It took its name from the dense, overshadowing woodland around it. A demonic power lurked in this place, and the shepherds who grazed their flocks there often worshipped it, so that the animals they pastured might supposedly be kept safe from harm by it. The herdsmen heard these demons, as though they were talking with one another and gloating, say that Syracuse had been taken the day before, and that everything in it had been razed and given to the flames. When some of the herdsmen told this to

certain people, the story reached Hadrian himself. He summoned the shepherds, questioned them closely, and found that what the shepherds said matched what had been reported. Wanting to hear it with his own ears, he went to the place with the shepherds. Through them he put a question to the demons: when would he reach Syracuse? And he heard that Syracuse had already been taken. He was overcome with grief and helplessness, but he recovered himself, thinking that one should not believe what wicked demons say, since they have no foreknowledge. He did not know that this was not foreknowledge at all. It was a report of things that had already happened and been done, for because of their subtle nature and swift movement the demons outrun the news that comes when human beings arrive. Still he did not believe it. But ten days later some of those who had escaped the destruction, men who belonged to the Mardaites and Taxatoi of the Peloponnese, came in person to tell the dreadful story. When Hadrian had received full confirmation from them, he hurried back to the capital with the fleet as fast as he could, since the winds that had blown against him on the voyage out had now become favourable for the return. There he fled as a suppliant to the great sanctuary of God, in which the name of His Wisdom is proclaimed. But the size of the disaster had cruelly torn the emperor's heart and driven him almost beyond measure in anger and grief. So neither the holy church itself nor the high priest who interceded for Hadrian could rescue him from punishment altogether. The patriarch saved him from the ultimate penalty, which perhaps he deserved, but he could not win him complete acquittal from a moderate one, which was imposed as a warning to others. Thus the emperor, who kept his anger moderate and restrained in private matters, was not at all lenient in public ones. 71. So the enemies in the West were growing strong again, and it was expected that, encouraged by their present success, they would also campaign against the regions nearer to us. Stephen, who was also called Maxentius, a Cappadocian by origin, was therefore sent as general of the forces in Longobardia, with Thracians and Macedonians and picked troops from Charsianon and Cappadocia. He reached the province assigned to his command and tried to take the city of Amantea away from the Saracens who held it. But he was slow and sluggish, it seems, or rather cowardly and fond of luxury, and he could achieve nothing worth mentioning or worthy of the force he had with him. He was relieved of his command, and in his place Nikephoros, called Phokas, was sent. He was a diligent and watchful man, noble in action and wise in counsel. He brought with him a larger force drawn from the commanders of the East, along with the well-known Diakonitzes, who had once been a servant of Chrysocheir of Tephrike and who brought a band of men who took their

religion from Mani. Once Nikephoros had joined the forces under Stephen, he showed many proofs of intelligence, warlike courage and nobility. He immediately captured the city of Amantea, routing the enemy forces drawn up against him with great slaughter. He brought the fortress called Tropai and that of Santa Severina back under Roman rule, to which they had formerly been subject, and he loaded the army with plentiful booty. These things he accomplished while Basil, renowned among emperors, was still alive. He added the rest later, under the gentlest and wisest of all emperors, Leo, Basil's son. These battles did not follow one another in time as they do in the narrative. But since the exact date of each action was unknown, they have all been set in a single sequence, as was promised. Such, then, and so many were the deeds done in war by the emperor Basil, both in person and through his subordinate generals, by land and by sea, in East and West, as far as they have come to my hearing. 72. Now the narrative must go back to the deeds the emperor performed himself, and tell how he was always occupied with public affairs and kept his mind constantly fixed on the care of the world. At times he steered affairs as they required by prudent management. At other times he lent his ear and listened carefully to historical narratives, political precepts, moral teachings, and fatherly and spiritual admonitions and counsels. At still other times he trained his hand and guided the writing pen. Now he investigated the characters, lives, conduct of affairs and military campaigns of generals and emperors, and after examining them he picked out the best and most praised of these and was eager to imitate them in his own actions. Now he carefully studied the lives of men who had excelled in the best way of life, the life according to God, and he pruned back the irrational impulses of his soul, wishing to show himself master of himself before being master of what lay outside him, and he reaped great benefit from this. For this reason he also counted it of great importance, and took great pains, to get to know, to meet and to converse with those blessed men still living, who led the immaterial life in this fragrant way of life and had transferred their citizenship to heaven. Out of his great reverence he did not summon them to himself. Instead, setting no store by the imperial dignity, he went to them, shared in their prayers, was crowned, as it were, with their blessings, was strengthened in the fear of God, and was guided toward the ordinances of God [the page ends here, followed by editorial variant readings:] “Stephen” A. “narrative” A. [?] A. “he made” P. [?] Patrologia Graeca 109.

[continuing the last sentence of the previous paragraph]. As a result one could see the four virtues dwelling with him constantly. People admired his prudence joined with courage, and his justice joined with self-control, and everything advanced toward the better. Life seemed to return once more to its ancient good order and stability. He took constant care that his subjects should live in security and that no one should be wronged by anyone. Those appointed to office at any time strove to imitate their master's reverence toward God, his respect for priests and monks, his mercy toward the poor, and his justice and fairness toward all. For it was his command and precept that the lesser should not be oppressed by the greater, nor the man of high rank be insulted or slandered by the needy. Rather, the powerful man should embrace and care for the poor man as a brother, and the poor man should bless the powerful man as a common father and saviour, and sincerely pray to the Lord for blessings upon him. Because he ordered his life in this way and made his own affairs depend on divine providence, he was often clearly taught in his sleep what needed to be done. When he went to bed thoughtful and troubled with anxiety over some public matter, he often saw in a dream what was going to happen, and then he took good hope and calmed the turmoil of his soul. And it is no wonder that those who exercise authority on earth as a kind of public service, who truly carry out a divine ministry here below among us, and who model themselves as far as possible on the higher pattern, should be encouraged by Providence, guided toward what is beneficial, and taught the future in advance. 73. There is something that the momentum of the narrative swept past and did not allow to be told at its proper time, and it is fitting to record it here, now that the narrative has finished with wars and accounts of battles. I mean the emperor's remembrance and repayment of those who had served him while he was still of humble fortune, and the fact that he did not forget them once he had risen to brilliant fortune. These were the superior of the monastery of St Diomedes and Danelis, the woman from the Peloponnese, and he repaid them more than they had hoped. He clearly adorned Diomedes, great among the martyrs, with magnificence: he dedicated costly offerings, provided a large number of books, and presented other treasures and splendid vestments. He brought the monastery named after him to prosperity by the gift of large estates and by a generous and abundant supply of ample revenues, and he secured for it complete freedom from want in every respect. He made it splendid with costly buildings, and in every way he raised it up and enriched it.

[…] once he had become master of the empire, he sent for him, honoured him with the rank of protospatharios, and granted him free access to himself because of the bond of spiritual brotherhood they had formed earlier. His mother, though she was by then considered almost an old woman, somehow conceived a great desire to see the emperor and to enjoy rather greater honour herself in her old age, because of the prophecy the pious monk had made and because of the other kindness and hospitality she had shown. So at the emperor's command she came up to the capital with great honour and with a large escort and retinue. Since she could not ride in a carriage or on a horse, and perhaps also because she was used to luxury on account of her vast wealth, she reclined on a litter. She chose three hundred of her servants, young men with strong bodies, and ordered them to carry her up. And so, with ten men at a time carrying the litter and relieving one another in turns, she completed the journey from the Peloponnese to this queen of cities. A reception was held in the Magnaura, as the Roman emperors customarily do when they are about to receive some illustrious and great ruler of a nation, and she too was brought in to the emperor with honour and splendour. She brought costly gifts, such as almost no foreign king had ever brought to an emperor of the Romans up to that time. There were five hundred household slaves, among them a hundred handsome eunuchs. For that wealthy old woman knew, it seems, that there is always room for eunuchs in the palace, and that they swarm about it more thickly than flies around a sheepfold in springtime. That is why she had prepared them in advance, so that perhaps, because they had once been her slaves, she would find them acting as her bodyguards whenever she entered the palace. There were also a hundred women skilled in weaving [?], and a hundred richly varied [?] fabrics of the kind that are now called *sendais*, perhaps because the ignorance of the many has corrupted the name. There were a hundred *linomalotaria*, woolly linen cloths (for it is well to use the common words for these things), two hundred plain linen *amalia* [?], and a hundred more cloths finer than spider's threads, each of which was rolled up inside the joint of a reed. There were also many different costly vessels of silver and gold. 75. She was received graciously and entertained magnificently, as her generosity and nobility deserved. She was honoured with the title of the emperor's mother and shared in many imperial receptions and honours. She was delighted and overjoyed, and she acknowledged that she had been repaid in full, or rather far beyond what she had given. For this reason she generously added to the gifts already mentioned no small part of the Peloponnese, which was her own property, and freely gave it to her son the emperor. She stayed in the great city

for as long as she pleased, amid honours and pleasures, and then went back to her own country like a mistress and queen of the people there, enjoying far more and greater honours than before. She made the journey down in the same way she had made the journey up. 76. At that time this most beautiful and conspicuous church that we usually call the New Imperial Church was being built. It was raised in the name of our Saviour Jesus Christ, of Michael the first of the angels, and of Elijah the Tishbite. The woman had the dimensions of its interior measured, and then she had great carpets [?] made and sent, of the kind that among us take their name from prayer. They were to cover the whole floor, which was made of various precious stones fitted together like mosaic tesserae and imitating the many colours and beauty of peacocks. The carpets were wonderful in size and beauty. Moreover, every year, as long as the emperor lived, she sent gifts no smaller than those she had brought in person. She happened to live a long life, and her life extended beyond the emperor's. While that clairvoyant monk was still alive, she heard from him that she would depart this life in two years' time. So she wished to go up and see the emperor's son Leo as well, who had by then attained sole rule. Once again, in the same manner as before, she was carried by chosen young men and covered that great distance easily and without hardship. She saw the most wise and gentle emperor Leo and brought him marvellous gifts as well. She made him heir to her property, since her son John had already departed this life, and she asked that an imperial official be sent who would register and take over her estate. Then she took leave of the good emperor and set off again for the soil of her homeland that had nourished her, so that she might lay aside the dust of her flesh there. And indeed, soon after she had returned, she died. 77. The protospatharios Zenobios had been appointed and sent to carry out everything the old woman had requested and arranged. He had already reached the fortress of Naupaktos when he learned from Daniel, her grandson, that she had departed this life for the life beyond. He went to her house, took the copy of her testament into his hands, and settled everything according to her will and instructions. He found a great quantity of gold in coin, and other wealth in silver and gold plate, clothing, bronze, slaves and livestock, surpassing any private fortune, or rather only a little short of a ruler's. Since her household

slaves were beyond counting, by imperial command three thousand of them were set free and sent to the theme of Longobardia, as if to found a colony. The rest of her estates, money and slaves were distributed as she had laid down in her testament, and eighty estates were left, separate from the rest, to her heir the emperor as his own portion. Some of these events took place long before the affairs and times related in this section, and others a good while after, and they did not seem especially necessary to the history. Nevertheless, to honour the old woman we have spoken of, and to show her wealth, her nobility and her generosity, let them stand here as a digression. 78. Between the wars, which he often directed as needed through his subordinates, like the president of the games, the Christ-loving emperor Basil restored many holy and divine churches. They had been split open by earlier earthquakes, and some had collapsed entirely while others showed by their cracks that they would soon fall. Through his constant care and his lavish supply and provision of whatever was needed, he raised some of them up from their ruin and added beauty to their soundness. Others he strengthened where they were weak, applying what was needed and repairing them so that they would not fall down, and he caused them to return to vigour and youth. These must be described one by one. 79. Take the famous and divine church that bears the name of the Great Wisdom of God. Its great and lofty western arch had cracked badly and threatened to fall before long. Using the skill of craftsmen, he had it bound tightly together and renewed, making it secure and lasting. On this arch he had an image painted of the Mother of God holding in her arms the Son conceived without seed, and he placed the chief apostles Peter and Paul on either side. He also repaired the church's other cracks with new construction and the most generous expenditure. He not only restored the walls that had become unsound, but also increased its diminished revenues with gifts of his own. The holy lamps were almost in danger of going out for lack of oil, so by the gift of a very large estate called Mantea he made sure that their light would remain unquenched. From the ample revenue of this estate he also generously provided stipends for those who serve in this divine church, and the estate supplies this service without shortfall or interruption. 80. He also restored the famous and great sanctuary of the Holy Apostles, which had lost its former beauty and soundness. He strengthened it by surrounding it with buttresses and rebuilding the parts that had cracked. Scraping away the old age that time had brought and removing its wrinkles, he made it beautiful and new again. And

The divine church of the Mother of God at the Spring had collapsed and lost its ancient beauty; he restored it and made it shine even more than before. Likewise the other church of the Theotokos, named after the Sigma, had suffered a terrible collapse; he rebuilt it from its foundations and made it sturdier than before. The church of Stephen, the first of the martyrs, in the Aurelianae had fallen to the ground, and he raised it again from its very foundations. Of the holy shrines of the Baptist and Forerunner in the Strobylaia and in the Macedonianae, he rebuilt the one from its foundations and the greater part of the other. He also cleared away the old ruins from the shrine of the apostle Philip, and from the shrine of the evangelist Luke lying to the west of it, and made them new. 81. The great precinct of the martyr Mocius had suffered many cracks, and its sanctuary had been thrown down to the ground [?], so that even the holy altar table was broken. He gave it the care it deserved and raised it completely from its ruin. Next to it on the western side stood the church of Andrew, the first-called of the apostles, which had fallen into decay through long neglect; with due care he brought it back to its ancient beauty. The divine house of Saint Romanus had also collapsed, and he built it again from its foundations. He made the churches of Saint Anna in the Deuteron and of Christ's martyr Demetrius new in place of old, and [?]. He saw that the church of the martyr Aemilianus, which neighbours the house of the Mother of God in the Rhabdos, had shrivelled with age, and he renewed [?] it, fortifying it on both sides with buttresses. 82. Further, the holy house of Nazarius, winner of the martyr's prize, had over many years not only collapsed but vanished entirely; he built it anew, far surpassing the former in dignity and beauty. In the so-called Porticoes of Domninus stood the beautiful church dedicated to the divine resurrection of Christ our God and to Anastasia the martyr. He restored and adorned it, making a stone roof in place of a wooden one and adding further admirable decoration. Likewise, seeing that the roof of the church of Plato, great among martyrs, was failing, he made it new, and where it was needed he strengthened the building with added walls. The divine house of the triumphant martyrs Hesperus and Zoe had been razed to the ground, and he rebuilt it almost exactly like the former one. Besides these, the divine church of the martyr Acacius in the Heptascalon had already nearly fallen down and was being driven to ruin. He renewed it, secured it with every kind of reinforcement, snatched it from collapse and made it stand firm. The church of the prophet Elijah at the Petrion was, as it were, fainting, and he revived [?] it
and conspicuously [?], freeing it also from the ordinary houses that surrounded it and pressed upon it

But why do we linger over his lesser works, even if they are very great, and not set forth the great and admirable work he built within the imperial palace itself, supervising it and labouring on it with his own hands? This alone is enough to show both his piety toward God and the grandeur and wonder of what he undertook. As if repaying the Lord Christ for his kindness toward him, together with Gabriel, the first of the angelic powers, and Elijah the Tishbite, the zealot, who had also been a messenger to his mother of her son's future elevation to the throne, he built a divine and very beautiful church in their name and for their everlasting memory, and also in honour of the Theotokos and of Nicholas, foremost among bishops. In it art and wealth, fervent faith and the most generous intent came together, and the finest things flowed in from every quarter—things which, I know, are believed by those who see them rather than by those who hear of them. This church he presented to Christ, the immortal Bridegroom, like a bride beautified and adorned with pearls and gold and the brilliance of silver, and with the variety of many-coloured marbles, compositions of mosaic and hangings of silk. Its roof, made up of five domes, gleams with gold and flashes with the beauty of its images as with stars, while on the outside it is adorned with bronze that looks like gold. The walls on either side are variegated with costly marbles of many colours, and the sanctuary of the church is decorated and enriched with gold and silver, precious stones and pearls. The screen that separates the altars from the outer parts, the colonnades in it and the parts above that serve as lintels, the seats inside and the [?] in front of them, and the holy tables themselves are all made of silver overlaid with gold and of costly precious stones set about with pearls. The floor itself would seem to be covered with silk fabrics or Sidonian embroidery spread out, so fully is it beautified and variegated by the many colours of the marble slabs laid in it, by the various bands of mosaic that border them, by the precision of their fitting, and by the abundant grace that runs through everything. There he also appointed a multitude of singers to serve, and assigned ample revenues, which he ordered to be distributed generously and magnificently to those devoted to this place of propitiation; in his munificence in such matters he strove to surpass almost all who had come before him. 84. Such, then, is the church, and so

it holds its features, so far as great things can be shown in a brief account, and it fills the minds of those who behold it with every kind of amazement. And what of its exterior? To the west, in the very forecourt of the church, stand two fountains, one to the south and the other to the north, displaying every excess of art, brilliance of material, and the munificence of the maker of the works. The southern one is made of Egyptian stone, which we usually call Roman. Around it one can see serpents, which the stonecarver's art has shaped superbly. In its middle stands a conical, perforated pinecone, and around it stand small white columns, hollow inside, arranged like a ring of dancers, with a crown running round above them. From all of these water gushes from above into the middle and bottom of the basin and waters what lies beneath. The northern one is built of the so-called Sagarian stone, which resembles the stone some call Ostrites; it too has, projecting from the middle of its bottom, a much-pierced pinecone of white stone. Above, along the crown that runs round the basin, the craftsman fashioned in bronze cocks, goats and rams, which also spout jets of water through pipes, as if spewing them out onto the floor beneath the basin. Cups can also be seen there, around which in those days wine bubbled up from below, giving drink to passers-by and welcoming them. 86. As you go out through the north door of the church, a long vaulted gallery receives you. Its ceiling is resplendent with paintings that depict the contests and struggles of the martyrs; at once they feast the eyes and rouse the soul to divine and blessed love, as the senses are led toward that love by the martyrs' feats of valour and strive, so far as they can, to rise beyond themselves. If you go out by the doors toward the south and the sea and wish to make your way east, you will find another gallery, equal in length to the northern one and running parallel to it, which likewise extends as far as the imperial court where emperors and the sons of the wealthy customarily play ball on horseback. This court too was made by the same celebrated emperor. He bought up the houses that had stood there before, demolished them to the ground and cleared the site, and on the seaward side of the court he built beautiful buildings, which he designated as a treasury and steward's house for the church just described. The purchase of the buildings and the construction of the court were rightly undertaken, because the court formerly set aside for the emperors for this kind of exercise had been taken up by the building of the divine church. The area enclosed between the two galleries, on the eastern side of the church, he made into a garden [?]

planted toward the east, itself like a new Eden, luxuriant with every kind of plant and abundantly watered. Because of its position we usually call it the Mesokepion. 87. But enough has been said about these, lest someone charge us with bad taste. The account must now turn to the remaining works of this industrious emperor, so mindful of fine things. In the palace itself, which of all those ever remembered for munificence in such matters did he not surpass in costliness and beauty, in novelty of design and in grace in everything admirable? He did so not only in the beauty, costliness and delights of churches, but also in the buildings of truly royal and magnificent residences, which joined delight to costliness and to delight much usefulness and wonder. But since such beauties are not open to everyone's sight, though sight is by nature the more exact teacher of such things, they must be set out in writing for the ears of the studious, so that their maker may be worthily admired and those barred from entering the palace may not be wholly ignorant of them. Right on the eastern side of the palace stands a church built to Elijah the Tishbite, not only its interior but its exterior too full of every costliness and beauty. The whole roof above shone with gold, made entirely of well-fitted tesserae, although by now, in the course of time, the frequent onslaught of rains, the winter snows and [?] have spoiled and ruined much of its beauty. Joined to this church he also built the oratory named after Clement, the much-suffering and most enduring of martyrs, and in it he deposited Clement's divine head and the holy relics of many other martyrs, from which he himself and those after him receive strength of soul and body. Next to these stands the house of prayer he built in the name of our Saviour and God. Its costliness and preciousness will seem incredible to those who have not seen it, so much silver and gold and such a multitude of precious stones and pearls have been laid out within its walls. The whole floor is made of solid hammered silver with niello work, displaying the exactness of the goldsmiths' art, and the walls on the right and left are likewise overlaid with abundant silver, flowered with gold and studded with precious stones and gleaming pearls. And the screen that separates the sanctuary of this divine house—by Heracles, what riches it holds! Its columns and lower parts are made entirely of silver, and the beam resting on their capitals is wholly of pure gold, with all the wealth of India

lavished on it on every side. On it, in many places, the divine and human form of the Lord is depicted in enamel. What beauties and holy things the sanctuary itself contains and guards as treasure, the account declines to reveal; it prefers to leave the sanctuary inaccessible and untrodden by words as well, for in things beyond speech silence is more fitting. These, then, are what one might call the eastern beauties of the palace, which rose like the dawn from the faith of the celebrated emperor Basil.

88. The rest are found in other parts of the palace. Among them is the venerable oratory of Paul, the herald of sacred things. It had the same builder, who built it with the same wealth-bestowing hand; its floor too has silver enclosing the circles of marble, and in costliness and beauty it is seen to fall short of the others in nothing. Likewise there is the divine church in the name of Peter, the chief of the apostles, which he built at the end of the galleries of Marcian like a citadel tower; joined to it is the oratory of the Archangel. And the church of the Mother of God, which lies further up—what surpassing comeliness and beauty did it not possess? Whose eye would it not feast, whose soul would it not [?], and what beholder would it not make altogether happier? 89. The beauties of the halls that the emperor Basil built within the palace itself, like a palace of palaces, would need more brilliant words to herald them, and a more accomplished hand to be able to show in words what works themselves cannot imitate. This novel hall, called the Kainourgion, which he raised from its foundations—which of its beholders does it not rouse to amazement? Sixteen columns standing in a row support it. Eight of them are of Thessalian stone, which has a leek-green colour; six boast the name of onyx, and these the stonecarver adorned in every way, carving on them the form of a vine and working into it the shapes of all kinds of animals. The other two are also of onyx, but the stonecarvers did not give them the same form: the smoothness of their surface was cut away by spiral grooves, because the craftsman wished to vary them in this way, seeking comeliness and charm through variety of form. Above the columns up to the ceiling, and in the eastern half-dome, the whole hall is gilded with beautiful tesserae. Presiding there is the maker of the work, attended by the generals who fought at his side, who offer him as gifts the cities he captured. Higher still, on the ceiling, are depicted the emperor's Herculean labours, his toils for his subjects, the sweat of his struggles in war and his God-given victories, through which the hall shines forth surpassingly bright, like heaven with its stars. There is also a bedchamber, crafted by the same emperor, beautiful, lavishly furnished [?]

and richly varied, and carrying off the prize for beauty over almost all others. Right at the very centre of the floor the peacock, the Median bird, is fashioned of brilliant tesserae by the stonecarver's art, enclosed in a perfectly round circle of Carian stone, from which rays of the same stone extend to another, larger circle. Outside this, like streams or rivers, bands of Thessalian stone, which has a leek-green colour, are spread out following the square shape of the room. In its inner corners they enclose four eagles made of fine, many-coloured tesserae, all so exact in their likeness that one would think them alive and eager to fly. The walls on either side are covered with plaques of many-coloured glass and seem adorned with the shapes of various flowers. Above these runs another ornament, flowered with a design in gold, which seems to divide the lower parts from the upper. Above it comes another delight in gold tesserae, showing enthroned the emperor who made the work and his consort Eudocia, adorned in imperial robes and crowned with diadems. Their children are depicted around the room like bright stars, they too resplendent in imperial robes and crowns. The sons are shown carrying books containing the divine commandments, which they were taught to follow; the daughters too are seen holding books containing divine laws. Perhaps the artist wished to show that not only the male offspring but the female too had been initiated into the sacred writings and had a share in divine wisdom; and that although their father had at first been unfamiliar with letters because of the circumstances of his life, he nevertheless made all his offspring partakers of wisdom. This, beyond the history itself, he wished to convey to beholders through the picture. These beauties cover the four walls up to the ceiling. The ceiling of this bedchamber does not rise up to any height, but rests on the walls in a square shape, entirely gilded and glittering. At its very centre it bears the victory-bringing cross, formed in green glass, around which you will see, shining like stars in heaven, the celebrated emperor himself and his consort with all their children, raising their hands to God and to the life-giving sign of the cross and all but crying aloud: "Through this victory-bringing symbol everything good and pleasing to God has been done and achieved in the days of our reign." There is also an inscribed thanksgiving, spoken to God by the parents for their children and by the children in turn for their parents. That of the parents is shown worded more or less as follows: "We thank you, O God supremely good and King

of those who reign, that you have surrounded us with children who give thanks for the magnificence of your wonders. Keep them in your will, so that none of them transgresses any of your commandments, and so that in this too we may give thanks to your goodness." That of the children, in turn, is shown declaring: "We thank you, Word of God, that you raised our father up from Davidic poverty and anointed him with the anointing of your Holy Spirit. Guard him with your hand, together with her who bore us, and count both them and us worthy of your heavenly kingdom as well." This, then, is our description of the works and beauties of the bedchamber. 90. Of the same hand and mind is the very great triclinium by the galleries of Marcian, also called the Pentakoubouklon, which itself carried off the first prize for every kind of beauty and comeliness. There too stands the beautiful oratory of Paul, who traversed the heavens, mentioned earlier, to which is joined the oratory of the martyr Barbara built by Leo the most wise. The other imperial apartments as well, which lie further east than the Golden Triclinium and higher up, to the west of the New Church, and which received the name Aetos (Eagle) from their great height into the air—where there is also the beautiful and delightful oratory of the Theotokos—are works of the same emperor. By the costliness and abundance of their precious materials, the novelty of their forms and their magnificent design, they display the man's magnanimity and love of beauty. [?] The pyramid-shaped dwellings to the west of these, where there is another oratory of the Mother of God the Word, record him as their patron and builder, and they carry off the first prize over many others for the excellence and novelty of their construction. Below them, at the very entrance of the so-called Monoouros [?], is the most delightful oratory of John the Theologian. The same emperor built this too, together with the airy, sunlit, marble-paved walkway that begins there and runs as far as the Pharos, and also the very solid buildings to its east, one of which is the treasury and the other serves as the wardrobe; along with delight, these were granted exceptional security. And the finest, largest and brightest bath of the palace, which lies above the so-called Phiale—a name left over from the stone fountain of the Blue faction that once stood there—was harmoniously [?] built by him, a work at once of beauty, luxury, bodily well-being and rest. The fountain of the other faction, I mean the Greens, stood in the courtyard on the eastern side of the palace; and in [?]

[?] … the divine church there happened to be moved, the use made of the parts around them was changed, and the rites performed in them came to an end.

91. Besides the works already mentioned, the same noble emperor also built the imperial house called the Mangana and the house called the New House. He built them for the following reason. He did not want to spend public money, which grows from the taxes paid by his subjects, on his own needs. Nor did he want to make pleasant, or to supply, the table of those he invited every year out of the toil of others [?]. So he devised these houses and assigned to them enough revenue from farmland that the imperial banquets, both his own and those of his successors, would always have a plentiful and honestly gained supply. At the place called Pegae the same emperor also raised from their foundations the imperial lodgings and residences used for a change of air. He adorned them with beautiful churches. Among them are the church of the holy prophet Elijah [?], the church of Elisha, his successor and disciple, and the church of Constantine the Great, the first of our emperors to reign in piety. There is also the church of the forty-two recently revealed martyrs, and besides these, two other houses of prayer piously built in the name and to the glory of the Mother of God. In the palace of Hieria he also built a sacred oratory of the same prophet Elijah, which is judged second to none of the others in beauty and grace.

92. In these imperial residences, used for retreat and a change of air, there was also a reservoir of water, large and spacious. It was the work and labour of the emperor who first adorned the suburb. But Emperor Heraclius had it filled in with earth and made into a bed for planting trees and vegetables. The same had been done to the reservoirs inside the imperial palace: the one in front of the Magnaura, and the one between the Triclinium of Justinian and that of the Ekthesis. These too had held plenty of water and bred fish for the emperors' pleasure and sport, but the same emperor turned them into dry land and they became gardens. The reason was that Stephen the astrologer had looked into that emperor's horoscope and said that he would die by water. For this reason the cistern at Hieria had also been turned into a garden. The celebrated Emperor Basil saw that the place had ample and suitable ground for planting gardens but was rather short of clean drinking water. So, with many hands and great energy, he carried the earth out again. He brought the meadow, only lately seen thick with plants, back to its old form, and in place of a garden he made a reservoir of plentiful and lasting water.

93. These, then, are the works that the celebrated emperor built, with diligence and piety, within the imperial precincts.

Now let the narrative leave the palace and go on to the emperor's next works in this imperial city and around it: the building and rebuilding of holy churches. He saw that the townspeople and working crowd who spent their time in the market called the Forum were absorbed in the needs of daily life. Because there was no house of prayer nearby, they were forgetting the care of their souls. So he built in the market a very beautiful and venerable church of the Mother of God. It was meant to be a shelter for the crowds from rain and storms, and a delight and help toward the salvation of their souls. He also saw that the other church of the all-praised Mother of God, the holy church of the all-venerable and holy Reliquary (Soros) in the Chalkoprateia, was low and dark. He raised windowed arches on both sides to let in light and lifted the roof high, and so he made it bright with dignity and gleaming with flashes of light. As for the holy church of the first of the angels at the place called Tzirou, together with the charitable service and provision for the poor attached to it, he is the one who secured them. He made the church splendid and brought it to the beauty now seen. He increased its revenues so that its ministry lacked nothing, and he gave the poor more generous charity. He also rebuilt the very great church of the priest-martyr Lawrence in the Pulcherianae, which had collapsed, and filled it with great charm. Around the city he raised about a hundred other sacred buildings. He renewed poorhouses and hostels, and he restored most of those that had grown old: hospitals, old-age homes and monasteries.

94. He did not do such works, out of love for God and generosity, only within the city. Outside it he showed the same care. In this spirit he rebuilt the church of the apostle and evangelist John the Theologian at the place called the Hebdomon, which had been worn down by time and had fallen. He beautified it with ornaments and made it secure with supports. Near it stood the church of the Forerunner, which had collapsed very many years before and was a ruin rather than a church. He cleared it of rubble and heaps of earth, and by very quick building and careful work he made it equal to the famous and great churches. The sanctuary of the chief of the apostles at Rhegion could not be entered because it was threatening to collapse. He himself pulled it down and rebuilt it from the foundations, as a lasting and unforgettable memorial of himself. At Justinian's bridges over the river Bathys he raised the church of the martyr Callinicus, which had fallen into ruin [?], making it better than before. And at the place called the Stenon, by which I mean the neck of the Euxine, he built the all-venerable church of St Phocas in a way pleasing to God and loving toward him. He gathered there a community of devout monks and enriched the place with buildings and

estates, and so he made it a monastery gathered by God and a hospital for souls. On top of all this there was the sacred church of the commander-in-chief of the angels, Michael, at Sosthenion. It had been decaying for a long time and had sagged with many cracks. It was by now almost brought to its knees and had lost much of its beauty. He raised it from its ruins, restored it to its former prime and showed it full of every beauty. Such, then, was Basil, celebrated among emperors, in his care for sacred buildings and their restoration, the thing by which piety toward God is most clearly shown.

95. He knew that God rejoices in nothing so much as in the salvation of souls, and that whoever brings out the worthy from the unworthy is as the mouth of Christ. So he did not show himself careless or idle in this apostolic work either. First, as far as it lay in his power, he drew into Christ's net, to submit to him, the nation of the Jews, uncircumcised and hard of heart. He ordered them to bring the proofs of their religion and come to public debates. There they had either to show that their teachings were strong and could not be refuted, or else be persuaded that Christ was the sum of the law and the prophets, and that the law was a shadow that the rising sunlight scatters, and so come over to the Lord's teaching and be baptized. He also gave honours and offices to those who came over. He released them from the burden of their former taxes, and he promised to raise them from dishonour to honour. In this way he freed many from the veil of hardness of heart that lay over them and drew them to faith in Christ. It is true that most of them, after the emperor had departed this life, went back to their own vomit like dogs. But even if they, or rather some of them, stayed unchanged like Ethiopians, the God-loving emperor was still to receive from God the full reward for his zeal in this work.

96. He is found to have acted in the same way toward the Bulgarian people. That nation had earlier seemed to accept the change to true religion and to come over to Christianity. Yet it was still unsteady and unsettled in the good, easily shaken and blown about like leaves in the wind. But through the emperor's frequent exhortations and splendid receptions, and also his lavish generosity and gifts, it was persuaded to accept an archbishop and allowed the country to be filled with bishops. Through these, and through the devout monks whom the emperor called out of the mountains and the caves of the earth and sent there, it gave up its ancestral customs and was wholly caught in Christ's net.

97. Then there was the nation of the Rus, very hard to fight and utterly godless. By generous gifts of gold, silver and silk garments he drew them into agreements and made peace treaties with them. He persuaded them to share in saving baptism and arranged for them to receive an archbishop ordained by Patriarch Ignatius. When this archbishop arrived in the country of that nation, he won its acceptance through the following deed. The ruler of that people called an assembly of his subjects. He presided with the elders around him, who clung to their superstition more than the others because of long habit. As they were deliberating about their own faith and that of the Christians, they summoned the prelate who had just come to them, and the ruler asked what it was that he preached and what they were to be taught. The archbishop held out the sacred book of the divine Gospel and told them some of the miracles of our Saviour and God, and he set out for them the wonders God had worked in the old history. At once the Rus said, 'Unless we too see something like this, and especially something like what you say happened to the three young men in the furnace, we will not believe you at all, and we will not lend our ears any longer to what you say.' He trusted in the truth of the one who said, 'Whatever you ask in my name, you will receive,' and, 'Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater ones than these,' whenever what is done is meant not for show but for the salvation of souls. So he said to them, 'It is not permitted to put the Lord God to the test. Nevertheless, if you have resolved with all your soul to come to God, ask for whatever you wish, and God will certainly do it because of your faith, even though we are lowly and the least of men.' They asked that the very book of the Christians' faith, that is, the divine and holy Gospel, be thrown into a pyre that they would light. If it were kept unharmed and unburnt, they would come over to the God he preached. These terms were agreed. The priest raised his eyes and hands to God and said, 'Glorify your holy name, Jesus Christ our God, now too, before the eyes of this whole nation.' Then the book of the holy Gospel was thrown into the furnace of fire. Many hours passed, and then the furnace was put out. The sacred volume was found to have stayed untouched and unharmed. The fire had done it no damage or loss at all. Not even the tassels on the book's clasps had been damaged or changed in any way. When the barbarians saw this, they were struck by the greatness of the miracle and began to be baptized without hesitation.

98. In this way such works were being accomplished in the years of the reign of the wise Emperor Basil. His affairs were going well and as he intended, and life flourished from day to day. Good cheer danced through the city and the palace, and calm spread over almost every island and mainland. Then suddenly a hurricane, a squall and a tempest of disasters burst into the palace. Mourning and lament, an Iliad of sorrows and a tragedy of afflictions danced through the palace. For the emperor's dearest and firstborn son, Constantine, fell into an acute illness in the very flower of his age, in the prime of youth, just as he was beginning to run in rivalry with his father's noble qualities. He burned with fever for a few days, and the violent, unnatural fire quickly used up all his vital moisture. He departed this life and left his father unspeakable grief. Yet an educated man ought to master irrational passions by reason. Basil knew that he was himself human and mortal, and that his son too had been mortal. So he left immoderate mourning over what had happened to the women's quarters, as something ignoble and unmanly, and quickly came back to himself. He spoke the grateful words of noble Job: 'The Lord gave,' he said, 'and the Lord has taken away again [?]. As it seemed good to the Lord, so it has come about. Blessed be his name.' And he said, 'What is so astonishing if the one who gave has taken back, as he willed, what he gave [?]?' Instead he became a comfort to the mother and the brothers, and he was back at his usual work. He protected orphans, helped widows, provided for soldiers and the poor, and defended those who were wronged. He listened gladly and kindly to those who fear the Lord as they explained and recommended to him things that were profitable, things that brought salvation and won the kingdom above.

99. Those placed in charge of offices and administrations often like to make a show of their loyalty. Perhaps they also think it will make their own position more secure. So they propose measures to raise receipts and increase revenues. With this sort of intention the official who then held the office of the genikon once suggested to this noble emperor too that the so-called inspectors and assessors should be sent to all the themes under Roman rule. That way, he said, they could hand over to others the fields and estates whose owners time had swept away in its currents through some misfortune, and so bring the imperial treasury no small revenue. The emperor pretended to accept the suggestion. He urged him to choose and make ready the men who could carry out the work well and

bring them to him. The genikos considered the matter and took thought, chose what seemed to him the very best men, and brought the names of those chosen to the emperor. But the emperor thought him deserving of heavy blame and rebuked him sharply for putting forward such men for such a task. When the official said that he had no better men among the civil officials, the emperor replied, 'In my judgement the work of the proposed service is so important that, if it were possible, I would go out myself to carry it out. But I know that this would perhaps seem unfitting and impossible. So I have no choice but to rest my hopes on the two magistroi of the state. Through long years and experience, and through the many civil offices they have held over their long lives, in which they have been tested, they have given an unalloyed and pure proof of their virtue. I am confident that the service will be properly carried out by them. So go,' he said, 'and tell them yourself how useful this service is and what my will is. If they are willing to go, I too approve and put my seal on the plan.' When the men heard this they were dismayed. Pleading their old age, along with their many labours and toils for the common good, they begged that the cup of such a service might pass from them. So the man who had been sent had no choice but to come back with nothing done, and he reported the magistroi's answer to the emperor. When he heard it, the emperor said, 'If it is thought and said to be impossible for me to go out, and the most illustrious magistroi also decline the service, then I have no worthy administrator for the matter. So I wish what has been proposed to be left, as it must be, uninspected and uninvestigated. For it is better,' he said, 'that some people should wrongly profit from what is mine than that anyone should be wrongly brought into ruinous harm and a crushing disaster.' For this reason, throughout his whole reign, the people of all the themes under Roman rule remained uninspected, so to speak, and unassessed, or rather free and untaxed. The estates and fields were left for the neighbouring poor to enjoy. Such was the good emperor toward all his subjects, and especially toward the country people, showing them a father's concern and care.

100. But again envy stirred up another squall and storm around the palace, throwing nature into confusion and turmoil against itself. The emperor's dearest son Constantine had only just departed this life, and the father's affection and hopes had passed to his second son, Leo. It seems that the envious race of demons could not calmly bear to see the gentleness, quietness, piety and good order of the one who was to succeed to this imperial

rule, or the prosperity that would come from this upon [?] under his reign, and its growth in everything worthy of praise. So it prepared itself for the fight against him and struggled against him in roughly this way. Among those whom the celebrated Basil greatly favoured and trusted was a man who seemed to be a monk and a priest, his friend and capable assistant, called Santabarenos. Although the emperor was fond of him, he had no good reputation among the others and was not thought blameless. For this reason the very wise Leo often mocked him as a sorcerer and a cheat, who led the emperor astray into things he should not do and drew him away from his duties. When that cheat and villain learned of this, he put on a show of goodwill and pretended to be a friend to the good Leo. He said to him, 'You are already a young man and loved by your father. Why do you not secretly carry a sword or a knife when you ride out with your father in the countryside? Then you could hand it to him if he needs it against a wild beast. And if some plot [?] is ever made against him, as often happens, you would not be found unarmed, but would have something with which to fight off your father's enemies.' Leo did not suspect the trick or see through the man's cunning, for whoever is not inclined to wickedness does not easily suspect evil. He accepted the advice and was persuaded to carry a knife inside his boot. When the plotter knew that his scheme had worked, he reported to the emperor, 'Your son is plotting to kill you. If you do not believe it, when you are about to leave the capital to go hunting or anywhere else, order the shoes taken off his feet. If he is found carrying a blade, know that he has got it ready to murder you.' So an imperial outing was announced, and the whole usual retinue went out with him. When they reached a certain place, the emperor pretended he needed a knife and asked for one urgently. His son was there with him. He suspected nothing of what his father was thinking, and quite innocently and without any guile he drew the knife he was carrying and handed it to his father. When this happened, the charge against him at once seemed believable, and his defence seemed empty and worthless. As soon as they had returned to the palace, the emperor turned on his son in anger. He had him placed under guard in one of the palace buildings, called the Margarites, and stripped him of his red boots. The enemy and avenger even provoked him to the point of putting out the lamps of his son's eyes. But the archbishop of the capital and the senate prevented him from doing this. Even so, he kept him in prison. A long time passed. Nature did not recognize itself but was made harsh by evil spirits, and of the [?]

[?] The men of high rank had often wished to plead with the father on the son's behalf, but had been prevented [?] at one time by one thing and at another by some other cause. Then the following pretext gave them a reasonable opportunity to bring it about.

101. In the palace a winged creature hung in a woven basket. It was a mimic with many voices, and it is called a parrot. Whether someone had taught it or it learned some other way, it often cried out, "Alas, alas, Lord Leo!" Once a banquet was being held for the emperor, and the leading members of the senate were dining with him. When the bird kept uttering these words, the guests grew gloomy, stopped [?] feasting, and sat lost in thought. The emperor noticed this and asked them why they were not eating. Their eyes filled with tears, and they said: "What food can we be seen to [eat?] [?] when we are reproached like this by the voice of a dumb creature? We are thought to be rational beings and to love our master [?], yet this bird calls out for its own master, while we live in luxury and have forgotten our lord's son, who has done no wrong. If he is proved guilty and shown to have raised his right hand against his father's head, then let all of us be his executioners and glut ourselves on his blood. But if he escapes conviction on the charges brought against him, how long will the slanderous tongue prevail against him?" These words softened the emperor. For the moment he ordered them to sit down and promised to look into the matter. Not long afterwards he returned to his natural feeling. He brought his son out of custody and into his presence, changed his mourning clothes, ordered the long hair that had grown during his grief to be cut, and restored to him his former rank and honour in the empire. 102. Not long after this the emperor fell into a wasting sickness, brought on by a flux of the bowels that began with one of his hunting accidents, and from then on he slowly wasted away under this consumption. [?] He arranged the affairs of the empire in the best way and named his heir. He considered what was fitting in each matter and settled it wisely. At last a burning fever flared up in him, drew out and used up all his vital moisture, and he departed this life. He had reigned jointly with Michael, his predecessor, for one year, and for another nineteen years he had won distinction in sole rule of the empire. He ordered civil affairs excellently and conducted military affairs very well. He enlarged the borders of the realm and drove injustice and violence away from all his subjects, so that Homer's testimony about the best of kings fits him: "Both a good king and a mighty—"
He was succeeded in the whole rule of the empire by the one who, both by nature and by virtue, was called to the

inheritance of his father and was asked for in the prayers of his subjects: Leo, most gentle and most wise, the eldest of the sons still living. So the history of the pious reign of Basil of blessed memory has now been told and recorded, as far as we were able and as the nature of the truth required: all of it that has not been swept away by the streams of oblivion or faded in the time between. This includes his upbringing before he became emperor and everything that the story of his whole life contains.

THE REIGN OF LEO THE EMPEROR. [?] He reigned as sole emperor for twenty-five years and eight months. His brother Stephen, a cleric and synkellos, lived with the patriarch Photios, who brought him up and educated him. The emperor sent the general Andrew to Chrysopolis with other senators, along with clergy, candles and spices [?]. They took Michael out of his tomb and laid him in a coffin of cypress wood. They placed him on a bier, shrouded him with honour as befits an emperor, and brought him into the City. They escorted him with hymns as far as the Holy Apostles, and his brothers also followed him there. There they laid him in a sarcophagus.

[?] Coming there, they read out the charges against the patriarch Photios in the hearing of everyone [?]. They deposed him from his throne and sent him into exile at the monastery of the Armonianoi, called the monastery of Bordon. The emperor appointed his brother Stephen the synkellos as patriarch, and he was ordained by Theophanes the protothronos. Stephen lived as patriarch for six years and five months, and when he died he was buried in the monastery of Sikeai. 3. The emperor appointed Stylianos Zaoutzes magistros and logothete of the drome. 4. The city called [?] was betrayed [?],

and all its inhabitants were taken captive by the Hagarenes. There was also a great fire near the Sophiai, which burned the church of the holy apostle Thomas, and the emperor Leo later restored it splendidly. 5. The emperor sent to Euchaita and brought Theodore Santabarenos into the City. Andrew the domestic of the scholai and Stephen the magistros of Kalomaria had both often been slandered to Basil by Santabarenos. They now suggested to the emperor that Photios and Theodore Santabarenos had intended to make one of Photios's relatives emperor. The emperor gave orders, and they brought both men [?] to the palace of Pegai, and he ordered them to be guarded separately. Judges were sent to examine the charges against them: the magistros Stephen himself, the domestic Andrew, the patricians Krateros and Goumer, and John Hagiopolites. They brought the patriarch Photios and seated him with honour on a throne, then sat down themselves and began the inquiry. The domestic Andrew said to the patriarch, "Master, do you know the abba Theodore?" He replied, "I do not know an abba Theodore." Andrew asked, "You do not know the abba Theodore Santabarenos?" The patriarch answered, "I know the monk Theodore, who is archbishop of Euchaita." When Santabarenos was brought in, Andrew said to him, "The emperor declares to you: Where are the money and the property of the reign of my father [?]?" He replied, "Where the emperor of that day assigned them. But now that the emperor is asking for them, he has the power to take them back." Andrew said, "Tell us: whom were you planning to make emperor when you prompted the emperor's father to blind his own son? Your [?] relative, or the patriarch's?" He replied, "I know nothing of the things you accuse me of." Then the magistros Stephen said, "Then how did you send word to the emperor that you would convict the patriarch on this charge?" At once he threw himself at the patriarch's feet and said, "I adjure you by God, master: first depose me, and then, once I am stripped of the priesthood, let them punish me as a criminal. I never told the emperor any such thing." The patriarch said, "By the salvation of my soul, lord Theodore, you are archbishop both in this present age and in the age to come." This angered Andrew, and he said, "Abba, did you not send word to the emperor through me that you would convict the patriarch on this charge?" But he denied knowing anything about it. So they went back and reported to the emperor what had been said. The emperor was seized with uncontrollable rage and fury, because he had found no reasonable charge against the patriarch. He sent men who had Santabarenos severely beaten, and he exiled him to Athens. Later he sent and had him

blinded and exiled him to the East. Many years later he recalled him from exile and brought him back into the City, ordering that he receive a food allowance from the New Church. Theodore died in the time of Constantine and his mother Zoe. 6. In Leo's day the Lombard duke, who had become son-in-law of the king of Francia, rose in revolt against the emperor and brought the whole country under his own control. When the emperor learned of this, he sent Constantine, the official of the table, with all the western themes to make war on Aio [?]. When battle was joined, Constantine's men were defeated and slaughtered, and he himself barely escaped. At that time there was also an eclipse of the sun at the sixth hour of the day, so dark that the stars could be seen. There was also a violent rush of wind, with lightning and thunder, so that people were struck by lightning on the steps of the Forum of Saint Constantine.

7. Samos was besieged by the Hagarenes, and Paspalas, its strategos, was captured along with it. The emperor Leo honoured Zaoutzes with the title of basileopator, a dignity he created himself. For he had already become intimate with Zoe, Zaoutzes's daughter, after her husband Theodore, surnamed Gouniatzitzes, had been done away with by poison. 8. When the patriarch Stephen departed this life, Antony, surnamed Kauleas, was appointed patriarch in his place. 9. News arrived that Symeon, the ruler of Bulgaria, intended to march against the Romans. His pretext for war was this. The basileopator Zaoutzes had a eunuch slave named Mousikos. Mousikos made friends with two merchants from Hellas, Staurakios and Kosmas, men greedy for gain and for gold. Hoping to profit through Mousikos's influence, they moved the trade with the Bulgarians from the City to Thessalonica, where they levied harsh duties on the Bulgarians. The Bulgarians reported this to Symeon, and he made it known to the emperor Leo. But Leo, swayed by his partiality for Zaoutzes, dismissed it all as nonsense. Enraged, Symeon took up arms against the Romans. The emperor sent Krenites, who was a general, against him and equipped him with a large army and many officers. Battle was joined in Macedonia and the Romans were defeated. Krenites himself was killed, along with the Armenian Kourtikes and many others. Symeon also captured some Khazars from the emperor Leo's hetaireia, cut off their noses and sent them to the City to shame the Romans. When the emperor saw them he was filled with anger. He sent Niketas, called Skleros, to the Danube with dromons, to give gifts to the Turks so that they would make war on Symeon. Niketas met them, persuaded them to take up arms against Symeon, and returned to the emperor with hostages he had received from them.

The emperor decided to make war on the Bulgarians by both land and sea. By sea he sent Eustathios the droungarios. By land he sent the patrician Nikephoros Phokas, who had become domestic of the scholai after Andrew's death. When they had reached Bulgaria, the emperor sent the quaestor Constantinakios to Symeon, because he still valued peace and wanted to make a treaty with him. But Symeon seized him and shut him up in prison, suspecting that he had come to him with some trick. While Symeon was occupied with Nikephoros's army, the Turks overran the whole Bulgarian land and plundered it. When Symeon learned of this, he turned against the Turks. They crossed over [?], joined battle with the Bulgarians and defeated them so completely that Symeon barely escaped to Dristra. The Turks then asked the emperor to buy the Bulgarian captives from them. He did so, sending citizens to ransom them. Symeon begged the emperor for peace through Eustathios the droungarios. The emperor agreed and sent Leo Choirosphaktes to conclude it, and the domestic Nikephoros and the droungarios Eustathios were ordered to return with the army. But Symeon did not even deign to speak to Leo Choirosphaktes and kept him confined in prison. He marched against the Turks and slaughtered them all, since they could get no help from the Romans. Returning in triumph over his victory, he said to Leo, "Unless I first receive all the Bulgarian captives, I will not make peace." The emperor agreed to hand them over. So Theodore the Bulgarian, a close associate of Symeon, came with Leo and took charge of them. 10. The emperor was extremely fond of the domestic Nikephoros, so the basileopator Zaoutzes favoured him as a man of power and wanted to make a marriage alliance with him. Nikephoros refused, so as not to give the emperor Leo any cause for suspicion. This enraged Zaoutzes, who stirred up charges against him and removed him from office. In his place the magistros Katakalon was appointed domestic of the scholai. After a long time without office, Nikephoros was again appointed strategos of the theme of the Thrakesioi. He performed many brave feats in war throughout his life and set up many trophies over the Hagarenes and other nations. He died at a good old age, leaving two sons, Bardas and Leo. Bardas was very close to the emperor Leo, who cherished and loved him, and he served in offices attached to the emperor's person. As has been said, the emperor appointed Katakalon domestic and sent him against Symeon, together with Theodosios, patrician and protovestiarios. When all

the themes and tagmata of the East had crossed over, battle was joined with the Bulgarians near Boulgarophygon. The Romans were badly routed and all of them perished, and the protovestiarios Theodosios perished with them. At this time the inhabitants of Cherson also killed their strategos Symeon, son of Jonas. Koron in Cappadocia was taken by the Hagarenes as well. 11. The emperor went out to the Damianou palace, taking with him Zoe, Zaoutzes's daughter, and Zaoutzes himself. Theophano, the emperor's wife, was not there. She was devoting herself to prayer at the holy reliquary at Blachernai. When the emperor decided to stay on at the Damianou, Zaoutzes's people, his son Tautzes and the others, held a council and plotted to do away with the emperor during the night. Zoe was sleeping with the emperor. She heard the noise, leaned out of the window and silenced them [?]. When she had understood the full danger of the plot, she woke the emperor and told him what was afoot. He immediately got into a boat and crossed to Pegai, leaving everyone there, Zaoutzes included. Early in the morning he entered the palace, dismissed John the droungarios of the watch, and appointed in his place Pardos, son of Nicholas the hetaireiarch. This Nicholas was a loyal friend of the emperor and kept him fully informed of all Zaoutzes's secrets. From then on the emperor did not enter Zaoutzes's chamber, until Leo the magistros, surnamed Theodotakes, reconciled the two of them. 12. The Augusta Theophano died after reigning for twelve years. She was shown to be a wonder-worker. She had risen above the passion of jealousy, meekly endured seeing Zoe preferred to her, and spent her whole life in almsgiving and prayer. 13.
