The emperor Leo crowned Zoe, Zaoutzes's daughter, and the marriage was blessed by the palace cleric surnamed Sinapes. The man who blessed it was deposed. Zoe reigned for one year and eight months and died. They found a sarcophagus to lay her body in, which bore this carved inscription: "Daughter of Babylon, the—"

14. Mousikos and Staurakios were denounced to the emperor for taking gifts from the strategoi, and from the officials as well, in return for acting as their go-betweens with the basileopator. Once Staurakios had gone in to the basileopator with letters from one of the strategoi. The emperor saw him as he was standing in the solarium, went in after him and took him by the neck. He led him out as though he meant to ask about the strategoi, brought him to the [?] door, snatched the letters, flung him out and handed him over to those standing nearby, to be taken out of the palace and tonsured as a monk. When Mousikos learned of this, he fell into despair. The emperor then went in to where Mousikos was standing beside Zaoutzes, shoved him out by the neck, and ordered Christopher the koitonites to have him tonsured in the

THEOPHANES CONTINUATUS. Stoudios monastery. Shortly afterwards [?] died in the palace. They carried him down by way of the Boukoleon and buried him in the monastery of Kauleas. 15. Basil the epeiktes, who coveted the imperial dignity, struck up a friendship with the koubikoularios Samonas, a man of Hagarene descent. He confided to Samonas: "Now that our aunt Zoe is dead, the emperor will certainly marry another woman and get us out of the way. Give me your word that you will keep the secret, and I will reveal [?] to you everything we are planning." Samonas did so and was told everything. Then Samonas went in to the emperor and said, "Master, I wish to tell you something in private [?]. If I speak it, it brings death on me; if I keep silent, it brings death on you." And he related to the emperor the whole of Basil's plot. The emperor did not believe what he was told and suggested that he might be saying this out of some ill will [?]. Samonas replied, "If you want to be fully assured, send whomever you wish to my chamber. I will hide them in a concealed place, and they can write down whatever Basil and I say. Then you will be certain that nothing I have told you is false." So the emperor sent Christopher the protovestiarios together with Kalokyres the koitonites, who went up into Samonas's [chamber?] and hid. Samonas lured Basil on, gave him his sworn word, and persuaded him to state the whole plot openly once more, along with the names of those plotting with him. Kalokyres and Christopher listened and took it all down in writing. While the others were at lunch [?], these two came down, informed the emperor and read him the record. The emperor at once summoned Basil and gave him 24,000 miliaresia, supposedly appointed as alms for the soul of his aunt Zoe, and sent him off to Macedonia. Pardos, the droungarios of the watch, had been Basil's accomplice. The emperor sent him to Stypiotes, supposedly to bring Stypiotes back, but Stypiotes had been forewarned by an imperial letter and put him in chains. The emperor also banished Nicholas the hetaireiarch from the City. Then he had Basil brought from Macedonia. He interrogated him, had him severely beaten, had his hair burned off and paraded him through the middle of the City, and then exiled him to Athens. The emperor summoned all the magistroi and the high officials and read out before them what Samonas had disclosed. They praised Samonas highly for having saved the emperor's life and declared him worthy of the highest honour. The emperor at once raised him to the rank of protospatharios and made him his own close confidant in—
16. The patriarch Stephen [?] died, and in his place the mystikos was ordained patriarch:

Nicholas, a man of many outstanding gifts in learning, together with a dignified bearing. The city of Demetrias, in the theme of Hellas, was taken by the Hagarenes. 17. The emperor Leo crowned Anna, his daughter by Zoe the daughter of Zaoutzes, because the customary banquets could not be held while there was no Augusta. The emperor then took as his wife a girl from the Opsikion theme, fair and very beautiful, whose name was Eudokia. He married and crowned her, and she bore him a son, but at the birth both she and the child died. 18. The emperor built a church near the church of the Holy Apostles, dedicated in the name of his first wife Theophano. He also built the church of Saint Lazarus at the place called Topoi, and established a monastery of eunuchs in it. There he brought and laid to rest the bodies of Saint Lazarus and of his sister Magdalene. While the fleet was busy with the work on these churches, Taormina in Sicily was taken by the Africans, and many Romans were slaughtered. Lemnos was also seized by the Hagarenes, and a great many people were taken captive. 19. On the day of Mid-Pentecost the emperor went in procession to Saint Mokios. As he was entering and drew near the holy doors, a man leapt out from the ambo and struck him on the head with a thick, heavy staff. He would have killed him on the spot, but by some providence the end of the staff struck the polykandelon, which checked a little of the blow's force. As blood poured from the emperor's head, the officials were thrown into confusion and fled. His brother Alexander had pleaded illness and had not come down for the entrance, so he was suspected of having contrived the attack. The man who struck the emperor was seized and endured many tortures. Since he maintained that no one else had known of it, in the end his hands and feet were cut off and he was burned in the Sphendone of the Hippodrome. From then on this procession was discontinued. Some time later Mark, a very learned monk who was steward of that same church, and who also completed the tetraode of the great Kosmas for Holy Saturday, was dining at table with the emperor. He begged him not to let this procession be abolished. When the emperor refused, Mark said, "Do not be angry or vexed, O emperor. The prophet David wrote long ago that you would suffer this, for he foretold it when he said, 'All the evil that the enemy has done in your sanctuary,' and so on."

…those who hate you have boasted in the midst of your feast.” “So, master, you will hold the empire for ten years from now.” And so it came about: when the ten years were complete, he died on the same day on which he had been struck.

20. Zoe, the emperor's fourth wife, was living in the palace with the emperor, but she had not been crowned. While Bulgarian raids were wearing down the Romans, the sons of Hagar learned of this and sent out a war fleet. They put it under the command of Leo of Tripoli, who had come from the city of Attaleia and had abandoned the Christian faith. Tripoli in Phoenicia got its name because it was divided into three communities of settlers from Aradus, Tyre and Sidon. The emperor had gone out to the market of [?] to dedicate the monastery of his protovestiarios Christopher when the news reached him that Leo of Tripoli was coming against Constantinople with a Saracen fleet. So the emperor sent Eustathios, who was then droungarios, against Leo of Tripoli with a fleet. Eustathios could not stand against him and came back with nothing done. Leo of Tripoli came after him, entered inside Abydos and got as far as Parion. When the emperor heard this, it threw him into deep despair and left him at a loss. So he put Himerios the protasekretis in charge of the naval forces and sent him against Leo of Tripoli. [?] to Abydos, passing the one on the Hellespont, which colonists from Miletus had settled. The Hellespont is named after Helle, the sister of Phrixus, who was thrown into the sea there. The Aegean Sea got its name from the motion of its waters, which dart about like a goat. Next he put in at [?] (called Strobelos from its location, and Kibyrrha after Kibyrrhos, the brother of Marsos and Kidramos), and at Lampsacus. Lampsacus was named for a light that shone from God at night while the Phocaeans were praying as they laid its foundations, and the base of the foundations was made firm. After that he passed Imbros, which is named after Imbros, son of Anthus, whose father was Staphylus, the dearest grandson of Dionysus. He crossed over to Samothrace and approached Thasos, which people in earlier times called Chryse. Samothrace was once a peninsula in Thrace called Therioussa, because it was full of wild beasts, and was sacred to the Nymphs. Later the current broke through and it became an island. Settlers from Samos took possession of it, and it was called Samothrace. [?]

…carrying a hundred [?]. He fell ill and went into Thessalonica to bathe and get some relief. Leo of Tripoli seized him. Learning that he was carrying gold, Leo tortured him severely and killed him, although he insisted that he had nothing. And in fact he had left the gold on the road. Symeon the asekretis came by and picked it up, and later this Symeon became patrician and protasekretis. When Leo of Tripoli meant to destroy the city, Symeon sent him word to take gold and spare the city from destruction, and that is what happened. Then the Saracen fleet turned back and went home. When Himerios found this out, he set off in pursuit of them. But they put in at Crete and gave the people there a share of the plunder. From there they sailed home, leaving Himerios at Lemnos with nothing accomplished.

22. The emperor had as hypostrategos of the Anatolikon the patrician Eustathios, who came from the excellent and noble family of the Argyroi. He campaigned against the Ishmaelites and routed them, not once but many times. He was honored and distinguished for strength, power, intelligence, courage, prudence, temperance and justice, and he had Andronikos Doukas with him as well. The Hagarenes feared Eustathios Argyros so much that the mere mention of his name filled them with terror and fear.

Samonas claimed that he was going out to his monastery called Ta Speira, at Damatrys, but instead he took flight with his money and horses. At every relay station he hamstrung the public horses. So the emperor sent Basil Kamateros the hetaireiarch and George Krenites after him to hunt him down. As Samonas was about to cross the Halys, Nikephoros Kallonas the droungarios overtook him and held him. Samonas begged him at length and promised to pay him. When this did not persuade him, Samonas took refuge at the cross in Siricha, pretending that he had come there to pray. Constantine, the son of Andronikos Doukas, overtook him there, took him in charge and brought him back to the city. The emperor ordered him to be kept under guard in the house of the Caesar Bardas. He asked Constantine whether Samonas had really been fleeing to Syria. When he learned that it was true, he told Constantine not to say so if he was questioned before the senate, but to say that Samonas had gone to Siricha to pray, because the emperor wanted Samonas to be pardoned. He summoned the senate, brought Constantine before them and asked him: “By God and by my head, was Samonas fleeing to Syria, yes or no?” Constantine respected the oath. He had said earlier that if he was not put on oath but simply asked, he would not tell [?]. So he admitted before everyone that Samonas had been fleeing to Syria. The emperor dismissed him in anger,

and Samonas was kept from the emperor's sight for four months, staying in the house of the Caesar. After that he was again admitted to the emperor's presence and conversation.

23. Leo had a son, Constantine, by Zoe, his fourth wife. At his birth a comet appeared with its rays toward the east, and it was visible for forty days and nights. He was baptized in the Great Church by Patriarch Nicholas on the holy day of Lights. His sponsors at holy baptism were Alexander, the emperor's brother, the patrician Samonas and all the officials. At that time the Kyphe also became a home for the aged, and the prostitutes there were driven out. The emperor Leo was married to Zoe by the priest Thomas, who was deposed for it, and he proclaimed her empress. For this reason the patriarch barred the emperor from entering the church, so he would go through the right side to the metatorion.

24. Samonas was promoted to parakoimomenos because he had become the emperor's partner in every lawless and wicked act. They began to plot against the Church. They summoned Patriarch Nicholas (it was the first of February) and pressed him hard to accept [the marriage]. When they could not persuade him, after a banquet they put him in a small boat at the Boukoleon and took him across to Hiereia. From there he could barely make his way to Galakrenai, because deep snow lay on the ground. Euthymios the synkellos was ordained patriarch. He was a man worthy of the priesthood, self-controlled and devout, and they say that he accepted the high-priestly office because of a divine revelation. For the emperor intended to issue a wicked law allowing women to have three and four husbands, and many very learned men were helping him with it.

25. In the month of June the emperor Leo was invited by Constantine of Lips to his monastery near the Holy Apostles to dedicate it and to dine. A wind called the lips arose and blew violently until the third [?]. It shook houses and churches, so that everyone fled to open places, saying that the end of the world had come. But God's loving-kindness stopped the storm with rain.

26. When a Hagarene fleet set out against the Romans, the emperor appointed Himerios, logothete of the drome, commander of the whole fleet. Andronikos the doux also agreed to go with Himerios and fight the Hagarenes. But Samonas was Andronikos's irreconcilable enemy, and he was digging a pit for him and laying snares for his feet, because he resented him for foiling his flight. He got someone to write to Andronikos secretly, telling him not to board the ships. “Himerios,” the letter said, “has received orders from the emperor, at Samonas's prompting, to seize you and blind you.” Although

Himerios urged Andronikos many times to board the ships, since the Hagarenes were close at hand, Andronikos balked and refused to do it. So Himerios alone joined battle with the Hagarenes on the feast of the holy apostle Thomas, and he won a great victory. When Andronikos learned of this, he gave up hope. With his relatives and slaves he seized a city called Kabala and went into rebellion. Samonas had long been waiting to seize just such an opportunity, and he said to the emperor: “Master, haven't I always said that the doux is a rebel and a traitor and an enemy of your majesty?” At once the emperor sent Gregoras, known as Iberitzes, to fight him. Gregoras was domestic of the scholai and a relative of Andronikos by marriage. When Andronikos learned this, and also how Patriarch Nicholas had been driven from the Church, he fled with his whole household to the Hagarenes, who had then come out against the Romans. The Amermoumnes received him with honor and splendor. The emperor was grieved over Andronikos and wanted to send him a signed assurance so that he would return to the Romans. Some people advised the emperor to win over one of the Saracens of the praetorium with gifts and send him to Syria with the signed letter. So he did this. He wrote the letter in cinnabar, sealed it with a golden bull, and enclosed it inside a small [?] candle. When the Saracen came out from the emperor, Samonas called him aside and said: “Do you know what you are holding?” He meant the wax the man was carrying. “It is the ruin of Syria.” He gave him money and told him to put it into the hands of the vizier. The man went and did so. Andronikos was arrested and put in chains along with all his relatives. When he learned that this had happened through Samonas's treachery, he and those with him were forced to renounce their own faith. His son Constantine knew that it was impossible to get away from there, so on his father's advice he escaped from Syria and returned to the emperor with his companions. The emperor showered him with gifts. Standing at the east-facing icon of our Lord and Savior, he said to him: “Do not deceive yourself because of the saying that many repeat, that a Constantine will reign over the Romans. I swear to you by the all-seeing justice and by the icon of our Lord that the empire is not yours because you are called Constantine. God has given it through my forefathers to my dearest son, as many holy men have assured me. If you try to lay hands on him, your head will come in through this gate without your body.” And so it came about. After he rose up as a usurper, his head, fouled with blood, gore and dust, came in through those same gates.

27. The emperor removed Eustathios, surnamed Argyros, from the command of the

Watch because of some suspicion and sent him home to Charsianon. On the way, at Ara, he was given poison by one of his own men and died. He was buried at Spynin [?] on the summit of Ara. Then his sons Pothos and Leo, who held the rank of manglabites, took up his body and buried him in their family monastery of Saint Elizabeth in the theme of Charsianon. It had been dedicated by Leo the tourmarch, their grandfather. He also took the name of the Argyroi, whether because of the purity and chastity of his body, or because of the beauty and nobility of his appearance, or because of some trait of his family and his courage. For the man was such that no other soldier like him was found under the emperor Michael. Many times he engaged the Hagarenes of Tephrike with his men and put them to rout, flight and destruction, and they cowered and trembled when his name was spoken.

28. For an exchange of prisoners, the famous Abelbakes and Samonas's father came out from Tarsus. The emperor received them, having decorated the Magnaura with great splendor. He also adorned the Great Church completely and showed all the precious vessels to the Hagarenes. This was unworthy of Christian order, to display the vessels of God's liturgy to the godless and foreigners. Samonas's father wanted to stay with his son, but Samonas would not allow it. Instead he urged him to return home and keep to his own faith. “And I,” he said, “will come back to you soon, if I can.”

29. On the day of Pentecost the emperor Leo had his son Constantine crowned by Patriarch Euthymios. Samonas gave his own man Constantine, who had earlier served Basil the magistros and kanikleios, to the Augusta to serve her. This Constantine was so loved by Leo and by the empress herself that Samonas became jealous of him and slandered him, saying he was having an affair with the Augusta. The emperor suspected that this was true. He sent and had him tonsured in the monastery of Saint Tarasios, and he entrusted Samonas himself with doing it. A little later the emperor wanted to take him back, and he ordered Samonas to bring him to the monastery of Ta Speira. So the emperor went out to Damatrys. While he was dining at Samonas's monastery, he saw Constantine and gave orders at once. They dressed him in secular clothes and put the emperor's cup into his hands at the meal, and he returned to the palace with the emperor. When Samonas saw the emperor's affection for Constantine growing, he wrote a pamphlet with [?] the koitonites and Michael Tzirethon, full of endless insults against the emperor. They had it composed by Constantine the Rhodian, his secretary, [?]

and threw it into the metatorion. The emperor entered the Great Church and went into that metatorion. He found the pamphlet in the place where he prayed, read it and was overwhelmed with grief, and he tried to find out who had written it.

30. There was an eclipse of the moon. The emperor summoned Pantaleon, metropolitan of Synnada, to learn from him what the eclipse would bring about. As Pantaleon was coming to the emperor, Samonas asked him: “Who will the harm fall on?” He said: “On you. But if you get past the thirteenth of June, you will suffer no harm after that.” To the emperor he said that the eclipse would strike the second person. The emperor suspected it would fall on Alexander, his brother. Afterward Tzirethon admitted to the emperor in private that Samonas had written the pamphlet. At once the emperor sent Samonas down to his house, had him tonsured as a monk and took him off to the monastery of Martinakios. He made Constantine parakoimomenos and built a monastery for him at Nosiai. He went there with Patriarch Euthymios and dedicated it.

31. In the month of October there was a sea battle between Himerios the logothete and Damian and Leo, the Hagarenes. Romanos, who later became emperor, was then strategos at Samos. Himerios was defeated and barely escaped, and almost all his men were in danger.

32. The emperor Leo fell ill with a bowel disease and grew extremely weak, so much so that he could barely address the people at the beginning of the fast, as the imperial custom required: “You see me wasted and chilled by disease. Perhaps I will not live to see Christ's resurrection with you again.” There was also a fire in the candle stores of the Great Church, and the record rooms and archives of the patriarchal treasury burned. On the eleventh of May, a Tuesday, in the fifteenth indiction, the emperor Leo died, handing the empire over to his brother Alexander. They say that when he saw Alexander coming to him, he said: “Here comes the bad time after thirteen months.” He pleaded with him again and again to protect his son Constantine.

[?] Theophanes Continuatus.

…from the patriarchate Euthymios, and enthroned Nicholas himself a second time. Alexander held a silention in the Magnaura and brought Euthymios down from the monastery of Agathos, and sitting together with Nicholas they carried out his deposition. Immediately, as if they had turned into wild beasts, they leapt on that holy man, plucked out his venerable beard, struck him on the neck and inflicted other unbearable punishments on him. They called him a usurper and an adulterer, a man who had leapt upon another's wife. But that holy and venerable man bore it all meekly and quietly. So he was exiled to the monastery of Agathos, and when his life came to an end he was buried in the city, in his own monastery. The patriarch's cleric who had plucked out his gray hairs in the Magnaura when he was being sent into exile went back to his house, and at that very hour his house was consumed by an unseen fire. He also found his daughter struck and paralyzed in her hands, her mouth and her speech. She lay bedridden, begging for her daily food, until the time of the emperor Nikephoros [?].

2. Alexander had long made it his business to live in luxury and devote himself to hunting, because his brother Leo looked down on him. He did none of an emperor's work but loved luxury and spent his time in debauchery, and when he ruled entirely alone he did nothing noble or worth mentioning. As soon as he became sole ruler, he made the priest John (surnamed Lazanes) raiktor [?]. This man came to a bad end after Alexander's death while playing polo at the Hebdomon.

3. In the same way Alexander made Gabrielopoulos and Basilitzes the Slav very rich and poured palace money on them. They say that he often considered making this Basilitzes emperor and having Leo's son Constantine castrated. But the plan was thwarted by those loyal to Leo, who pointed out sometimes that the boy was a mere child, and sometimes that he was sickly. In Alexander's time a comet appeared in the west. They called it the swordfish, and said it foretold bloodshed in the city.

4. This Alexander gave himself over to deceivers and sorcerers, and they persuaded him that the bronze wild boar standing in the Hippodrome was his stoicheion, his talismanic double. For, they said, it was fighting a lion, that is, his brother, and they hinted that the fool was the piglet. Taken in by them, he restored the boar's genitals and tusks, since these were missing. Trusting in this delusion, he held races, and he took the sacred veils and the lamps of the churches and decorated the Hippodrome with them. So the wretch gave the honor due to God to idols. For this reason God very soon took his own honor away from him.

5. When Himerios the logothete returned after his defeat by the Hagarenes, Alexander sent and confined him in the palace monastery called Kampas [?],

after threatening him as someone who had shown himself an enemy during the reign of his brother Leo. Himerios was confined there for six months and died miserably, worn down by distress.

6. Symeon, the ruler of Bulgaria, sent envoys to Alexander about peace. He let him know that he welcomed it and wished to be treated kindly and honored, just as he had been under the emperor Leo. But Alexander was overcome by folly and senselessness and sent the envoys away in disgrace. He threatened Symeon, thinking he could frighten him. So the peace was broken, and Symeon [?] to take up arms against the Christians.

7. Alexander, after dining and drinking wine in the dog-day heat, went down to play ball. There he was struck by a sword sent by God. He went back up, with a great deal of blood flowing from his nostrils and genitals, and two days later he died, on Sunday the sixth of June, in the first indiction. He left as guardians Patriarch Nicholas, Stephen the magistros, John Eladas the magistros, John the raiktor, Euthymios [?], Basilitzes and Gabrielopoulos, and he handed the empire over to Leo's son Constantine. They laid Alexander to rest in the tombs of the emperors, and he was placed with his father Basil.

THE REIGN OF CONSTANTINE, SON OF LEO.

1. When his father Leo died, Constantine was still a child (he was in his seventh year). His uncle Alexander left him the empire, but he was under guardians. He reigned under his guardians and with his mother for seven years. Then he reigned with Romanos, his father-in-law, in a subordinate position, for another twenty-six years, and as sole ruler for fifteen years. So his whole reign lasted [?] years. Patriarch Nicholas took control of the palace, since he too was a guardian, together with Stephen the magistros and John Eladas the magistros. He looked after public affairs and every day managed the business that concerned the empire.

2. While the empire was in this state, word was sent to Constantine Doukas, who was domestic of the scholai, by some of the magnates in the city. They admired him as brave and sensible and well able to govern the empire, and they urged him to come into the city and take power without any effort. When

…some, and the patriarch Nicholas, not knowing that under Alexander's will he had been entrusted with the regency of power, handed a letter to Artabasdos, who was in holy orders, and sent him to Constantine, the son of the Doux, urging him to enter the imperial city and take hold of the empire. For carrying the letter, Artabasdos was made first of the clergy of the renowned Sophia. He was the father of Andrew, who in our own day carried the art of painting to its height, as Apelles and Agatharchus, Heracleides and Philinus of Byzantium had once done.

3. Constantine had long dreamed of the throne and always coveted the crown, so he reached the capital as fast as he could, together with the picked men of his troops, who were enough for the purpose. He came in by night through a postern of the protovestiarios Michael, which was near the acropolis, and spent the night without sleep with his companions in the house of his father-in-law Gregoras. Nicetas the asekretis, who later became protonotarios, reported Constantine's arrival to the patrician and monk Constantine Helladikos. That same night both of them came to the Doux Constantine and took counsel. Before day had broken they seized the gate of the Hippodrome with torches, a great many people and a crowd, acclaiming Constantine as emperor. There his groom was speared by the men inside the Hippodrome gates and killed. Constantine was not let in there but was driven off. As though possessed by some demon, his reason no longer steady because of his lust for the throne, he withdrew from the Hippodrome gloomy and downcast, judging the slaughter of his groom a bad omen. From there he went on to the Chalke amid acclamations, entered by the [?] gate of the Chalke itself, and came as far as the Excubitors. The magister John Eladas then made a selection from the Hetaireia and the oarsmen and sent them armed against the Doux. They came as far as the Chalke and battle was joined. Many fell on both sides, cut down by the sword, so that the place became a pool of blood flowing like a river. Among the dead were Gregoras, the Doux's son, Michael his cousin, and Kourtikes the Armenian. When the Doux Constantine learned this, in the very great confusion that followed, he rode out of the Hippodrome. But his horse slipped on the paving slabs laid there and threw its rider to the ground. Someone found him lying on the ground alone, since all the others had scattered, and cut off his head with a sword. It was brought to the emperor and displayed to all as a warning against treachery. This undertaking of his had also been revealed [?] in another way. A certain Nicholas, who had been entrusted with collecting the public

revenues in Chaldia, had gone over to Syria and renounced our faith. Living there, he practised astronomy, or rather a kind of astrology. He wrote on a black-dyed cloth and sent it to the logothete Thomas. When Manuel, the interpreter for the Hagarenes, washed it in water, the letters on it appeared: "Do not fear the red cockerel, the Doux. He will rebel foolishly and be destroyed at once."

4. When these things were over, Gregoras, Constantine's father-in-law, fled with Leo, whom they called Choirosphaktes, to Hagia Sophia, the church of God. They were dragged out of it by force and tonsured as monks in the monastery of Stoudios. Constantine Helladikos was flogged with ox-hide whips, dressed in rags, seated on a donkey and paraded in mockery through the middle of the city. Then he was taken to the monastery of Dalmatos and confined there under sentence. Leo Katakalites and Abessalom, the son of Arotras, were blinded and sent into exile. Philotheos, son of Dampoudes [?], the eparch, beheaded Constantine, the son of Eulampios, and others with him in the Sphendone of the Hippodrome. They searched hard for Nicetas the asekretis and Constantine of Libos [?] but did not find them, because they had fled. As for the notorious Aigides and his many brave companions, he impaled them all on double stakes all the way from the Heifer at Chrysopolis to Leukatos. These so-called regents would have killed many of the officials of the time without mercy or cause, had not some of the judges [P. 238] curbed their unjust fury, saying to them, "The emperor is a child. How do you dare do such things without his order?" They tonsured the Doux's wife and sent her off to her house in Paphlagonia, and they also castrated her son.

5. In the month of August Symeon, the ruler of Bulgaria, marched against the Romans with a heavy host and reached Constantinople. He encamped before it and threw a palisade around it from Blachernae to the so-called Golden Gate, buoyed by the hope of taking it without effort. But when he saw how strong the walls were, and how well defended by the multitude of troops and by the stone-throwing and arrow-shooting engines, his hopes were dashed. He withdrew to the place called the Hebdomon and asked for a peace treaty. The regents accepted this most gladly, and Symeon sent his magister Theodore to discuss the terms of peace. The patriarch Nicholas, Stephen and John took the emperor with them and came to Blachernae. They brought in Symeon's two sons, who dined with the emperor in the palace. The patriarch Nicholas went out to Symeon, who [?] his head to him. The patriarch said a prayer and then, they say, in place of a crown he took his own epir-

rhiptarion and placed it on Symeon's head. Symeon and his sons were treated kindly with gifts beyond measure and very great, and returned to their own country. They parted without agreement on the peace in question [?].

6. The emperor Constantine, being a child, kept asking for his own mother, whom the emperor Alexander had already put out of the palace, and so they brought her back up again. Once she had taken control of the government, she brought up to the palace Constantine the parakoimomenos and the brothers Constantine and Anastasios, known as the Gongylioi. On the advice of John Eladas they removed the people of the emperor Alexander's household: John the rhaiktor, the man called Gabrilopoulos, Basilitzes and the rest. The Augusta appointed Dominic as hetaireiarch. The magister Eladas fell ill and was given up by the doctors. He left the palace, went to Blachernae, and there died, overcome by his illness. On the advice of Dominic the hetaireiarch, Zoe removed the patriarch Nicholas from the palace together with his associates, telling him angrily to look after the affairs of his own church. [P. 239] Not long afterwards Constantine the parakoimomenos denounced Dominic the hetaireiarch to the Augusta as trying to seize the throne for his own brother. As a pretext they made him a patrician, and when he went down to the church to receive a blessing, as was the custom, they ordered him to stay at home. Zoe appointed John Garidas as hetaireiarch and the eunuch Damian as droungarios of the Watch. Dominic went off to his house, lamenting to no purpose.

7. When Symeon the Bulgarian was again plundering Thrace, the Augusta and the officials were anxious to find a way to put a stop to his arrogance. John Bogas asked to be made a patrician, promising to bring the Pechenegs against Symeon. His request was granted. He received gifts and went off to the land of the Pechenegs, made a treaty with them, took hostages there and brought them to the city, the Pechenegs having agreed to cross over and make war on Symeon. At that time Ashot also came to the city, a man very famous for his strength, the son of the archon of archons. They say that he could take an iron rod by its ends in his two hands and, with his surpassing strength, bend it into the shape of a circle, the stubborn nature of iron yielding to the force of his hands. When he arrived the empress received him with great honour and then sent him back to his own country.

8. In the month of September of the third indiction, Pankratoukas the Armenian betrayed Adrianople to Symeon. The city was formerly called Orestias, after Orestes, the son of Agamemnon. With righteous zeal, because Clytemnestra had treacherously murdered his father, Orestes killed her together with Aegisthus and was driven quite mad. He bathed at the confluence of the three rivers, the Hebrus, the Arzus and the Artakos, and was freed of his

sickness. There he built this city and called it by his own name. Later the Caesar Hadrian enlarged it with well-built houses and renamed it the city of Hadrian. It lies three days' journey for a quick traveller on the road to Philippopolis, embraced by Mount Haemus, beside which the three rivers bring their rainwater together. Not long afterwards Zoe sent Basil, patrician and kanikleios, and Nicetas Helladikos the protospatharios with many gifts, and recovered the city. [P. 240]

9. The emir Damian came to the island of Strobilos with warships and a great force. He would have taken it had he not fallen ill and died, and the Saracens went home empty-handed. The inhabitants of Hellas and Athens were constantly abused by Chase, the son of Joube [?]. Unable to bear his profligacy and greed, they pelted him with stones and killed him miserably inside the sanctuary of the church at Athens.

10. The empress Zoe, seeing Symeon's arrogance and his attacks on the Christians, took counsel with the officials. They decided to arrange an exchange of prisoners and a peace with the Hagarenes, and to bring the whole army of the East across to make war on Symeon and destroy him. The patrician John Rhodinos and Michael Toxaras were sent to Syria to carry out the exchange. When it had been done, the customary distribution of pay was made to the tagmata, and taking these together with the themes they crossed over into Thrace. The domestic of the Schools at that time was the magister Leo Phokas, a man more given to bravery than to prudent command. Constantine, the protopapas of the palace, called Kephalas, and Constantine of Balelias brought out the venerable and life-giving wood of the Cross in Thrace. All venerated it and swore to die with one another, and then set out in full force against the Bulgarians. John Grapson commanded the tagma of the Excubitors, and the son of Maroules that of the [?]. Romanos Argyros was in command as general, together with his brother Leo and Bardas Phokas. With them were Melias with the Armenians and all the other generals of the themes, and besides all these there was the patrician Constantine Lips, who accompanied Leo the domestic as his counsellor in all matters. On the twentieth of the month of August, in the fifth indiction, battle was joined between the Romans and the Bulgarians at the river Achelous. Then (how unsearchable and untraceable are the judgements of God!) the whole Roman army was routed. There was a total rout and a dreadful wailing, as some were trampled by their own comrades and others were killed by the enemy, and there was such a shedding of blood as had never happened since the beginning of time. Leo escaped by fleeing to Mesembria. Among others who were slain in

the clash of battle [P. 241] were Constantine Lips, John Grapson and a good many other officers. The patrician Romanos, droungarios of the fleet, had also been sent with the whole fleet to the river Danube to help Leo Phokas, and John Bogas too, to bring down the Pechenegs, as has been said. The droungarios Romanos was ordered to ferry them across against the Bulgarians to fight alongside Leo Phokas. But Romanos and John fell into quarrels and disputes, and when the Pechenegs saw them fighting and feuding with each other, they went back to their own lands. When the war was over and Romanos and Bogas had returned to the city, proceedings were brought against them [?]. The droungarios Romanos was put in such danger that a sentence was passed condemning him to lose his eyes, for negligence, or rather for malice, in not ferrying the Pechenegs across, but withdrawing too quickly and not even taking on board his ships the Romans who were fleeing. He would have suffered this, had not the sentence been overturned by the patrician Constantine Gongyles and the magister Stephen, who had great influence with the Augusta. The Bulgarians, elated by their victory, marched as far as the city. Leo, the domestic of the Schools, John the hetaireiarch and Nicholas, the son of the Doux, went out against the Bulgarians with a very large force to a place in Thrace called Katasyrtai. During the night the Bulgarians fell upon them unexpectedly. The domestic fled, and Nicholas, the son of the Doux, was slain, and many others with him.

11. Theodore, the tutor of the emperor Constantine, saw that Constantine the parakoimomenos was trying to seize the throne for his own brother-in-law Leo. He advised the emperor Constantine to take Romanos the droungarios to his side, since he had been his father's servant and was well disposed towards him, so that Romanos might be with him [?], guard him, and serve him as ally and helper whenever needed. Romanos was approached about this many times and refused. So the emperor Constantine had a letter drawn up in his own hand, secured it with his signature and sent it to him. Once he had it in his hands, Romanos promised to make the move against the parakoimomenos Constantine and his relatives, [P. 242] as was needed. As this rumour spread, the parakoimomenos pressed Romanos, who had received the customary pay, to set out with the fleet. While Romanos was fitting out and preparing the ships, Constantine the parakoimomenos came out as if to hurry him into sailing. Romanos met him with a servant's bearing and promised that he would gladly do what he was ordered. When Constantine said to Romanos, "If you have handsome and well-born men fit to row the imperial trireme…", Romanos at once beckoned with his hand to those men, who were standing ready,

to come near. They knew the plan. When Romanos was already right beside the dromon, walking behind the parakoimomenos Constantine, he seized him with his hands and cried out, "Take him!" At once they seized him, brought him into the trireme of the droungarios Romanos and held him in custody. There was no one to defend the man or to pity him, since all his companions had taken to flight. When the Augusta Zoe learned of this, she summoned the patriarch Nicholas and her magnates and sent them to Romanos, wanting to learn what had happened. When they did this, the people drove them off, pelting them with stones. At dawn Zoe came out onto the terrace of the Boukoleon and called out to the people [?] and to everyone, "How has this revolt come about?" Theodore, the tutor of the emperor Constantine, said to her, "This has happened because Leo Phokas has destroyed the Romans, and Constantine the parakoimomenos the palace." The emperor took the patriarch Nicholas and the magister Stephen to be with him in the palace, drawing the authority away from his mother to himself. The next day he sent John Toubakes to remove the Augusta Zoe from the palace. But she clung to her son with wailing and tears and moved him to a son's sympathy and pity, so that the emperor said to those leading her away, "Let my mother stay with me." At that word they let her go. The emperor and the patriarch summoned John Garidas and appointed him domestic of the Schools, fearing that Leo Phokas might turn to revolt. But he would not consent to this unless he appointed Theodore Zouphinezer, his wife's brother, and his own son Symeon as hetaireiarchs. Reassured by them with oaths, he went down to his house. [P. 243] But they immediately removed his relatives from the palace. When these came to him and he saw them, he was seized with trembling and his wits deserted him. He went out at once to Romanos and told him what he had suffered. He was reconciled with Romanos, and they gave and received oaths that the two of them would have one soul. He became of one mind and one spirit with him, so much so that they also agreed to make a marriage alliance, tightening the bond of friendship still further by it.

12. On the twenty-fourth of the month of March, Romanos sent John the priest, a close and most trusted associate of his, and Theodore Matzoukes to the palace to explain himself: "What I have done was not done in revolt. I suspected an attack by Phokas and feared that he might attempt some coup against the emperor. That is why I resolved to come up to the palace and guard the emperor." The patriarch Nicholas did not agree to this, so Theodore, the tutor already mentioned, sent word to Romanos to come with [hetaireiarch P; hetaireiarchs in the margin.]

his whole fleet to the Boukoleon. He took counsel with his men (for what was driving him drove him on), and on the day of the Annunciation of the all-blameless Virgin and Theotokos, which was a Thursday, he came armed with the whole fleet to the Boukoleon. Immediately the magister Stephen left the palace, and the patrician Nicetas, whose child was married to a child of Romanos, went up into the palace and brought the patriarch Nicholas out of it. The people of the palace, after Romanos had reassured them with oaths, sent him the life-giving and precious cross. He venerated it, confirmed his oaths to them, and went up with them and a few others into the palace to do obeisance to the emperor. He entered the church of the Pharos with the emperor, and after they had given and received pledges, the emperor at once appointed him magister and grand hetaireiarch. Straight away an imperial order went to Leo Phokas, charging him by no means to contemplate any sedition. Constantine the parakoimomenos was likewise ordered to write letters giving them the same instructions: to plan nothing hostile, but to remain in submission to the emperor Constantine. Andrew, the primikerios of the imperial wardrobe, took these and carried them to Leo, who was in Cappadocia. When he had received and read them, he went off to his own house and kept quiet. [P. 244]

13. In the fifth week of the holy Fast, in the month of April, the emperor Constantine gave a pledge of marriage to Helen, the daughter of Romanos, in whom intelligence flourished along with physical beauty. On the Tuesday of Easter week, which is called the Tuesday of Galilee, she was blessed and crowned together with him by the patriarch Nicholas. The emperor appointed Romanos basileopator, and Romanos made his son Christopher hetaireiarch in his own place. Not long afterwards Leo Phokas, misled by some of the officials and by his own tagmata, moved to revolt. He took with him Constantine the parakoimomenos, the brothers Constantine and Anastasios Gongylios, and Constantine Malelias the protasekretis, assuring them all and confirming that he was making this move on behalf of the emperor Constantine. Romanos the basileopator had signed chrysobulls drawn up as if in the person of the emperor Constantine. They declared the plot overturned, and stated that those who abandoned Phokas and fled to the emperor were on the emperor's side. He gave them to Anna, a shameless and bold woman whom they also called Basilike, and to a certain cleric named Michael, and sent them into Phokas's camp. These two took the documents and secretly spread them through the whole army. Michael was caught by Phokas, beaten without mercy, and had his nose and ears cut off. He later received a fitting reward from Romanos, and so did the woman who had been sent with him. The first to desert was Constantine, the son of Barymichael, commander of the tagma of the Hikanatoi, who abandoned Phokas and went over to Ro[manos?]…

[?] ran over to [Roma]nus, and became the beginning of the end of this rebellion. With him also went Balantios and the man called Atzmoros [?], who were tourmarchs, and both [?]. Phokas, then, having reached Chrysopolis with a very large and heavily armed host, drew up his battle lines from the Stone Heifer as far as Chalcedon, striking fear into those in the City. So Symeon, the keeper of the imperial inkstand, was sent by Romanos in a dromon, carrying a letter signed by the emperor Constantine, which declared: "Having found among my subjects no guardian of my sovereignty and empire more vigilant, more loyal and more faithful than Romanos, I have entrusted my protection to him, after God, and have taken him in place of a father, since he has shown me a father's compassion and a parent's [?] affection. As for Leo Phokas, who has always [?] been plotting against my reign, I have now found him by his very deeds [?] rising up like a tyrant against my rule. Therefore I do not wish him to be domestic from this time on. For I declare that he did not carry out this revolt with my consent, but made this attack of his own free will, [?seeking] the empire for himself." When this was read out to the troops, they all began to withdraw and stream over to Romanos the basileopator. Phokas, at a loss and in despair, as one who had missed every hope, took to flight and came to the fortress of Ateous and was received there; [?] in a place called [?] he was caught. Romanos sent John Toubakes and Leo, his own kinsman, to bring him into the City. But they seized him and blinded him, although they had received no order about this and had done it on their own initiative, so that the basileopator Romanos was angered at it. 14–15. In the month of August the plot of Constantine Ktematinos, David Kamoul[?], and Michael, curator of the Mangana, was denounced; these men were blinded, paraded through the middle of the City and sent into exile. They also brought Leo, magistros and domestic of the scholai, into the City, and he passed through the middle of the marketplace seated on a mule. 16. The Augusta Zoe too was caught plotting against Romanos by means of poisoned food, prepared by Theoklitos, notary of the hypourgia. They removed her from the palace, tonsured her, and took her away to Petrion, to the monastery of St Euphemia. Theodore, tutor of the emperor Constantine, and his brother Symeon were invited to lunch by Theophylact, patrician and count of the stable. While they were eating, John, droungarios of the Watch, called Kourkouas, came in with a large force, seized them, carried them off to the Opsikion, and exiled them to [?their own] estates, on the ground that they were plotting against Romanos.

17. On the twenty-fourth of September Romanos is honoured with the rank of Caesar; and in December, on the 17th of the month, the Sunday of the Forefathers, he is crowned with the imperial diadem by the emperor Constantine and the patriarch Nicholas.

THE REIGN OF ROMANOS. 1. In the year 6428, in the eighth indiction, on the 6th of January, the day of the Holy Lights, he crowns his wife Theodora. In the month of May, on the 17th, the day of holy Pentecost, he has his son Christopher crowned by the emperor, and the two of them alone went forth in that procession. In the month of July, in the eighth indiction, on a Sunday, Romanos brought about the reunion of the Church, all the metropolitans and clergy who had been divided between the patriarch Nicholas and Euthymios being united. 2. On the eighth of February, in the ninth indiction, Romanos sent Stephen of Kalomaria into exile on the island of Antigonos, since he had been accused of aspiring to the throne, and had him tonsured a monk [?], together with Theophanes Teichiotes and Paul [?the tutor], his men. 3. The emperor Romanos held a procession in the Tribunal, everyone having gathered there under arms [?as for] a muster; and suddenly Romanos and Constantine return in great haste to the palace. For a plot of Arsenios and of Paul the manglabites had been denounced by Leo, a man of Arsenios. They were flogged, their property was confiscated, and they were exiled. At that time the presbyter John the rhaiktor held the chief influence, and he made Leo, Arsenios's man, a hebdomadarios, having brought him into the emperor's favour. Romanos, son of Leo Argyros, whom I mentioned earlier, the emperor Romanos made his son-in-law, giving him his daughter Agatha. He was a man of outstanding stature, graced with beauty of body, good looks and intelligence, and above all with almsgiving and generosity, goodness and simplicity. 4. There was a certain Rentakios from Hellas, a kinsman of the patrician Niketas, uneducated and a parricide [?]. He pursued his own father to murder him, and since the father, fleeing his attack, boarded a ship and sailed away, and by the Saracens

of Crete was taken captive, this Rentakios, finding himself unchecked, plundered all his father's property, and coming to the City took refuge in the Great Church of God. The emperor Romanos, learning of his lawlessness and plundering, resolved to remove him from the church and punish him. But he forged letters to the Bulgarians and wanted to desert to them. Seized and convicted, he was deprived of his property and his eyes. 5. When the Bulgarians again marched out as far as Katasyrtai after the death of the domestic [?], Pothos, son of Argyros, a most excellent and very experienced man, was appointed domestic of the scholai. He marched out with the tagmata as far as Thermopolis and sent Michael, son of Moroleon, who was topoteretes, to spy on the Bulgarians. Falling unexpectedly upon their [?ambush], he killed many of the Bulgarians, but was himself wounded, and after entering the City he died. 6. Then, through Theoklitos, notary of the hypourgia, a plot against the emperor Romanos was denounced: that of Anastasios, the sakellarios and head of the goldsmiths' workshop [?], Theodoretos the koitonites, Demetrios, imperial notary of the eidikon, Nicholas [?], and Theodotos the protokarabos, who were supposedly acting on behalf of the emperor Constantine. Being convicted, they were flogged, paraded through the Mese and banished abroad. Theodoretos was flogged privately in the Trikonchos of the palace and was likewise exiled. Anastasios the sakellarios they tonsured [?] in the monastery of Elegmoi, where he also died. 7. Seizing on this pretext, Romanos demotes the emperor Constantine and makes him second, and puts himself forward in first place, out of fear of plots and the death that might come of them. In this he fell, alas for human affairs, into perjury, for he had earlier given his assurance that he would not proclaim himself autocrator ahead of Constantine. 8. Symeon again takes the field against the Romans. He sent a host of Bulgarians, together with Chaganos, Menikos and others, and ordered them to march against the City as fast as possible. Passing through the mountains, they came as far as [?]. Learning of their approach, the emperor Romanos, reckoning that they might come down and set fire to the palaces of Pegai and the Stenon, sends John the rhaiktor together with Leo and Pothos Argyros, who had with them a sizeable force drawn from the imperial guards, the hetaireia and the tagmata. With them was also the patrician Alexios Mousele, droungarios of the fleet, with his men. It was the fifth week of Lent. They drew up their force on the flat, low-lying ground at Pegai. When the Bulgarians appeared above them in arms, raising a wordless and terrifying shout and charging down on them with great violence, John the rhaiktor at once takes to flight,

while Photeinos, son of Platypodes, is slain fighting to defend him, along with many others. The rhaiktor barely escaped and got aboard the dromon. Alexios Mousele the droungarios also came fleeing in his armour, and being unable to climb all the way up the dromon's gangway, he fell into the sea together with his protomandator and drowned. The Argyroi, Pothos and the patrician Leo, fled into the fort and were saved. As for the marines and the whole host, some, fleeing from the enemy's hands, drowned in the sea, others fell to the sword, and others were captured by the Bulgarians. The Bulgarians, with no one to stop them, set fire to the palaces of Pegai and burned the whole Stenon. So terrible a thing is folly, together with inexperience, when it has rashness for an ally. 9. On the twentieth of February, in the tenth indiction, Theodora, Romanos's consort, dies, and her body was laid in the house of the emperor Romanos himself, which he had turned into a monastery. In the same month Sophia, wife of the emperor Christopher, is crowned. At that time also the kouropalates of Iberia came to the City. He passed through the middle of the marketplace, which was splendidly decorated, and was received with great glory and honour. They took him to the Holy Wisdom of God to see its beauty and size and its costly adornment; for they had embellished it and hung it with gold-woven drapes and every kind of ornament, and only then led him in. He was astounded at the marvellous and enormous work of the church and greatly admired its costly adornment. Saying that this sacred place was truly the dwelling of God, he returned again to [?]

10. When the Bulgarians again took the field, came as far as the [?palaces] of St Theodora and set them on fire, the emperor Romanos invited the commanders of the tagmata to lunch, among them also the man called Saktikes. He exhorted and urged them to go out against the enemy and fight for their homeland. They readily agreed to die for his majesty and for the Christians. So the next day the said Saktikes, armed by the emperor, showed that his loyalty and courage were genuine. Getting behind the Bulgarians, he entered their camp and slaughtered everyone he found there. When the Bulgarians learned what had happened, they returned to their camp, and when battle was joined they routed Saktikes, who had only a few men. He fought nobly and killed many, but since he could no longer hold out against the great number of the enemy, he gave his horse its head and rode off in flight. As he was crossing a river that flowed nearby, his horse got stuck in its mud, and he was wounded in the buttock and thigh. With difficulty the horse was pulled out of the mud with the help of his men, and he was brought safely as far as Blachernai; and

being laid in the holy reliquary chapel, he died during the night, since the wound was mortal. 11. At that time also the most reverend Petronas, at the command of the emperor Romanos, brought a splendid small sarcophagus, along with two others without carving, from the men's monastery of St Mamas, which is near the gate called Xerokerkos. In these, they say, Maurice lies together with his children. They were placed in the monastery of the emperor Romanos, that is, the Myrelaion. 12. A certain Adrian, a Chaldian, together with Tatzakes, a very rich Armenian, at the prompting and advice of Bardas Boilas, then strategos in Chaldia, prepared a usurpation and revolt against the emperor Romanos, seizing the stronghold called Paipert. John Kourkouas, domestic of the scholai, defeated and captured them. He blinded the more prominent of them and confiscated their property, but ordered the poor and obscure to go free wherever they wished. Tatzakes fled to another very strong fortress, and having received a pledge that he would suffer no harm, came into the City. He was honoured with the rank of manglabites and lived under guard in the house of the Mangana. But he planned to escape, was caught, and was deprived of his eyes. Bardas Boilas they tonsured a monk, the emperor taking pity on him because he was his friend. 13. The patrician called Moroleon, or more fittingly Thymoleon, was strategos of Adrianople. He was most able in war and very skilful, and had performed a great many feats of valour against the Bulgarians. Symeon the Bulgarian surrounded that city with his whole army, threw a palisade around it, and besieged it vigorously. When the grain of those in the city ran out and a severe famine pressed on them (for they could get supplies from nowhere), they were driven by want to surrender themselves and the strategos to the Bulgarians. Symeon, having taken him, put chains all over his body, punished him with countless tortures, and finally killed him by a bitter death, worthy of his own most cruel and savage soul. Then he handed over the guarding of the city to Bulgarians and withdrew. But when they heard that the Roman army was marching against them, they abandoned the city and left, and it came under the Romans again. 14. When Leo of Tripoli set out against the Romans with a great force and warships and reached the island of Lemnos, the patrician John, droungarios of the fleet, called Rhadinos, suddenly attacked him. Battle was joined, and with God's help the Hagarenes under Leo were routed; the man of Tripoli alone barely escaped by flight. 15. In the month of September, in the second indiction [?],

Symeon, ruler of Bulgaria, marches with his whole army against Constantinople. He plunders Thrace and Macedonia, burning everything, laying it waste and cutting down the trees. When he had come as far as Blachernai, he asked that the patriarch Nicholas and some of the magnates be sent to him, so that he might meet with them about peace. So both sides took hostages from each other, and first the patriarch Nicholas went out, then the patrician Michael called Stypiotes, and John the mystikos, who held the chief influence. For John the rhaiktor had by then been slandered to the emperor; pleading illness, he had left the palace and been tonsured in his own monastery near Galakrenai. These men, then, discussed peace with Symeon, but he sent them away and asked to see the emperor Romanos himself, for he had heard from many about his prudence, courage and intelligence. The emperor was greatly delighted at this, for he longed for peace and for an end to the bloodshed that took place every day. So he sent men to the shore at Kosmidion and had a very strong landing stage built out into the sea, so that the imperial trireme could sail up and moor at it. He had it fenced in on all sides and ordered a partition wall built across the middle, where they were to speak with each other. Meanwhile Symeon sent men and burned the church of the all-holy Theotokos at Pege, which the emperor Justinian had built, together with everything around it. By this he made it plain that he did not want peace but was deceiving the emperor with empty hopes. The emperor came to Blachernai with the patriarch Nicholas and went into the holy reliquary chapel. He stretched out his hands in prayer, then fell on his face and wet the holy floor with his tears, beseeching the all-praised and immaculate Theotokos to soften the unbending and implacable heart of the arrogant Symeon and persuade him to agree to peace. Then they opened the holy casket in which the revered omophorion of the holy Theotokos was kept. The emperor took it up and put it on like an unbreakable breastplate, and set his faith in the all-blameless Theotokos on his head like a helmet; and so he went out of the church fortified with sure armour. Having equipped the fleet that was with him with shields and weapons, he reached the appointed place to speak with Symeon. It was a Thursday when this took place, the ninth of November, at the fourth hour of the day. Symeon too arrived, bringing a multitude divided into many units: some with gold shields and gold spears, others with silver shields and silver spears, others adorned with arms of every colour, all of them clad from head to foot in iron. Taking Symeon in their midst, they acclaimed him as emperor in the language of the Romans. All the members of the senate stood on the walls

and watched what was happening. Then one could see a truly imperial and noble soul, and admire his undaunted spirit and the firmness of his courage. Seeing such an onrush of enemies, he was not dismayed; he did not shrink back or retreat, but went forward calmly, as if going among a crowd of friends, all but offering his own life to the enemy as a ransom for his subjects. He reached the landing stage first and waited there for Symeon. When hostages had been taken on both sides, and the Bulgarians had searched the landing stage carefully in case there was some trick or ambush, Symeon dismounted from his horse and went in to the emperor. After greeting each other, they began to speak of peace. The emperor is said to have spoken to Symeon as follows: "I have heard that you are a God-fearing man and a true Christian, but I see that your deeds do not match your words. For it is the mark of a God-fearing man and a Christian to embrace peace and love, since God is love and is called love; but it is the mark of an impious unbeliever to delight in slaughter and in blood unjustly shed. If, then, you are a true Christian, as we have been assured, put an end at last to these unjust killings and the shedding of unholy blood, and make peace with us Christians, since you yourself are a Christian and are called one. Do not seek to defile Christian hands with the blood of Christians who share the same faith. You too are a man, and await death and resurrection, judgment and recompense. Today you are here, and tomorrow you will be dissolved into dust; a single fever will quench all your arrogance. What account, then, will you give to God when you go there, for these unjust killings? With what face will you look upon the fearful and just Judge? If you do these things out of love of wealth, I will fill you to overflowing with what you desire; only hold back your hand. Embrace peace and love concord, so that you yourself may live a peaceful, bloodless and untroubled life, and so that the Christians may at last be freed from their misfortunes and stop killing Christians; for it is not right for them to take up arms against those of the same faith." Having said this much, the emperor fell silent. Symeon, put to shame by his humility and his words, agreed to make peace. They embraced each other and parted, the emperor having honoured Symeon with magnificent gifts. 16. I shall now relate a portent that happened at that time, something strange to those who know how to interpret such signs. They say that while the emperors were conversing, two eagles flew over them from above. They screeched and came together, and then at once separated from each other: one went toward the City, and the other flew off toward Thrace. Those who study such things closely judged this to be no good omen, for they said that the two rulers would part without reaching a lasting agreement on peace. Symeon, on reaching his own camp, [?] to the [?]

…he reported to the magnates the emperor's intelligence and humility, and praised to the skies his appearance, his strength and the unshakable firmness of his spirit. 17. On 25 December Romanos crowned his sons Stephen and Constantine in the Great Church. The patriarch Nicholas also tonsured his son Theophylact as a cleric. He ordained him subdeacon and appointed him synkellos, after Theophylact had first passed through the order of subdeacons into the sanctuary. 18. In the month of April, on the 19th of the month, Romanos honoured John, the mystikos and chief minister, with the ranks of patrikios and anthypatos. For this very reason envy was stirred up against him, and he was accused by

12 [?]. On 15 May, in the 13th indiction, the patriarch Nicholas died. In his second tenure he had held the patriarchate for thirteen years. His body was laid in the monastery of the Galakrenoi, which he himself had built. In August Stephen, metropolitan of Amaseia, a eunuch, was installed as patriarch. In October John, the mystikos and chief minister, was accused of aspiring to the throne at the prompting of the patrikios and logothete Kosmas, who was giving him his daughter in marriage. For this reason he was removed from the palace, but he was allowed to come and serve the emperor and to manage the relevant affairs together with him. The emperor Romanos had the greatest affection for him, as a man able to serve him in everything, and did not want to cast him off entirely. But the accusers kept pressing the emperor and offering clear proof of the charges. The emperor investigated, learned that they were true, and was about to arrest and interrogate him. John, however, learned of this in advance and took flight. He reached the Monokastanon and was tonsured a monk. Constantine, son of Boilas [?], master of the table, who was his intimate and friend, also fled. He reached Olympus and put on the monastic habit. He too was afraid, since he was a fellow initiate of the mystikos and shared in his more secret affairs. The emperor had the patrikios Kosmas flogged in the Horologion of the palace and replaced him. In place of John the mystikos he appointed Theophanes the protovestiarios as chief minister. At that time there was also a terrible earthquake in the theme of the Thrakesians, and a great and frightening chasm opened in the earth, so that many villages and churches were swallowed up together with their people. 20. On 27 May, in the 15th indiction, Symeon, ruler of Bulgaria, moved an army against the Croats. He engaged them in battle, was defeated, and lost every one of the men under him.

21 [?]. John the astronomer saw the emperor Romanos and said to him: "Master, the statue standing on the arch above the Xerolophos, facing west, is Symeon's [?]. If you cut off its head, Symeon will die at that same hour." The emperor Romanos sent men by night and had the statue's head cut off. At that very hour Symeon died in Bulgaria. He had been seized by madness and struck by a disease of the heart, and so he perished, having done wrong to no purpose. He appointed as ruler his son Peter, whom he had by his second wife, the sister of George Sursuvul, and Symeon also left George as guardian of his children. Michael, his son by his first wife, he had tonsured a monk. John and Benjamin, Peter's brothers, still wore Bulgarian dress. 22. When the surrounding nations, the Croats, the Turks and the rest, learned of Symeon's death, they planned to march against the Bulgarians. At the same time a very great famine, together with locusts, was severely oppressing the Bulgarian nation. The Bulgarians feared an invasion by the other nations, but they feared an attack by the Romans still more. So they took counsel, marched against the Romans and occupied Macedonia, intending, as is likely, to strike fear into the Romans. Then they learned that the emperor Romanos was about to march against them. Peter and George secretly sent a monk named Kalokyres, an Armenian by race, who carried a chrysobull. Its contents declared that they welcomed peace with the Romans and were eager to conclude it. More than that, if the Romans wished, they were ready to make a marriage alliance as well. The emperor received this monk most gladly. He at once sent off on a dromon the monk Theodosios Aboukes and Constantine of Rhodes, an imperial cleric, to discuss peace with the Bulgarians at Mesembria. The town was formerly called Menebria, from Menas the Thracian who founded it and from "bria," which among some of the Thracians means "town"; it is called Mesembria for the sake of euphony. The envoys arrived, discussed what was fitting, and came back by land together with Stephen the Bulgarian. After them came George Sursuvul, Symeon Kalouterkanos, Ousampsos [?], and Symeon, brother-in-law of the ruler of Bulgaria, as well as his kinsman Stephen, and also Magotinos, Kronos and Menikos. They came to a firm agreement with the sovereign Romanos. They saw Maria, the daughter of the emperor Christopher, and were greatly pleased with her. After first concluding the terms of the peace, they wrote to Peter to come quickly. Niketas the magistros, father-in-law of the emperor Romanos's son, was sent to meet Peter and bring him to the city. When Peter the Bulgarian arrived,

the emperor Romanos boarded a trireme and went to Blachernae. There he saw Peter as he came up to him and embraced him. When they had spoken with one another as was fitting, the treaty of peace and the marriage contracts were signed. The protovestiarios acted as mediator in these matters and guided them wisely between the Romans and the Bulgarians.

23. On 8 October the patriarch Stephen went out to the church of the most holy Theotokos of the Spring, together with Theophanes the protovestiarios, Maria the daughter of the emperor Christopher, and the whole senate. He blessed Peter and Maria and placed the bridal crowns on their heads, while Theophanes the protovestiarios and George Sursuvul acted as groomsmen. A splendid and lavish banquet was held, and all the customary wedding rites were joyfully completed. Then Theophanes the protovestiarios went back into the city with Maria, the emperor's daughter. On the third day of the wedding the emperor Romanos gave a splendid feast at the landing-stage of the Spring. He had decked it out with silk hangings, and the imperial dromon was moored at the landing-stage itself. There Romanos met with Peter the Bulgarian, together with his son-in-law Constantine and his son Christopher. The Bulgarians strongly insisted that Christopher be acclaimed first and only then Constantine. The emperor Romanos gave way to their insistence, and what they asked was done. When all the wedding ceremonies had been completed, Maria was about to set out for Bulgaria with her husband Peter. Her parents went out with her as far as the Hebdomon, together with Theophanes the protovestiarios. When she was about to depart, they embraced their daughter and shed many tears, as is natural when one is parted from a much-loved child. They kissed their son-in-law, committed her into his hands, and returned to the palace. Maria, now handed over into Bulgarian hands, went off to Bulgaria both rejoicing and grieving. She grieved because she was parted from her dearest parents, from the imperial palace and from the company of her kin. She rejoiced because she had been joined to a ruler as her husband and was proclaimed mistress of the Bulgarians. So she departed, taking with her wealth of every kind and countless baggage. 24. At that time also John Kourkouas, magistros and domestic of the Schools, had been ably commanding the Roman army almost from the proclamation of the emperor Romanos. He fought the Assyrians every day, ravaged their cities, fortresses, villages and lands, and took captives. Among these places was the famous and renowned, very strong and powerful fortress of Syria called Melitene. He attacked and plundered it in various ways and brought it to the brink of ruin,

and he burned the surrounding villages and lands. Then he laid siege to the fortress itself, which had never been conquered or taken by assault, set up siege engines, and reduced the inhabitants to complete helplessness and perplexity about what to do. They sent envoys to the domestic again and again asking for terms. The wise and prudent John Kourkouas, domestic of the Schools, considered their tears and pitiful pleas and the turns of fortune, since such are human affairs, and he gave way and granted them terms. Apochaps, grandson of Amer, who was emir of Melitene, and Aposalath, a most noble and wealthy general in Melitene, came to him. John the domestic of the Schools received them and sent them on to the emperor. They made a peace agreement and returned home. From then on they campaigned with the Romans against their own kinsmen the Hagarenes. They even entered the city together with the Romans in the triumphal processions, leading Hagarene captives. This was a wonderful and strange sight, and a sign of the misfortune of the godless Saracens. But when the emir [?], a sensible and wise man, died, the inhabitants of Melitene broke the peace. So John Kourkouas, domestic of the Schools, marched against them once more with the themes and the tagmata, and so did Melias with the Armenians. They made many raids and seized much plunder every day. By continual incursions they took captives and despoiled the inhabitants, and they reduced Melitene to such straits that they very quickly sacked it and razed it to the ground. They did the same not only to Melitene but also to the neighbouring cities and lands, which were very fertile and rich and able to yield large revenues. The emperor made Melitene into a kouratoreia and had many thousands in gold and silver paid from there as tribute every year. 26. Niketas the magistros, father-in-law of the emperor Christopher, was accused of urging Christopher to rise against his own father and drive him from the throne. So they expelled Niketas from the city, tonsured him a monk and exiled him to his own

25. On 15 July, in the 6th indiction, the patriarch Stephen died, after being patriarch for two years and eleven months. On 14 December they brought in Tryphon, a monk who lived in the Opsikion and was well attested for piety and holiness. They ordained him patriarch for a fixed term, until Theophylact, the son of Romanos, should reach the proper age, since they intended to ordain Theophylact patriarch of Constantinople. 26. On the 25th of the same month an indescribable winter set in, so that the earth was frozen for [120?] days. From this came the great famine, which surpassed every famine that had ever occurred, and there was great mortality from it, so that the living could not

carry out the dead. The emperor Romanos saw the unbearable violence of this disaster and made provision worthy of his compassionate and merciful nature. He relieved the want caused by the famine with many alms. He closed off the porticoes of the colonnades with shutters and boards, so that the snow and cold could not get in to the poor who sheltered there. At that time he also built the so-called arklai in all the colonnades. He ordered money to be given every month to the poor who lay in them, and the monthly trimisia to be distributed to the poor in the churches. All that was given to the poor in the arklai and in the churches came to twelve thousand in coined silver. His compassionate soul, in its care for the poor, did not stop at these measures. He also ordered that three poor men should dine with him every day, each of whom received one nomisma. On Wednesdays and Fridays three poor monks dined with him, each receiving the fixed nomisma. He also did what is customary in monasteries at mealtimes: he set a double table for himself and his guests. The body was nourished with the usual food, while the soul delighted in the fitting pleasure of words. He listened to these readings attentively, was moved to compunction, and let flow many fountains of tears. Who could describe how great the faith he had in all monks, and above all in those renowned for holiness and piety? He never met a monk devoted to virtue without confessing his own deeds to him with many tears. Being most faithful and most orthodox, he splendidly adorned and brightened all the churches of the city with transparent veils and lamps. He also never failed to send annual stipends to the monks on the mountains: on Olympus, on Kyminas, on the place called the Golden Rock, and on Mount Barachaios. He cared and provided for them, summoned to himself those who were renowned for the active and the contemplative life, and reaped the blessings of their prayers. More than that, he never failed to supply the annual stipends he had decreed to those who for God's sake had shut themselves up as recluses in very narrow cells, and to all the monasteries. We have recounted these few out of his many good deeds and acts of charity. 28. John, the brother of Peter the Bulgarian, plotted against Peter together with other magnates of Symeon. When they were found out, John was flogged and shut up in prison, and the rest were subjected to no ordinary punishments. Peter made this known to the emperor Romanos. The emperor then sent the monk John, who had been rhaiktor, ostensibly to arrange an exchange of the captives being held, but in truth to seize John and bring him to Constantinople. And that is what happened: he went on board a ship together with

John and came from Mesembria to the city. Not long afterwards John cast off the monastic habit and sought a wife. The emperor gave him a house, a great many estates, and a wife who came from his own homeland of the Armeniakon. He also held a splendid wedding in the house of the Caesar, with the emperor Christopher and the monk John, the former rhaiktor, as groomsmen. 29. Michael the monk, also Peter's brother, was eager to seize power in Bulgaria and rose in rebellion on his own account in a certain Bulgarian fortress. The Scythians who had broken away from Peter's rule flocked to him. After Michael's death these men attacked Roman lands, so that they passed from Macedonia [?] to Hellas and Nikopolis and plundered everything there. Nikopolis is named after the victory that Augustus won over Antony and Cleopatra, when he brought the rule of the Egyptians under the Romans. 30. On 2 March a cornice in the Forum fell from the columns that stand in a row there, and it killed six men. There was also a great and terrible fire in the colonnade of the Forum, near the church of the most holy Theotokos, so that the candle-sellers' shops and the furriers' shops of the Forum burned down as far as the

31. The emperor Christopher died in August of the fourth indiction.
