His father mourned and lamented him greatly, more than the Egyptians did, since he himself had already reached old age and Christopher's sons were still infants. His remains were laid in his father's monastery, mentioned above. 32. In August of the [?] indiction they also deposed the patriarch Tryphon, since he had completed his fixed term. He went off to his own monastery and died there. The Church was widowed for one year and five months because Theophylact, son of the emperor Romanos, had not yet come of age; for, as has already been said, it was him they intended to install as patriarch. 33. A certain Basil, a Macedonian impostor, called himself Constantine Doukas and drew many people after him. He was arrested by Elephantinos, a tourmarch from the Opsikion, and brought to Constantinople, where Peter the eparch had one of his hands cut off. Later he seized an opportunity and went back to the Opsikion. He fitted a bronze hand in place of the one that had been cut off and had a huge sword made. Then he went about, once again deceiving many of the vagabonds into believing that he was Constantine, son of Doukas. Drawing them along with him,

he stirred up a great [?] rebellion against Romanos. And [?] … excelling in everything, and also outstanding in his achievements as well as in his learning, legates came up from Rome bringing a synodal tome that declared on his ordination; and they installed him on the patriarchal throne. 35. Maria, the granddaughter of the emperor Romanos mentioned above and wife of Peter the Bulgarian, often came from Bulgaria to the city to visit her father and her grandfather. The last time she came with three children, after her father Christopher had already died. She received much wealth from her grandfather and returned home with honour. 36. Romanos [?] took a wife, the daughter of Gabalas [?], surnamed [?] Katakyla, called Anna. Along with the bridal crown, the crown of empire was also [placed on] her.

37. The first campaign of the Turks against the Romans took place in the seventh indiction, in the month of April. They raided as far as the city and carried off every soul in Thrace. So the patrikios Theophanes, the protovestiarios and chief minister, was sent to arrange an exchange of prisoners. He dealt with them admirably and wisely and accomplished everything he wished, and they greatly admired and praised him for his prudence and good counsel. On this occasion the emperor Romanos also showed his magnanimity and humanity, sparing no expense to ransom the captives. 38. The emperor Romanos took a wife for his last son Constantine. She was Helena, of the family of the Armeniakoi, the daughter of the patrikios Adrian. When she died on 2 February, he joined him to another wife named Theophano, a descendant of the famous Mamas. 39. In the fourteenth indiction, on 11 June, the Rus sailed against Con-

who are also called Dromitai and are of the race of the Franks. So the patrikios [?] was sent against them with the triremes and dromons that happened to be in the city. He fitted out and readied the fleet, and fortified himself as much as he could with fasting and tears, and then waited for the Rus, intending to give battle at sea. They came up to him and drew near the Pharos (the Pharos is the name of a structure on which a beacon is placed to guide those who sail past at night). He was lying in wait at the mouth of the Euxine Sea. (This sea is so named by antiphrasis, for it was "hostile to strangers" because of the constant raids made on strangers by the robbers there; when Heracles, as they say, destroyed them and travellers were able to pass safely, they called it the Euxine, "kind to strangers.") He fell upon them suddenly at the place called the Hieron, which received its name because the Argonauts, when they passed through there, set up a temple on the spot. He sailed out first in his own dromon, broke up the formation of the Rus ships and burned a great many of them with the prepared fire, and he put the rest to rout and flight. The other dromons and triremes followed him, ran out against the enemy and completed the rout. They sank many ships with their crews, killed many men and took a great many alive. The survivors sailed across to the eastern side, to the place called Sgora. Then the patrikios Bardas Phokas, a former strategos, was also sent by land with cavalry and picked men to shadow them along the coast. The Rus sent a sizeable detachment to the regions of Bithynia to obtain food and other supplies. Bardas Phokas came upon this detachment and dealt harshly with it, routing and slaughtering its men. The most wise and prudent John Kourkouas, domestic of the Schools, also came down with the whole army of the East. He destroyed many of them, catching stragglers here and there, so that out of fear of his attacks they huddled together by their own ships and did not dare to venture out anywhere. But before the Roman army came down they had done many very great evils. They burned the whole of the so-called Stenon. Of the captives they took, some they crucified, others they nailed to the ground, and others they set up as targets and shot down with arrows. Any members of the priestly clergy they caught had their hands bound behind their backs, and the Rus drove iron nails into the middle of their heads. They also gave many holy churches over to the flames. As winter came on, they were short of food, and they feared the army of Kourkouas, the domestic of the Schools, which had come against them, as well as that prudent, sensible and wise commander himself; and the ships

[?] and the hostile preparations of the patrician Theophanes, they decided to return to their own lands. And so, eager to slip past the fleet, they set out by night in the month of September of the fifteenth indiction to sail across to the Thracian regions. But they were met by the patrician Theophanes already mentioned, for they did not escape his most watchful and noble spirit. At once a second naval battle was joined, and that man sank a great many ships and killed many of them. A few were saved with their ships, put in at the shore of Kyle, and escaped as night came on. The patrician Theophanes returned with a brilliant victory and very great trophies, was received with honor and magnificence, and was honored with the rank of parakoimomenos.

40. The John already mentioned, magistros and domestic of the Schools, proved outstanding in war. He set up many great trophies, extended the Roman borders and sacked a great many cities of the Hagarenes. Because the man's excellence was so renowned, Emperor Romanos wished to take his daughter as a bride for his own grandson Romanos, the son of his son Constantine. The daughter of Kourkouas was Euphrosyne. The son of Constantine was the Romanos who was later castrated by Constantine Porphyrogennetos and honored as patrician and praipositos. But because this matter stirred up the envy of the other emperors against John, the emperor removed him from office. By then he had served as domestic for twenty-two years and seven months, with no one succeeding him in that time.

41. It is worth telling of his family, his upbringing and his way of life, the nature of his soul and body, and his deeds, and of how faithful and upright he showed himself in our generation. He was of Armenian stock, from Dokeia, from the village of Darbidous [?]. His father was a man of some standing, a very wealthy palatine, the son of John, domestic of the Hikanatoi. He is also said to have been taught the sacred letters by Christopher, metropolitan of Gangra, who was his kinsman. The story goes that the prelate said: "This John will bring redemption and relief to the Romans." And he did subdue many, indeed very many, cities, fortresses, lands, castles and places of the Hagarenes, and he made Romania twice its size. Before, it had been occupied by the deniers of Christ as far as the fortress of Charsianon, Hypsele and the river Halys. John, domestic of the Schools, faithful and zealous toward the emperor Romanos, set the borders of the Romans at the Euphrates and the Tigris and brought these lands to Romania as a dowry and a gift. From there the emperor gained people and an army as well. John also imposed many tributes to be paid yearly, and he brought back from there much spoil, many weapons and many Hagarene captives.

He threw himself into the greatest struggles and sacked the cities of the deniers of Christ. Who could list by name all the cities that John Kourkouas, domestic of the Schools, subdued and [made] tributary to the Romans? In twenty-two years he took nearly a thousand cities, and more, and brought them under Romania. One could see the sleepless John Kourkouas drawn up for battle, addressing the Romans with speeches and persuasive exhortations, and one would liken him to another Trajan or Belisarius and call him by that name. Anyone who sets the man beside them will find that the brave deeds and exploits of Kourkouas are the greater. Those who earnestly long and wish to learn of the exploits of John Kourkouas, and of what has been written about them, will find them set out in eight books by Manuel, protospatharios and judge.

42. It is also worth telling of the exploits and brave deeds of Theophilos, patrician and strategos of Chaldia, the brother of the magistros and domestic of the Schools John. When he became sole strategos in Chaldia, he did not give himself over to luxury, extravagance and pleasure, as many do. Instead he devoted himself to toil and hardship and to plundering the villages and lands of the Hagarenes. As a result, the Hagarenes living in the very strong and altogether marvelous fortress of Theodosioupolis and in the fortresses around it were carried off as captives and made tributary and subject to the magistros John. In Mesopotamia too he proved himself an excellent general. He did not merely appear so but was shown to be so, and he was revealed and recognized as another Solomon, the one of Justinian's time. He also left behind for posterity his grandson John, called Tzimiskes. For his natural talent, courage and tirelessness, this man was honored as patrician and strategos of various themes, and later, under Nikephoros [?], the emperor called [?], he became magistros and domestic of the Schools. But these men too must be described in their proper sequence and order. The same is true of Romanos, patrician and strategos of various themes, the son of the magistros John called Kourkouas, who also proved excellent and brave.

43. These men were at the height of their success. They held fast to the faith of the Christians and fought for it, brought cities, lands and villages under the empire of the Romans, and made the deniers of Christ tributary to Emperor Romanos. But Beliar, who is forever at war with the race of faithful and upright servants, could not bear the great and boundless thanksgiving of the Christians, and he put ideas into the heads of certain people. They slandered the magistros and domestic John to Emperor Romanos, claiming that he aspired to the empire of the Romans and had a people ready for the purpose [?], and that he had committed a great many wrongs and seizures of lands and estates.

Romanos sent men to investigate, but they found nothing, and he gave John back his share of the command. But because these matters stirred up the envy of the others against him, he fell from office, and Pantherios, a relative of Emperor Romanos, was appointed domestic in his place.

44. Emperor Romanos paid all the debts of the City, those of the rich and the magnates, of the poor and the needy, as far as they could be openly proved. Some say that he gave nineteen kentenaria. He burned the bonds at the porphyry omphalion of the Chalke, and everyone called down blessings on the emperor. In the twenty-second year of his reign he paid the rents of the whole City, from the least to the greatest. On Wednesdays and Fridays he went out to the metastasimata [?] and gave every citizen two silver coins each, and he gave the male and female recluses three nomismata each. He built many churches and monasteries, and he also gave gold-woven altar cloths, patens and chalices. He founded a hostel in the quarter of Mavrianos, and he built stables, very fine lodgings and furnished beds there for all the provincials who came to the City with lawsuits. He also ordered provision for their maintenance and for that of their animals and their servants, and he assigned houses to it so that it would be supplied without fail. He did this for the provincials who came to the City with lawsuits, so that they would be fed and maintained from it. For his tomb he ordered that thirty thousand loaves be given out every day. On Wednesdays and Fridays every person in the Praitorion, the Chalke and the Noumera was to be given fifteen folleis, and on Good Friday every prisoner was to receive one nomisma. He also ordered that the monks of Olympos, Kyminas, Athos, Paracheus [?] and Latros should all receive one nomisma each, and that they should receive it from his own monastery.

45. In April of the first indiction the Turks attacked again with a very large force. The patrician Theophanes, the parakoimomenos, went out and made a peace treaty with them, taking prominent hostages, and as a result the peace was kept for five years. Emperor Romanos rebuilt a great many cities in Macedonia and Thrace, some from their foundations, while for others he arranged repairs. In the imperial City as well he renovated splendid palaces, and also shady and fruitful meadows that give no common delight. He built homes for the aged, hostels for strangers and residences for the sick too, hoping for a reward for his soul.

46. In the second indiction Emperor Romanos sent Paschalios, protospatharios and strategos of Longobardia, to Hugh, king of Francia, to ask for his daughter as a bride for Romanos, the son of his son-in-law Constantine. The said Paschalios took her and brought her to the City with great wealth. The wedding took place in September of the third indiction. She lived with her husband for five years and died in the days of the sole reign of her father-in-law Constantine.

47. In the month of December a violent and fierce wind blew down the so-called Demoi in the Hippodrome, which stood opposite the imperial throne, and they smashed the steps beneath them and the so-called stetheia. When the year had come round, in that same month, Emperor Romanos's own sons brought him down from the palace.

48. The city of Edessa, in which the precious imprint of Christ was kept, was being besieged by the Roman army and was reduced to the direst need. Its inhabitants sent envoys to Emperor Romanos to negotiate an end to the siege, promising to hand over the holy imprint of Christ. In return for this favor they asked to receive prisoners from among the notable men, and also a chrysobull guaranteeing that their land would no longer be plundered by the army of the Romans. And this was done. The holy imprint, that is, the mandylion, was sent off, and when it was already approaching Constantinople, the patrician Theophanes the parakoimomenos went out to the river Sangarios and met it with a brilliant display of lights and with fitting honor and hymns. On the fifteenth of August he entered the City with it. The emperor was at Blachernai and venerated it there. On the next day the emperor's two sons, Stephen and Constantine, and his son-in-law Constantine went out to the Golden Gate together with Patriarch Theophylaktos. They received it with fitting honor and carried it on foot to the church of Hagia Sophia, with the whole senate going before it and a very great display of lights leading the way. After it had been venerated there, they brought it up to the palace [?].

49. In those days an Armenian prodigy arrived in the City. It was a pair of conjoined male children who had come from a single womb. They were complete in every limb of the body, but they were joined from the pit of the stomach down to the parts below the belly, and they faced each other. They spent a long time in the City and were looked on by everyone as an extraordinary prodigy, but they were driven out of the City as an evil omen. Under the sole reign of Constantine they came back. When one of them died, some skilled physicians

skillfully cut through the joined part, hoping that the other would live. But he survived only three days and then died.

50. As was said above, the emperor had boundless trust in all monks, but he especially honored and revered Sergios, who shone among the monastics. He was the brother of the magistros Kosmas, the first of the judges. The emperor also restored the monastery of Manuel. Likewise he built from the foundations the church and monastery of Saint Panteleemon, at the place called Ophrou Limen. There he tonsured eight hundred monks, and he also laid down solemnia for them to receive for their maintenance, entrusting these to the monk Sergios, his spiritual father. He took pity on all those in exile and gave them a great deal of money, so that when he was brought down from the palace not a single exile was to be found. This Sergios was a nephew of Patriarch Photios, but his nobility of soul brought him more honor than his kinship of the flesh. He reached the summit of both virtue and knowledge, so that it was hard to decide in which he excelled more, so thoroughly had he cultivated both. Besides his other gifts, there blossomed in him the glow of discernment, a graceful character and a modest mind. He did not raise his eyebrows like the wise men of today, nor did he seem boastful or arrogant. His speech dripped sweeter than honey, his character was firm and steady, and his mind was humble. The emperor kept this celebrated man constantly by his side as a true rule and plumb line by which to order his life. Sergios often urged the emperor to take care of his sons and not to leave them undisciplined and inclined to wickedness, lest he too suffer the fate of Eli and pay the penalty for his sons' lawlessness. And that is just what happened.

51. When his sons brought him down from the palace and exiled him to the island of Prote, he again had this man as a comfort in his misfortunes and as a remedy to soothe the pain of his afflictions. With him at that time was also Polyeuktos, a most devout monk, who no less than Sergios gave him fitting comfort. Afterward, because of his sincere life, Polyeuktos was appointed patriarch by Emperor Constantine when Patriarch Theophylaktos died.

52. Emperor Romanos, worn down by long old age and illness, settled the affairs of the empire by testament. In the year 6453 he named the Porphyrogennetos Constantine as first sovereign, with his own sons following in second and third place. He made express provision concerning them that if they wronged the first emperor in any way, they would be removed from the throne at once.

53. But since God wishes in many ways

453 BOOK VI. CONSTANTINE PORPHYROGENNETOS 454

to save humankind, he allowed Emperor Romanos to fall into an unexpected misfortune, so that, chastened by it and brought to an awareness of his own transgressions, he might be counted worthy of salvation. For he allowed his son Stephen to rise up against him, as Absalom once rose up against his own father David. Stephen took as his advisers in this the former monk Marianos Argyros, the protospatharios Basil Peteinos and Manuel Kourtikes, and the other emperors also knew of it. He wickedly brought his father down from the palace, exiled him to the island of Prote and had him tonsured a monk.

THE SOLE REIGN OF CONSTANTINE

1. So Constantine, his son-in-law, was left as sole ruler on the twentieth of December of the third indiction, in the year 6454. He at once honored Bardas, son of [?], with the rank of magistros, since he had often shown his valor in war over a long period, and appointed him domestic of the Schools. He made Constantine Gongyles commander of the fleet, and he appointed certain capable men as generals. Next he made Basil, surnamed Peteinos, patrician and great hetaireiarch. He had Marianos, of the family of the Argyroi, put off his monastic habit and made him patrician and count of the stable. Likewise he made Manuel, surnamed Kourtikes, patrician and droungarios of the watch. Not long afterward the just judgment of God overtook these three, because they had behaved outrageously toward the Lord's anointed and had unjustly laid hands on him in their greed for the throne. They were caught in treason, and every one of them ended his life by a most pitiable death. I will set out what concerns them more fully and in greater detail in the main account.

2. Forty days later, on the twenty-seventh of January, Constantine came to suspect Emperor Stephen and his brother Constantine of planning to do the same to him. He reasoned, as was only likely, that if they had not spared their own father, they would hardly spare him. So he invited them to a banquet. When they were already seated at table, with food still in their mouths, the men called the Tornikioi, the patrician Marianos and the others who had been made ready for the purpose seized them and brought them down from the palace. They confined them on nearby islands and tonsured them as clerics.

[?] and from Prokonnesos to Rhodes, and from Rhodes to Mytilene. Constantine was taken to Tenedos and from there to Samothrace. There he plotted a revolt and killed the protospatharios Niketas, who had been entrusted by imperial command with guarding him, and he himself was slain by his guards. His body was brought back and buried with great honor where [?] his first wife, named Helena, lay. Constantine Porphyrogennetos took the imperial sandals from Michael, the son of Emperor Christopher, and made him a cleric, a magistros and a rhaiktor. As for those who had a hand in the deposition of Emperor Romanos, this is what they suffered. The magistros Basil was brought in, paraded and exiled, and ended his life in exile, groaning and trembling. As for Marianos, a woman threw a tile down on his head from a height, and he met the fate of Judas. Diogenes, the strategos, was speared by two atzypades of Malelias [?] and died an evil death. Kourtikes was drowned at sea with his dromon while sailing to Crete. Kladon was caught in a mutiny, and his nose was slit and his ears were cut off. The same happened to Philip and the rest.

4. Emperor Romanos saw in a dream two eunuchs dressed in white. They took him by the hands and led him, stark naked, into the Trikymbalon [?]. The polo ground was full of fire, and he was being [?] by many atzypades. Then he saw the Theotokos come to him and speak to the eunuchs on account of his almsgiving. The Theotokos clothed him [?] and led him into the Tropike [?]. Then the lord Constantine, the one who had been slain, and Anastasios, metropolitan of Herakleia, passed by in chains, led by atzypades, and they were handed over and thrown into that fire. On the same day on which the emperor saw the dream,

the two men also died. Emperor Romanos sent to all the monasteries and lavras, and also to the Holy City and to Rome, and summoned holy monks, three hundred in number. On Holy Thursday he took off the tunic and robe he was wearing and stood in the church in front of everyone. When the priest was about to elevate the divine and holy bread, he took out a sheet of paper on which all his sins were written and read them out publicly in front of everyone. While the monks cried out "Lord, have mercy" and wept, he made a prostration before each one of them and asked forgiveness. All the monks granted him forgiveness, and he received communion. As they were going up to the refectory, he gave a rope to a young boy [?], and the boy struck him on the feet while he said: "Go in to the table, you wicked old man." When everyone had sat down, the emperor sat weeping and [?]. He sealed the paper on which his sins were written and sent it to the [?] that remained, and likewise to Dermokaites, who is among the saints. He also sent two kentenaria to the monks on Olympos, asking them to pray for the salvation of his soul. Dermokaites took the paper and the money and ordered all the monks to fast for two weeks and pray for the emperor's sins. One night, as Dermokaites stood praying, a voice came to him from someone unseen: "The love of God for mankind has prevailed." When he had heard this voice a third time, he took the paper, opened it and found it blank, without a single letter on it. He called all the monks together and showed it to them, and they all glorified God. All the monks then made an act of absolution and sent the paper to Emperor Romanos, and it was buried with him.

5. While Emperor Romanos was on the island, Patriarch Theophylaktos and the patrician and parakoimomenos Theophanes laid a plan to bring him back to the palace. They shared the plan with him and won him over, and then they watched for the right moment to carry it through. But the plan was discovered and reported to Emperor Constantine, and he punished those involved. He exiled the patrician Theophanes. George, protospatharios and epinkernes, and Thomas the primikerios he had flogged and tonsured and then sent abroad into exile.

6. In December of the 6th indiction certain men plotted against Emperor Constantine, wishing to bring Emperor Stephen, who was on the island, back to the palace. The plot was revealed to Constantine by Michael, called Diabolinos. The emperor seized the conspirators. Some he had their noses and ears cut off, and others he [?] with a flogging [?] [?].

[?] overthrew them, and seating them on donkeys he paraded them in triumph through the middle of the City and sent them into exile. 7. On the fifteenth of the month of June, in the sixth indiction, the emperor Romanos died on the island called Prote; and his body was brought back to the City and laid in his own monastery. 8. But I have passed over a great and remarkable story without telling it. When the emperors Stephen and Constantine had been brought down from the palace at the instigation of Constantine Porphyrogennetos, a [?] took place in the house of the magistros John Kourkouas, the former domestic of the schools, and in that of the magistros Romanos Saronites, and in various other houses, and it brought plunder and poverty upon them. The emperor Constantine, pitying them because they were suddenly and all at once seen to be poor, ordered the eparch Theophilos to gather these goods together and give them back. Theophilos assigned the task to his protokankellarios together with the man called Zonaras. Being a clever and wicked thief, Zonaras took possession of their dwellings and with great zeal appropriated everything, glutting his insatiable mind, and barely returned a tenth part to them. Who could recount the great and boundless deceit and wickedness of this deceitful man, who became a plague and a disease to the Roman state? In what evil was the man not found foremost? He confirmed everything with persuasive talk and with oaths, so as to seem trustworthy and upright to all. As the story goes, he called on the help of demons and prospered in everything, so that even the emperor Constantine, when he wished in various ways to remove him, could not do so, but instead bestowed benefits and gifts on him. Concerning his fawning and flattery and great shamelessness, his faithless disposition and his wicked and unparalleled greed, I shall set these out more broadly and in more detail in the preceding [?] account. 9. After Constantine was left sole autocrat, he appointed Basil, his protovestiarios, the natural son by a concubine of Romanos, the emperor before him, as patrikios and parakoimomenos and chief minister over the senate. He was a sensible and learned man, and served the emperor in all things auspiciously and fittingly. Then the humane Constantine resolved to make an exchange of prisoners with the Tarsians and to ransom the Romans held captive by the deniers of Christ, because they had been ill-treated for many years in chains and afflictions. He sent the aforementioned magistros John called Kourkouas, who had been domestic of the schools, a wise and prudent man experienced in civil administration, [P. 276] and Kosmas the magistros, a wise man learned in the law and foremost in the civil courts; and to the river Lamos

[?] they made [?], without anything hostile or treacherous occurring. Having done this they returned, and were kindly received by Constantine Porphyrogennetos. 10. The emperor, having fresh in his mind the injustices and losses that the pitiable and wretched poor had suffered at the hands of the strategoi, protonotarioi, soldiers and cavalrymen in the time of his father-in-law Romanos, sent pious and virtuous men to lighten the heavy burden of the untimely exactions imposed from time to time on the miserable poor. To the Anatolikon he sent the magistros Romanos Saronites; to the Opsikion the magistros Romanos Mosele; to the Thrakesion the patrikios Photios; to the Armeniakon Leo Agelastos; and so on to the remaining themes in turn. At the emperor's urging they granted the poor a little respite. And this was a prize and a distinction of the sovereign, with God working alongside him. For he cared for his subjects as an eagle shelters its own brood. He was never angry with any of the officials, or the middle ranks, or the common people, even though he found many who had committed great outrages against the public and against himself; but being an imitator of Christ he rather repaid them with benefits and gifts, and looked to the One who judges justly. The eparch of the City, Theophilos, a learned man and competent in civil law, he promoted and honored as patrikios and appointed quaestor; and in his place he appointed as eparch Constantine the protospatharios, at that time mystikos and teacher of the philosophers, praiseworthy in word and deed, so that no one else in the senate equaled the man in knowledge and wisdom; and so he made the eparchy distinguished for good order and justice. 11. The patriarch Theophylaktos fell ill and came near to death, and when he had recovered a little he did not give up his wicked depravity [P. 277], ordaining bishops for gifts, and his [?] for horses and his follies. And overcome once more by the illness, he reached the end of his life, having been patriarch for twenty-four years. In his place Polyeuktos was ordained, a monk shining in the ascetic life, who had been a monk from his tender years and was distinguished in every virtue and in orthodox doctrine [?], so that he was known and called by many another John Chrysostom; and he was not only called this but was seen to be so. Seeing him, Constantine, the lover of beauty, rejoiced and exulted at having found such a man in his days. 12. The God-loving and beauty-loving emperor Constantine, finding Joseph the patrikios to be of like character with himself, and

praipositos, and sensible in civil duties and swifter than a bird, appointed him sakellarios, then droungarios of the fleet, and entrusted all his authority to him. 13. As I am about to describe the love of beauty and the cultivation of Constantine Porphyrogennetos, his concern for [?] and improvement, and how piously and justly he preserved his subjects, I lack the means to praise the man as he deserves and fear to attempt it, so it would rather be fitting to keep silent; yet it is worth telling a few things here and there out of the many. 14. Finding everything in a state of uselessness and [?], and virtuous men degraded and despised, as a lover of God and of the good he preferred the bold and brave to the cowardly and unmanly, and by handing them over to the magistros and domestic of the schools Bardas Phokas he secured victory for the Roman realm. And since much that was fine and praiseworthy in our state—knowledge, the verbal arts and the sciences—had somehow been neglected and overlooked, what does that most philosophical mind devise? Because he knew that action and contemplation bring us close to God [P. 278], action being suited to civil affairs and contemplation to intellectual ones, he advanced each through the other: he arranged for the practical side to be trained through the art of rhetoric, and the contemplative through philosophy and the natural study of beings. He selected the best teachers: to Constantine the protospatharios, at that time mystikos, he gave the school of the philosophers; to Alexander, metropolitan of Nicaea, that of the rhetors; to Nikephoros the patrikios, son-in-law of Theophilos Erotikos the eparch, that of geometry; and to Gregory the asekretis that of the astronomers. The emperor took great care and pains over the students, making them his daily companions at table, giving them money, and conversing kindly with them. Not much time passed before, through the encouragement and understanding of the emperor, they mastered the great sciences and arts; and choosing judges, secretaries and metropolitans from among them, he honored them, and he adorned and enriched the Roman state with wisdom. 15. He also restored and renewed the imperial robes and the ancient crowns and diadems, which had decayed; he beautified the Boukoleon with statues brought from various places, and made a fishpond there. He also investigated and visited the prisoners held in the prisons of the City and of the outer themes, and from their bonds [?]

he released them, so that everyone acclaimed the good and Christ-imitating sovereign Constantine as savior. He honored virtue and knowledge as no other [?] of those who had reigned; and anyone he found to have knowledge and a natural gift and aptitude for the laws, he promoted and set on a higher seat. One could see justice and good order in everything, since the Porphyrogennetos cultivated and embraced them. The emperor also issued a law. For he saw that much greed had poured forth from the insatiable, and from the officials [?] in the provinces and [P. 279] villages, who were oppressing the wretched poor, and that the powerful had acquired estates by seizure through various devious pretexts; and he resolved to take these away from them. What does the man wise in all things do? Gathering his council, he makes a decree: the rich who had crept in since his accession and had bought or received as gifts and taken possession of plots or fields in the villages were to be expelled without compensation. And so he wiped away a little of the outrage and greed of the insatiable. 16. The gentle and serene master did not refuse to judge in person the disputes, pleas and claims of those who came to him, nor did he hesitate to sit in judgment alongside the judges. When the judges, the advocates and the litigants stood before his tribunal, he refuted their pleas and their deceptions; for nothing escaped his sharpness of mind—not falsehood placed beside the truth, not plausibility mingled into a narrative, not elaborate documents secretly composed, which escaped even very vigorous men behind a curtain of truth. As a result, schooled by fear before the trial, each person became his own judge and settled the case with the one he had wronged. 17. We must also speak of the sovereign's public concerns and his countless reforms and administrative measures. When letters sent from the strategoi everywhere, from the imperial protonotarioi, and from those in villages, provinces and cities, and also those to the leaders of nations, were read by him, he at once determined how each should be handled: what was to be done about matters in the East, and what about those in the West. And he went through most of these like a bird, receiving embassies, writing to officials, and correcting changes made rashly. This same Constantine showed himself councillor, administrator, general, soldier, commander and governor. Who could tell or describe such excellences? 18. We must also speak of the hospice of the holy man. [P. 280] The emperor Constantine, [seeing?] that it was very small, enlarges it with very large buildings,

so that all who were in the grip of that disease might be gathered there; and having their flesh anointed with ointments and providing them with unfailing supplies, he left it as an everlasting memorial for those who come after us. 19. We must also speak of the stable converted into a home for the aged. Behind the most wondrous Great Church and close to it there was a stable for the horses of the patriarch Theophylaktos. When the good emperor saw it, judging it not right, he turned it into a dwelling and made it a home for the aged, and decreed that those living there should receive a yearly provision of food and clothing. 20. We must also tell about the roof of the Nineteen Couches. Seeing it rotted, collapsing and very unsightly, he renews it. For its gilded ceiling had decayed over time, and he himself took it in hand and made it look new and splendid. He put together octagonal coffers [?], and adorned them with openwork and various carved shapes, formed into vine tendrils and leaves and the forms of trees, and sprinkled them with gold; and so he made [?] so beautiful that those who behold it are amazed. 21. For his son, the emperor Romanos, he built [?] more palaces than the emperors of old, raising houses from their foundations. The varied forms of these buildings astonish the mind and thought, draw them in many directions, and fill the beholders with wonder. In the Tetraconch of the apostle Paul he had various images made, and since it had lost its old beauty, to give it a new consecration he set up many figures and images of gold in it. 22. The man understood the art of painting so precisely that I think no one before him or after him did so. He corrected many who labored at it, and showed himself an excellent teacher; and not only did he show himself so, but he was admired by all and was a great wonder to those who saw him, being skilled in things he had never learned. [P. 281] Who could tell of the corrections the Porphyrogennetos made to craftsmen? He corrected stonemasons and carpenters, goldsmiths, silversmiths and blacksmiths, and in all things the sovereign showed himself the best. 23. Constantine, the lover of beauty, built the silver doors of the Chrysotriklinos; and his diligence produced a silver table for receiving guests and adorning the dining hall, which he beautified with many-colored materials and [?] and natural color, so that it gave the guests more delight than the sweetness of the food.

24. In front of his bedchamber he also built a porphyry basin, constructing a reservoir for water, which he surrounded with marble columns whose smoothness gave off a soft gleam. What then did that great-minded

soul do? It set a silver eagle on the water pipe, not looking straight ahead but turned sideways, arching its neck and proud as if returning from a hunt, with a snake coiled around its feet, which it is strangling. And in the vestibules of the imperial bedchamber he made artful mosaic images, varied in their colored materials and their forms. 25. Nor was the emperor inexperienced in shipbuilding; for he gave instructions for the construction of warships: which timbers suited them, their fastenings and joints, and how they fit with one another.

26. As for the palaces of Hieria, I reflect in my mind on the sweet and delightful buildings with which the Porphyrogennetos adorned the place. Formerly it served the Chalcedonians as a burial ground, but now it rests on four arches, and its corners form further imperial residences, surrounded by the breath of summer winds and breezes. One cannot say into what pleasure and joy it casts whoever takes his rest there. 27. What could one say of the buildings of the empresses' palace in another place? These too, surpassing and outshining Hieria in form and elegance, and in the fragrance of delight rising from the ground, because of the restoration of their beauty, are far superior and excel it, like the newly built church near the Holy Apostles, beautiful to look at and lovely to admire. [P. 282] For though it falls short of the old one in size, it far surpasses it in inner splendor. And what does the faithful emperor do? [He appointed?] the patrikios Theodore Bilonas as his collaborator on the splendid and resplendent church. 28. Who could tell of the sacred vessels and veils he presented to the great and most wonderful common sanctuary? Whenever he went there, he did not see fit to appear before God empty-handed, but he greeted and repaid him with great gold-wrought offerings, with pearls and stones and fabrics, which adorn and make resplendent the Holy of Holies and proclaim Constantine who offered them. 29. We must tell of the expedition of the patrikios Basil Hexamilites, strategos of the Kibyrrhaiotai. This patrikios Basil, strategos of the Kibyrrhaiotai, was young in body but gray in prudence, with experience beyond his years. When warships had set out from Tarsus with prominent Hagarenes aboard, and the strategos saw them attacking Roman lands, intending to seize them like a nest, the strategos [drew up] against those

his own ships in battle array, although they were very few and insufficient against such a multitude. But since he had judgment and resolve stronger than the multitude of warships, and boldness joined with prudence mightier than many allies, the two sides meet; the clash of ships began, battle was joined against one another, and a violent war cry and shoving rang out from the ships on both sides, until the strategos Basil himself, coming into the midst of the deniers of Christ, leapt aboard. When this happened and liquid fire surrounded the deniers of Christ on all sides, they were at once defeated and cut down [?] and taken captive into slavery, their leaders and commanders above all being captured alive. These he sent to the City to the fortunate emperor Constantine, and they were paraded in triumph in the Hippodrome. 30. The emperor Constantine assigned a military force against the Lombards and the Neapolitans and sent the patrikios Marianos as its commander, [P. 283] because the western regions had revolted and broken the bonds of the Roman yoke. For those who had been allotted the land of Lombardy as their home, and those of Calabria, had grown insolent, emboldened because they were far distant from the capital. So, constantly rebelling, they reached such a pitch of insubordination that they paid tribute to the Hagarenes and put the neighboring cities, forts and villages to the sword. The Neapolitans too, falling away from their subjection to Christ, agreed to act as [?] slaves, and turned to open revolt. So that the rebellious multitude should not grow still more arrogant, as if they had enslaved the nations subject to the Romans, the Porphyrogennetos, unable to bear it, repels them with Thracian and Macedonian armies, and with warships carrying liquid fire he checks their insolence and folly. The patrikios Marianos Argyros fell upon Naples by land and sea with the Roman army; they burned everything on the landward side and secured all the outlets to the sea, and surrounded them on every side. Pressed and humbled by famine and captivity, the Neapolitans sent up petitions and supplications to the sovereign Constantine, submitting to him as they had from the beginning. The Lombards and the Calabrians did the same; and therefore the barbarians of Sicily also concluded peace agreements. 31. One must also marvel at the war against the Africans. They at once engaged and clashed, the ships grappling with one another; and then a violent wind blew, fighting on our side and helping us, but fighting against and opposing the barbarians. Defeat followed for them, and they were sunk into the deep with their weapons and ships. And so their emir [sought?] peace treaties [?]

…was pleading with the emperor. Not only did these acknowledge their subjection to the emperor; the barbarians who live in the Gauls, every household of them, also showed goodwill toward the Porphyrogenitus sovereign and sent magnificent gifts to the emperor with their envoys. The fortune of the Porphyrogenitus brought them all into subjection, servitude and the yoke.

32. When the emir of Egypt heard of the Romans' great victory, the naval battle and the defeat of those who deny Christ, he at once laid aside his hostility in friendly letters and promised concord. The emir of Persia, having met Roman armies on various occasions and been defeated in various assaults and wars, was reconciled with the emperor by a bond of love. The emperor sent envoys to him. They reached that parched land, venerated and kissed the tomb of the apostle Thomas, lit the lamps sent by the emperor, and bought precious stones and pearls. For besides his other great achievements, the emperor had been so richly gifted that he gathered and collected one thing after another and turned it into something lovely.

33. Now I must also tell about the Chrysotriklinos. The most ingenious sovereign [?] it into a fragrant rose garden full of flowers, made of very fine tesserae of many kinds and colours that imitate the hues of freshly opened flowers. Enclosed within spiralling interlaced bands and shaped by the composition, they are beyond compare. He crowned this with silver, setting it all round like a rim, and it gives those who see it a delight they never tire of.

34. The emperor loved the citizens like his own children, or more, and held them in high regard. He made those of noble birth [chosen men?]. Some he made illustrious with the honours of high rank; others he honoured with magnificent gifts. He made them share his table and his daily life, and so increased all the more the charm of his goodwill. In place of many bodyguards, sentries and protectors he preferred these men as faithful and [?], and they put their sovereign before their own safety.

35. Next I must tell of the [?] of the Brumalia of the Porphyrogenitus. It was a custom observed by the emperors of old, and the Porphyrogenitus put it into practice. On the day allotted to the letter of his name, kappa, he celebrated a most splendid festival and made it a crowded occasion. With those costly and [?] banquets [he entertained] the senate [?].

…entire, receiving them with the most generous largesse, and he [?] the brightness of the feast with gifts of silk garments, much silver and [?], purple robes and fragrant Indian woods, such as no one had ever heard of or seen.

36. Everyone knows that music is a divine discovery and a benefit to human nature. What, then, did the pious and most magnanimous sovereign do? He devoted himself to it and never ceased to hymn God through it. Because of this, bright festivals were made brighter, the feasts of the martyrs shone, and the commemorations of holy pastors and teachers glittered. The man was so gifted that he assembled choirs of hymn-singers and devised leaders for them, while he himself was present among them before anyone else, listening to what was chanted, his soul delighted and rejoicing…

37. He loved it as no other of the faithful emperors before him had done. He also honoured the genius of Chrysostom with a most splendid commemoration, praising the arrangement of his words and periods, his long, drawn-out sentences and his arguments. In it he splendidly and brilliantly magnified the herald of repentance.

38. He cherished and loved his son, the emperor Romanos, as no one else ever did. Above all he urged him to keep godly piety; then he trained him in imperial speech and manner, walk and laughter, dress, and the way an emperor sits and stands. For this reason the Porphyrogenitus was also granted divine visions, and it was foretold to him: "If you keep these things, you will reign long over the empire of the Romans."

39. He gave his son, the emperor Romanos, a wife of noble ancestry, beautiful in body, lovely in appearance and modest in soul. Her name was Anastasia, the daughter of Krateros, and the Porphyrogenitus fittingly named her Theophano, as one who had appeared and been chosen by God. The bridal chamber was announced and the wedding celebrated in the most wonderful triclinium of Justinian Rhinotmetos, and joy and gladness shone around the Porphyrogenitus and Helena the Augusta, since they had betrothed such a maiden of ancient lineage to their son.

40. When the Augusta Helena was worn down by illness, the kindly sovereign did not slacken in his affection and love for her, but granted all her wishes in every respect. The Augusta asked the sovereign to assign estates, chrysobulls and revenues to the hospice and old people's home that she had recently built in the old Petrion [?], called "Helena's", and the Porphyrogenitus granted this with joy. And one could see her…

…delighted and rejoicing in soul and body, since he provided her with boundless revenues and wealth. She rejoiced most of all to see her son, the emperor Romanos, and her daughters Zoe, Theodora and Agathe together with her, sharing the joy with her and with the emperor Constantine. He too honoured and loved them, and Agathe above all, since she served the emperor tirelessly in his illnesses, and through her the emperor was informed of the business of the bureaus and of the officials. She appeared as an intermediary, and not only appeared so but was also recognized as such and…

41. Because the magistros and domestic of the Schools, Bardas called Phokas, had become infirm and reached old age, the Porphyrogenitus removed him from the office of domestic. In his place he appointed as domestic his beloved son Nikephoros, patrikios and strategos of the Anatolikoi, a man who had distinguished himself in many different wars and proved himself most excellent. Having heartened the armies with his most pleasant speech and [?], he advanced against the enemy Hagarenes, so that all the troops took courage and camped as if in their own country. They did not hide, or run wild, or turn back, as had been their habit; all of them advanced boldly against the enemy, fenced about with shields, defending themselves with spears and destroying the Hagarenes by force. Those who watched were amazed and astonished to see the victorious Nikephoros cutting down and beating back the battle lines, forces and divisions of the godless Chambdas, and they marvelled at and extolled the good fortune of the victorious champion. He burned cities, villages and whole regions to ashes, led away captives and brought tributaries to the empire of the Romans. When he came to the faithful Constantine, he received praise and honours from him such as the Roman generals of old would have won.

42. The sovereign Constantine would not allow any of his father's buildings to fall into ruin. This included the great bath built by his father Leo at the quarter of Marina, very spacious and a marvel of our city. Through neglect and carelessness it had earlier been reduced to complete ugliness and disorder, and nothing of it could be seen but its foundations. This Constantine, glorying and delighting in his father's works as if they were his own, renovated it and restored it again. He not only brought it back to its former beauty but made it much better, everywhere… [Apparatus: "only"] "indeed" [?]; "allowing"; "his" [?]]

…beautifying it on every side, and [restoring?] the earlier comfort for the bathers. It amazes visitors and astonishes the local people.

43. The emperor Constantine appointed the patrikios Theodore, called Belonas, eparch and father of the city. He was a capable and learned man, with wide experience of the law and natural talent for it. For the common good, his orderly conduct and fair judgement gave litigants a nourishment they had not had to plough for.

44. The Porphyrogenitus sent the patrikios and parakoimomenos Basil against the godless [?] with an expeditionary force, many troops and much equipment. Armed with the emperor's God-inspired counsels, Basil set out from the imperial palace and from Byzantium and came to the lands of those who deny Christ. First he again sacked Samosata. It had been settled long ago by Syrians and lies on the bank of the Euphrates; it was hard to take, populous and laden with great wealth. The army advanced there, with him leading them against the barbarians themselves. Puffed up with their native arrogance, the barbarians were boasting of their victory before any fighting had taken place. But when they engaged the Roman army they could not withstand its onslaught and turned to flight, each man striving to save himself as best he could. Then the dead were stripped, the prisoners bound, and a great quantity of spoils gathered, and all of it was received in the public theatre and in the triumph at the Hippodrome.

45. The emperor appointed the patrikios Leo, son of Bardas the magistros [?], strategos of the Anatolikoi in place of his brother Nikephoros. He was a most excellent man and a formidable fighter against the Hagarenes and other enemies. One could see both [brothers?] contending for the Christians, advancing against the enemy and slaughtering them, while the enemy could not withstand their onslaught.

46. There was also a great and terrible fire near the church of Saint Thomas, which burned down the portico that leads to the Iron Gate. In his great goodness the emperor, who loved and cared for the citizens as his own children, comforted them all by helping them rebuild their burned houses. The citizens praised the sovereign as a second god and benefactor and gave thanks.

47. When the Turks made expeditions…

…against the Romans, raided as far as the City at the feast of holy Easter, and carried off every soul in Thrace and much booty, the emperor at once sent the patrikios and domestic of the Excubitors, Pothos Argyros, with his tagma, together with the strategoi of the Boukellarioi, the Opsikion and the Thrakesioi, to cross over on their heels. Helped by the Porphyrogenitus' prayer, which was acceptable to God, they fell on the Turks by night, slaughtered them and defeated them, and recovered the booty and the captives. The Turks, ashamed of their defeat and rout, went back to their own land.

48. It is also worth telling of the fearful sign that God showed as a forewarning of the passing of Constantine the Porphyrogenitus. They say that at the sovereign's birth a bright comet appeared for forty days. Now, at his illness and death, a star was again seen in the sky, but with a murky, dim light, and it was visible for many days. This showed that Constantine the Porphyrogenitus had been fashioned by the higher power. Many sensible people know this and have passed the marvel on to those who did not know it: even the elements mourned the end of the Porphyrogenitus.

49. Even if most of the emperor's deeds escape my memory, I shall add this last one to what I have said and so come to the end of my account. A longing and desire had grown in the sovereign to go to Mount Olympus, to visit the holy Fathers there and enjoy their precious prayers, and to recover his health through a change of place and the mild climate. A hidden illness was smouldering in him, for which he had been placed under medical care, and he needed above all to make the journey to Olympus. Seized by this longing, he at once boarded the dromon and went to the land of the Bithynians, to Prietos, which the local people call Prainetos, taking its name from an ancestral god of the Bithynians. From there he went on to Nicaea, a city of ancient wealth and many people. From there he came to a monastery lying on the road [?], dedicated to the martyr Athenogenes, who is honoured there. The abbot there showed the sovereign a document written in cinnabar by his father. For they say that the pious emperor Leo passed that way when he was travelling to the heights of Olympus to pray that a son be given him as heir to his throne. Peter, then abbot of the monastery, foretold that he would beget a son to succeed him as emperor, and that this son would come out to [this place?] at the end of his life. The Porphyrogenitus recognized the handwriting as his father Leo's own and declared that the…

…monk's prediction was true. From there he went to the [foothills?] of Olympus, the Olympus that ancient writings also call Mysian, because the Mysians lived there in ancient times. With difficulty the sovereign made his way through the [?], the hardships and the winding, precipitous ascents, and reached the cells of the holy Fathers. He saw them, embraced them, and took their prayers, which profit the soul, as provisions for the road. Then he moved on to [Prusa], the city of a man who ruled the Bithynians long ago and built this city as a memorial of his valour and of the wars in which the kings of that time were [overcome?]. Not far from it he saw [?] underwater [?], watching the hot springs welling up, in which the myths say Heracles, wandering in search of Hylas, washed off the gore of the [?] murder.

50. The holy Fathers told the sovereign that on the summit of Olympus there lived in a cave an ascetic, an old man who wore [iron chains?], and he hurried there out of longing to see him. The old man, made aware by divine illumination that the emperor was coming to him, came out of his cell, made a prostration and said, "Bless me." The emperor asked him, "Who are you, where are you from, and how and where are you going?" He said, "I learned of Your Majesty's approach to me, and so I have come to you instead." Recognizing [?] the old man as sent by God, the emperor took his prayers as provisions for the road, and learned of the end of his own life. He returned to the cells of the holy Fathers, dined with them, and quickly went down to the sea. Most people did not notice that he was ill, but inwardly he was being consumed and wasted away by an intestinal disease and fever.

51. But O laws of mortal nature and turns of fortune, to what laments am I being hurried and driven! From there he crossed over, set his course straight for the imperial City, and arrived, worn down and stricken by the illness that gripped him. When the formidable emperor was being overcome by his illness and the hopes for his life were fading, there was no one who did not weep for the Porphyrogenitus and lament the good sovereign: sweet, gentle, approachable, serene, and whatever other names one should call the man to whom they were bound by longing. While the Porphyrogenitus Constantine was breathing his last [?], he made his son Romanos autocrat emperor and entrusted him to Joseph, patrikios and praipositos, binding him by oath to protect Romanos with his skill. And [?]. For such was the man: shrewd, upright and faithful, swifter than an eagle in civil administration, impartial, pious and just, so that no one else like him was known…

…and the patrikios and parakoimomenos Basil and the chamberlains, when they saw the sovereign Constantine breathing his last and fading, crowded round the bed. Weeping and lamenting without measure, they mourned and bewailed such a master, yet they achieved nothing more than to wash that imperial body with mute and empty tears. While both groups surrounded his bed and beat their breasts with many wails, and the sweet, wealth-giving emperor was at his very end, choirs of saints and righteous ones, of monks, martyrs and hierarchs, stood by and committed his all-holy spirit into the hands of angels. They quickly washed him and laid him out in the Hall of the Nineteen Couches. When they had sung the psalms over him, they at once carried him out and set him down at the Chalke. There the patriarch, the priests, the magistroi, the patrikioi and the whole senate gave him the last kiss. The master of ceremonies cried out, as was the custom: "Go forth, O emperor; the King of kings and Lord of lords calls you!" The great crowd raised a cry of wailing and lamentation, and when he had called this out the third time, they at once lifted the sovereign and carried him out of the imperial palace onto the main avenue. They bore him to the church of the Holy Apostles, with the whole senate escorting him and honouring his departure with [?] processions.

53. What need is there to speak of the people and the crowd of the city who gathered? Some looked down from above on that imperial [bier?]; others watched from close by; others leaned out of lofty, high buildings and houses and strained toward the sight of the bier. Some wept in secret, shaken by heartfelt groans; others were torn by lamentation; others wailed more shrilly, crushed and mourning the common misfortune; and some poured out tears in torrents, soaking and sprinkling the gold-inlaid bier. When they drew near the church of the Holy Apostles and the imperial body, escorted by guards, appeared inside, the patrikios and parakoimomenos Basil wrapped his all-holy body in its grave-bands with his own hands, as is customarily done for the dead. When the tomb, that is, the sarcophagus, had been made ready and its lid raised, he laid him beside his father, the emperor Leo. So even after death and burial the most beloved son did not turn away from his union and love with his father.

54. In appearance the Porphyrogenitus emperor Constantine was tall, with skin as white as milk and fine, bright grey eyes. He was hook-nosed, that is, aquiline, long-faced, ruddy and long-necked, as straight in stature as a cypress,

[broad?] in the shoulders, of good character, gentle toward everyone and for the most part timid. He loved the table and loved wine, was pleasant in speech, and was generous with gifts and help. From his birth to his death he lived fifty-five years, two months and [?] days… He died in the month of November, on the fifteenth, in the third indiction, in the year 6469 from the creation of the world, leaving as autocrat Romanos, together with Helena Augusta, Romanos' mother.

The Reign of Romanos, Son of Constantine the Porphyrogenitus

1. The emperor Romanos was left as autocrat by his father, Constantine the Porphyrogenitus, at about twenty-one years of age, while Basil the Porphyrogenitus was one year old. Romanos ruled together with his mother Helena and his wife Theophano, from the month of November, on the sixth, in the sixth [?] indiction, in the year 6469 from the creation of the world. He at once honoured his father's chamberlains and men with the ranks of patrikios and protospatharios, promoted them to other dignities as well, enriched them with gifts, and sent them down out of the imperial palace. As his chief ministers and the foremost members of the senate he chose and preferred Joseph, patrikios, praipositos and droungarios of the fleet. Soon afterwards he promoted him to parakoimomenos and entrusted him with all authority and care of the subjects. He appointed the protospatharios John, called Choirinas, patrikios and great hetaireiarch, to protect the sovereign from suspect persons. He appointed the protospatharios Sisinnios, formerly of the sakellion, eparch of the city. He was a learned man and well suited to public service, and shortly afterwards Romanos promoted him to patrikios and logothete of the genikon. In his place he made the patrikios Theodore, called Daphnopates, formerly of the military treasury, eparch of the city. Sisinnios distinguished himself in the eparchate by good order and justice and brought lustre to the sacred praetorium. Those who stood before his tribunal could see him repelling and rebuffing the appeals and counter-pleas of the litigants, and each man became, through himself, a judge of the case against the one who had wronged him [?]. The emperor also gave the eparch assistants, by the choice and [?]… [Apparatus: "of Constantine" [?]; "of Basil" [?]]

...(of Joseph the patrikios) and parakoimomenos, and of the eparch Sisinnios: Theophylaktos the asekretis, called Mitzitzikos, and Joseph, spatharokandidatos and judge, whom he made logothete of the praetorium. By the eparch's good counsel these men served the state well.

2. We must now also speak of the emperor's public concerns. As soon as his friendly letters had been sent to every leader and royal general, and to the nations of Bulgaria, of the West and of the East, all of them hailed the fortune and friendship of the emperor as most excellent and agreed to treaties of friendship. We must also speak of the citizens. The emperor Romanos loved the land that bore him as he loved the mother who gave him birth, and he set great store by the families in it. For this reason he chose out the noble and pure-blooded families, and some he made illustrious with honours of rank, while others he honoured with magnificent gifts. At times he also made them his table companions and gave them silver, so that he increased and kindled their affection still more; and he valued their goodwill above many garrisons and guards.

3. His sisters Zoe, Theodora, Agatha, Theophano and Anna he brought down from the imperial residence to the Kanikleiou, where Sophia the Augusta, wife of the emperor Christopher, had been tonsured a nun, and he had them tonsured as nuns. Helena, mother of Romanos and of the girls, lamented greatly, and they wept bitterly, clasping one another's hands and hanging on one another's necks, but they achieved nothing more with their deaf and empty tears. Then after [?] days the emperor moved them from there again: Zoe and Theodora and [?] he assigned [?], and Agatha he sent to the monastery founded and established by Romanos, who reigned at that time and was the emperor's grandfather. He ordered that they be supplied with whatever they had been given in the palace.

4. Nikephoros Phokas, domestic of the Schools, he honoured with the rank of magistros and sent against the deniers of Christ in the East; and Nikephoros's brother, the patrikios Leo, he appointed general, and not long afterwards made him magistros and domestic of the [?]. And one could see the emperor enjoying himself and living entirely in the countryside, in hunts and the chase, as though he had wholly turned his back on the imperial palace and had entrusted the care of the army to the brothers. He himself took his pleasure and [?] in hunting outside Byzantium, keeping company with his peers, with flatterers and evil counsellors [?].

5. What could one say of the emperor's tirelessness and uprightness and valour, his courage and goodness? In a single day he sat in the Hippodrome, dined with the senate and made the distribution of silver; in the afternoon he played polo in the Tzykanisterion with skilled and experienced players and beat them many times; then he went over to a resting place at Anoratai, and there he hunted and took four enormous boars and crossed back to the palace in the evening. For he was young in years, vigorous in body, wheat-complexioned, with fine eyes and a prominent nose, rosy-faced, cheerful and sweet in his speech, tall and straight like a cypress, broad in the shoulders, calm and gentle, so that everyone marvelled and was amazed at the man. The state rejoiced with him, since he was prospering and prevailing over the nations. And in Byzantium rich supplies of grain and provisions were furnished.

6. The emperor Romanos also fathered another son after his father's death and named him Constantine. Not long afterwards the child was crowned by the patriarch Polyeuktos in the ambo of Hagia Sophia. The Augusta Helena, who lay sick in the palace and [?] with the emperor, and had been ill for a long time, died piously on the nineteenth of September. He honoured her in royal fashion; laid on a bier and escorted by the senate, she was buried in the monastery founded by her father, the emperor Romanos, at the Myrelaion, in a sarcophagus near and close to her fa-

7. Then the good emperor, the kind, the gentle—and by whatever fine names one ought to call and name the man—ordered the magistros and domestic of the Schools Nikephoros Phokas to set out for Crete with an expedition and a great force, equipped with warships and liquid fire. For ever since the Cretans had taken this great island they had inflicted many terrible evils and taken captives every day in the land of the Romans. They seized it in the time of Michael the Amorian, father of Theophilos. When the armies went over to the revolt and usurpation of Thomas the Slav, Michael's companion (for the usurper held Thrace and Macedonia for almost three years or more), the Saracens who had come up from Spain found their opportunity and seized the island with a great fleet of warships. Their rule and occupation lasted until the day they were vanquished by the magistros and domestic Nikephoros Phokas, a hundred and fifty-eight years.

8. So the emperor Romanos, moved by divine zeal, on the advice and good counsel of the parakoimomenos Joseph, gathered ships and warships from every quarter, with liquid fire and a picked [?]

army of Thracians, Macedonians and Sklavesianoi, and resolved to send it to Crete. But some of his own servants in the senate were unhappy about the Cretan expedition. They reminded the emperor of the expeditions and ventures under past emperors, and of the countless sums poured out to no purpose, especially under Leo of pious and blessed memory and Constantine Porphyrogennetos, when so much money and so many men were spent and lost. They feared the danger of the sea, the great alliance of the neighbouring Saracens, the fleet of the Spaniards and the Africans, and also the rumour going about that whoever took Crete would reign and seize the sceptre of the Roman realm.

9. But the parakoimomenos Joseph, that good and upright and wakeful mind, stood up among them and said: "Master, we all know what terrible things have befallen us Romans at the hands of the deniers of Christ. It is right to consider the slaughter, the defiling of virgins, the destruction of churches and the captivity of the coastal themes; it is fitting to struggle for the Christians and [?], and not to fear the length of the journey, the open seas, the uncertainty of victory or the impossibility of the rumour. Above all we must obey your God-assisted counsel and command, for this thought has come to you from God. For 'the heart of a king is in the hand of God'—and all the more since the domestic of the Schools, an upright and faithful servant, is being sent by your God-guided majesty."

10. When the emperor heard this he could no longer hold back his resolve. He armed and paid the army, gave money to the magistros, and sent him off together with the koitonites Michael, the epistates, in the month of July of the fifth indiction. There were two thousand ships with liquid fire, a thousand dromons, and three hundred and seven cargo ships carrying provisions and weapons of war. The domestic Nikephoros set out from the Queen of Cities and reached Phygela, and there he made sure that the whole fleet would sail together and come to anchor together. The prudent man sent swift galleys ahead to reconnoitre and ordered them to capture someone for information. They went and seized some men, and brought them to the magistros. He questioned them closely and learned that the emir of Crete and the leading men of the fortress were away on their own estates. At once he sailed on with all speed and haste and put in to shore. Disembarking from the ships, he built a palisade and dug a deep ditch, and then went out on a raid, urging everyone to stay together and not to ride off before they had learned his strength. Advancing on the fortress, he shut out all the Cretans who were outside the for-

tress, with fear [?]. From then on many deserted to the magistros every day. Nikephoros learned that those shut out of the fortress had taken refuge in the narrows and passes, the ravines, the marshes and the mountains. So he drew up an army of mounted archers, Rus, Anatolic officers, Thracians and Macedonians and sent it out, while the prudent and brave domestic himself stayed behind at Saka [?]. And by the man's good counsel all of them felt as though they were in their own country. The troops overtook and overran the places where the enemy's cattle and flocks and possessions were hidden and where they themselves were camped, plundered everything, and returned in joy and victory. From then on the Romans camped without fear or anxiety where there were clear springs and an abundance of every kind of fruit. Each man had his hut among the fruit trees, and with fruit pouring down and everyone enjoying it they rejoiced and called down blessings on the magistros who led them so well.

11. The emir of Crete, called Kouroupas, informed the neighbouring Hagarenes of Spain and Africa of what had happened, and asked for help and alliance. They sent swift galleys to learn about the commander, the army, its condition and its obedience to its commander. With great speed these reached Crete and by night entered the fortress by means of a rope. They met the emir Kouroupas and the leading men of the fortress, who were helpless, dispirited and in despair, not knowing what to do against the Roman army and the magistros. These men threw their arms around the envoys' necks and could say nothing else; clasping their hands, they wept and lamented, begging that the emirs march out to their aid and alliance, and sent them back with all speed. The envoys hurried back, and each came to his emir and told of the great armament and the expedition of ships, of the allies assembled from various nations, of the general's vigilance and intelligence, his faith in God, his justice and his aversion to every kind of passion. The emirs, filled with astonishment, were by no means willing [to send] them help or alliance

12. The army was encamped on the island when a fierce winter set in with rain and cold. Their grain and provisions were used up, their clothing fell apart and left them bare, and the soldiers lost heart and wanted to return home. But Nikephoros, their brave and prudent leader, held them all back by his speech and the sweetness of his words. For he said to them: "Men, my brothers and fellow soldiers, let us take to heart the fear of God; let us strive to avenge the insult done to God; let us stand nobly [?] and the impious enemies [?]

[?] let us take [?] the fear [?]. Let us consider that we are inside the island of the Syrians. Flight from here brings great danger. Let us avenge the defilement of virgins; seeing honoured limbs wounded, let us set our hearts [?]. The toil and the danger are not without reward. Let us stand firm and endure in battle against the deniers of Christ, and Christ our God will fight with us and destroy our enemies, and the fortress of those who boast against Christ will be taken." [?] When he had exhorted them with many other words as well, one man answered on behalf of all: "You have opened our hearts, magistros. Your words have steeled and sharpened our strength and our resolve. You have given wings to our minds; we follow your counsel and command, and with you we will die."

13. In the month of October of the second year of Romanos's reign there was a shortage of wheat and barley in the City: wheat was selling at four modioi to the nomisma, and barley at six modioi. And one could see the wakeful mind of Joseph providing for the common good. At once he sent ships to the East and moved to stop the grain dealers from hoarding grain, for the man was just, impartial and trustworthy. Not much time passed before wheat was selling at seven or eight modioi to the nomisma. Such was the man, so diligent and fervent that no one before him or after him could equal him.

14. In the month of March the magistros called [?], named Basil, was accused of plotting a mutiny at the prompting of certain evil counsellors. The emperor sent him into exile, and he died there. The patrikios and domestic of the East was sent to the East in his brother's place, so that the godless Chamdas would not find the East unprotected and make raids, take captives and plunder the land of the Romans. He joined forces with the general of Cappadocia, the patrikios Constantine Maleinos, and with the other generals and the tagmata. He met the braggart's expedition at a place called Andrassos, engaged him, defeated him decisively, crushed him and put him to flight. Then one could see corpses being stripped and the boastful Hagarenes slaughtered, put to flight and taken alive as slaves, caring nothing for arms or horses or steeds or money or kin; each man saved himself from his own calamity as best he could.
